So do you not find it a bit weird working six days a week and people just taking it for granted like you got to go with it or something? It's not like it's something you chose, is it? Or at least not all of it.      I mean, it’s not exactly glamorous, but there’s more to it than that. I enjoy the actual work when I’m not stuck on a train or in meetings. It's like everyone thinks you're just there to fetch them coffee and not take holidays. And I’m not saying you're like that, but I think it's just how people see admin jobs — as something you can do when you're not actually working.      Yeah, I get that. Everyone thinks admin is easy, or that it's the lesser job. But you still have to stay on top of deadlines and juggle emails and spreadsheets. I think people forget it’s still work. I dunno, maybe I’m just in a better position because I work in a more technical field. People take consultants – even junior ones – fairly seriously, I think.      Maybe, but it’s not just about what you do. It’s the hours and the expectations. Like, they never want you to say no. It’s always “we can sort it out, can’t we?” You’re just expected to be there. It’s not even being flexible — it’s just being taken advantage of.      Yeah, I hear you. I mean, the flip side is that I get a bit of control over projects now that I’ve been in the role a bit longer, but that’s just because I’m part of the “consultant” team. Still, I get it — I’ve done some internships where I was the low man on the totem pole. I could see the same thing happening.      Exactly. It’s weird, right? Like you can do the same amount of work, you can deliver the same results, but if the title is different, the treatment is different. I sometimes wonder if it’s just because I’m a woman, but I don’t know.

I was meant to meet Vicky and go to the pub tonight for her 21st but I’m now considering bidding my chips to survive on for the next 72 hours.      Oi, calm down. My uncle owns a kebab van—you know the one on the High Street, the one that smells like a pastry bomb and sad dreams? They deliver. Or you can just dress as a gigachad breakfast, and pretend your “dinner” is a lifestyle choice.      Great plan, Kart, ordering puff pastry and edible glitter. That’ll definitely pass for a meal and not just, like, inappropriate Halloween leftovers. What I don’t get is why we’ve still got to pay for “vinaigrette on the side” here. What is this, a Michelin star or a funeral?      Listen, I had to pay an extra pound the other day because my chicken and “cheese” casserole “didn’t contain any additives” which is fair, because someone at the canteen suspiciously sounds like a bag of Ritz.      Honestly, this place would charge you money for being thirsty. Can I just  literally  drink the tap water and then pay them to not let me? That should be an option on the menu.      You know what? Forget the canteen. Let’s run to that student café, ‘cos they just opened up that “fancy” one with vegan everything and 60% less brain cells required to microwave it. I hear they even give you a free spoon if you ask “In what way do these eggs not taste like sadness?”      If I have to do the vegan egg emoji face  one more time  by a vending machine, I’m goin’ on a life mission to start a cult or at least open my own student café. Call it “Fableggs” – it’s your soul and a sandwich at £13.      We’d go viral, honestly. Just put photos of your “rainbow proteins” and overpriced hummus and call it art. Now go get my cousin to deliver us a meatball sub and tell Vicky we’re coming to her pub crawl looking like we haven’t seen sunlight since the last lecture she missed.

So did you lot actually manage to get anything to eat in that supermarket the other day or did they just sell you all the weird organic stuff again?      Honestly, I've given up trying to find anything that isn’t gluten-free or vegan these days. It's either that or it's branded 'multi-vitamin enriched'. I swear the bread they sell now has more nutrients than medicine.      I feel you, but I think that's just a result of everyone watching what they eat now. When I was a kid, the only thing people worried about was when the biscuit tin was empty.      Still, it made me chuckle when I saw the guy at the checkout trying to work out what turkey alternative was. I just watched him read the label like it was some kind of code.      I think he turned round at the end and said, “Thanks for the protein breakfast, no doubt about that.” Like he was marking some exam paper at the same time!      Ha, I had the same kind of moment when I was trying to decide between lentil and chickpea pasta. I looked it up online while queuing to see which is better for you. I ended up buying both—just to hedge my bets.      Honestly, I just want one holiday where I can eat normal food again. Not that I'm picky or anything, but when you're at a place where the only burger you can get isn't even a burger, someone has to win.      That's the absolute truth. I went on this trip to the south of France, and I thought being able to eat decent food would be one of the highlights. Instead, I ended up buying a salad every day from the supermarket near the campsite.      That sounds like my parents’ holiday in Greece. They managed to eat out three times in a whole week. The rest of it was just tzatziki with bread and yoghurt. I think their idea was to immerse themselves in the local culture, but I think they just lost their appetite for anything that came in a sauce.      I think it's related to TV as well. I mean you don't even get nice telly any more—just documentaries about nutrition or celebrities eating healthy food while trying not to look like they’re enjoying it.      And the box sets—oh man, your streaming service will tell you what you  should  be watching, not what you want.

Rather skip the newfit and go to London to see dad.      Yeah, he’d be right in his element with the tubes and the museums. Not a bad idea himself.      Not bad at all, I mean what would be the problem? We’ve got two eeny weeny passive incomes and the one from the   farmhouse  .      Aye, but I think he’d want to see Harrow again, you know,   where’s he came from  .      Didn’t you get the kids staying at the hostel in Cornwall to sort of get away from everything? I remember you saying the   youth hostel had a bunkhouse that Myra still liked   even after she was thirty.      Oh right yes, them and their friends. She said the   B&B was run-down but the view of the sea breakfasts made up for it  .      Aye, you ever looked at that place, the views near the   Pentire Point, or that cliff walk over there  , you get the sea and the sky and I don’t think land leaves as much as water and air do, it just remembers you.      I remember when we got offered that   house for sale down near Royal Tunbridge, and I said no because I wanted to stay in Birmingham flat  .      Oh what was the price on it?      Around forty-three. But I   reckon it was a good catch at the time  . Some nut had bought it thinking they were sorting out the   kitchen underfloor heating  , which in the end, it was about   stone floors and a bad drain  .      Not much underfloor heating in the   1800s era houses  , is there?      You’d be surprised. My sister nearly   burned down the loo at her place trying to fix a faulty socket  , said the   elephant plug just melted when she turned the kettle on  .      Websites like   eBay were handy for the memorabilia we’ve got  , but you want to be careful, I got this telly that the bloke sold as   new on the outside, ancient on the inside  , and it made my   ‘Chike show’ go completely fuzzy  .      Reckon we should invest in a   Minibike rally in Cambridge  , those days are gone but not altogether.      It’s either that or start watching them on   weather forecasts and keep my fingers crossed for warm temperatures for our garden flowers  . They both thrived under the   sunshine, frost made them all sad and slightly dirty-looking  .      Speaking of weather, have you two heard about the   new Health tax  ?

So did you go and pick up Joshua from your mum’s earlier then?      Yeah, I got there just after she’d fed him. He’d been crying a bit, but he calmed down once he spotted me. Poor thing, I think being at the day nursery knocks him out. Got on the bus at about half past one, you know, and he was basically asleep as soon as I sat down. A lot less stressful than trying to do anything social, I tell you.      Oh, wasn’t that the bus service that doesn’t run when it rains? I remember you saying something like that last week. I mean, I don’t get why the roads are still such a mess in this area. It’s not like we’re anywhere near the motorway or anything dramatic, just little back roads, Potton and all that.      It is, isn’t it? The council doesn’t seem to care much about us. Mum says I should’ve just driven, but I haven’t even got my keys back yet. Still waiting for my driving test date, which I swear the DVLA have lost on purpose. Honestly, I don’t know what it is with them and human error.      It’s so sad how much work it is, being a parent. I remember my nan used to say that you’re still learning how to parent long after your babies grow up. It’s not like you finish the first level and then everything gets easier.      Oh God, don’t remind me. I’ve been trying to get the hang of the whole ‘feeding on demand’ thing, and let me tell you, being woken at 2am to make a bottle is not in my top ten most enjoyable activities. I’m the kind of person who used to hit 8am and still not be out of my pyjamas, let alone be up for mixing formula. My sister Lucy tried to help the other day, but she clearly misunderstood the word ‘demand.’ She sat there timing it like he was on the clock.      Oh, your sister Lucy’s such a drama queen. I saw her once when we were at your parents' house and she was like, "Right, well if you're serious about this parenting thing, the baby has to go every hour on the hour if you ask me."      I was like, “Lu, he’s not Time Lord’s kid.”

Rather skip the newfit and go to the request and see.      Yeah that sounds better.      I’m more than happy to take cover.      Right. So we do this the same time as yesterday. Just like the timing was.      I don’t think they want that.      Yeah? I mean obviously I wouldn’t want to walk in too early but if we can stretch it into as long a session as possible and we might be doing the same. Didn’t take them long the last time either. Only like three-quarters of an hour.      What’s the point in rushing? You want to look like you’ve got somewhere to be though.      We had the sandwiches, didn’t we? I think the first round went quite well actually, far as Catsfield goes. I mean no doubt if I said something about mudflats in there they might not be too impressed.      Well the mudflats are fairly directly related to Waterfurlong, yes. But I think they would have understood if we were a bit more candid. I think initially, when I asked the first question, I didn’t have quite enough confidence.      Mate, you got fairly sidetracked, yeah.      Yeah, well I did try and stall them for a while.      Mmm. Well what someone said in one of the previous ones:  "We are extremely grateful for the support we received from the local residents and parish council in particular."        Sighs  Yeah, I about blocked at that. I thought "But the problem is that the parish council didn’t support what we wanted at all!"      Yeah, unhelpfully mentioned that.      "But it’s very much part of the ongoing work at the centre."      I mean, I tried to frame my questions carefully, but I just lost it when they started going on about partnerships and community spirit with people we don't even know!      You lost it, yeah.      Yeah, go back to the pond life if you like, but don’t forget the ducks line in the pond that was filled with mud, blokes.      So I said I was seriously concerned about how the wildlife in the area would be affected by the proposed new development to the farm. And that went over very well.      Mm, so what I did at the end was just say I thought the Waterway Improvements would be a waste of money and time for the local residents and I support the Friends of the Pond as far as their long-term goals go.

So did you get your science test back yet? I still haven’t got mine. I’m  dying  to know how I did.      I did! I got a 93%—so pleased with myself. I panicked during the actual test but somehow pulled through. You’ll get it back soon, I’m sure. Miss Ward always puts them on the table outside her room.      Ugh. I  failed  my quiz last week. She makes those quizzes so easy and I still messed it up. I got distracted by that new stamp collection I’m doing. You know I like to add a page in my homework journal dedicated to British stamps every time I finish a test.      Yeah, I’ve seen. You got that one from the 1840s Oliver Cromwell one and the Queen’s head? That’s so cool, by the way. I wish I could do that instead of just doodling in the corner like I do. I’m more of an art person, to be honest. I got into trouble for painting on the science worksheet one time.      Oh, really? I never would’ve guessed. Did you draw like a flower on it?      No, it was this weird little sea creature—I think it was a jellyfish but with five eyes, and one of the eyes was crying. Mr. Brown nearly had a heart attack. Anyway, enough about that. Have you seen the Christmas display in the hall? They’re putting in one of those big plants at the front like they normally do.      Yeah! Mom got me a little plant for my room as well—an aloe vera. I water it every day, even though I’m not sure I’m doing it the  right  way. I just pour water into the leaves because that looks like it works in the photos.      That’s not the way! You put it in the soil, not on the leaves. I’ve done gardening with my grandad all my life, so I can tell you that much. We grow sprouts and carrots. He says they’re the easiest things to grow for a new gardener.      My grandad used to grow tomatoes. He had a secret method—he used goop he made from his compost and ant food or something. I swear half the garden was alive with bugs. But he said they tasted amazing.      So are you planning to go to the Christmas market this year?

Rather annoying this new bus route, isn't it, Doris? I had to get off two stops early yesterday, and I nearly lost me brolly as well. Not a bit like the old days when yer knew exactly where the stop was and the bus came as regular as clockwork.      Oh dear, William, I felt the same! I tried to go into Norwich to get me eyes tested last week, and I missed me connection so bad I ended up taking a taxi home. It cost me a small fortune! You’d think they’d keep the old routes when they change.      That’s because they’re trying to modernise, Doris. County council’s always tinkering with things like that. Though, I have to agree, it can be a bit of a mess if you’re not used to it. Still, at least the buses are running most of the time, and they’re cleaner than when I was your age!      Clean or not, I still think they should keep the old ones running for the folk who aren’t so tech-savvy. I nearly had to get me grandson to download this new app for me yesterday. What did he call it again? Something like ‘Bus Times Plus’… Sounds like it's for rhythm and blues performers, not old people trying to find their bus!      Oh, I tried that app once, William. It took me longer than just phone the company and ask a real person! Though, I must say, I did enjoy the one time I saw a rat puppet on a seat just down the road. That was a sight! Someone had a red nose on and was bobbing around like it was a ballet performance! You’d have about laughed yourself sick.      Oh come now, Doris, they call it ceilidh puppetry these days. I saw one up near Loughton last year. My, they've gone all fancy with them. All LED eyes and bell actions. Rather impressive, if I do say so myself. Though I’d still take a decent handbell performance over a rat any day. Those handbell choirs from the Churches always bring a proper crowd.      Handbell ringing, yes, you remember when the church had that course on the village green? I tried it once, ended up ringing the wrong one and nearly pulled me arm off in the process! I don’t think God was particularly impressed.

I can't believe we've never done this before. Venice is such a classic. Honestly, I got to visit with work ages ago, but more than once! You should've come with me. Yeah, I know, I wish I had. I can't believe how pretty it is—especially now, with the sun out. It's not all roses though, I remember it being a proper rush in the height of the summer, so busy you could barely get through the streets. Oh I heard that. Didn’t it get so full with tourists that they had like signs saying "maximum number of visitors"? Oh, don’t get me started. It’s a bit of madness, especially near the Rialto Bridge and the Piazza San Marco. But if you pick your day right, you can actually get a bit of peace. Yeah, I figured if we do a coffee here and walk in the early morning, we’ll avoid the worst of it. That’s why I suggested this spot—Café Venice, a bit off the main drag. I remember it from my last trip. The coffee is strong and the cachetti are just on another level. Oh, cachetti? What's that? Little rectangular, like Venetian baps, but sweet and salty versions. They do one with mascarpone and chocolate—worth every calorie. Now you're just making me hungrier. What else would you recommend? I’ve heard so much about the fresh pasta and the seafood. Oh it’s next level. You  have  to try the sarde in saor—they’re sweet-and-sour sardines, a Venetian classic. And don’t even get me started on the risotto al nero di seppia—served in a shell! Sounds fancy. Are we going somewhere tonight? Like a real Venetian restaurant? I’ve made a reservation at Arlequi in Burano. It’s a bit of a ferry ride, but the lunches there are outrageously good—sea bream, oysters, you name it. Oh man, I can go for that. But what about the gondola ride? I thought we were doing that today. That’s the plan, yes. After we finish our coffee, I’ve booked a gondola tour in the afternoon. It’s supposed to take in the quieter canals—like the ones over near the Arsenale. We'll avoid the tourist traps. Perfect. I was about to suggest that, actually. I really want to see the side of Venice that's not full of selfie sticks.

So did you go to the gym this weekend? I saw you posted a photo of your squats on Instagram... got to keep up with you, Gemma!      Oh, please! You’re the one who can do a full Turkish get-up at seven in the morning. I just went on Saturday because my ex-kept badgering me saying he’d book a spin class for us. I told him not to but he did anyway. I got stuck in a Ladies' Only session by mistake.      Oh my God! Didn’t you get thrown out or shouted at?      No! Someone just laughed and said, “He’s only here for the view,” and the instructor just rolled with it! So I left halfway through. Ten minutes, to be exact. Ditched him and went for a long walk instead.      That sounds better honestly. I’ve been thinking I need a break from the gym in general. Maybe I’ll book a holiday instead, you know, for some proper rest. Spain? Or maybe Portugal—something with beaches, not a gym.      You need a holiday as much as you need oxygen. You’ve still got that project at work, right? The one with Bupa? You’ve been at the office until nine at night again last night, haven’t you?      It’s not as if I have a choice! I’m stepping into a managerial role, and the HR team want everything formatted in a new system. God, it's chaotic. But I can’t not do it. Also, I’m in the process of being housed in a new flat in Cambridge. Staggering all my life crises at once.      That’s exciting though, isn’t it? New flat! Going out there to see it? I remember your old student digs in Milton. My, what a dump.      I know! The shower used to cut out every time someone flushed the toilet. But this flat is way better. It’s a two-bed flatshare with a barrister who’s doing a PhD in law. She’s a complete whiz—typing away at midnight with no music.      A PhD student and a barrister? That sounds like someone from  Law & Order: UK Edition .      You know it. But I can live with it. It’s way better than pestering my brother to let me stay one more week.      It’s a win on the life board. Also, I’ve met someone, by the way.

Rather skip the new landlord’s meeting. You know what they do. They promise internet, and they deliver potted plants and a showerhead with a mind of its own.      Yes, and it’s not £20 a month for the bollards either. But it was interesting writing about Porden. You remember the spire collapse in   Chichester  ? Quite the disaster for a man who only built it to last ten more centuries.      Imagine   Philip of Spain   journeying to   Spain   to.Fatalfanstay chase his wife into the Spanish fold. I saw the Spanish archives in Seville. They were like a spider’s nest of bureaucracy and wet ink. You had to wear gloves, even for Mary Tudor’s coronation scroll. Ten layers of napkins between you and history, if you ask me.      Well, the Catsfield housing estate doesn’t have that problem. The architect’s still a boy in his early twenties, planting evergreen desktop hides, thinking he’s   Philip of Spain  . I would’ve told him to give it a spire for character, but they’d have put a bollard in it and called it   enterprise  .      You know, we had a little boy who was born in   France  , near   Orange  . His mother, she just thought: why settle into a British flat with black mold when you can have a   provincial farmhouse   with a tile roof, and the   anarchists in the village square   making cheese from manure. He’s oddly British at school—keeps saying “merci” and then pulling a tea towel out of his pocket.      I daresay the   French   prefer the English here too. I had a young man in my flat not long ago who was   horse-riding   down the street with his mobile phone on, like he thought he was in a   royal procession  . Bumped into me by the bookstall. I asked him if he’d tried the   Open Day photo exhibition  ? Not to be confused with the   art competition  , which is truly the saddest thing I’ve ever seen. Children took the paintbrush like it was a sword.      Oh yes, and he kept recounting about the   Austrian battleship disaster   like it was a Sunday constitutional. He’s a bloke who’s read your book cover to cover at the   British Library  . Thought it was about   Philip of Spain  , not   landlords  . I had to say, “No, this one is about them alone.”      I did indeed intend for it to sound like   land   suffering romantic seduction from above.

So did you lot actually finish your homework for maths or are we doomed again?      I got it sorted, man. Miss Chen keeps giving us these graphs to draw like we’re plotting a heist or something. Why do we have to do so many lines?      I didn’t do mine. I’m bad at graphs. I reckon it’s not fair. You don’t need that in real life. Who draws graphs every day, apart from like, Miss Chen?      My brother was doing one for his job. Apparently, he works with Chinese car parts or something. It’s all bar charts and line graphs. He said the boss gets cross if they’re messy.      Oh please. My cousin’s a chef and he says the only charts he uses are pastry charts and sad cake graphs. No, he just rules a ruler every now and then for breakfast, no graphs involved.      Ha! That’s not even science. Anyway, speaking of food, have you tried the sweet and sour chicken here? I had it last time, and it was like edible fireworks. I mean in a good way.      That’s only because they probably gave you the secret sauce extra. I asked for mild and it still made my tongue feel like it was trying to leave my body.      Same here. I reckon they just say mild for tourists. Next time we should bring our own chilli sauce from home.      Nah, my mum tried to teach me how to make her chilli sauce, but it ended up like tomato and being sad. Not the same as China, mate.      My sister says the same story. She tried to make “crispy duck” once and ended up with crispy wallpaper. My nan fixed it. She said it was like the duck reborn.      My gran once tried to make something at home and the smoke alarm told us to all move out. I think it counted as a new sort of biscuit though. Like mysterious yellow sprite crisp.      Ha! Grans ruin everything. Anyway, have you all read the new  X-Men  comic yet? The one where Cyclops is really on fire—literally.      I got it, yeah. It’s wild. That bloke isn’t even your normal superhero. He’s just like, lost and on fire and someone paints his face black so he looks even more confused.      It’s brilliant, right? They’re trying to make him the new Spider-Man of like, existential dread or something.

Right, thanks for having us today, Doreen. We’ve been trying to get all the presents sorted for Jonathan and the house is starting to feel like more of a birthday warehouse by the minute.      Aye, seems like I’ve lived in a storage unit all week. But it’s all good, I’ve been keeping busy clearing out that old junk in the attic anyway. You don’t know how many things I’ve found lying around!      I thought we might dump that old upright piano we had in the corner for a while. But Doreen revealed under the dust sheets was a box of photos and letters—pre-war, goodness.      Oh, now that’s a proper find. I remember you had that photo of you and Ken standing outside the Post Office in Kendal, and I think he turned 14 that year, was that you, Margaret?      Aye, that was me in the tartan dress, and Ken in that fawn suit looking like a model! Young fool.      Can I see those photos, Nanny?      You can have a look, Tom, but careful with them—Doreen says some are over sixty years old.      I’ll get them out, no bother. It just goes to show, the more you move out of a house, the more you remember what it held in the first place.      Well, speaking of moving, I think my mum wants to clear out the spare room now—piece by piece, of course. You can’t be accused of clearing out all the best stuff, or you’ll have about five calls from disappointed aunts!      Aye, and I’ve already warned her sister Sarah that she shouldn’t be expecting any of the ‘best bits', not with her ‘ upmarket antique’ guest list  at the last tea.      She told me she was bringing three of her ‘ sparkly little ones ’ who insist on calling her  Nana Nominator .      Anyway, speaking of clearing out—what about the food? Tom’s delivering something around five, and I told the local bakery go ahead and get the cake if it’s not going to be late.      You don’t go to town until you’ve had your cake and you don’t have your cake until it’s had sprinkles, okay?      It better have more than just ‘ best wishes ’ written on it, this is Jonathan’s big one—keeping it to five digits for now.      And let’s keep the speeches short.

So did you pick your GCSE options yet? I’ve been stressing about it for weeks.      I did last week. I’m doing art, music, English, and geography. What about you?      I got maths, biology, English lit, and drama. I kind of wish I’d done art instead of biology. I reckon it’s easier to get an A  in that.      Honestly, I’m not sure anyone gets an A  in art anymore. Mrs. Johnson was saying the standards have gone sky high, but the coursework is not too bad if you put in even a little bit of effort.      Yeah, but I like doing the science stuff. I’ve always wanted to be a vet or something. I mean, I’m not good at chemistry and I think physics is just nonsense to me, but at least biology is better.      I used to want to be a vet too, but then I looked into what they actually earn, and it was like, why would I work that hard for that little? Might get into something like fashion or maybe IYTS — international youth traineeship scheme. It sounds fancy.      You know, I’ve been watching all these YouTubers who talk about their jobs. I mean, some of them are just 15 and have already picked out their careers like they have a million followers. It’s a bit annoying, isn’t it? They all make it look so easy.      Yeah, I hate when people pretend you just need to upload a video and money rolls in. Like, I’ve had a ballet blog for ages and I about earn pocket money. My dad used to say it’s all just “bogs and bloggers” now.      My brother’s into it too. He does that astronomy channel, like for little kids. He got sent free rockets once by some brand and it was all over his Instagram. But he still can’t get a job, you know. His dream is to get to be as big as Jamie Oliver or something. He’s obsessed with celebrity chefs.      Wasn’t there a new programme where chefs had to learn how the food is made in the countryside? It wasn’t bad. I think they had this lad who just started out baking sourdough.      Oh your dad used to tell me stories about when he was a lad and wanted to be a clarinet player. He said he was in a massive band in Cambridge and they used to do gigs at the local theatre.

Rather skip the new model entirely eh?      Aye, I mean, they’re like... got the seats, they’re got the dash, and I can tell by the smell in that car that it's full of new things they don't need.      Honestly, if it’s not broken, don't fix it. My dad used to drive his Ford Escort all the way until a bearing let go in the engine. That car was like a second home; it even watched me through university.      Oh, I once looked after a little boy whose toy car he named "Rover". Horrible habit! He made me talk to it when the wheels fell off!      My son still drives the same Clio I left him in 1998 – I told him if it falls apart I’ll weld the bonnet shut and make it a garden ornament.      Heh, I mean, with the state of roads in Norfolk, you could probably drive that thing on the windings and the exhaust!      I was over near Thetford Forest the other day—there I was in the landrover, and this fox ran off, followed by two cubs… watching it all, trotting through the heather. Absolute delight.      I love watching wildlife, but the other day, I had a heron in the garden. Stood there for an hour. Then it hit me—it was toilets and bins in the background. Spotted my mistake. Just said to it, “You don’t belong here.” It flapped off!      Hey, you know what I missed when we were building bridges? The birds about it. Herons, swallows, the lot of them watching us from the beams.      You know, you guys mentioned wildlife and it reminded me—I mentioned to the uni kids the other day that the construction of the A11 actually cut off bird migration paths. You would think a few bloody environmental scientists would’ve noticed that before you poured the concrete!      Aye. You think of old engineering projects—like the Roman roads and canals—wasn’t the same as today where you bash something up with a machine and the birds get up goosed.      It does make you wonder, though—if the Romans had computers, would they be arguing with blokes on forums about your iTunes install?      Oh, software—now there’s a nightmare. I tried to upgrade the photos on my tablet, and now it tells me I need a “cloud subscription” like I’m some sort of Victorian railway needing steam and tracks to collect passenger info.

Rather skip the school uniform lark entirely.      That’d be a real maverick move, wouldn’t it?      Not a bad idea if you ask me. I always thought uniform was more about the school than the kids. Just keeps the place looking tidy and smart, and saves a fortune on laundry.      My lass went to a secondary with that ‘optional uniform’ policy, so every Friday half the school wore jeans and the other half came as if they were going to the Prom. It looked like half of them belonged and half of them didn’t.      Oh I remember that, we used to supply the blazers for the poorest kids so they still fit in. There was a bit of a knack to picking the right ones who weren’t going to pick fights about it.      God, the old school slogans. "We are the walrus," "Nitpicking for the soul," the lot. Only teachers would come up with that lot.      Or the bloke who decided the school should have a mascot in the image of a falcon with a face as if it were grief itself. Poor old bird.      You remember Mr. Beadle? “It takes one to know one.” True enough, in my experience.      Yeah, but don’t get me started on the new system. I blame the universities as much as the schools. Our kids walk into full-time work with bucket-loads of debt and none of them want to do farming—job’s as good as gone in thirty years and here we are still trying to make future ballet teachers out of them in Year 8.      Oh come on, Charlie, let’s not be too gloomy. You were telling us about the time the delivery lad tripped over that bunch of tulips on the doorstep.      Oh yes, and landed head-first into the wheelie bin full of old newspapers. I tried not to laugh when he started muttering about how “never again am I being sent out in the rain with lunches to a madhouse.”      That's Tom, delivering the fish fingers and custard on his moped go-kart on a life mission to save everyone else’s supper.      I had a delivery person once bloke turned up at one o’clock in the morning with flu tablets and a kipper after I tweeted hours previously that I had bellyache and a migraine.      That’s not a tweet that needs a follow-up, my missus used to do that when the cat was being a supreme little turd, casting runes on the windowsill.

‘Ey Mark, you seen this snow? It’s mad. I came out for the bins and it looked like we was in some sort of Christmas card!      Yeah, it’s proper mad, hun. Not quite enough to cancel the football match at the weekend though—Deirdre’s een invitat to play host to the lassie who’s got the stag do next Saturday. Should be a laugh.      Deirdre, yeah, I remember she was on  Come Dine With Me  years ago..Fatalfailed the whole time, but still had a right good time. You thinking of joining in with the stag do, or are you just supplyin’ moral support and beers?      Ha ha! Yeah, I’ll be there, but I reckon you’ll have to pick me up in the morning cos I might be in too much of a giggle by breakfast, no doubt. But this weekend’s for the garden—before this snow’s even half gone! I told you, the new raspberry canes came.      Oh right, you’ve had them in? Yer not going full vegpatch on us now, are you?      Nah, not full, but we’ve been talking about this for months. We can’t wait til summer to start, least way it won’t be a rush. You lot join in? You’ve got the whole back yard to play with!      Honestly, I just don’t have time with work. But my man, if it’s a mad evening of stargazing and mulled wine, I’m in. Still, maybe I’ll make a curry for us all at some point.      That’s the spirit! We can have our own cooking night, and maybe you can be the judge!      Maybe I’ll do better than  Come Dine With Me . Although if I drop a spoon on the floor, Deirdre’ll probably assume I’ve spontaneously combusted.      Hey, stick to my good side and I’ll tell her you’re always like this.      Thanks, Mark. And speaking of things coming up—any plans yet for the holidays? I reckon goin’ on a road trip up the North York Moors would be bricking in the snow, but maybe we can boxset binge instead.      Road trip’s too risky with this weather, you’re right. I was thinkin’ of a proper getaway—maybe somewhere with a little less walking up hills and more sitting down sipping coffee. You up for Spain?      Only if you’re cooking my paella, and you’re not getting hen do vibes again.

Rather skip the newfit meat eh?      Well I know it's not real mutton is it dear.      It isn’t I can tell by the smell. Proper mutton is strong. Not like that stuff they pass off as meat these days. It’s more like card een fritter if you ask me.      Dad, it’s actually not that bad. It’s plant-based. Healthier than a lot of processed meat anyway.      Healthier? What’s wrong with you? You can’t chase a football or run miles on some meat that’s not even meat. I used to be able to eat a whole Sunday roast and still go for a walk after.      Yeah well, you’re over 70 Dad.      I’ll be the same at 80, thank you very much. Still breakfast, still roast, still me.      Oh don’t be too stubborn, love. You ate the puff spare ribs the other day and claimed they were the best you’d ever had, and we both know those were vegan!      Well they might be fake meat, but that still don’t make them better than the proper ones. I’d rather have a good Sunday roast – no alterations.      Let’s just eat and not argue about it. We don’t get to see you both that often.      Absolutely. So what did you make someone at the childminding centre used to tell me a recipe once for lentil stew – rich and warming.      Oh yes, she was a good cook! We had it every other Wednesday in about ’89. I think you were the one who invented it Charlie?      Charlie? You know that was you! I remember it had a lot of spices and the smell stayed in the kitchen for hours.      I was trying to impress. It turned out bloody nice though.      Not as nice as your mutton pie, queens.      That always comes with a bit of Gravy from the steak.      Still, I’m happy with this meal! The beetroot lasagne was really good.      Yeah – I think I might try it myself when I get back. Who knew plants could taste like that?      Well maybe I’ll give it another try one day – but don’t expect me to like it better than a good old steak and kidney pie.      We won’t. You can go back to your mutton once we’re finished.      You saw the colour of the beetroot used in it though, right?

Rather skip the new house and go to our old one in Cheetham.      We can't do that it's not registered.      Erm sure we could we could borrow it.      That's not what you were saying about the lease was.      Well I don't think they'd really know if we just borrowed it for a bit.      Like would you have a problem?      No not if there's no problems and we give it back.      But the kids.      They're with their brother.      What the hell are you two up to?      We were going to go to our old house.      Again.      I think it's just.      Again and again.      To look at it.      Walk through it.      Just to see it.      To see that it's not been trashed and sold.      I think we should just walk to it and look at it and then come back.      You'd get a little kick out of it no.      I think it's normal it's our memories.      It's got to be something that will be beautiful to see again.      I suppose just someone else in it now.      When they sold it we had a house warming and had the key.      But Ernie still has the house key in his possession because he nearly about blocked the kettle.      Oh the kettle had to be unplugged a few times.      Cos it was boiled dry every bloody day.      Should've put the kettle in guest.      The house warming was lovely the day before Christmas was was nice.      Everyone was waiting till we could all get there.      Then we went to Ernie's to keep the kettle from boiling dry.      Still remember Ernie saying this is like a man's house.      The man's house was.      Yeah it was.      That bloke Ernie what a man.      The man was a soldier and he knew his way around.      True to say.      Yeah and when we moved them out the window was the problem so he refused to move out.      Right so they had to take it down.      To take the window down because it was like it was.      Broken.      Broken.      Was that a problem.      Like it's our memories you see.      So yeah typical.      The memories and the stories.      Yeah I mean the window was broken for ages ages.      Like when we first moved in he was the one that said I'm not taking the window out without the window.

So do you ever find that kids just aren't engaged in lectures these days? Even in secondary school?      Oh absolutely. I’m always trying to figure out what grabs their attention. I mean, we tried with a few viral video clips in our classroom — you know the kind — short, funny, and relevant? The kids were hooked for about five minutes before it became background noise again.      That’s interesting. We had a similar problem when we started our education start-up in Wellington. We tried to make learning interactive, like short video prompts that led into discussions or mini-projects. The key was giving them a  story  to follow, something to solve, not just information to absorb. It worked surprisingly well.      Oh, I like that idea. Storytelling as a framework for learning. If you turned history into an adventure quest, or a problem to solve, I could see that working at university level too. You know, like a narrative-based approach to lectures.      Exactly! We used to call it ‘edutainment’ — education, but presented like entertainment. Think of one of those viral videos where someone walks you through a mystery or something. You want to watch until the end just to figure it out. That’s how we designed modules for our start-up.      That’s brilliant. I’ve seen some of those TED-Ed videos and they use a similar idea, but universities tend to stick to the old 'lecture someone at the front' model. Maybe because they don’t have the resources to push a more modern approach?      It’s frustrating, isn’t it? I remember one of our early successes was about problem-solving techniques. We designed a project where students had to solve a real-world business issue in teams and present their solution. Not just theory — real application. And we recorded the whole thing and put it on social media. It actually went reasonably viral — not TikTok viral, but enough to get attention from some education forums.      That’s amazing. Would you ever consider expanding that kind of approach to higher education? Because from the teacher’s side, it feels like the same thing over and over. Still trying to get students to  want  to learn.      If I had the funding again, I would push into university partnerships, no doubt. The team I had in Wellington was small, but incredibly driven. We all believed that education didn’t have to be one-size-fits-all.

So did you go out at all this weekend? Or were you hiding away like me?      Well, I went out on Saturday for a bit. I helped a friend with a Halloween fancy dress party in Leicester. Not quite my scene, but it was a good laugh. Went as a nurse again, just because I liked the outfit. It was actually   tricky   getting in without them thinking I was part of the decor.      Haha, classic. I stuck close to home, just cooked a massive meal and was lazy. You know me. But, I  did  manage to get out to Kent on Sunday for a family thing. That’s the weird thing, right? You can be like minutes from London, but it feels like a different country.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been to the Kent countryside—so peaceful, compared to the place I grew up, which was more East London. I still can't believe how rural it’s out there. There’s no way I could have imagined that from the train station.      Exactly! I’ve always loved that about England. I mean, we’re a small country, but we’ve got  everything  in there: cities, countryside, coastlines... Well, almost. You ever been to the Lake District?      I’ve seen pictures, but I haven’t actually been. I did grow up near the north of the country, so I’m more used to the Pennines. But I hear the Lakes are beautiful. Maybe my sister wants to go there next spring. You ever think about moving out of London? I imagine the air is better up there!      Honestly? I about considered it. Not permanently, but just to get out of this chaotic city vibes for a bit. My job is quite location flexible now. I’m a project co-ordinator in mental health projects, so remote work works well for that. I might even rent a place up near Exeter or something—south west, nice weather.      That sounds mad, honestly. I’m tied down here for a few more years—my hospital job’s not exactly flexible. But I do have five-year plans… like you do, right?      Oh yeah, go on then. What’s your five-year plan?      Well, I’m thinking of doing a bit more in leadership within mental health. Possibly moving into policy or something that can make a broader impact. I’ve seen too many issues that don’t get fixed fast enough.

Rather annoying isn't it, this weather.      It's like it's pretending to be spring and then it snows. I’m so ready for summer.      Me too, love £200 worth of winter clothes at the back of the wardrobe. Never wore half of them.      Which puts me in mind—when you were my age, did you have all these cycles of fashion? Like, I feel like now you’re into a trend and you stick with it for three years, but back when you were in your twenties, it was different every month.      Oh, don't get me started on that. One minute it was wide legged trousers, the next it was jelly-legging bursts, you know? I had one pair of Dungarees and I think I turned into a piece of furniture for about a year.      You look back and go, “Why in the name of all things holy did I dress like that?”      Oh, yes. I remember I went into town, and I had this headband up here that covered my whole forehead. Someone asked me if I'd got lost and ended up in a bonnet factory.      Sounds dramatic.      I replied, and mind you, I said, “You weren’t around in the sixties, so you wouldn’t understand the fashion language.”      Oh, someone said that to me the other day. I was at work and one of the older production guys said something about how I look “too modern” and “all zipped up” which I understood fully because he was about forty. I told him the same: “You weren’t around in 2014, so you wouldn’t be up to speed with the lanyard fashion.”      Oh, I like that. “Lanyard fashion.” That’s a new one on me.      I don’t know how long that will last, though. It’s either going to become a status symbol or go out with a whimper and join the digestive belt trend of the 90s.      Now, that was something. I had one for a while and I had to go to the loos at the cinema, but only between films.      I can picture it. So, have you made the special dinner yet?      I’ve got the ingredients in, more or less. I’ve overcomplicated the recipe and I’m missing a few things I might have to go out and get. Again.      You could order online.      It’s not the same.

So did you watch the Euros last summer? That match between France and England was wild, innit?      I did, yeah! Though I was watching from Cambridge, so I gotta say, it was probably more of a nightmare for the locals with all the fans. But it was epic. I still can't believe England made it that far.      Proper madness. Though I reckon we only got so far because of that kid from Oldham, the one who started as a sub and scored. What’s his name? Bukayo Saka?      Yeah, he’s brilliant. Honestly, I’m still annoyed I missed the live stream because I was doing this stupid biology prac that lasted five hours. You know how it is in sixth form—science teachers go off if you dare miss a lab.      Haha, I was lucky. I bunked off breakfast, sat in the park with a bagel and watched in peace. Blooming cold it was! But, you know, I’ve always hated the uni environment, so that’s why I’m still in sixth form. Just can’t get into it.      Fair play. I’m dreading starting uni properly next year. I’m studying chemistry and then doing some French modules. My brother says it’s easier because I can speak it, but I’m like, no, no, don’t test me. I couldn’t even translate “I’m going to the shops” without looking it up.      Lmao, I tried once. I told a barista in Paris “Je voudrais une croissant” and they looked at me like I’d spoke in code. I about died. But you know what’s bugging me the most? I had to present a project on scientific methods yesterday. I was trying to explain the difference between a hypothesis and a theory. My teacher nearly flipped.      A hypothesis is like a guess? A theory is something you’ve tested a million times and it still works, right? You must’ve been so lost.      Pretty much! Except I said a theory is just “something scientists think happened in the past”. The guy gave me a look. I was like, “it’s go or bin it” and I blurted out “It’s like gravity—it’s a theory, not a guess!” That might have saved me.      That’s actually kind of smart. You’re not wrong. And speaking of smart people, have you seen that new indie band that went viral this summer?

Rather annoying to wake up and find a load of cobwebs in the corner of the hallway, wasn’t it? What was I thinking not putting the vacuum on more than I have been this week      Aye, we had a bit of a pest problem last winter. We found a proper house spider, the sort that likes to drape itself all over your things. My George wanted to squish it with a newspaper but I said nay, too much like me dad.      Aye, and you never end up squishing them anyway. Just end up with a squashed newspaper and the poor bug still sitting there.      What I found odd is how some spiders like to set up shop in the living room. Ours’s one tried to spin a web from the ceiling rail on the banister right in the middle of the room. Had it about a week ‘fore we noticed, and then of course I happened to trip over it in my slippers.      They are bloody cheeky when they settle in. We’ve had mice before—though not for a while now—but nothing says ‘clean home’ like a mouse dropping in the middle of the hob, does it?      You'd think a little cleaning would sort it out, but no. Once you’ve got one, you’ve got a queue of them lining up. Now don’t get me started on the birds. I swear one of them outside our kitchen window’s watching for food.      Aye, I reckon they’ve got good taste. Left out a bit of bread a few days back and next thing you know, I’ve birdsmith ballet, there it all is about five at it. I don’t blame the little blighters, mind. It’s what you call ‘a wasted chance’ if you ask me.      Aye, they’re smarter than you’d give them credit for. My cat tries to have them but the birds just fly off ‘fore it can get anywhere near. I think the ones with the blue on their backs know what they're doing.      You keep the cat from the table, do you, or do you let it jump around with bits of roast chicken all over its goody? I usually tell mine off and give it a swat—no respect in the house, I don’t know where it learned it from.      That’s the way to go, mind.

Rather skip the new DVD and go through the request cards first.      Ah, typ...typical. Never mind. You've already sorted out my family tree then?      Most of it. I'll have to wait until you've sorted things out with your brother again.      Oh, you know   he's   fascinated with all that genealogical stuff. A lot of his documents are in this box, if you'd like to take a look.      Right, the one under the piano?      Yes...and the one with photos mostly.      What I found fascinating was how detailed your mother’s MySpace profile was. I thought she was left-handed, you know. I didn't know she had a brother in Manchester who used to send her letters.      Oh yes, Dave, he wrote to her religiously. They had some sort of betting system, you know, for the fai-in’s results.      Faith in—?      Championship, sweetie. I mean, F A Cup. They still play it in Wales, even today.      Oh right, sorry, of course. I’m used to Baptists talking about faith, not football. Anyhow, her illness was...cancer of the liver, right?      Oh yes, it was. She didn't want anyone panicking, which is why she never said a word. It just sort of...overtook her in the end. I didn't even know until it was too late.      That must have been so hard. I remember the last time I saw her, she was telling me about cooking lasagne and not needing her glasses to see the sauce bubbling.      That was her way of being humorous. To her, cancer wasn't funny. But at least she finished her recipe book before she went.      I haven’t had time to crack into it yet. I’m being asked to write a proposal with lunches and a new budget from the caretaker, and let me tell you, delivering something around this budget is like the holy grail.      Aww, I feel for you. I remember in my day, I was always arguing with the county about getting the proper amount of pens. It was never enough! Eventually I gave up and just started using those plastic ones from the supermarkets, they work like a dream.      We do them now. I tell the kids they feel like prison stationery. My job is kind of like trying to keep 200 teenagers out of trouble.      It’s a noble job. Always wondering, what would I have done with so much time on my hands had I retired earlier.

Rather annoying isn’t it? Power lines everywhere. You'd think they could run them underground somewhere like this. I got the kids to paint them once as part of a community project—put up little bluebirds and hares on poles with proper signs. Looked lovely for a month, then the council took ’em all down.      It was ridiculous. I reckon someone just wanted to "tidy up" but forgot about the artistic value. Imagine! I mean, what are we, backward? We could be in a Dutch painting out here if the lines weren’t snaking through the fields like some sort of... like some sort of electric broom.      You know, I was thinking about that hot-air balloon event again. You remember the one Terry got involved in? Ten years ago, was it? Drove up from London with a whole bunch of local lecturers in a Mini Cooper and got stuck for breakfast, no doubt about it.      Oh yeah, Terry’s idea of an adventure was driving somewhere and not planning the journey. They got excluded from the hot-air balloon over weather conditions, and had to spend the night in some tent two miles out.      And sent back by the council the next morning—very politely, by the way, from what Terry said. Made a very good point about planning, didn’t they? Anyway, imagine if we had a balloon of our own.      If we had one we could at least make sure the power lines were someone else’s problem. Although I don’t know—count me out for that. I once tried camping and ended up with a muddy dog named Alfie who washed under the tent for a week and never came out.      That does sound rather the thing, doesn’t it? Not much of a walk—that’s if you call trudging through the undergrowth with a sandwich for both of us and a ‘very useful wet wipe’ a proper countryside activity.      Well, the wildlife is a positive uplift, I have to say. The other day when I was marking past papers, I saw this fox trotting across a field like it owned the place. Watching it from my study window, the glass tinted just right, it looked like it was pacing the campus of some gothic university on the edge of the world.      I like that—our study-to-wildlife ratio might need a bit of adjustment, though.

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather? One minute it’s sunny and warm, the next it’s like someone’s turned on the hose. You’d think April would be more predictable by now.      Aye, I know what you mean. It’s enough to put a bobbly on your boots if you ask me. It was like proper spring this morning—still, better than the wet we’ve had all winter. Not that I’m complaining, mind. Warm stretch makes for a better warm-up before the class.      Didn’t your class today? I saw you doing a demonstration to the newer coaches earlier.      That’s right—morning class and then that session. Just showing them how you get the members engaged without making them feel like they’re back at school. Know what I mean? A bit of encouragement goes a long way.      I can imagine. I do a lot of education myself—language teaching. It’s the same in a way, building confidence. You can shout words at someone all day, but if they don’t feel comfortable using them, it won’t stick.      So what you sayin’ then, we’ve got something in common? You and me both in the “pushing people out of their comfort zone” business?      Something like that. Though I’m quite happy to sit in the classroom with a good book and a cup of tea most days. I’ve just finished  The Midnight Library —such a read.      Never heard of it. Not really a book type, I’ll be honest. Can’t even remember the last book I read before I did  Harry Potter , and that was a mammoth effort.       Wait , you mean you never got around to the rest of the  Harry Potter  books? My, my! You must’ve been mighty busy working at the gym.      Oh, aye—I was bringing up two daughters and running them from dance to drama while I was at it. Books could wait. But what about you? Do your students ever act out while learning French like Harry and his mates? Though I expect learning verbs is a bit more tedious than fighting dragons.      Haha, some of my classes could very well be called “living libraries.” I had a bloke the other day who told me  “passer”  and  “pass”  in English are the same, and I’m not sure he’s wrong either.      Sounds like them translations went sideways.

Right, love, I’ve got to go to the post office. I was just wondering if you fancied coming with me and helping me carry the shopping back, or would you rather do your homework?      I don’t mind. I’ll come with you. Just let me grab my coat real quick.      Oh, you’re taking young Davey with you? Don’t forget a bobble hat and gloves. It's that wind off the Humber; it’ll take the skin right off your face!      Oh, don’t be such a drama queen, Nell. It’s a mild January. Last time I listened to you the fire department’d have had to fetch me out the turkey shop. I was fine. I left with a hat and well, I was back in the house, so no harm done!      Ed, you’ve got to stop going out when you’re ill. The doc’s told you for the last time. I know you want to keep shopping, but your chest won’t thank you for it.      Nell, don’t start on me again. I’m fine, honestly.      It’s okay, Mrs. Harrison. I’ll walk with her. I don’t mind the cold. I used to cycle miles every day in York, and I barely noticed the wind.      It’s Mrs. Norris to you, David! And no one’s stopping your riding, but don’t forget someone older in the house also breathes the same air. It just does oddly sometimes. That’s all.      Alright, love. Be back in a bit. We need more bread, and I’ve got that milk to collect. Don’t know where the heck it is. I think it’s in the larder with that tin of marmalade we bought for your nan’s 80th. I still can’t find that tin.      You mentioned that tin  last  year, Miss Norris!      Oh, leave her be. That’s the only marmalade that tastes right. Not that posh shop stuff the rest of you like. No, no. This is the real stuff. Walter go and bin the soap again if you don’t mind.      I don’t see why we always go through this charade every week. It’s not like I have a clue.      I think I’m gonna go to the farm shop sometime and get something proper. They’ve got fresh quiches and homemade soups there.      Quiche? Oh, you cheeky rascal.

Rather skip the new road and go through the village, is that right?      Yeah, got to follow the maps on the phone unless yer fancy getting lost again by the old sawmill.      Oh aye, that one frightened me well. Thought me satnav had een taken a holidays!           Aye, well next time you might take a proper map or ask one a the locals, like we said last time.      Nonsense, me navigation skills are just fine when it don't rain.      That’s mostly it, innit? All roads are fine until the rain comes down and they turn into turkey soup.      Aye, and then I’m stuck like a Daffy Duck and I’m late for your concert.      Good thing we’re going to a ceilidh after. They always know the roads in the village, and they’ve got fiddles to distract you.      Aye, I’ll do me best not to spill the pint of ale I’m gonna get out of you to calm me nerves.      Make it two pints, and I reckon you’ll be fine. Though I don’t know if yer fairly good with a fiddle will help if you’ve had a few.      Silly man, I can still hit tune even if I’ve had a bob.      Just trying to keep a sense of humour, sour face. Anyway, speaking of tunes—what instrument you thinking of picking up next? The bodhrán or are yer moving on to flutes?      No, the flutes are fickle. I’ve already got the sheepskin that I dip and the spinning wheel. I think next I’ll do something proper like pottery. Maybe make you a vase for your next book.      Oh glorious. A vase with pottery cracks and I’ll write about my loneliness in Kendal while the townsfolk tut and I type.      Aye, and maybe you’ll do a chapter about our journey here—nearly lost in Darlington, muddy roads, and a gooseneck pond we stopped at.      I like it, “The Writer and the Woolly Companion.” You’ll be your own character.      I shall, and I won’t miss a single exit again. Unless it’s to buy wool for my dolls.      A fitting ending. Now—close my door and hold on, we’re taking a bend and I want to see if it’s flatter than Darwin’s nose.      Aye, and pray no sheep are marching across the road again like they did last time.

So did you talk to Lucy last night?      No, she hasn’t been replying to anything. I’m starting to get worried. She said she had a meeting with the client about that university project… and honestly, I don’t think things went well.      I saw the brief she shared with the team—and honestly, I think it was clear as mud. The client said they wanted a "modern yet traditional" academic space but didn’t specify a single detail. It’s like trying to design based on a dream.      Exactly. And now Lucy’s probably frozen, thinking she has to fix everything on her own. That’s just her style.      Ugh, I’ve already got my breakfast. Eggs, avocado, toast, and I’m already worrying about her. I should’ve asked her for help with assembling the tender documents yesterday. Now I’m stuck with a coffee and this pile of paperwork.      You ever considered communal living, by the way? Like a shared flat where everyone does chores and helps each other with work stuff? We need a Lucy-life backup system.      Haha, only if we can avoid someone cooking on a Saturday. I once lived with a guy from Stoke who tried to make a “haute cuisine” omelette with 12 eggs and a bottle of somerset apple cider. Disgusting.      That’s Stoke for you—passionate about everything, even breakfast. Honestly, I miss my Stoke accent. Trying to blend into a London architectural firm with all this posh talk and architectural lexicon is exhausting.      Don’t try to do it. I walk into the site every day talking about "external envelopes" and "sustainable vernacular" and it kills me. I’d rather just say,  “We’re putting the roof up over the wet bits, yeah?”       Classic. And the client bites. But bloody hell, the university project—the way it’s structured makes me want to crack my head off the wall. They’ve written a 20-page brief with no budget and a timeline like we’re going to build it all by next Tuesday.      That’s the problem with public-sector architecture. It’s all policy and no practicality. I swear, if I hear one more mention of “educational experience” without a single mention of acoustics or daylight factors, I’m going to scream.      True. I had a girl from my old university walking past the site the other day.

So did you manage to sort out that weekend trip with your mates then?      Yeah, got the house sorted out in Wisbech. It’s got a few bunk beds, which I was totally thrown by when we arrived—I thought I was being sarcastic, like "Deer in site," but no,  bunk  beds. But it’s all good fun. Classic "let’s pretend we’re thirteen again" vibes.      Bunk beds are alright as long as someone doesn’t light a fire in the loft and cause a chase through the house with garden hoses. Which I  might  have done once.      Oh, I’d forgotten about that! So that MySpace friend of yours, Emma—you know the one who tried to throw her dinner around the café in Diss, right? I think she turned up. Or did she just text us and say she’d "run out of petrol and therapy"?      No, she showed up. She hides behind plants now, but she was there. Good to see her, even though I still can’t get over the amount of Diet Coke she put in her coffee one night.      Honestly, I’ve been thinking—maybe I should have asked her to bring the Diet Coke. We were all dead hungover the next morning and I had to eat a whole packet of mint chocolate chip ice cream to try and sober up.      You know what, dear? When I was your age and my friends and I would read books like they were poison, I definitely  should  have taken better advice. Or at least more painkillers.      Ooh, I did take painkillers! Paracetamol and orange juice, like it was a cooking show. Not very effective.      Well, if we ever do that again, I’m planning on just hiding in the garage with a sofa, some blankets and at least a month’s worth of crisps. Lock the door, no interruptions.      Join my squad and we’ll do it together. Next time we’ll do a  proper  trip—maybe somewhere with an actual bathroom that you don’t have to shoot tippex at the walls to go in. I think someone had a  hidden  monologue in loos at our last trip.      Oh yes, Tom. He went full  King Lear  in the loo. Thought we were his court.      It was both confusing and beautiful.      Which reminds me—speaking of places I go—how’s that traffic problem at the ring road in Grantham?

So did you read the job description throughly? I remember you saying it was for a media post in Yorkshire... What was the job called again?      Yeah, I've gone over it a few times. It's a senior media producer role at a local broadcaster—sort of a hybrid between radio and digital. They want someone who can manage content across platforms and maybe even pitch new shows. Sounds interesting, though ambitious.      Sounds right up your street. You’ve done so much in radio already. But have you tailored the application properly for this role? I mean, the person specification looks different from the others I’ve seen you apply for.      I’ve only just started on the personal statement. I know I need to make sure I highlight my experience in team leadership, cross-platform content production, and maybe push how I’ve adapted to new technologies—like in podcasting and live streaming. That must matter.      Definitely. You should be thinking about what’s different about this job from, say, the others at the national radio station. They probably want someone with a local connection, maybe? You applied to that one last year and didn’t quite nail their tone.      Yeah, they went local-love-local, and I was too all-singing-techy at the time. This one’s similar, and I know they’re trying to modernise without abandoning the community vibe. So I need to show I can understand both.      Exactly. And what about the interview? They’ll probably ask you to pitch a show idea on the spot or talk about how you’d restructure existing content. I’d be tempted to suggest something that’s future-friendly but still builds on what they’re already doing—maybe a show that blends talking heads with interactive voting or user-generated content.      That’s not a bad idea. I’ve wanted to experiment with formats that let the audience shape the show rather than sit back and listen. It would show initiative without alienating the traditional core. What do you think?      I think that could stick out from the rest. Just make sure you’re also prepared to talk about why  you  are the person to do it. Show that you’re a manager as well as a creative. They’ll want go-to coverage on your track record.      True. I just need to remember that between technical stuff and box-ticking, I’m also telling them a story about why I’m the right fit—someone who understands the audience, the local scene, and new tech.

So do you think you could go back into teaching or would you want to try something different now?      Honestly? I’ve been thinking more and more about it, and I think I’m ready for a change. Teaching has been the bulk of my career, but now—it just feels like it’s time to do something more… aligned with the things I enjoy outside of work. You know, creative stuff.      That makes sense. I mean, you're used to working with people, so you could go in a few different directions. Didn’t you want to start that arts-based workshop for kids ages back?      Yeah, I did. I still remember how stressed I got trying to juggle planning for that with school duties. I just never gave it the time it needed. But now, with the kids in school and your place here, I could totally do something part-time. I could run those workshops during term time. Maybe even online in the summer.      You should absolutely do it. And I could help you set it up—set up the website, maybe even handle some of the business side of things. Like taxes, billing, and supplying the materials. Small businesses might not be your thing, but it’s definitely in my wheelhouse.      Are you sure? I mean, it’s not like we’ve talked about this seriously before. You already have your entrepreneurial hustle going on.      It’s exactly why I want to help. I remember when I first started up, it took years to get a proper system in place—especially with things like suppliers, and being able to scale without burning out. If we do it right, we could make this something fulfilling for you and efficient for both of us. It’s a win-win.      That sounds amazing. But what if we run into problems? Like, what if the response isn’t as good as we hoped, or people just aren’t interested? I’d hate to go all in and then feel like I failed.      That’s understandable. But here’s the thing—this isn’t about jumping into the big leagues. It’s about starting small, testing things out, learning as we go. I started with nothing more than a really bad Excel spreadsheet, and now I’m sourcing from overseas and employing a part-time designer. You don’t go from zero to hero overnight.

Right, I just wanted to say thank you to everyone for coming. I know it's been a busy week with all the changes at the school—well, more accurately, the  lack  of changes.      Aye, the school in our area is getting near full, and we’re hearing all about the  Polish  families coming in. I reckon it’s not all bad, don’t you think, Harry?      I do, Bessie. It brings new life to the place. My own school was full of immigrants when I was a lad. Migrants from Germany, Italians, even a couple who'd made it from Kenya. Diversity's nothing to fear, especially when it brings that vitality you see in young families.      I suppose you're right, Harry. But with the housing shortage, every new family is just one more added strain. My cousin is still waiting for a place for her child to start. They’ve been in temporary accommodation for six months!      Ah, I remember the fights we had over school places in the fifties. Not a lot has changed, really. I mean, we even had one boy with a  bottle-green  mohair jumper and a  beard , pacing in the playground like he owned the place – cheeky bugger!      Ha! Sounds like Bertie, your former pupil! I remember him turning up for his GCSE English exam with a mohawk and a tattoo. Who wears a beard to a schoolyard at twelve?      [mumbles with a mouthful of potato] Papa wants to talk beards again?      Oh, come on, about time you stopped mopping up everything like the little pig you are. [pauses] But yes—heartily sorry that your school barely noticed the housing crisis until  your  class filled up.      [giggles] I did not fill up the class! You did!      Oh, I dunno, I remember passing a doughnut shop on the way over that had "Healthy Options" in their window. One of the “healthy” ones had  bacon in it .  Bacon , Patricia!      That's the world we've created, Bessie. Just give it six more months and we'll see a food delivery van box blooming on every doorstep.      I  refuse  to start one of those high tea diets, though. You know I’ve been on them twice, and each time I gained five more pounds! It's a  vicious circle !      Aye, and once you start throwing things in the waste bin instead of the bin-bag, it’s all over.

Rather do I though I haven't seen anything about it in ages. I was just reading the paper this morning and got to the end of it and thought oh, not another one of these.      Yeah, I can see that, I mean what's the point really? We make our own problems, and now we've got to vote on 'em.      Yeah, I mean I don’t know if I'll even bother voting. Trouble is, you don’t know what’s going to come of it. You vote one way, and then it turns into ten new things you didn’t sign up for.      That’s the problem with politicians, innit? They like to think they know best. Still, enough about that. How’s the boy doing on the piano?      Oh he turned six last month and is now officially a Grade 1 waiting to happen. He plays 'Chaqueta' a mile a minute and his teacher says he’s got a good ear for it.      That’s brilliant! I remember when my Bob played piano, he got so fed up with scales, ended up dropping it and taking up the saxophone instead.      Oh, Bob! How is he these days? Still at the works down in Royal Oak?      No, he retired a couple of years back and now he and Sil’s in the states looking after the grandkids. Last time he wrote, someone got chickenpox and he was trying to count the blisters.      Sounds like Bob. So, you seen the new sixth form block at the school?      I did actually, walk past it every day to the shop. Looks shiny enough. I said to my Jane, you know that place you barely left when you were a student?      Oh yeah, I always tell her if I'd known how much I’d use it as a sales rep, I might’ve stayed there myself!      Ha! Not sure how you managed that. I’ve seen you dealing with the lunches, keep the whole canteen running, and you've got more energy than the kids.      That's because I need the money if I'm going to pay for that car park pass in the morning, otherwise I’d go mad trying to park on the road all the time. It’s like a treasure hunt down there first thing in the morning.      True, I had to start going in over an hour earlier last winter

Rather skip the newfit one eh?      Aye, it's such a mawel. Just another Insta filter dream, y'know? Not a real place unless ye live there and it's probably £20 for a coffee.      Ten out o' ten eeny weeny barstool vibe. Not my cuppa if I'm wearin’ wellies. I’ve only posted once. Got tae this year cos me mam checks it nae. She’s obsessed with clout now or somethin’.      Oh aye, my grannie’s takin’ photos o' her dead cat wi' captions like “Still here guid lad” and hashtag  nostalgia . I’ve told her to left it, but she’s gon’ upload the funeral if she gets a good sad filter.      Sounds like a job for the better half. I’ve been usin' it more for wark in truth. People’s profiles and opinions are like, you ken, intellectual gymnastics? I once had to block a man who decided I looked like a “Scottish Ferris Bueller” in a poll.      And did ye explain that we dinnae have mini Ferraris? I use it like a giant staffing list at times. Real ones, not fake, like, “looking for a new role” and somethin’ to say next to their photo. Dinnae they ever cook or walk the dogs for real life?      Aye. I had a rush of admin staff following me after I posted about the new farm policy. Got real strange comes through inna comments like  “So are there actual cows”  and  “Is the Wifi reliable” .      Not th’ worst ones. My sister posted that she was moving up the housing ladder. Next day I got two messages,  “Update me”  and  “Happy 50th” . She’s 32.      At least someone knows how to keep it real. We should run our own group. “Edinburgh Websites and Yellow Flags: A Town Hall Grumble Thread.” Post quotes from the recent budget meeting and let folk rant anonymously.      Yeah, go viral or get censored if the council finds it. I think I saw one of the estate managers liking a rant he himself wrote last week.      So summat o' it's all kina roles inna mix. On the plus side, I found a guy on there selling sausages out o' his van. Didn’t last a week, so I guess he's done wi' the trend.      Aye, probably backs out on a real job when the cheese runs out. I just use it now as a reminder to buy tickets fer some festival we’re probably nae goin' to, but it feels responsible on a Wednesday.

So did you survive the weekend? I barely saw you all week.      Honestly, it was a bit of a blur. I’m still recovering. Went to this event on Saturday with a colleague, and then spent Sunday helping my nan sort out her attic. You can’t imagine how much old cheese she has hidden in there.      Oh no, not  that  again. I’ve heard all about your cheese-filled Sundays!      It was worse, there was a loaf of bread from the 70s. I literally had to wear gloves. Gloves, Jess!      Okay, fair enough, but at least you’re not working on Monday like me.      Oh, I’m working this week too, but I had the weekend off, which was a rare treat. I actually had a really nice time, even with the cheese.      Well, I had to work both days. Organized five different meetings, plus some last-minute catering notes to sort. One of the vendors thought "vibrant palette of flavors" meant they should start adding glitter to the ice cream. I’ve still got glitter in my keyboard.      Ugh, really? That was from the last event.      No, last night, it was  another  event. I swear, someone thought that making everything sparkly will make the clients less grumpy.      They just don’t get us, do they? You’d think they’ve seen  The Great British Bake Off  before.      Exactly! I mean, I  would  be there, waving a flammable feather duster if the gold standard of events was blinking and shiny. Honestly, I’ve lost all respect for some of these people.      Maybe they’re just trying to ‘stand out.’      Stand out? They just stand me on the edge of a breakdown. Do they think I haven’t got enough to deal with already? We had to clear up  five  glitter bombs out of the venue after people started sneezing from the "sparkle."      You’re not joking. That’s gross.      It was like some kind of allergic ninja apocalypse. I just wanted to wash my hands for a week.      Okay, you deserve all the glitter flu and nose bleeds in the world after that. On the bright side, I did get to talk to some interesting people over the weekend. We had this new guy at the clinic I really like.      Oh really? You haven’t romanticized a colleague since Phil, and that didn’t end well.      He’s not like Phil.

Rather skip the new car for a while.      Well, it would be a bit of a stretch for me to afford it now, so I’m not going to be able to lend you any money until probably next summer.      I wouldn't dream of it. Got eenough to sort out with the nephew coming down and   Johnny   being fascinated with all the shiny new kitchen stuff. A lot to think about before that.      Yeah,   Johnny’s   been a bit obsessed with the interior design lately. Didn’t even want to sit with us at dinner because he was too busy checking out the new oven.      That’s   Johnny   for you.      So, what’s the deal about the voices? I heard you two talking about it earlier.      It’s just about the old place. You know, the old lady up the hill. She says she used to live there, and ever since we started felling the trees near the back, she’s claimed she can hear—      Voices, yeah. She says they’re talking about land and old disputes and things like that. Bit old-school, but she’s not the first to have such a legend.      Mate, I’ve heard enough ghost stories from these parts to last a lifetime. You lot are telling me there’s   now   a new one.      It’s not a ghost.      No, it’s a   voice   now. Funny thing—  you’d   have thought the wind would sound more like that than some conversation in your head.      I’m just saying it’s a bit uncomfortable for the kids. Both our son and his friend—he even said he heard something like a child’s voice.      My, my. Then I certainly wouldn’t want to go near it. Though I have been to the property before.
