You have?      Yeah. Couple of years back. Looked like a right bit of a rabbit warren in there with all the old pipes and glass. Defo not a place for anyone who doesn’t like their peace and quiet.      So does that mean you think it’s just the wind making that noise?      I think your son’s imagination might be running faster than it should. Thought we were having a nice quiet dinner, not some sort of hearing analysis.      Yeah, but honestly, I’m just worried. You know my job is sensitive enough without someone claiming the property is haunted.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think when you get to a certain age it would be easier learning a lass language, but no—Spanish keeps giving me a right old rollick!      Aye, I know what you mean—some days I feel like I’ve leared eeny weeny, and then the next I can’t even remember how to say  I like  or  I don’t like ! Got so mixed up I’m wonderin’ if  me gusta  or  me gustar  was the one for yesterday!      Told you I like to go with apps mostly. Bit more gamified, keeps the interest, don’t it? You like that My turkey one, where you duz duz bursts on the back o’ the head for the wrong words! Always used to make me laugh! But then you’ve got to do the grammar proper, when you wanna actually talk to proper people.      Blooming grammar! I tried one of them courses online once. One lesson and I was like  bless me bones , tell you—person, place, thing, verb, adjective, adverb. It’s enough to make a man take to drink!      But it does make sense once you get the hang of it. I got a chap in my class once, from Catalonia, and he said somethin’ that made me think. He was sayin’ that in his home town, they all speak Catalan an’ castilian. Saying two languages is like breedin’ naturally for ’em. You hear it from the bairns, the way they chatter through their day in one or t’other!      Ah now, that’s a mammoth difference from us, isn’t it? We stick to one and are lucky if we barely manage the lingo o’ the local accent. My sister ‘eard someone talking in Catalan once in Barcelona and said it sounded like Spanish with a posh uniform on. ‘Course I had to argue that Catalan is a language in its own right. She didn’t like that answer.      Course it is! They do’t even call it ‘Spanglish’ or nothin’ like that. It’s proper co-off goin’ on. The same as in Wales with Welsh and English—still some in the older generation who don’t go further than  bore da  and  diolch , but plenty who’ve been brought up speaking it full-time. It’s just… not as common to learn a foreign lass where we are, unless you go to learn it specifically.

Right, so this pile here is all the old tax stuff. I’ll just scan it and upload it to the cloud, yeah? Saves it getting lost in a box somewhere.      That's probably for the best. When I was your age, things were simpler—just a file cabinet in the corner! I never liked sorting paperwork. It was always   "where did I put the last receipt?!"        Fair enough, Dad. But honestly, with a digital scan, it’s like it never gets lost. You just have to remember the password. Or maybe the password gets lost...      Still, better than me fumbling with paper and spilling tea on it again. Last time My turkey curry exploded all over the counter and left a brown mess on the invoice for the Hoover.      I think the world has changed since you were using paper, Dad. Now we’re talking about cloud storage and corpus linguistics for a living!      Corpus what?      Corpus linguistics—basically, analysing large sets of texts to see how language is used in real-life situations. I’m building a corpus as part of my studies. Kind of like ... creating a language database.      Oh, like the way Kelly Brook used to do it in that show she was in, where they study slang and all that?      Sort of, yeah. If Kelly Brook could analyse sentence structure while riding a motorbike in a leotard...      She’d probably have the top corpus by midnight. Anyway, back to this lot. What about these old   documents   under the photo of your grandmother and me? Are those about   banking  ?      Yeah, this is an old savings account statement. Should I   scan   it too? I can label it clearly so you can find it easily.      That’d be grand. I did all that electronic stuff with my last job—customer services was all about typing up complaints and smiling on the phone. I could rant about how people   don’t know how to read instructions  .      At least your job had some drama. My day is mostly delivering grammar rules with a bit of patience and lots of go-to examples on Word docs.      I respect that. You sure are making a better go of it than I ever could with my reports about dodgy appliances at 10 am on a Friday.      Well, maybe I’m helping the future by training foreign students to sound more polished in interviews or business meetings.

Rather annoying this, innit? These queues at the pumps. I swear, it's always busy when we're in a rush.      Yeah, I know. I've been over to the Shell station at the roundabout and they're even worse—half the motorway drivers stop there. Got eeny weeny staff and plenty of cars.      Aye, I heard most a the places ‘ave these self-checkout things too. I’m not fae rushing into a tech disaster like that. Who knows what the machine'll do when you're in a queue.      Not to mention the bikes! Have you seen how much they’re everywhere? I only got stuck behind a biker the other day, and I’m still wondering whether I was supposed to overtake him or not.      I think the law is you can if it’s safe, but you better make sure, innit. I’ve been behind bikes a few times, and they usually fly past as soon as they can. Some of them don’t even stop at red lights, I swear.      That’s true—some are way too confident. I did see this one guy last week, he went through a junction on a flashing amber, and it was only the car next to me that caught it. I nearly misted, I swear.      Awh, no don’t go mistin’ at me. I’m already grumpy at this whole car situation. Our car’s got full fuel, so maybe we shouldn’t be here anyway.      Oh, come on, it’s not that bad. I filled up at the Tesco one near St Albans and it was pain-free. Couple a girls there just chatting and the machine didn’t fanny off like the ones in the town centre.      Yeah, but we went past that. My sister ‘ad to go back for something. All I saw was queues. I’m not stopping again. If I was on my bike, I’d just race past them waiting ones, but in this—      Let’s not speed, love. I’m a professional engineer, not a biker extraordinaire. Still, I did ride with a friend once on his Kawasaki. He was a lunatic—nearly took off a cat at 80 on the A12.      Oh, I’ve ‘eard you like your bikes. I’ve asked why you don’t ride one. Why settle for a car like this tin pot?      Well, I do like bikes, but I’m a bit too old-fashioned for motorbikes.

Right, I just popped the chicken in the oven, so that’s sorted. Richard, would you mind piling those salad leaves into a bowl while I’m at it?      Course not. I was just putting the washing-up away, anyway—get a bit of a head start on chores on a Saturday. Keeps the weekend runner.      You’re a saint. Though I reckon that plate from yesterday still has custard on it, so be warned.      M’um, I was just wondering—do you think it’d be a good idea if I saw a proper coach again for tennis? I’ve been practicing with Dad every morning, and I’ve noticed I’m doing the same thing wrong each time.      Ten to one it’s the same problem I had at your age. A good teacher can spot those little quirks faster than you can say "two-handed backhand." I used to have a coach in Seoul who was relentless. Told me once, “If your elbow is higher than the racquet, you’ll never hit over the net, and I will throw a ball at your face if you do it again.”      Honestly, sounds terrifying. But maybe not the worst way to learn.      It does sound a bit strict, but I think it worked for you, Dad. You were smashing serves by 14.      I wasn’t that good, but the coach was someone who knew what to fix. And let’s be honest, your mum’s racquet knowledge outstrips mine by about ten miles. If you ever want advice between coaches, she’s the woman to call.      I’ll be your accountability partner, yeah. I used to be a keen player myself—pre-kids, you barely saw me handle a racquet for ten years. My form’s a little rusty now, but I can at least spot when someone swings at 60 degrees instead of 90.      So you’d help me out while you’re proofreading that book of yours or whatever it is you do all day?      Haha, far be it for me to shoot birds with two hands tied behind my back. But I’ll tell you what—I’m going to a local open event next month, entry is free. Fancy coming along and watching some high-level stuff? Mike’s in the doubles, I think.      Yeah, that’d be cool. It’s just been a while since I’ve seen proper tennis up close.

Right, who wants some turkey? I’ve carved up a mountain of it, and it’s only just piling back on the plate faster than it’s going off it.      Pass it over, hun. Not to be dramatic, but this looks like the best turkey in the history of turkeys.      It smells like      a million dollars.      Why’s he smiling like that? Is he going to dump someone over Christmas dinner again or what?      Lay off the lad. He’s just frozen to death in America, apparently—Managed to get a short holiday back, only to find it’s like minus one turkey outside.      Oh, you flew over, didn’t you? D’you pick up any of that weird American sandwich stuff while you were about? Catsup sandwiches, breakfast tacos—give us a tip while you’re at it.      I got a fidget spinner, some Casper the Friendly Ghost onesie pyjamas, and three servings of deep-fried everything. My cousin Emma put me straight—"In Florida, you either fry food or you're dead inside."      Deep-fried Christmas dinner? Sounds like a cult – Baptism of baps, with extra grease.      Well, better than the fried turkey and sprouts with a side of ‘don’t bring your opinions around the table’ this someone got in one of their aunt’s houses.      [pointing at Speaker_3] That was  her  cousin’s lot. Can’t even  say  the Prime Minister without nearly flinging mashed potatoes.      Anyway, listen to this—Last year, my sister Jackie decided it would be brilliant fun to get up at ungodly o’clock and dance ‘Ring Around the Rosie’ with her kids. Said it was 'traditional'. Well, the music box was broken, so it just played it in a loop for 45 minutes while the turkey turned into charcoal.      That’s not traditional—that’s sabotage with a lullaby.      You know what I like about the dinner here? There's always the ‘Downton Abbey’ vibes—that one aunt always calls me “Chike” now because I go to university. "Chike your potatoes," she'll say. I’m 16, not a dairy cow.      It’s a Northern adaptation of ‘chum’—called ‘Chike’ now you’re a big boy at uni. You’ve evolved.      Speaking of, always remember to poke for the wishbone. Got mine and Leon last year—probably worth more than your student loan, that bone. One side of it, you're rich. The other, you're a loser who needs to write a best man’s speech in 2025.

So did you talk to Auntie Gwen about sorting out that cottage then?      Oh yes, dear. She’s letting it now for more than I can afford, mind you. But she was very kind. She said I could have the season as long as I can get it cleaned up again.      That place was like a tip if you walked in without your wellies on!      That’s exactly what I told her, but she just laughed. She said it’s just how it was after the last tenants.      Were they the ones who brought the cat?      The same! I found cat hair in the airing cupboard that could’ve been used for a duvet!      I’m volunteering to help clean. But only if I get the good cupboards to take back for my kitchen.      Not if I get there first! You know I’ve been collecting vintage crockery for years, you didn’t think I was going to miss that, did you?      This is brilliant, though. I mean, with your job as it is, and the economy, having somewhere cheap to go…      Yeah, it gives us a reason to actually stop looking at our phones and, you know, talk to each other.      You’re sweet talking now, aren’t you? You don’t talk much when you’re in your work head. But yes, it’s a way to get out of the city. I remember what you were saying at dinner last week, Deb.      I was ranting about my project deadlines again, wasn’t I? Ugh, the thing is, it’s not just work stuff. My flatmate and I… well, things are getting a bit tense.      You’re not ending it, are you?      Not me, the flatmate. She got offered a job in Manchester and wants to move out at the end of the year. So I’ll have to find a new space or take over the rent on my own.      That sounds expensive, love.      Yeah, go on then. But it’s more than that. Just… it made me think about what I really want. And I’ve been working non-stop since uni, and you two are the only people I’ve been able to talk to about it.      We’ve been doing alright in that department over the years, haven’t we?      Oh I think so, yes. And love, you’re welcome to come stay with me for a few weeks when the cottage is sorted, if it’s helpful.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      What's that love?      Our blender. Never mind the appraisals at work I've got something far more serious to worry about – it's broken again.      Again? How many times has it been fixed now? I swear if I had a pound for every time I've had it fixed I'd have a second fridge by now.      Honestly I don't know why we don’t just get a new one. We've had the same one for nearly ten years. It's practically prehistoric.      Maybe it's time to treat ourselves. With the new Marks and Spencer opening up near the town centre what’s a bit of shopping for?      Ten o'clock on a Wednesday and you're talking about shopping?      Why not? For a nice smoothie blender and breakfasts and whatever. I've been thinking about making some of those quiches you like so much from the new food section they have.      Oh that new food range, it's fantastic. I bought some of the pesto shortbread the other week to go with my coffee.      Sounds good to me. You'd think I’d be used to it by now – but it's better than my last supper, that's for sure. I remember my first flat in London and making my own pesto was the pinnacle of culinary sophistication at that point.      Well, speaking of cooking – shall we actually make a move here before we end up on the table for dinner at half ten again?      Can we not make a pizza? This chicken and mushroom about to fall off the shelf as it is.      Alright, pizza it is. But not that bog-standard stuff you make. I'll have a classic cheese and tomato. My,  very  adventurous tonight.      Mm, and I'm going the whole hog – any fresh basil I can get I'll add it on.      As long as it's not the one out of the blender with weird bits in. So do you ever imagine going back to a different time in history and living it out?      All the time, honestly. I’d probably run away to France in the 1700s pretending to be a nobleman and have no idea what a keyboard is. But it’s interesting—do you ever think about where  you’d  want to live if you could choose?      Oh, definitely the 1920s. Cocktail dresses, jazz, flappers, interesting personalities. Plus, you had these big parties and people who lived life to the full. I’d love that kind of energy. What about  you ?      I’d go medieval. Somewhere in the 1400s. I’d start a blacksmith business, live in the country, forge some weapons and say nothing more. No Wi-Fi, no emails, just hammer and anvil. I’d probably be best friends with everyone because there’d be nowhere to hide from each other.      You’d be so grumpy. I can see you taking everyone’s sides, then ending up in a duel because you misunderstood someone’s words.      Touché. But what would we do in those parties you mentioned, then? If we could throw imaginary ones?      Oh, I’d go full Versailles—crystal chandeliers, dance cards, and everyone has to wear something period-accurate. And at the end, they all dance out someone who wins an award for the best personality. Like a soul-mate award.      That is a great idea. I’d be disqualified in under five minutes for talking too loud or swearing at people about how cold it is.      Exactly! Whereas I’d probably be a terrible judge and make everyone cry because I can barely choose outfits for real events, let alone soulmates.      Fair enough. But seriously, are we not both just bad at acknowledging the one we already have?      Oh, you mean you? I could stick you in the middle of that soulmate party and you’d probably take someone else home and forget your own name.      That’s a risk I’d happily take! But hey, if I did escape my soulmate, you’d be there to drag me back, right?      Only if you promise not to complain about your spiritual journey for the next two years. I’ve been there and I’m still recovering.      It was enlightening, though. I went on this retreat, met someone who told me I’m the “star of my own cosmic story,” and now I kind of believe it.

So do you ever find it tricky running a small business, Sarah? I know you do it through your own company, and I always think it must be so pressurised.      Oh, it is at times. You do feel the weight of being your own boss. But it’s also pretty freeing, if you can handle the admin. I actually handed over most of the HR stuff to Helen a few years ago, and it’s made a massive difference.      Yeah, I get that. As Head of Admin and HR, I do get the run of the mill stuff done for big organisations, but Sarah is juggling everything independently—accounting, sales, the lot. That’s got to be stressful.      It is. And the holidays are always last-minute, because if I’m not careful, the whole business grinds to a halt. But I’m lucky—I’ve got a really loyal team. And then I’ve got knitting to help me unwind!      Knitting? You, Sarah? I had no idea!      Oh yes! I started during a particularly busy spell last year. I found that the rhythmic stitch really cleared my head. Plus, it gives me something to bring to events—and it’s quite a hit. I’ve even started selling some of it online now. I call it ‘Stress-Derived Knits’.      That’s brilliant! You know what I find interesting? The way people from different parts of the country knit. Some patterns are so region-specific. I remember seeing a cobbler’s shoe out in Cumbria—only a local would know it!      That’s so true! I nearly did an A-Level in linguistics, just to touch on different cultures and languages. It fascinates me how local traditions shape identity. I mean, even down the road in Boston, the dialect, the way they say "’ave a bit o’ lunch" versus Grantham’s more clipped version—it's got to be part of their heritage, you know?      Definitely. I was talking to a customer last week from Yorkshire, and we were both laughing about "marmalade o’er toast"—such a slight difference but like a cultural stamp!      But it’s not just language. Just the other day, someone in the office asked me why we don’t have graveyards with tombstones all over like in America. I nearly choked!      I know those jokes, don’t like them. But honestly, it’s not just over guns or graves—there are so many stereotypes.

So did you lot hear about the new tax break for students? My sister was on the phone going on about it all weekend.      Yeah, I think it's all a load of nonsense to be honest. £20 a month? What are they supposed to do with that? Buy a cheese sandwich and call it a week?      Honestly, I’ve been thinking about moving out of our flat. Like, I mean this place isn’t even on fire and I’d rather dump someone to do it than rent here another month.      Oh come on, you can’t be serious. I mean it’s not like we’re in the middle of nowhere or anything. From here you can get a bus to town in ten minutes.      London bus for you, Aine. I swear it’s like Watergate or something, it’s political.      Well, least we’ve still got grief. Gav’ll still be there on a Saturday night with that packet of crisps from Sainsburys and a Mate’s Mate with two shots, and he swears it’s the best drink he’s ever had.      If that weren’t the case I might be tempted to follow you out.      Just not my man, though. He’s got a €7 hotter than the借錢 he borrowed in the first place. Still replying to all my messages in Pig Latin because he reckons it's ‘trendy.’      You’re worse off than me. At least my boyfriend doesn’t know what a week is. He just turned up to the uni pub like it was the treble guest.      And you told him the football match was on ‘at quarter to kick-off’ and you meant 5pm. We’re not even speaking since.      Oh, that’s a new one. I’ve got a friend whose landlord said “yaar” for ‘year’ and the bloke got goaded into paying twelve months’ rent in advance.      I love hearing that word. I go to blokes’ cafes and say “would you like summat to eat” to see how long they live out the shock.      Oh right? I say that and they either run the other way or try to teach me how to ‘keeping’ properly.

So do you lot reckon we’ve got enough to eat, or do we need to get any more?      I think it’s fine, love. We asked for enough portions. Let's see how much they eat.      I’m stuffed. This place is proper good, Mummy.      Yeah, I reckon this is about as close to a Bolton pie and mash as you can get in Croatia!      Haha, fair point, Dad. We’ve had the best few days here. The kids are getting sunburned and grinning like maniacs.      I got the sunburn on my back from the moped Myk, you said I could sit back left.      I know, love. But I thought I told you to put a shirt on in the morning. Next time better wear a hoodie.      Honestly, I’m just glad he’s not jumping off cliffs like he did in sixth form. That was the end of my pyjamas for a year.      Haha, I remember that well! Still, he's a sensible lad now. Tell me, how did you reckon the bus trip over from Manchester was?      It was bbbboring, like, 9 hours long. I had my headphones on and watched four TikTok videos.      And did your teacher let you go in the first place? That moped ride was not exactly on the school-approved list.      Yeah, he let me as long as I got my mates to promise not to get stopped for speed. I did five over the limit once.      Oh Charlie, I'm not surprised you've got that tattoo that says “Live Fast.”      That’s just nonsense. Burgundy hates it, constantly texts me about it. Parents are supposed to stick to the boring stuff like Facebook groups and pottery.      You mad, girl? Burgundy is as un-boring as they come! Did you take her to the new café with the dogs?      Speaking of dogs, have you thought about the proposal we made goin’ on your own? Burgundy does love walking two at once, even in the heat. You might be the only bloke in Europe who walks dogs for sport.      I think it’s about time we start thinking about houses and all that. I’ve been talkin’ to a fellow at the hospital, he said property prices in the North are up again.      I’ve started looking at part-time things once I graduate, y’know, to help the bills. Burgundy said maybe you could work from home while we save up.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do you?      Well, I got to wave at one of the volunteers at the gate. He asked what I was doing, and I said, “Just watching my granddaughter in the race,” and he went, “Deirdre again, then?” Like he’d seen it all before.      Aye, they don’t forget that A listing, do they? Such a show she put on in '92.      You lot are still talking about that when she won the under-16 cycle race? I was three years old!      That’s right! You were only a little blob in a wellington boot then, bless you! But it left quite a mark on the village.      I know, I hear the stories now. Something about crabs at the lighthouse?      Oh yes! That’s still a local legend. See, the YHA group we stayed at near Hayle—it had the most dreadful clambakes. The lighthouse keeper’s wife, a pleasant enough woman, but the crabs were from somewhere near Hereford and were clearly only alive on the table because they looked good on it.      Sounds like one of those places that should be in a film. Bit like  The Wicker Man , but with more tea and scones.      I’d already seen enough of that in the classroom. Our geography teacher took us to a lighthouse near Whitby once. It had one blind bulb and an out-of-tune piano.      But you weren’t in  that  class, love. No, I daresay your teacher was brought round the right way by the YHA.      Speaking of which, how d’you get on with the Cornwall letch? I mean, I tried volunteering at the local guest house last year, but after five days I told them the biscuits had a mind of their own.      You volunteered? I thought you just live off the goodwill of your niece’s Websites and grandkid’s lunches.      That’s not the way to speak to your granddad, Joseph!      Then go write a novel. Start with  The Elderly Volunteer of Gwithian Beach , and I’ll buy it.      Now what your dad’s talking about is something else. I’ve been to see one of the old lighthouses regenerated in Cornwall, and it’s worth it. They turn over half the lights to be used as Airbnb string lights—marvelous!      Again, I’m not surprised they romanticize things in Cornwall. They did the same for Yorkshire’s  Yorkshire in a Day  tourist brochure.

Right, I just brought the last of the chips in. Cheesy sticks and everything—the lot came in like... one big wave, didn't it, Tom? Blows my mind how they pour over the plate like that.      You wouldn't say that if you had eenie weenie  not  covered in aioli. I reckon half the bucket was sauce.      Honestly, if I saw that every night, I'd move out and into a wok place. Real ones know the difference between a doughy crust and a charred brick.      Speaking of which, how’s the girlfriend? Still keeping you on the straight and narrow?      What straight and narrow? She says “Tom, it’s not about the bins—it’s about you caring more.”      Romance is overrated. Relationships are just shared dirty dishes and arguing over Spotify playlists at 2 a.m.      Oh, I dunno. She texts him at the same time every night. 8:47 p.m. bang on. Gave her a tick list of things to do before he replies.      “Consistent” or “boring”? Sounds like he’s programmed to fall asleep with her photos on a loop on the telly.      Or maybe he’s stringing her along so he doesn’t have to get round to proposing. I swear, women romanticise things so much they don’t clock the red flags until the roses are rotting on the doormat.

So did you survive Barcelona? I was practically checking WhatsApp every 10 minutes just in case you passed out from sangria and forgot to call a taxi at 2am!      Ha, ha, very funny. I’m fine, I promise! But wow, that place was incredible. I wish we had  more  weekends like that, honestly.      Yeah? I mean obviously I love watching your DMs blow up with cute seaside selfies, but are you going back there soon or is it going to be another "once-in-a-lifetime" thing?      I’ve already booked a longer trip for next summer, actually. I found this Airbnb in Sants that’s super cute, and I’ve even invited my brother’s partner this time. I’m terrified I’m gonna upset them by eating too much tapas and then complaining about the bill, but hey — better safe than sorry, right?      I’m just jealous because I’m still stuck in the “student-in-the-city” phase of my life. I mean, I work full-time, I’ve got bills and a credit card I don’t struggle with , but still, I only live on takeaways and Netflix.      Oh come on, you’re sarcastic at the best of times, but I know you’ve got proper plans! What are you saving up for? Paris? A weekend away with  whoever  is gracing your couch tonight?      Oh ha ha ha. No boyfriend to grace the couch, thank you very much. But yes — Paris is the dream. I want to go through Eurostar and actually  take my time . You know, do museums, sit outside a cafés, the full lit cuisine experience.      Oh! You know that new French film I told you about?  The Coffee Break  — it’s on TV tonight. It’s based in Paris and it made me want to run to the airport.      Okay, that sounds exactly like the kind of thing I need to watch as I hoard cereal like it’s the end of the world.      Speaking of, want any Moroccan chicken delivering after the film? I’m feeling fancy tonight.      Oh my God  yes . But hold on — do I need to pretend to like olives with this or something? I can’t remember the latest food trend that’s supposedly healthy but tastes like someone’s poached a sock.      Ha, okay — zero olives this time. We’ll go basic. I’m not in my health-nurse mode tonight.

Rather skip the new barista café near the dock, isn’t it?      Oh, I don’t know—new place, new music, new blend of something or other. Beans imported from, like… £20 a cup and a card says "say thanks to our sponsor" at the beginning and end of the ad.      Yeah, well, I’d rather a clean cup of instant any day. Got one from my aunt, brought it over last summer.      Instant? You’re a pioneer woman!      Told you already, I taught in Dorset. People there still pour tea from the spout into another cup to test the temperature.      Dorset? The one where they throw tomatoes at you for bad service, or is that Somerset?      No, no, wait—Somerset breakfast, Dorset tea. I mean, here in Cyprus in the summer, I remember the milk bottles melting on the doorstep.      That would’ve been a treat—steamed, lumpy, sweet, and proudly British.      You’re not wrong. But let me tell you: I’ve had some proper work placements in my time. You ever worked at a primary school with thirty hyperactive, cheery, slap-happy, sugar-coated balls of energy?      If I had, I don’t remember. I owned a business at twenty-six. That’s what I got: my own company, office meetings, coffee machines that didn’t work, and a sense of responsibility I didn’t ask for.      Ooh, I envy you. I worked a bit of hospitality to get through my degree—crashing at a friend’s flat between shifts. One manager used to say, “Keep the change, I’ll pay for your ‘Positive Attitude’ pin.”      That’s bleak. Sounds like it was a chain restaurant with a soul left in another county.      Not to mention the time I served to a lady who always topped up her builder’s and demanded that I do the same. Once I said no, she said, “Well, you’ll never get away with that in my day.” I wanted to say, “And I’m very glad I don’t live in your day.”      Laughter aside, I think I’ve made it to the other side of that kind of grind now, though. You ever think about changing it up?      I have, believe it or not. I’ve been toying with the idea of taking an online course in photography—I mean, who doesn’t want to look at someone else’s holiday snap-takes and say, “Oh that’s lovely, quite professional, by the way.”

So did you talk to James about us using his room for the weekend?      No, not yet. I’ll text him after this road calms down a bit. He’s been a bit awkward about it since we said we might have friends over as well.      Why’s he so fussed? I mean, it’s only for one weekend. He's had us over before. What’s changed now?      I don’t know. Might be the fact it’s someone new. We’ve never invited anyone else from uni up before. He said he's got some "stuff" to sort out in there. I’m assuming it’s more Facebook photos taken at another house party he’s never told me about.      Yeah, typical. Tenants, right? I mean, we pay the bills just as much as he does. It's not like we’re crashing or anything. He just wants us to feel like he has a say in everything.      I know, but I don’t want to start an argument over it now. I mean, it’s not a big deal. If he doesn’t want people in there, we can still stay and just use his spare room for gear. It’s not like we’re going to sleep in there.      Well, maybe he doesn’t like the idea of other people in his personal space. He gets quite territorial when he gets the sniff of something. Last week he almost flipped when I put the Hoover in his door.      That was just a bit of a test, wasn’t it? Just to see if he’d notice.      A test! Look, it’s because he’s about to fall off the wagon with whatever he's trying to avoid this time. Honestly, I’ve seen this coming since he started that mindfulness course two months ago. Next thing you know, he’ll say ‘no energy’ and refuse to even open the door.      I don’t think he's got the attention span to do that properly. I mean, I could see him giving it a go for a day or two and then trying to find a new hobby by watching YouTube videos of people doing pottery.      Pottery, or maybe the mandolin? He tried that on his own about three or four times and gave up.      Hopefully, this mindfulness lark might last a bit longer. It’s better than all the nights I’ve spent cleaning up after one of his 'mental health' mornings where he says he just needed time to ‘process’.

Rather do this than sit in the living room with the telly on the whole Sunday, eh?      Aye, it was a bit of a trek getting all the toilet roll and cleaning products, but at least we’re not the only ones being frightened by the weather on the telly again.      Oh, they’re   always   frightening us with all that “stormy conditions expected” lot. Like they know more than us, who’ve lived through thirty winters in this dump of a place!      Funny you say that, Fred. The lad at the shop said to me, “Do you need a shopping trolley, love?” and I said, “If you mean one of those plastic inventions that you push about like it’s the Ten Commandments, then I do, yes.”      Oh, typical you, June! Back in my day we used to wheel old prams to do our shopping in — in fact, my dear old mum used to say shopping was the only kind of transport working women had!      That’s if they had one of those老爷爷 special rations — no, wait, I mean  rations , Fred.      Well, we’ve been lucky. Mind you, I remember the first time I got a proper paper round, it was  harrowing . I delivered newspapers in Costessey and the whole village was covered in one of them winters that made your nose look like a frozen Berlin Spree.      And you thought you were doing a  glamoring  job?      Er —  glamorous , June,  glamorous , and I meant to! And you can just leave the  telepathy vibes  out of it this time.      Apologies, Fred, I thought that was just standard delivery for you.      Anyway, here — let’s open this lot. Got a bag of those microwave chips, I see — you know when I was your age, you had to  make  your own chips!      And what with? A spanner and a saucepan set on a  tinderbox ! Fred, I can go back to my day-vading suffragette life or whatever it was, just leave the history alone.      You know what your problem is, June?      Oh good, we're starting those “you never had a  proper childhood ” games now, are we?      No — you always  think  I'm going to say that. My point is, you always romanticize things in Harrow, back when you were childminding at that big posh house and before that when you were married off by some bloke you met in the  post office .      Fred – that was a red-haired man, not “married off,” and he  used to pay real wages .

Right then, John, don't be slumped on that chair like a sack of spuds — come on up off the seats, or I’ll be having more tea than I need by the time you move!      Oh, don’t fanny about with them, Jean. Let ’em eeny if they like — we’ve got the day off and if it kills ’em, they won’t be botherin’ us no more!      Oh Grand Nan, don’t say that! Please! You and Grandad are the best!      T’was a jest, love! Still, if we can keep me legs crossed and out of the way, Jean, like that one’s been doing for years!      Ten out of ten for the attempt, John, but no: not unless you’re a piece of furniture, you’ve got to leave space when guests are in. Look at us all! Huddled in like a posh chicken coop!      I told you, Nan, I reckon we can rearrange the chairs, if we try. I’ve got the side table free — maybe shift that to the middle and the armchair by the bookcase. It’ll give you proper room.      Oh, who needs room when we can all be squashed together like sardines and laugh like somethin’s wrong?      Bless ‘er, Jean — always the one for comfort. Who cares if it’s squashy — we’re all a bit old for that anyway.      Just mind the tea, then. Don’t spill it all over your new coat, John. I did wash that for you!      Actually, Nan, I meant — what you said earlier about me doing the school trip to the museum. You said you used to do something like that for your work. What was it?      Aha! You mean before I was too old to do anythin’ accurate, Jean and I went out once. Me and her and that lad of ‘ers — always trying to catch fishin’ boats with cameras.      Still remember that time she nearly tumbled into the sea ’cause she was too busy snappin’ away at a boat. Nearly made her dent in the water, I did.      Properly? Cos you two are both supposed to be past jumpin’ roles!      T’was a case of professional aggressiveness, lad. Jean was keen on gettin’ the right shot. I reckoned I did her head in when the clouds were soft.      Right, right — and then you nearly drowned the lens cover in my tea, you old bee.      E’en them days, she never had a tea out.

So did you lot see the latest health supplement everyone’s raving about online? Some kind of ‘glow from within’ powder or something.      Yeah, I saw it on Instagram! All these influencers were chugging bowls of this stuff like it’s a fruit smoothie. It was prob bright pink and full of goji berries or whatever they call them now.      Sounds a bit dodgy to me. Like, I mean, I don’t hate the idea, but what if it's just sugar and glitter in disguise? They call it “wellness” but it's probably not doing much more than making your urine neon.      Honestly, I’ve only started paying attention to health stuff since uni. I’m living off cereal and left-over takeaways most days, so I reckon I need a shot of something that’ll fake the healthy vibe. But I’m far too broke to spend forty quid on a bottle that just makes you fancy.      I hear you, mate. I’m ordering online now and the ads are targeting me like I’ve got a medical degree. One told me I’d lose five stone by adding two drops of acai to my water and only eating kale for the rest of my life. Bloke, I’m a student. I live off pasta and paranoia about exams.      Yeah, and don’t even get me started on the tech side of all this. I use a fitness tracking app that tells me how much sunlight I’m getting and that I need to “hydrate more” because my tongue is dry and I watched three hours of  The Mandalorian .      I’m not even using mine! It’s been in my bag since about half way through term. I used it the other week when I finally had a gym session. Managed to make it to the bench press and the thing started beeping at me like I was on a time limit. I left it there.      That’s the vibe man. I used mine once too, it told me I stared at my phone 14 hours a day and had a  digital wellness score of 2%.       At least your digital score is higher than mine. Still trying to figure out how to Instagram Stories without looking like a goon. I tried it yesterday and posted a photo of my microwave.      I had a go the other day and posted a video of me trying on some new trackies I bought online.

Right, so we need to get through our list tomorrow. I’ve got milk, bread, maybe some pitta bread and hummus cos I’m doing that for lunch again. Erm, we’re out of soap for the kitchen and we need more loo roll as well. Oh, and lemons for the fish—have we got any more?      I think there's one left in the bottom of that fruit bowl by the door, so yeah, we’ll probably need a couple. Let me check the fridge. We’ve also got to get some eggs. The last ones are past their best.      Can we also get crisps? I want Monster Munch, and can we get some of that squishy sweets? The melon ones.      I’m not saying yes or no, Dad and I’ll be the ones cleaning your teeth in the morning!      Hmm, maybe if you do your greens for dinner tonight, we’ll see, love. But we will get some fruit as well. We’re down to one apple.      Yeah, and we need some cat food too. I think we’re a week to go. And maybe some kitchen roll as well—Dad’s been using paper towels again and then just leaving them scattered everywhere.      I’m not leaving scattered paper towels—just resting momentarily. Anyway, enough of shopping. We need to talk about the large issue: the emergency situation with the creature in the hall.      It bit me! It was a big one, like, definitely not a normal house spider. I think it wants to come and live in my room!      Oh no, did you clean up after it? You can’t leave the body around for the cat to find. Use a tissue or something next time.      Or we could just step over it, like normal people. There’s no need to make it a drama. I have no problem with it being a spider.      But it bit me! I had a big red mark for hours.      Next time, take a shoe or a big book to the hall and be ready. Defuse the situation.      Maybe get a jar go-to plan on your phone if you see one again so you can trap it and chuck it out the window. We don’t want infestations, your mother allergic to them.      Or, you know, maybe we can just co-exist like humans do with everything on the planet?

Rather skip to the front of the queue, I suppose, since we both know her—the matron in charge here. You've had a long enough day already, and I can take care of the ticket forms. And go—oh my, how you could travel. I still remember your story about the time in Dresden, when you accidentally knocked a framed engraving from the wall during a setup.

Rather skip the new house for a while.      Well, it’s only temporary. I mean, the builders had no choice but to run down the garden path, left himself over a long time doing it.      Mm. It is to me, and I used to work in a field where I had to live in the car just driving forty hours a week.      Oh yeah, I remember when you were in the oil industry—what was that, the late ‘80s?      Mid ‘80s, actually. Built up quite the map of different areas I had to drive through. I’d head for the motorway and just drive, wondering if my radio was playing the right side of the wind or not.      Bit before my time, I think, but I remember when I first moved to Birkenhead, I got lost for three hours going from the airport to the town center.
