Well, I’ve been trying to perfect it since I moved to Germany. Some things don’t transfer well across the continent. Take being able to just pop to Tesco in five minutes and not have to drive thirty minutes to a Lidl. But I still found a way to get decent stuff in Wegberg.      I hear you. Moving house up here in Cardiff was... a  project  itself. Got my bins wrong for  weeks . The health and safety board were probably petitioning for my removal.      Bins? I once accidently put my cat's  poo  in a recycling bag by mistake. Town hall nearly called pest control.      You’re  mentally unwell , Mark.      Look, I didn’t know that our  black cat  counted as medical waste in the scheme of things. Sue the box for bad labelling, why don’t you?      While we’re on moving house – where you off to next?      Just made admin manager in a new university’s international office. Start next month. S’all set up near Cambridge. Very posh. My kind of thing, all the white goods included, no need to move my washing machine again.      Congrats! Yeah, I left college behind a couple of years ago.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it?      It's always like this when you try to get out of East London. I’m just glad I remembered to bring my earbuds in case it gets too heavy.      Yeah, well, at least it gives us a chance to catch up. I’ve got an assignment due on the digital versus print media debate next week. You’ve got a good grip on that one from your job, right?      A little. We’ve been doing quite a bit at the TLS about how the industry is shifting. It’s not just about print dying, it’s about how much value we place on physical versus digital content. You like that sort of thing, don’t you?      I do, actually. You know, I was reading about how some people still buy printed books just for the tactile experience. It’s weird, isn’t it? I mean, with a tablet in your pocket, why would anyone want a paper book or even a newspaper?      Well, I think it’s nostalgia, maybe. Or it’s just the ritual of it — the smell, the weight, the way the pages feel. I’ve got a couple of books I bought secondhand when I got back from France last year. Real ones, not e-books.      Oh, you were in France again? Did you go to Lyon or Marseille this time?      Lyon, this time — full of old bookshops and great French pastries. I thought I’d bring you something back, actually — a Mont blanc and some candied ginger. You used to love that when you were younger.      That’s gold. I’m still partial to candied ginger. Honestly, thanks for not buying me that ‘inspirational’ mug every time, like most people do.       laughs  Oh, I did once — and it ended up smashed. You told me you were sleeping and dropped it.      That’s not my fault you filled it to the brim!      Anyway, what’s the assignment? Was it about media trends or something more specific?      It’s about how the TLS fits into the whole transition. You know, how you guys started digital subscriptions, but you still print the paper version. I’ve been reading some of the older issues you keep in the hallway and comparing the language against the online stuff. It feels like it’s trying to be the same, but online it’s more … casual, I guess.

Right, so we've got the fish and chips coming in a minute, and I swear, if any of you mention the  "Great Barcelona Pasta Incident of 2022"  again, I will scream into this pint of lager.      Lottie, you can’t lie. That was  the  best holiday we ever had—and you   did   eat the pasta all on your own. You’ve got no one to blame but yourself.      I was   hungry  , Kevin. We’d walked three hours to that cheap little trattoria, and the menu was in Italian   and   Russian. I couldn’t read a word, so I just pointed at the first thing on the menu that looked like a vegetable. Marco   told   me it was pesto, and you know what I get? Chocolate and fig in a cream sauce.      But you still had breakfast, didn’t you? I mean, you had croissants and panini for five days! That’s, like,   eleven   meals.      I do not, and I will not listen to this. I’m still sore about that.      Honestly, we’ve got much better stories than that. Remember when Becca got left behind at the –?      – Swiss mountain train? Yeah, she was the only one left because she got distracted taking selfies at the cheese museum. And then when the train came, she didn’t hear someone yelling in four languages that the next train was in an hour and a half.      I was   not   left behind. I was  strategically late .      Strategically late? Becca, you were   ten minutes early  . Not one of us left without you.      Honestly, it does sound like Barcelona was the most successful trip for us. At least you didn’t get lost in the French countryside at 10pm with a bag full of pottery.      You’re getting your comeuppance for that, Lottie.      Please, I walked out with a dozen mugs and a   very   confused waiter after I tried to say “I need the loo” in my best approximation of French. He thought I wanted a camping tent.      And he took you seriously. You were handed a tent and a map.      You were in France, you spoke broken French and then gave money to a man for a tent and a map at the end. That counts as a win.      Honestly, I think Becca and I both need to start saving up for our own trips. No more group holidays, no more waiting for someone to accidentally eat chocolate in a pasta dish again.

Rather you than me, luv. Winter camping? Cold enough outside the tent, let alone  in  it. I once went glamping—glamour and camping!—and that nearly did me in. I was warmer with a cup of tea and a jacuzzi on the deck.      Oh dear, William, don’t start twitching again. Ay, I read all about it on a recent course I took, this wild winter camping—cold water therapy, bushcraft, survival skills, pulling yourself out of a snowdrift like a modern-day Cro-Magnon. Sounds gloriously exhausting.      Aye, and I’ve been involved in the odd weekend myself. You know, wild camping in the Highlands during December? Colder than a pike’s belly in a ditch, but the benefits are, well, I think it’s transformative. Living with nature, breaking free from the gadgets and breakfasts—there’s something about mastering your own comfort zone in the wild. It teaches you discipline and hides, you know, all the softness we’ve accumulated since we were kids.      Discipline, aye—what I lack in spades. I’ve still got grief from the time I went for a walk on Hampstead Heath in January without a jumper. Was only a half-mile, but it nearly got me summarily buried by the cold.      But seriously, the benefits? You do talk about grounding and all that mindfulness jazz? I find, even in my work, that people are craving a sense of authenticity. Nature offers that, don’t you think? Some folks just need to be a bit shaken up and rubbed down in frost and snow to remember who they really are.      Exactly! And you’re not talking just blinking at the trees. It’s about preparing your own firewood, learning to make a windbreak, sourcing water, and sleeping two feet from a bear—or so you’re told. All that fosters resilience. And at 6 a.m., shivering bloody murder while trying to relight your stove, your whole world is reduced to fire and warmth and that cup of lukewarm porridge with your name on it.      Blimey, you make it sound positively idyllic! I’d be more goin’ on about how I lost my teeth to the cold or how my dentures are no longer secure because I bit a bloomin’ chunk out of an icicle. No, I’m quite content with my heated home, thank you very much.      But still, it’s fascinating how people are drawn to it, innit?

So did you watch The Last of Us on HBO yet? I’ve been trying to get you into it like... forever.      I did actually, binged it all in one weekend! It is genius. Not quite like the games, obviously—some bits condensed—but the acting was top-notch. That finale episode? I was a wreck for like two days.      Oh I know! A lot of people swore at their TVs. I had to watch it with the volume turned down just to keep from crying in public.      Honestly, the slow-motion walking away... like, I get it, it’s tragic. But man, the people who still haven’t played the game are missing out on all the little Easter eggs and left-hand-path decisions.      Duh, of course I played it. Game of the decade in my opinion. But you better not get me started on Naughty Dog’s mastering of emotional trauma for profit.      Fair point, but even if it guts you, it’s worth it. It’s like one of those books—personally I’m thinking of  Life of Pi —where it knocks you sideways and leaves you reeling in a good way.      Oh yeah,  Life of Pi  was something else, right? I still think it was way more powerful in the book. The movie was beautiful, but the whole Pacific was just... big and empty in that way, you know?      Yeah, they adapted it well, but the book is so layered. Some readers still debate what was real. I mean, it’s supposed to make you  feel  something, not necessarily have all the answers.      Exactly. It’s like The Last of Us too, really. You know that line Joel says about putting it out of its misery? That’s just, like, the story being so emotionally manipulative that it actually becomes poetic.      You mentioned ‘manipulative,’ which brings me to my next question: did you crack my request for  The Midnight Library  by Matt Haig? I left a copy by your computer the other day.      You did? Ugh! I owe you so much for ghosting that book from your shelf. But real talk, I read the first few chapters and it genuinely felt like a bloke Googling ‘how to make people feel something’ and then pasting it into a manuscript.      Oh, come on! Is it not that ‘buddy, we’ve all had bad days’ kind of vibe? The genre is like emotional comfort food.

Right, who’s ready for a story tonight? I’ve just raided the bookshelf, and I think we’ve got a few good ones.      I want something with dragons in it! There was that one with the green castle… and the fairy!      Okay, I think I remember  The Dragon Inside the Castle . But just to be clear, do you two share a story or do you want to take turns?      I don’t want a dragon story. I want one about the space robot and the ice planet.      That’s not a real story. You just made that up last week when the real stories were all gone.      Touché, Maddy. Alright, let’s see – I’ve got the dragon one, and I might’ve bought a new one called  The Adventure of the Lost Typewriter . Wait, does anyone even know what a typewriter is?      It’s like an Xbox, but for old people.      Well, almost! It’s like the computer Grandma used before we had the PlayStation. You tap keys and it prints words. And the story is about a boy who finds one in an attic and goes on a treasure hunt. Sounds good, right?      Can I read it tomorrow? I’ve got the Brownie Promise evening tomorrow and they said we have to know what “truth and honesty” means.      Well, I’m telling the truth: my promise is already broken. I left my Brownie scarf in the PlayStation cupboard.      Again? Oliver,  every  week! You know we about to find it in a different bin every time!      Maybe it’s in the recycle bin. I saw you throw a yellow handle in there earlier.      That was the  mixer  handle. And it was  not  yellow. It was beige. But don’t distract me – I am trying to read your story!      What if we made up a story? Like with a computer?      That sounds like work. Still, maybe something fun. So… once upon a time, in a world ruled by Excel spreadsheets and clip art –      Oh no, not clip art! That’s bad magic!      It is! The evil clip art wizard had turned everyone’s Microsoft Word into a never-ending table of column widths and unsavable files. And the only one brave enough to rescue the world was…  a Brownie with a lanyard who knew where to find the escape key .      YES. I want to be that Brownie.      But what if the spreadsheet has puppies in it?

Rather skip the new coat of paint for now, Christopher. I’ve got more practical things on my plate—like figuring out how to get rid of this house before it drives me mad. It’s just me and the cat now. Not to mention the junk mail that’s stacking up.      Aye, I can imagine. I’ve got one like that just north of Harrogate—three floors, a roof that needs re-doing, and more land than I can use. Sold it last year, dump of a place. Put it in the hands of a young couple who want to make it a B&B. Bit of a gamble, but at least I don’t have to deal with the hippo of a mortgage anymore.      I’m not so sure. It’s not just the mortgage—this place has ghosts, if not quite in the haunted sense. Living in it for forty years means you’re almost part of the walls now. I mean, there are kitchen clocks that don’t tick, and cupboards that loudly reek of preserved raspberry jam from the 80s. I swear I dream about jam.      Hah! You don’t say. We still sell it when we clear out. My wife was attached to it, though. She kept arguing that the fruit orchards at the back were worth something. I told her, it's not exactly a Yorkshire nectarine farm—more like a patchy strawberry attempt that ended up being a weed farm. Still, the old things someone might want. Clocks, maybe. Or just a sense of nostalgia.      Nostalgia’s a burden sometimes. I’m not sure I even  want  someone else living in those same rooms I raised two children in. But the alternative is to rent it out and deal with what passes for “decorative” taste these days. I looked at a Facebook ad last week. My house had to be reimagined as “strenuous boho.” I have no idea what that is.      You haven’t met them yet. I had a pair of twenty-somethings who wanted to live in the same house I sold. They demanded that I convert the garage into a studio, set up a herb garden with basil and oregano, and go easy on the pond life if they wanted to put in a pre-built solar power system. I’m not even going to mention the part about selling the house to plant a vegetable patch.

Right, I just wanted to go through the medication again before we get the rest of the food sorted. We’ve got the antibiotic, some painkillers, and the skin cream from the GP. Let me make sure we don’t mix them up. That ointment’s for the burn on your hand, not on your face, William.      Thanks, Margaret. I’m all right with most things, but I still slip up now and then. Last week, I almost used the ointment instead of the moisturiser and ended up with dry skin on the outside of my leg.      That’s easy enough to fix. I can throw a bit more hand cream in the shopping list for you if you’re running low. Oh, and while I’m at it, do you need the usual brands or are we branching out for a bit of variety? I’m thinking of trying that coconut oil one everyone’s going on about on Facebook.      Coconut oil? Sounds posh. I’ll stick to my old faithful, thank you very much. One thing I don’t need is a new fangled way of moisturising. My skin might survive two weeks longer.      It’s not that fancy, William. It’s just natural oil. I’ve used it on my burns before — much gentler than some of the stuff in shops these days. But if you’re happy with your current routine, by all means, carry on.      Fair enough, carry on in style. While we’re talking about products, have you seen the new app for local deliveries? You can order stuff from the farm shop now and have it here in an hour. Margaret, your curry powder’s out of stock, and I’m not sure the supermarket’s the best place to get it from.      No, it’s not. I’d rather have it fresh, not sitting in some warehouse for weeks. If the delivery’s quick enough, go for it. Though I have no idea how it works on any bloody phone app.      A little bit of technology won’t kill you, Margaret. You’ve sent me photos of your grandkids on a mobile before — I’ve seen it done. You just set your deliver time, pick what you want, and the thing go bzzz — it arrives.      Well, I like my directions given in full sentences with the box ticked on “will your delivery contain liquids?”

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode with Sarah’s scenes was just cringey as hell.      Oh God, I did not miss that. I was rolling my eyes so hard I thought they might fall out. Was Sarah really as bad as they made her out to be?      I don’t think they got it completely right, but c’mon, most people agreed that scene in the flat was unbearable. Why show us every squabble? I watched it while my mum was in the kitchen and she walked in and said “Crikey, that’s how we do it too!”       laughs  Classic. Honestly, the real drama only happens behind closed doors like that. Anyway, enough of TV meltdowns. How are you coping with work loads now? You’ve been pretty quiet on the group chat.      Oh yeah, it’s a nightmare. I’ve been swamped this month. They’ve taken on a new client, some big London advertising firm, and now I have to make a copy for like six different campaigns by Friday. I tell you, I haven’t left my flat since I got back from work on Monday. It’s only Tuesday and I’ve already written myself a note:  “Don’t burn toast” .      Ouch, I feel you. My survey programme’s been huge too. I’ve been trying to test out some new AI functions for the coding side and let’s say, it’s not going well. The client keeps changing their requirements every five minutes. I wish they’d just stick to one idea and finish the project.      Ugh, premium client energy  every time . At least your job about pays the bills though. I’m living the dream of £17 an hour and a clipboard of expenses.      Erm, it is a student job but to be fair, I’m part-time. My guest speaker last week called it a 'sustainable internship economy'. I called it something far less polite.      I haven’t started thinking about the future yet, which I know I should. My mum’s been asking questions about the “next step” like I’m going to drop out and get a stall at the market.      Honestly? I think life improvements sometimes come from weird places. I made my line manager go out with me to this obscure boxset last week and now he says I should be at the planning stage for a tech conference in May.

Rather skip the gym today, eh?      Aye, just ran out of steam first thing. You've been going in every day like clockwork. Not a bad idea to take a day off though.      That's kind of you to say. But it was my day off! I thought I’d make a proper breakfast and just enjoy the morning. I’ve been trying to eat clean but I’m so busy I often miss a proper meal.      Well, dump the guilt. What you making anyway? Something healthy, I hope?      Porridge with frozen berries and a spoon of honey—Managed to get some local oats last week, they’re from near Isleworth. Thought I’d give them a go.      Oh, I hear the local farm shops near me place are knocking it out of the park with quality produce nowadays. Catsfield Farm does breakfasts—smoothies, poached eggs, sourdough. Might be worth a trip?      If you're thinking of taking a morning walk or cycle—settle into it, get the heartbeat up a bit. I started walking with the dogs as much as I could last week, felt like ages since I did anything other than circle the office in the evening.      Mate, I often wish I could still afford that kind of lifestyle. I remember us growing up in the old place in Isleworth, was beautiful. Now that house? Absolutely unaffordable.      Tell me about it. That area has gone absolutely bonkers. I bought an old flat over the river a few years back—horrendous commute but at least I got in before the worst of it. Price per square foot? Ridiculous.      It’s just a generational gap. You know that place you told me you looked at near Bushey? £500k for a terraced bungalow. How do people afford that?      I'm told it's all about the student rental market. Everyone from London looking for somewhere a bit cheaper, as long as they can get a short commute. London prices are a little more bearable if you’re not going to live in it, you’re just staying.      There's a novel topic for you—gentrification and housing crises.      I suppose. Although I’ve been working on a bit of research related to property prices post-pandemic. It’s all quite depressing really. The market’s bouncing back like it was 2019, and people are squeezed hard.      That’s bleak. I appreciate you at least get to do something with it.

So did you watch the Budget last week?      No, I was working late. I got the gist from some colleagues—tax on gadgets went up, apparently.      Yeah, it’s wild. I read somewhere that things like headphones and smartwatches are being taxed more now. Who  knew ?      I’m all for making the rich pay their share, but this just feels like hitting people who are already squeezed. I mean, I got my laptop upgraded last month and was hit with an extra twenty quid just because the government decided it was a “luxury.”      Honestly, I’m just trying to budget for  Wicked  tickets. I’ve been saving for months!      I’m going next week, actually! I got two tickets off the discount site—front row, lucky sod.      Bucksy? I mean, I suppose I could crash at my mum’s again…      Nah, don’t do that. Borrow off me—settle it when you get your next salary.      Aye, fair enough. I’ve actually got that fancy coffee table in my flat now, so I’m basically set.      Mate, you got the same one I’ve had for years—it’s a classic.      Fair point! Anyway, what about you? Still at that civil engineering firm?      Yeah, but I’m branching out a bit more. I’ve started taking on freelance projects—small things like community walkways and park renovations. Not as stressful as giant infrastructure, at least.      That does sound better. I still can’t believe you let your boss talk you into that bridge inspection last frosty morning.      I still have the shivers over it. I swear that bridge was trying to kill me. Winds were sideways, the binmen were probably laughing at me.      You mad bastard. We could’ve gone and had a cup of tea instead.      And missed out on the “thrill” of icy road surfaces and dodgy scaffolding? Never.      You’re a man after my own heart. Let’s go grab a drink after this, yeah?      Only if your round.      Only if  you’re  paying next time. Mutual, innit?      You’re on—get walking, Crompton!      Oh I will, and I’m taking you with me to  Phantom  next time too.      Make it happen, and I just might forgive your terrible taste in furniture. 😄      Aye, and I shall thank you for it on my deathbed.      I’ll be there with a coffee, an umbrella, and a discount voucher.        That’s my kind of friend.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd do something about the gutters by now. We had proper rain and it just poured straight off the edge and onto the path again.      Yeah, I don't blame you, I'd be frightened to get near the place myself. Got a mate who tried fixing his last week, nearly fell off the roof.      Oh aye? A lot of people would rather just wait and see if it breaks off entirely. Makes it worth someone else’s while to fix it, maybe for them.      Still, looks like you've got your trowel and everything. You gonna do the whole fence too then?      My student, Elise, she's studying painting and she said she needed some "real world context" for her thesis. I told her the only context here is assembling a fence and dodging the council when they come to check up on us. She insists on helping though. Fetches me brushes and says we’re creating "contemporary art." I suppose anything beats paperwork.      Aye, well, I’ve seen the occasional painting in the landings as it is. I tell ya, colouring in bloody clouds and watching for leaf stickers. I remember when I got into acting. Back in the Eighties, I thought, "Right, I'll be huge." Instead, I’m telling people to “get the phone’s on the hook” and “don’t put your feet on the seat.”      Haha, tell me about it. Me, I thought I’d be writing the next great English novel and commanding the stage like some tragic bard. No, I end up reading Virginia Woolf to med-students who think "das Deutsche ist doof."      Still, you're living the life, innit? Lecturer, house, decent wage—don't laugh. I envy blokes like you. Me? I fix gutters and wait for a red light before I stop bloody moving.      Aye, I suppose. We all have our stages. I just wonder sometimes what we’d do with a bit of money. More importantly, if we ever would.      Money? Pfft! I’d buy a go-kart on the lake if I had a bob or two. You? Still in the books, I bet.      A bit. Me and Elise were talking about fluency and language acquisition earlier. She said she’d speak fluent Basque by now if she spent enough time in the Basque region. I said, "You’d better move there, then—second-hand books and language packs ain't gonna cut it."

Rather skip the new bar in Tarnów, what? I mean it does look nice, but when you factor in the travel, let alone the dining cost, it could all be a bit much. I’m holding out for some local fast food or, better still, a good pot of coffee and a chunk of cheese to nibble on.      Oh I reckon it depends on your mood. If I’ve been on the road for hours and the campervan feels like a museum of old travel detritus, a nice bar or restaurant hit makes sense. Didn’t your mum always say something about not living until you’ve embraced a bit of clutter and chaos?      That’d be her alright. She always said you don’t get rid of enough to live properly, you just get rid of the right things. She’d pick and choose what’s relevant and what’s not – which is harder than it sounds when you live in a van and surround yourself with novelty coasters and maps and what’s-his-name’s boots.      Yeah, but why do we always assume we need to do things the way other people say? I mean I don’t think your mother would’ve liked living in a van, cluttered or not. Still, it’s not like it’s a caravan park. It’s more –?      Mobile and scattered, yes. There’s something charming and somnambular about van life when you’re not constrained by one place. Everything comes with you and then you just chuck it in one of the two crates: read or unread, taped or untaped. You kind of make the rules yourself.      Anyway, speaking of rules, did you hear there’s a hitchhiker who’s been following the same route from Bialka to Tarnow for a week now? He says he’s heading east and back again, just doing the loop.      Oh really? Sounds rather lone wolf if you ask me. A bit too open-ended. I’d imagine something like that can be very intense if you don’t have anyone reliable to stick to or trust as your travel mate.      Yeah but there’s something to that freedom. Not everyone can let go like you do, you know. I like the idea of having plans go out of the window and just riding whatever comes along – depending, of course, on the food and the vibes.

So do we go via the motorway or down the old road through the villages again? I think mummy got lost last time.      Haha, I think I've fixed the sat nav this time. Let me check the route… No, we’re going motorway all the way. Got a bit of time, I don’t think the shops open until 9:30 anyway.      Lost? Like serious lost? I drove past that same roundabout three times last time! That road looked just like the one before. You’d never tell the difference if the signs weren’t different.      Yeah! And I was  this  close to getting out and asking for directions like a proper turkey. Although I probably still wouldn’t have known which direction to go, to be honest.      I think it’s just because we were in a hurry. Mummy was late breakfast, and I was late to work. Not a good combo.      Well, we’re not in a rush today so I’ll stop at the service station by Preston and do a full coffee run. Who wants one?      Me! And a chocolate bar. For exam fuel. I’ve got another test on Thursday.      Tell me about it—he’s doing three in one week! I still remember sitting my finals and crying over the paper because I didn’t know if I’d passed. Still don’t know, honestly!      Like I said at the dinner table—your generation gets stressed about a paper, and I had a baby with a broken pelvis and a cat with cancer and still didn’t know if I’d passed ballet school! You lot have about five choices and walk away all twisted.      You had a  cat with cancer ? That is brutal.      Aye, name of Tiddles. Had ‘em put to sleep when I was working at the bakery. Brought him into work with me once. Proper grumpy old minge.      I sort of miss the old days as well. My grandmother used to read to me every night—only the whole of "Alice in Wonderland" every night, for  weeks . Then she’d say, “Well, that goody really deserved to fall down that rabbit hole, didn’t she?” I thought it was a moral.      Time to lay off your moral preaching, Viv. We’ve made it to the 21st century where tea comes in a cup and morals are bought off a shelf in Boots.

Rather skip the newfit and go through the sorting table first.      Yeah, let’s be honest, it’s not like we're going to miss anything. I've been over this a thousand times in my head.      Course not, love. Just make sure it’s all clear before we chuck anything.      Why are we clearing out Nana’s stuff? A lot of this is cool! Why can’t I keep the cup with the lion on it?      Because the lion doesn’t chase the ambulance or the fire engine, sweetheart. That’s for a much older person—like me!      That’s not fair. It’s a cool cup. I’m not a baby.      I know you're not, Harry. I think it’s just about sorting what she wants to keep and what we can donate, okay?      Hush now, don’t get cross. Listen love, I saw the tele earlier and the programmes aren’t bad, mind you—there was one about the woman who used to listen to the radio in the bath.      It wasn’t that funny, though. The others were better. The one about the man who left the national gallery for three years and got misted up when he walked back in—it gave me the shivers.      Silly woman, I got the shivers too. It’s daft what someone can miss in three years.      Nana, can I watch something?      What’s the name of it?      Primeval. I’ve seen it on the tablet.      Oh, you mean the one with the creatures coming out of the ground like some kind of giant mole chorus?      Yeah, like the treacle ones.      Harry, remember to wash your hands after any tech, love.      You always say that.      Well, I did once go two weeks with no shower and ended up looking like someone took the paintbrush out of  The Last Supper  and left the rest to gravity.      Don’t talk about gravity at your age, Claire. It’s only going to cling on further.      Ha! You could have told me that 30 years ago, Margaret.      It was a different time back then, and you were walking up Cumbrian hills like a man on a mission. I used to sit inside knitting a cobbler.      Right, right. And I suppose that’s the kind of support system you needed back before social media, huh?      I had the telly and tea, that’s more than enough.

Right, lads, here we go — new laptop, brand spanking.      Oh nice, what’s it got in it? Intel i7?      Yeah, and it’s got £200 worth of games already on it, so you two better stop eyeing it like it’s the last biscuit in the jar.      Easy, I just might take notes for when I buy one too. I’ve been using a calculator from 1998.      You what? Do you want to test it first? Let’s boot it up and see how it handles.      Yeah, go on then. But if MyFitnessPal crashes, I’m blaming you. I’ve been tracking my carb intake like I’m training for the Olympics and I’m eating cereal for dinner.      Oh come on, you tracking carbs but you still haven’t bought a gym membership yet. When’s the next time you’re going to Bedford’s group hike?      Last week I went with that chap who had the Yorkie. Got halfway up the hill and said “I might be human, but I’ve only got legs for a domestic short-haired cat.”      Fair enough, some of us prefer to ride horses, not hike hills.      Yeah, don’t start again about the equestrian centres. Last time you brought that up, I had to pretend someone was in the next room.      Besides, we should talk about what you had for dinner. You still eating that strange Korean stir-fry you make with your grandmother’s recipe?      That’s not "strange," that’s heritage. It’s got stuff in it that grow in fields that aren’t called "rice." And it smells like my nan’s garden, minus the roses.      I tried it once and I could’ve sworn it had a wasabi bomb in it. I ended up needing water and half a spoon of honey to survive.      Ah, trying new lunches, right on brand with your social media posts. Still posting that “Me, learning South Korean martial arts in the woods” vibe go?      It’s not “vibe go” — it’s “character development.” I’ve got 999 views and 2 comments. One said, “Bro, why are you wearing ninja gear in a garden?” The other said, “You’ve got the same posture as my uncle at the golf club.”      You know I got into gardening because of a YouTube clip of a bloke reshaping his soil with patience and handcuffs.      Wait, what?

Rather skip the new bar across the road. That one, they serve the best pierogi, real home-made... got to go there often when I was doing more work here.      Yeah, this is nice. Not quite as scruffy as the places back in Bury. I was actually surprised how clean and smart Tarnow looks. Not like Kraków, but still... easy on the eyes. A bit more colour too. Not the same as anywhere back home, anyway.      That it is. You get the sense the people here are working hard, but still enjoying life. Which... I suppose is more than you can say for a lot of places at the moment.      It’s true. I mean, I’m not rich or anything, but I get to teach five days a week, pick and choose who I work for. Living with roommates, sharing costs... better than when I was stuck in that place in Manchester with a kitchen in the corridor. I didn’t want to finish my degree for a while. Just felt trapped, like I’d never escape.      I know what you mean. I left full-time work a while ago and didn’t tell many people for a while. It felt like a failure, admitting it out loud. Like “what if I can’t do anything else?” Sometimes, still, it does feel like that. You start questioning everything about yourself.      For sure. And that’s the thing about identity—when you lose someone’s label, like “teacher” or “engineer” or what have you, you kind of lose the scaffolding. So you have to be honest with yourself: what  are  you, when it’s about you, not your job?      Well, I still teach sometimes. I like that. Going into that school in Bielsko-Biała a few weeks back—being with kids, planning the lessons—it gives me purpose. But I also crave freedom. I used to go to the gym every day, now it’s once a week if I’m lucky. My knees are letting me down.      That’s life with age, I think. But hey, I took up running again. Still trying to get around this lake every morning before work. It's not much, but it keeps me sane. Gives me time to think, to dream, without the noise of the day.      Dreams are still important. I have them, too. I want to write again, you know—there was a bit of a scribbler back in the day.

So do you two fancy going to the Dorset Steam Fair next week? I think it starts on Thursday. It’s the big one down by the park, isn’t it?      Now there's an idea. Not sure I'll have the stamina mind you — been sitting on the sofa too much since I retired. But I used to love the old threshing machines.      Oh aye, I love watching those big steam engines chugging away. And the antique tractors — it’s like history brought to life. The girls used to get me to take them when they were little.      That sounds brilliant. I’ve never been, but the photos look amazing. You know, like that one of the old bakery cart with horses pulling it. It’s supposed to be vintage from the 1920s.      Blimey, that’s something special. And do you think they’ve got proper facilities for folk like me in a wheelchair? I wouldn’t want to miss out, even if I have to shout the details over to you lot.      I hope so — it should be accessible these days. A few years ago I worked at a care home and they were always on about watching for disability access. I’ll ring the staff and ask. Fancy a cheeky tea while I do, Elsie?      Love one, love one. You’re sweet as pie for thinking of me, Viv.      Honestly, this all sounds perfect. But also, I need to buy a ticket online before it sells out. Some years they’re like a goldmine and gone in a flash.      Oh, do make sure to get them early. And if you’re not the most techy, I can help — I’ve sorted my son’s iPhone more times than I’d like to admit.      Thanks, I’ll do that. Oh, by the way, Mavis — I was looking to buy a flat here in Bournemouth once the course is done, you know when I finish my postgrad next year. But the property prices are out of control.      Aye, the same with the land in Dorset. I remember when this place was just the seafront and go-karts on the beach. Now it’s got so posh.      I know. I’ve seen blokes on high street pay 500 quid for a flat-screen TV and champagne breakfast in Bournemouth. It’s mad. But don’t let that put you off, Ella.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break by now.      Oh it’s relentless isn’t it! I stared out the window this morning and thought, “Well, that seems like the kind of rain that wouldn’t stop until it’s tired.”      Yeah, it’s   pourin’   so bad I couldn’t even ride my bike to school. Dad said I had to skip riding unless I had a rain   suit   like a   robot   or somethin’.      That’s a bit poetic, like, “put on your  robot gear  and face the storm” – only Rob wouldn’t have made that joke, being too busy   hunched over his laptop   editing yet another short story.      Now I think he turned   Bates Motel   into a fantasy   inns breakfast  —I swear I read a sentence like “the clocks ticked backward, and the omelettes tasted of regret.”      That does sound like something out of a   Celtic fairytale   doesn’t it? Fancied as all and high and mighty, but with more   egg on the side  .      Mr Rob is a   writer  , though. He’s always got his head in the clouds or typing something about a   castle in the sky  , like   we   all live in one!      Well, what someone sees in an empty room filled with bookshelves and a desk is oddly therapeutic. You’d think I’d be going   insane   in here, but no – I’m just   revising a scene about a priest who plays the flute  .      Now that’s a proper   madcap idea  . Not that I mind really, it does sound like something that would be found in   a Gazette   if it were updated more often.      You know, I was thinking about it the other day—the way you can tweet about anything these days. Last week,   Tommy’s dad   mentioned how he’d recently moved a new   business to the village  , and he   put it on Twitter  : “New butchers! Still good at it go on then.”      That’s   wild  ! Is it? I only use Twitter for memes, mostly the ones where the dog looks like it’s about to die.      That’s where you get the best   insights into human emotion  —like that one where the dog’s like, “You said    vacation . I said   nap  .”      That’s one of those ones that goes   viral   for a week, then everyone’s like “No it won’t. No it won’t.”

Right, so today is rather special, isn't it? Both of you have birthdays today, and it's not every day you get to share a cake with your very own brother!      I know, it's really cool! We're like kind of twins but not really.      Yeah, we’re like “bithdays”      — don’t you mean "birthdays"?      Yeah, that. And I’m going to be 11 and you’re still 10, so I’m older now.      Not by much! Still older  by one week , so we’re practically the same!      My, my, such fierce competition. I left the cake in the oven, so if you two argue for too long, I’ll be the one serving brownies instead of birthday cake.      You didn’t say this happened last year... I only found out today’s my birthday by mistake!      Well, I thought you knew, darling. You’ve been getting birthday cards all week, and we’ve been texting Aunty Lydia about it to organise your party. You  were  asked to confirm if you wanted ice cream or cake, weren’t you?      She must’ve mistook it for fake because she thought her birthday was the 3rd of April and not the 4th. I told her the other day that we’d be turning ages this week — full on  big  ages: 10 and 11.      Also, I had a test in Maths today, and we did all this stuff about fractions and stuff. I did  really  well.      Only because I told you most of it on the bus! You know that.      Well, let’s not argue. Let’s focus on the good stuff. There’s also news — your friend Ashaad’s mum said he can come for the afternoon, so he should be over later.      Weee! Ashaad and I have been doing a project together in Science about growing plants and stuff. He even brought in some radishes from his veg patch.      Radishes? That's weird. I tried growing one and it looked like a carrot that gave up on life.      Children, plants can be sensitive. They also need you to water them sometimes, and to leave them alone, in cycles. Just like birthdays.      Do we talk about that trip over Easter? The school trip to that museum in Norwich? I read all about Monet and those big paintings — kind of like my colouring book, right?      Monet and colouring? No, Monet and  me  with a long coat and hat on.

Oh my god, am I still living in a world where people talk about eggs as if they're some kind of luxury product?      I'm not even exaggerating, Liv. Last week I went to the supermarket and the free-range, organic, pesto-flavoured eggs were more expensive than a pack of butter. I was like, “Is this a breakfast or a medicine?”      I know right? Like, I got this voucher from my dad for a “supermarket treat” or something. Spent it on six standard brown eggs and called it a win.      Your dad is a legend. I still can’t get over how the prices have gone through the roof. And don’t even get me started on melon. When’s the last time you saw a watermelon for under five pounds?      Last summer—when I was at uni and working part-time breakfasts at Bucksy’s. God, those were the days. Remember when we used to smuggle hides of bread to the spare room so our flatmate wouldn’t nick it all?      Oh, Laurie? She still nicks people’s toast.      And she once tried to hide a bag of crisps in her bin bag in the kitchen. So she thought she was doing it discreetly. I almost had a coronary just peering in.      Haha, Laurie never changes. Still the same old Laurie. Still living in her parents’ basement, just with full-time TikTok fame.      Honestly, I’d do anything for a chuckle at 2 a.m. looking at her videos now. Far more entertaining than the Prime Minister speeches.      I know! I watched the last one and I had to stop cooking lasagne and just sit there staring at the wall in disbelief. The lasagne turned out edible, just a bit overcooked. Mystery solved.      Hey, speaking of food—did I tell you about my lunch today? I fell in love with a little salad station near the train station. They had this sprite of kale, edible flowers, and this lemon poppyseed dressing—was like, "Congratulations, you just constructed a €12 birthday card for the system."      But it was healthy.      Healthy? Yeah sure, but I had to lie down three times post-lunch. Must’ve had some kind of post-salad seductive conference in there.      I had that new type of lentil casserole from the hippy shop on Orpington High Street. Served with quinoa oatcakes and beetroot. My dog looked at me like, “Was it worth it?”

Rather skip to the bar in the evening rather than going in for a glass of wine in the real world. I got to admit, I miss the dining room more than I thought I would.      Aye, we do. Look, the children would be well grown up by now if they een saw the place, I don’t think they’d even know what it looked like as it was. I remember that awful council bylaw policy where they swooped in and gave the building a lick and a promise of something better and then nothing was ever done for twenty years.      You'd fetch frozen fish from the market, mate—still no meat, no marble tables, only paint chipped and floors that slopped like seas under your boots. Fun to reflect on, sure, but the real action was in the dance hall and the old school turned community centre.      Oh aye, I remember that place. I used to take a drive in there at the weekends, play a bit of fiddle or piano for the folk who still came through. One bloke nearly took it out of me for tunes I played—said I put two words together wrong. But still, it was alive back then.      Well, we’ve been lucky with the rebranding here – it’s been a fairly radical, and sometimes bittersweet, thing. Let’s say the apple pie and clock tower approach have been revived rather well, and the old mill been turned into a coffee roastery with music nights. Strictly not bad.      I do wonder what made them decide to weigh in on the architectural side. The old way – all the lean-to, the sagging belfry, the walkways all twisted round the sides of buildings like veins—there’s a certain poetry in that.      Doesn’t sound uncommendable, to be honest, but for the sake of character, I’d much rather they took that route: minor modernisations here and a few fresh wooden decks there. I tried to make a little persuading when I was still on the planning committee. Let’s say... not very successful.      Perks do come with the reformations, though. I had a bit of the sun on my go in Prague on the cheap, and I had a real crack at loosening up in the spas and theatres. You could get in to places already due to be full with just a bit of begging to the kassiers in the gates.

So do you think an online version of our case study resource would have the same impact as the printed one? I mean, people are often glued to their screens more than books these days.      It would have to be interactive to compare, I think—maybe video case studies with interviews, student feedback, and even discussion prompts embedded. That kind of thing really draws people in.      Yeah, that sounds logical. Like, if we do a social learning angle, we could even integrate some sort of shared journey—maybe learners can post their thoughts or experiences during the study of the case. You know, like a digital journal space?      Oh, and we could link that to some kind of social media strategy. If teachers or students share their progress or takeaways on platforms, they could tag us or use a hashtag. I think it could create a buzz if people start talking about it.      Exactly. I've been thinking about how microlearning is becoming more popular. We could offer bite-sized videos or flashcards that break down the case studies into chunks that are easier to digest.      That would be perfect for short attention spans! I’ve read a few studies on how colour, design, and gamification can help retention. We could gamify the way learners unlock content—maybe they have to answer a quick quiz before moving on to the next part of a case study.      That’s a killer idea. You could almost see universities or even training companies investing in that. It’s also scalable—develop a few core case studies and just keep adding on with different themes each term.      And what about premium content? Maybe we offer a free version with a few case studies and then a paid membership for the full library and exclusive materials. Teachers and institutions might be more likely to invest that way.      Absolutely—and for the social networking side, we could create an online forum or even a Facebook group for educators using the platform. Peer support would really add something unique to it.      I remember reading a while ago about how good storytelling and emotional connection can increase learning retention. What if we include a narrative behind each case study—like the struggle, the process, and the results? People like a story with a beginning, middle, and end.      That ties in really well with the digital journal idea. People could reflect on how the case study might have affected them personally.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors.      They'd string us up if they found out.      I'd take my chances. It's a mad queue at the box office and they're not even letting you book online.      Right and now I've got to trudge all the way out onto the path and then come back.      If you're too tired to walk to the café then you're too tired to go.      Is that your solution when I don't want to walk too far like three times a day you just don't go.      That's not the solution that's you being a bit of a jelly though isn't it.      You're a jelly pick and I'll be the one that goes and gets the coffee.      Only if you don't drop it like last time in the car park oh you ever looked embarrassed that's you ordering a mocha and then spilling it all over that man's van and then you didn't even say sorry.      What did he expect.      You just ran out of the café with a cup of coffee like you were running from the –      Right and then it just slipped out of my hand and boom went into the back of his van.      And you didn’t even say sorry.      He looked like he didn't even notice to be honest.      Well he did have marshmallows and milk in his –      You know I about blocked his exhaust.      No you didn’t.      No he was doing that afterwards.      Maybe he was.      There he was.      And then you said the most awkward thing.      What was I meant to say I could stick out my thumb and go that’s a free wash for you.      At least do something do an oops emoji you don't even say anything and just run the other way away go.      It wasn’t like I meant to spill it in the back of the van.      But your hands were shaking.      I was in a bit of a rush alright I don’t like being late to everything.      You always say that and yet you end up the one who’s late to everything.      Right so what's the plan once we get out there.      What do you mean.      You said we were coming here for a bit of peace and quiet oh look.

So do you lot reckon I’ve got the whole "capsule wardrobe" thing right then, or does it just look like I’m wearing charity shop rejects?      No, come on, it's totally on trend. You know, the whole  quiet luxury  vibe. Minimalist cuts, earthy tones—very  Miuccia Prada moment . I reckon people are going to be stealing your look in a few months when they cotton on that fast fashion isn’t working for them anymore.      Yeah! And the way you layered that sweater over the collared shirt—it's like you stepped out of a magazine. I couldn’t even imagine doing that with my half-decent stuff!      My nan would’ve called it "trying to look like a shop window dummy" if I dressed like this at home, and I think she hated fashion. Living in Doncaster, there wasn’t a lot of, um…  fashion culture  to speak of in my early days, you know?      I get that. I grew up in Lewisham—there was  plenty  of fashion culture, but most of it was about what your mum was wearing to the shops or what colour laces were in on the trainers. You'd walk past about ten different styles in five minutes – very chaotic but also fairly authentic, in a way.      Yeah, Cambridge was more of a "academic chic" place when I got here. Everything was about neutrals, cardigans that looked hand-knitted by a 103-year-old, and boots preferably with some floring—there was a  lot  of being cold chic at the expense of your ballet tones.      I’m not averse to a bit of floring, but I’m just not made for that! Give me denim and a decent coat and I’m a happy lass.      True story. Speaking of denim, have you actually seen that new Max Mara campaign? I'm holding out for the jackets, but I hear the trousers are cult status already. We could talk about that  all  night.      Please do keep going because while I do like talking about Max Mara, I’m still stuck trying to style these jungle trousers my sister gave me that are supposed to be "streetwear meets boho". I made her promise not to do that again. Honestly, it might as well be what your cat walked over in the corner.      You’re not wrong. And speaking of questionable gifts—did I mention I got a "vintage" hippie skirt from my Aunty that looks like it’s been through a dozen Acid House raves and still came out alive?

So do you ever take photos of me anymore, Mum? Like proper photos? Not just when I’m pouting or falling over.      Oh don’t start with the pouting, Liv! You’re a teenager now, I know you hate being photographed! But yes, I do take proper photos. That one on my phone from last weekend was actually pretty good—standing by the beach with that sunset. You looked… peaceful.      Peaceful, yeah. Like I was trying to avoid someone. Please can we not post that one on Facebook again? I want to keep my dignity.      Dignity at 15? What is this, a competition? You know your dad still has a framed photo of you at two, covered in cake. Ten layers, gone.      Ugh, not the cake story. I told everyone it was a chocolate sauce accident. I still have nightmares about that!      Okay, okay. I’ll drop it. But, you were saying earlier—about working in college over the summer?      Yeah—there is this shop nearby that I can maybe apply to. It’s like a café and bookshop combined. I’ve been thinking about becoming a proper photographer one day, like actually studying it. Not just on my phone with filters.      That’s huge, Liv. Really exciting. I did love your Instagram page. You're not just taking photos of your mates, you’re starting to frame things in a way that shows you're thinking about the composition.      Thanks, I’d never have thought of that as a skill until recently. I used to panic about it all because I thought about how bad I was at it. But the more I take photos, the more I like doing it. It helps me not think too much about everything else, you know?      You mean like the whole world being a bit much?      Yeah. You know how I mentioned being scared of the sea? Sometimes when I take photos at the beach, it’s like I can calm myself down. Even if it’s just for a bit.      That’s amazing, Liv. I’m so proud of you. I wish I had even a fraction of your courage to try something like that.      Wait, you’re a receptionist with a postgraduate degree! You can do anything you want at 15.      Touché, Miss Know-It-All. But seriously, if you ever need advice, or someone to hold the camera for the selfie so I look like I'm taking it, I’m here.

Rather annoying lot, them builders. I'm sat in me own house and I can't shut a window without it creaking like a banshee on skates. I’ve asked them three times to put a little more care into it, but they just sort of shrug and say things like “nearly there, guv.”      You know, dear, it's not all their fault—they do work for wages now, but they must have this new sort of attitude these days. It was easier in my day. We had to build me house from scratch, and when it leaked, well, you just fetch the bucket.      Aye, and now the lot of 'em think "good enough" is good enough. I’ve seen enough shoddy fitting this week to fill a lorry. Damp, gaps in the walls, the lot. It's enough to make a grown man want to breakfast on brick dust. I've been trying to explain this in my application form, you know, for that 3D printing course. They’re asking why I want it, so I said, "I want to build houses properly—no leaks, no drafts, and certainly no cockerels raising hell on the roof!"      Cockerels! Oh, don’t get me started on that. I had one fairly recently, and mind you, it was up there at the crack of dawn every single day like it owed me rent. I went out with a ladder, a screwdriver, and someone said to me, “But you can’t just chuck it off the roof.” I said, “Well, who built a house with a cockerel in it—I did! And I’m buggered if I’m going to walk about with feathers in me ears for the rest of me life.”      You know that reminds me of the time we had a baby sparrow that fell out of the nest. Pokey little thing. Eddie passed it around with his handkerchief and said it was a “lost soul needing affection." I tried to put it back, but the mother bird was such a scold. Let me tell you, trying to catch a sparrow mid-flight with mismatched socks and a broom—it's a lost cause.      Yeah, go on then, but let’s get our heads back on straight for a minute. I was out last night with Sue—her bloke turned 70—and we were in this little Italian place, all chandeliers and chicken Parmesan.

Rather than going up there and paying through the nose for a few days and hurrying around, it just seemed... smarter to bring her down here. I mean, she could stay with me for a few weeks, see how it all works, and not have to break the bank on flights.      That sounds like a sensible idea. It’s not like Brighton’s far from London—she could pop over easily enough. Has she worked out where she’s going to stay permanently, or is she still figuring that out?      No, no plans yet. She’s still studying at the moment—trying to finish her degree in social work. She said she doesn’t want to rush into anything, and rightly so. It’s a bit of a big move for her, you know?      Aye, and I can imagine the parents up in Scotland must be a bit nervous about it. I mean, bringing your daughter this far south, after all—what if she’s not used to the weather, or the way we do things?      Oh, I know, and I had to explain it all to them properly. Told them that it wasn’t like I was shipping her off to some foreign country—it’s still Britain. She’s British. But I think they were just worried about her being on her own and not knowing anyone.      And rightly so, mind you. Brighton’s a beautiful city, but it’s not exactly a town for people who want to lie low. If she’s not careful, she could be out at some festival or bar hotter than the summer sun.      I know, I  do  know! I’ve nearly about blocked every place she’s mentioned on Instagram just trying to keep her grounded. But really, what can I do? She’s got to make her own mistakes.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? You can guide them, but eventually, they have to go it alone. But at least bringing her down here means there’s someone waiting with a spoon if the chips are down.      Something like that. I’ve got the spare room ready, and the kettle’s always on. I even got rid of the cat so she wouldn’t go back up North thinking life was full of danger.      Oh, no, you didn’t—!      No, no! I just moved her into the conservation centre in the garden.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's been on the news all week and I've had no luck getting across to her properly.      That's probably for the best. You wouldn’t have wanted her being frightened by all that talk about independence or whatever it’s called now.      Yeah, I reckon it's best to put it on a shelf for now. My Phoebe's too young to understand what's happening up north. But my wife said she heard her saying “indy” and “nay” at the toy shop. You'd think the shopkeepers were voting!      I'm still waiting for some kind of breakdown of whether university departments are going to get involved. I've got a job interview on the 13th, by the way — for the history of English language in Scotland — can you believe it?      That does sound interesting. You’d be teaching at the university in Stirling, wasn’t it?      That’s the one. It’s a combination of Scottish English and sociolinguistic changes — I mean, with all the focus on the vote and the language, it could be a really good opportunity. They asked me to give a sample lecture.      Well you’ve always been good with that kind of thing — you’ve the flair for it. All that time spent studying dialects and variations in English language universities will notice that, even if politicians don’t.      I hope so. I just hope it’s not a poisoned chalice — the politics weigh heavy in places up there. Anyway, enough about me — your colleague, Neil, he dropped about five times last week during the lecture. He had the students watching “The Theory of Everything” again and thought he was answering the plug-in question and it just snowballed.      Oh, I heard he was nearly in tears by lunch. The kids were terrible to him. Of course, he insisted it was due to tiredness, but when he started calling one of my students “Muffy”, I knew something was wrong.      “Muffy”?! That’s going back far too many years.      Oh, I reckon go back to my time at university. Not that I was Muffy.      Hopefully your students aren’t doing the same to your daughter — she’s at grammar school now, I heard.      Yes, she’s really adjusting well — new school, new town — and she seems over the moon. We moved here from Brighton last month.

So do you remember putting the mousetrap board together, Sarah’s dad? I swear it came in like 200 bits and no instructions. It took me three hours and by the time we got there, it was half collapsed.      Oh God, yes! And I was so cross because I thought  this is the one thing we   didn’t   need to be arguing over on a rainy day  and by halfway through the construction, I was muttering under my breath about why I ever agreed to do this.      Didn’t it end up with the wrong number of wheels on the cart? I remember watching and being like, “That’s not how Mousetrap is supposed to work.”      Oh it got worse. By the time the kids wanted to play, we had this whole game where the cheese just fell straight through the floor because the trap mechanism wasn’t secured properly. We had to use a pile of books to stop it falling. It was the most chaotic family bonding day ever.      That’s not even the worst one, though. You know when I got relocated up to Manchester two years ago for work? I had to tell the American branch of my department how much I didn't miss working abroad.      Yeah – what was that like? I’ve only ever worked in pubs and restaurants but the idea of working in another country sounds like a whole vibe.      It was a mix of business etiquette gone wrong and just missing home. I had to explain a million times that we don’t  actually  drink all the time in the UK. And being called “British” all the time in Maryland made me feel like I was in a history textbook.      Oh I remember going to a friend’s summer camp in Wisconsin when I was younger. It was the first time I’d met British kids, and for the life of me, I can’t remember what made me start calling them all “poi” – something to do with the tea they drank, I think. Honestly, the American kids I met always struck me as far more independent. When we went on school trips, it was like they all had cell phones, knew where everything was, and had marching orders from their parents on how to behave.

So did you go through all of my stuff to get me that glue sticks and markers or what?      No I just went through like your box I put in by the door where you said to leave your stuff. Do you think you want to have that sort of experience with your future kids? Like raising them on old-school stuff?      Eh, I’d like them to be tech literate at least. She just moved in to do her MSc for Healthcare and she’s already gotten herself passed out by sundown. I told her the minimal sleep thing was giving me nightmares.      You must be doing all the work for her then. You being academically-traumatized by her procrastination.      Yeah no, you remember when I worked with Gemma on the baby sign language go-to guide on pond life? It's not even real. But she calls me in the middle of the night with fish themed academic problems.      So how many siblings do you have?      Just one, my sister Lucy, but she’s doing her studies for a higher degree in Marine Mammal Science. I’m the one who runs the household.

Right, so you've got this Cyprus accent now, Eh? Blimey, it's like you've gone off and lived with some Cypriot goats or somethin’.      Nah, it's Luton and the fact that I've picked up some Greek from my mate Kostas. He’s always like “Come on,   paxto  ,” and I just sort of say it back now.      That’s weird, but cool. I mean, you speak fluent English and suddenly you’re halfway to playing a Cypriot shepherd in a Netflix drama. Have you ever thought about being in linguistics? You seem like someone who could accidentally become a specialist in mixed dialects.      Ha! Yeah, if I bottle this, I’ll sell it as a language learning tonic:   Luton Locarno Mix   — 50% East Anglian, 50% Cypriot mystery.      I teach English as a second language, so I get that. One time, I had a student from Vietnam tell me a story about a cat that turned into a hat — quite surreal. But still, it got me thinking about how we pass on stories and how accents kind of do the same.      Mate, I got a real one for you — the other day, I was sketching in the park and this guy comes over trying to buy my art for a fiver. I looked at 'im all serious-like and said,   “I didn't draw this with a fiver in my arse.”   He ran off.      That’s crude but fair. You know, most people I meet at work think I speak like a man talking to a donkey. I'm a gardener and not a very talkative one at that. But if a customer says something that’s just a bit over the top, I tell 'em I'm not here to protect feelings, I’m here to protect the bloody   hostas  .      I could see that as a catchphrase.   "I'm here to protect the hostas."   It's got the same ring as,   "You don't want to see me angry."        I'm more about   "You don’t want to see my line in the sand."   Which is basically three blokes on a garden chair with a bag of pork scratchings.      That’d make a good board game. You draw a card like “Someone spills chips on your chair” and you have to decide whether to move the poker chip up the   “line in the sand”   or risk losing all your scratchings.

So do you think I should go for the used car or just keep the bus for a bit longer?      Honestly, it depends on your budget. I mean, sure the bus is cheaper to run, but with all the waiting… I swear sometimes it takes twice as long to get home because I'm stuck at a stop.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been counting up how much I’m spending every month on fares. It adds up. But I also don’t want to go into massive debt for a car that’s just going to fall apart in a year.      No, I get that. Used cars can be hit or miss. You’ve got to go for something with a good MOT and not too many miles on the clock. I know this bloke, he bought a Fiesta off the kerb—looked alright at the time, then it breakfasts itself every time he starts it.      Blooming hell. I don’t have time to deal with that mess. I’ve got enough going on with work and the admin stuff—personally, I want the occasional smooth drive, not a breakdown timetable.      Tell me about it… I had the same problem last year when I got my first car. My Mate Joel showed me the ins and outs, but really, if you’re not confident, maybe start learning to drive next year instead. If you can save up enough for your own car and instructor, you won’t have to rely on the bus or my dodgy timing to give you a lift.      That might be the way forward. I’ve been thinking about it. If I start saving a bit more each month—maybe even move into the area a bit closer to work—then I can put more toward lessons. I’m tired of the stress of commuting.      That’s smart. Maybe you can guest sit my project meetings for a week and I’ll give you a few tips on how to wring money out of nowhere.      Ha! You know what? That’s tempting. But I think I’d rather keep the admin work I’ve got and just chip away at savings slowly. I’ve had enough of people's projects to last a lifetime.      Fair play. Just don’t let me catch you baking that sponge cake again—no one can eat it all and it’s not like I’m planning to fill up the car with desserts after every trip.

Right Aaron, the bins need taking out on Thursday, remember? I’ve had a few complaints about the smell already.      Yeah, I’ll do it, Nan. Don’t worry. I was just in my room revising for the mocks. They start next week, you know?      Revising, eh? Not like   I   had to worry about mocks when I was your age. I had to work in the factory and look after my younger brothers. Proper   work   that was. Not exams and fancy schools nowadays.      Oh, leave the lad be, Eleanor. We were all young once—well, me, at least. Eleanor only got her GCSEs well into her fifties, did you tell him that, love?      That’s true, dear. I think it was 1998, was it? Got better at breakfast, no doubt about that!      Ha! Well, I didn’t need exams to mark, didn’t I? Just a pencil and a red pen, like I do now.      Nan, you mark GCSEs? What did you teach back in the day?      I was a machine operator. Then I went back to college in my forties. Real late, I know, but better late than never, as your gran says.      Wow. Silly me thinking all teachers just jump out of the womb with degrees in their hands.      And not a bad one, mind you. She got an honours degree—  after   the kids, and   after   scanning all those papers.      I did alright, didn’t I? Decent salary now, too. Course, most of it goes into your father’s cabby toys.      Dad’s got another one now?      Aye, he’s passed up four cabs and counting. First red one, then silver, then white—and now it’s a blue one waiting at the garage. Not sure how he keeps them all apart.      Course, I think it helps he’s got such an excellent memory. Still remember my birthday come March 12th—usual time, usual place!      And   don’t forget   my denture appointment on the 13th, Arthur!      Don’t be getting ahead of yourself, Edith. You’ve still got plenty of time to live with your new ones!      Right, let’s not start bickering like I tell the Year Elevens not to. Now, Aaron, where’s your maths homework?      I haven’t done it yet—      —and here you are scribbling around in your revision guide like it’s a diary. I had a look earlier. You’ve written on it, “1+1= chocolate cake.”

Right, who’s up for helping me cut up some fruit for breakfast?      Can I have the cherry knife? The one that has the gold handle!      Only if you don’t eat all the cherries before we’ve even started, Martha. Come on, Jamie, you want to help as well?      Yeah! I wanted to be a pirate today. A real proper captain!      Oh, really? Well, Captain Jamie needs to keep his strength up, so fruit and eggs for breakfast it is!      Pirates have treasure, don’t they? I saw a pirate movie the other night and they had a real map that led them to a golden chest!      Yes! But they had to solve puzzles and avoid traps and things. A bit like solving maths puzzles in class, actually.      I’m going to buried treasure with a sword in my hand! I showed the teachers in school, they even showed me a bit of stop motion animation of pirates walking around! It looked like magic!      I remember seeing that! You did a great job with the movements, Jamie. You’ve got a proper eye for it.      What about Shakespeare – we’re doing that week next week and Mummy said we’re going to Stratford!      Yes! You know what? There’s a real-life acting workshop they’re doing at someone’s house in Stratford. They said it was a bit like a magic show. You can try being a character and shout in the way the actors do.      Did Shakespeare make pirates in his plays?      Interesting! Not many pirates, but there’s a lot of kings and queens and people arguing with swords. But if you want, we can imagine the pirates are in the background of "Hamlet" or something!      Can the pirates steal the crown from the king and run away with it?      Of course! Why not? Pirates can do what they want!      But Mummy, do the pirates in the workshops wear hats? Proper tricorn hats?      They do! And if you’re lucky, you might even find a real-life pirate making a hat for you in the costume tent. And what’s better than that? It’s part of the special Easter pictures we’re doing next week too!      Oh right, we saw the Easter posters yesterday – the ones at the doors of the school. I really like the one with the fluffy bunnies and the dragon!      Yes, very magical.

Rather skip to the part when we were all sat in Ahmed’s garden drinking tea and then we came up with... What was it, Roger?      I think it was called the  Ramsgate Rocket … Not quite NASA material, but we thought it was brilliant. We bought an old fishing boat, stuck a sail on it, got some ridiculous idea that we could just sail all the way from Jeddah to Cyprus by following coastlines and a few Google Maps print-outs. Very enterprising, very retired.      Very. You didn’t chase the spirit of adventure with a nettle, like. I had even packed  dental magazines  as bait to barter with fishermen. On the theory that Myron Keiser’s  Endodontic Update  is the most universally admired publication known to man.      Oh, the myth of the dental magazine, far more useful than gold. I still have a framed copy of the one with a smile in every language on the cover. But Roger, how did the arrest come into it?      It wasn’t an arrest, not exactly. Well, not from the police. It was the Coast Guard from somewhere. I think it was Jordan. We were in international waters, but it got quite hairy when we got picked up. They – very politely – said we were not licensed, had no navigation equipment, and the sail wasn’t quite big enough to qualify as a method of propulsion. Then they offered us tea and a GPS.      That’s the sort of arrest everyone should have—at least one oddly genteel one with a Coast Guard who feels sorry for you. I’ve only ever been removed from a clinic in枣庄 for forgetting to wear about five pairs of gloves during a lecture. But touch wood, I’ve never been arrested.      Oh, but you barely left the clinic, George. That was just the bin, wasn’t it?      A tragedy, yes. But I digress. I remember hearing something about all of this when I was teaching in Riyadh. You had your own little rebel mission, and I was stuck doing root canals in the middle of a sand dune.      That's where the alcohol comes in. We had a secret keg in the boat’s fake engine well. It was a French lager, deliberately unbranded, but that was our siren call to the sea.      We all have our vices, really. Although I think I was pretending to be a student of marine life to explain my wine stash hidden in the tool box.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the grannies. I know her hips are real touch and all, but I’m mid-editing this brochure yet and I can’t be running after Luke every five minutes.      No worries, love—grannie wouldn’t dream of missing her soaps, and she’s been more cheerful today than I’ve seen her in months. Proper self of her. She even asked me if I’d ever been to Africa, like I’m a Royal Geographical Society sort of woman. Know what I mean? Bit like dragging teeth for a holiday story.      I’m  not  a child, you know! I don’t do "mess about in the loo" for ages!      I know, Luke, but your gran’s downstairs with her slippers and she’s about as quick as a snail on glue!      Honestly, I used to live with six kids and not once did I get stuck in the loo—unless I was hiding from Dad after burning the Sunday roast, and that’s a different story altogether!      Right, and what grief when he got hold of me—absolute lecture on how the neighbour’s daughter had a proper job “with a desk and a collar.” But I’m not in a queue for a perk suit, am I?      You’ve done well, love. I’m just glad yours never led you down the full-time office path. I’d die in a seat like one of those magazine models—look at the sparkle in my eyes and my backside is in a sling!      Why are all you grown-ups talking about hips and slippers and whatever? I’m trying to revise for that history exam! I mean, what does  Eleanor of Aquitaine  have to do with anything?      Well, if you’re on the topic of explorers, you could do worse than start there. She was mad, but she knew how to move.      And speaking of moving lunches—Luke, d’you do anything today but play Xbox and sulk in the loo?      That's work! I'm building a rocket.      You’re building a catapult out of toilet rolls again, aren’t you?      Now there’s something I used to specialise in—building trouble out of tea-towels and bellyache. But I did alright in the end—got into the factories and them catering jobs. Now I’m my own manager, so to speak, during lunchtimes.

So do you lot reckon we’ve seen the last of truffles in the UK for this season?      I think so love, unless they find another patch in Cumbria where that fella is digging. Not quite as good as the Istrian ones though, mind you.      Yeah, I don’t think they compare. I reckon this bloke Luca, the Michelin chef we met in Poreč, uses this stuff in every other dish.      Can you just eat truffles? Like, on their own?      Oh aye, but it’s mostly shaved over pasta or meat, love. You don’t waste it on boring things like rice. Although, I’ve seen some eccentric chefs try.      I had a friend in America who said truffle oil is practically illegal in fine dining circles now. They’re like breakfast food—ketchup and mayonnaise for the posh set.      That sounds right to me. All the shouty chefs over here still love to flex over it, though—personally I think they’d be better off with a decent asparagus and a few potatoes.      Speaking of potatoes, Dad, I saw that documentary about stem cells. They actually used stem cell therapy on cows with bad joints.      Yeah, it’s not that far off for humans. If we can get the universities in Manchester and London to co-operate more, we’ll be looking at real medical breakthroughs.      You’d think the government'd have a clue by now. Between their heads and their shoulders, they’ve spent more on football stadium upgrades than med-research grants.      We had to do a whole project on stem cells at school. I thought it was weird that it’s kind of both science and... ethics.      Aye, that’s the rub. Just like with the whole education system. I think it’s gone a bit daft restricting what kids can learn until they're 16. You can’t just lock everything up with exams and keep the big secrets to the professionals.      I know, right? Sometimes I wish the schools would go back to the way it was when you were a midwife, Gran. You had more freedom, I bet.      Oh your dad’s the one who said that. Me, I was just grateful to get the hours off to feed the kids, let alone teach me anything.      Which is the real shame. We’re so busy focusing on producing managers and executives, we're losing out on scientists, artists, and even decent cooks.

Rather annoying isn't it when they play music too loud in here. I was just trying to read up on dialect shift and I couldn’t even hear the chair creak properly!      I mean, it probably helps stop people from feeling like they're at work, though. A little bit of soft jazz is okay, but this is full-on club banger territory.      I reckon they only do it to keep the interns from staring at their screens for longer than five minutes without pulling out a coffee. You start to forget the time when the music’s right.      Not to mention it helps block out other people’s conversations, which are mostly about SEO optimization and conversion rates anyway. My brain can only take so many mentions of "target audience" and "click-through rates."      I think it’s ironic given where we are, to be honest. Cambridge University Press, and we’ve got this playlist of house remixes of nursery rhymes spinning.      Have you heard the one that goes  Humpty Dumpty  with a bass drop? I had to listen to it twice I was laughing so much.      Honestly, it could be a meme at this point—and it'd get a million views. “Humpty Drops – Baptiste Remix.” I’m not saying it, but I’m not not saying it.      Anyway, enough about the playlist. How’s the dialect mapping project going for you, Jess? Spent any time in the archives lately?      Oh yeah—piece of work, some of the old transcripts. One lot from the ’60s in Norfolk had the most fascinating about how people used to talk about "the man in the hall" instead of the landlord.      That’s brilliant!
