I mean, it does sound like something out of a kids’ book. Maybe you should put it in one of your reports.      Or a podcast. Jess, you could pitch that as a mini-series. “Secret Histories of the English Language.” You’ve got a gift for this kind of stuff.      I’ve thought about it—though delivering it with this voice would make the tone a bit gothic. I might need you both to guest as the voice of "the man in the hall."      Deal. I’ll wear some virtual mustache and puff out my cheeks to really get into roles.      Just don’t forget to include a tracking link for our next client meeting. We can call it "Wit & Wisdom of Past Generations."

Rather skip the new road and go through the old part of town. I know her house is through there. It’s the quieter route anyway.      I can take it, if you’re sure. I don’t mind a bit of a scenic detour—we picked up some pastries from that Polish bakery in the van, and I’d rather enjoy them while I can.      Oh aye, I love those. The custard strudel, right? She used to send me boxes of it when I taught in Leeds. Bit of a guilty pleasure when I get the chance. You don’t often find decent Polish baked goods over here.      I found it easier to get in Poland, honestly. Every town has one of those corner places. It’s just more traditional, I reckon.      I think it’s just nostalgic for most of us who’ve spent time abroad. I still miss the coffee shops in Wrocław. They had this little barista who’d make the milk foam into little cats or puffins. Madness, the way they take their coffee over there.      That’s beautiful—makes you want to keep going back. We might need to plan a bigger trip sometime. Maybe in the spring. I’ve got some upcoming contracts from the local council here, but I could take a week off, and you could tag along if you like. I promise not to ask you to help with the lesson plans.      Aye, and I might just tag along with one of my books and a thermos of tea and let you do the teaching—job’s all yours. But a week sounds good. Even better if we can make a stop in Kraków on the way. I always walk away with a headful of history and a stomach full of pierogi.      Deal. We’ll take the campervan up for the whole lot of it. Burgers and lesson plans by day, beer and nostalgia by night. Just me and the minimal luggage I can carry as it is.      You’re getting your stick out to clear a path early on, aren’t you? Git with it, Jane.      Well, let’s face it, I’m the organized one. You the one who still goads her map app into telling you about “the real route” and ignores the traffic camera warnings.      I’m just looking out for some character. You can’t take the same road every day and expect it to give you anything new.

Look at that new strip, eh? You think they’re going to go with it for the whole season? I reckon the white with the red sash is more their look, not this neon nonsense.      Yeah, I know what you mean—some of them sponsors gone mad with the bright colours. I mean, I understand the branding, but   does every damn thing on your shirt have to be a logo  ? I swear last season they had like three ad names under each armpit.      Oh, I heard they're talking about a deal with McDonald's now. Can you believe it? Like, who  chose  that? I mean, I’d rather have some boring old bank on my chest than golden arches.      Probably the marketing department who never touched a football in their life. Fair enough though—if it pays for the kit, hey. Although honestly, I miss the old sponsors. Like, "Look at that classic Walkers crisps logo," you know? Nostalgia and a bag of hot ones, right?       [Laughs]  Yeah, nothing says I’m full of beans quite like crisps and a match-winning goal. But seriously, this whole thing with the stickers and sub-brands—ain't it taking the look away from the team themselves? I mean, it's  their  badge that counts, not some burger chain.      Absolutely. You don’t see the principles of the old clubs changing anything every season. Clubs like Liverpool or United—no rush to rebrand because they  are  the brand. Just a red badge and a name—say no more.      Exactly. I mean, I get marketing partnerships, but the   design of the strip itself  —this one looks like some kid drew it at school. I mean, is the sponsorship affecting the quality of the design too? 'Cos I swear that zip-up at the back looks like something from a discount store.       [Gestures at the muted TV where a goal is being scored]  Like  this  player clearly didn’t care what the kit looked like. Goals first, looks second, innit? Although you think a bit of branding might rub off on the players—imagine walking on the pitch if your whole strip was covered in a burger logo.      Honestly, maybe they should start selling McDonald's after matches. You could have a big screen showing the highlights and a burger stand. " Hugely successful match, now get a Big Mac and chips. " Yeah, why not? Make it all one big ad.

You’d think a recording of me going on about the train being five minutes late would get more hits on eBay than some naff CD by some boyband from 2003, wouldn’t you?      Uncle Alan, honestly, I don’t know why you keep doing it. You’ve sold two vocal samples, and one of them was to your sister-in-law for a joke. You don’t need to monetise your gripes about the Southeastern line.      It’s not just that. I’ve been recording me ranting about the whole of life lately. The gas bill, the frozen bank account, even Mary  —  no, forget it. I accidentally called another bloke in the queue at the Jobcentre "Mary" the other day. It was embarrassing. I’m not racist or anything, it just slipped out.      It must’ve been a bit awkward. Wait, Mary was a lady, wasn’t she?      Bloke, five o’clock, massive ginger beard, looked like a Mary from  Coronation Street . I said "Alright, luv" and he just glared at me. Like a wounded toad. I only live on benefits, but there’s something to be said for dignity, innit?      You should’ve apologised. I mean, you’re on the register now, aren’t you? It’s not like you can afford to burn bridges.      What, claiming the dole? Aye, I burn bridges every day. First thing every morning. I start the kettle with a chuckle and a moan and I swear it’s contagious. I even had your grandmother calling me a "pensioner misfit" the other day. She spent the day watching daytime TV and spending a week’s budget on lotto tickets.      Nana  is  that bad with her gambling. I just keep quiet about it so she doesn’t cut me out of her will. I’d be rich off all the bets she’s lost!      Aye, you’d be sipping sprite in a villa in Tenerife by now. Me? I’m still here, stuck with no grandad and a mortgage I can’t pay. I tried to set go-karts on fire outside Jobcentre Plus once. Just wanted a bit of line in, innit?      You’re lucky they didn’t arrest you. I’m surprised you haven’t been kettled in some protest for fun.      Oh I did go to that one over in Gillingham, the one about rising energy prices. Sat down near the bins and they said I was "offensive" to the environment.

Rather skip the new drive-through café near the station, have you noticed the queue for it yet?      Never mind queueing, I’d rather go to the usual convenience store where I know where I am. Not all of us have got time to sit in motor cars all day.       Ah yes, I was down that way the other day on the bus and heard a funny one—they had a flat tyre and got lost and ended up in some building site. It weren’t no road. Know what I mean?       Oh dear, I hope they weren’t far from home.       Nah, found their way back eventual and made a cup of tea. You’ve met enough eccentric drivers in this life, haven’t you? I remember Oliver, he’d used to drive the milk round. Once he drove off with a cow stuck under the bonnet—       Haha, hard to imagine, madam.       Oh he was the brightest one, mind you—set the sat nav to a bookshop and ended up in the park instead. Was a week before he twigged. Hilarious, really.       That’s a legend. Mind you, most of us just end up at the same roundabout, it seems.      Now don’t go making me nervous, will you? I already had a proper shudder on the road this morning someone almost sideswiped me.       Now that’s a proper drama. Much better to have a good stretch of road and tea in hand. Far more peaceful in the good old past, I daresay. My girls used to bring me chips and cups of cocoa most days. Ron always said I ran the house better than I drove the car. Know what I mean?       That’s nice. My mother-in-law here— gestures to Speaker_3 —still insisted I had to grow up before I knew what a cup of tea was.       And rightly so! Kids were growing up on biscuits and digestive biscuits and glass of water for ages, mind you. Now these days, it’s more go, go, go and if you don’t get takeaway at 10 o’clock, you’re a sinner. I say, when did your generation forget how to boil an egg?       Well, mind you, I had to learn from your lot, didn’t I, over this one’s food scraps and everything else.      Mother, if you were still in the kitchen, you’d be throwing things at me for leaving the saucepan on again and again.

Okay, I just wanted to say – do you know how long that science test was today? I think it lasted like, an hour and twenty minutes, and more than half of it was like,  why do volcanoes erupt?  Why do they care so much?      Yeah, honestly it was kind of dumb, wasn’t it? I mean, I got it basically right – pressure builds up in the magma chamber and stuff. But the way they asked the question was so confusing. It was like, “_How do you scientifically predict volcanic explosivity?_” when we’ve never even talked about that in class.      I just wrote, “You ask the volcano nicely first and then test the soil pH.” Just messing with you, but I left that one blank. I was so confused I nearly drew a cartoon of Etna wearing a party hat. It would’ve been more useful than what I put, honestly.      Haha, no, don’t get me started. I thought I was doing pretty well until the essay. “ Evaluate the role of human activity in geological events. ” What? Who says geological impacts in short words?      I only started halfway through. I just went on about how people cut down trees and then the ground collapses. Which is – kind of true, I guess, but way simplified. Do you think we’ll even get marks for effort?      If the trainee teacher marking it even knows what they’re doing, maybe. Oh no, remember when Miss Manning left to have her baby and we had that guy with the beret who wore a scarf and called us “students” way too much?      Don’t even remind me. That day I brought a sketchbook and drew him as an over-embroidered dragon. I know that was school inappropriate but I felt it. At least he never noticed.      I’d still like to see that drawing. By the way, did you hear about Geli? She asked the trainee teacher yesterday, “Why can’t we just stick to one good teacher and not have to get a different one every term?” and he just said, “This is how the system works, darling.”      Oh my God, I can go there all day. Like, why don’t we just give the kids highlighters in English class and let them colour in box sets until the exams are due?      Honestly, it feels like we’re roles reversed sometimes. We’re the ones doing all the explaining to the teachers.

So, I read an article today about a new group in town—some people think it’s like a cult... or maybe scientology? Have you heard anything about it?      Umm, is it the one we saw advertised outside the church hall? The one with the big sign saying “Discover Truth”?      Yeah, that one. Some of the neighbours are making a bit of a fuss about it. I think one of the nuns from the parish even came out to dump leaflets in front of their door the other day. Didn’t seem to get far with them either.      Nuns still exist? I thought they were all in The Matrix or something by now. My friend watched a documentary that said religion is like... a system of control, right?      Hmm, not sure I agree. Religion gives people structure, meaning. Sure, there are bad parts—maybe that’s happened in some areas—but in my opinion, it’s about belief and community, you know?       Chirps  Mum, do nuns get Christmas presents?       Smiling  They probably get them from other nuns, sweetheart.      But where do they put them? They don’t have houses.      They live in convents, like big houses where they all share everything.      Right, and they usually get food, clothes, and whatnot donated. But to get back to the cult—well, not a cult, maybe—should you talk to people about it or just let it be?      Why are people so scared of about new religions or groups? I mean, the Church of England had its time, and so did Methodists. Why is that new group so scary?      Some do take things too far. Like hiding stuff from their members or赚钱 off them. You need to be careful. Do you know anyone who’s gone?      Not really. Just some of our Auntie’s friends always trying the 'alternative religions' or whatevs. Some of them are weird—like, one of them wears a crown of thorns because she's really into medieval stuff.      Well, I just worry, you know. It’s a small town, and when people start getting too excited about stuff, it can get noisy.      Maybe we should ask someone from the group to explain it? I mean, over tea or something?      You’d go to that?      I’d go, as long as it’s not a test of loyalty. I’m not signing up for anything with initiation rituals.       Laughs  Fair enough.

Rather skip the dance class, eh?      Aye, it's not that I don't like it, it's just after a week of lectures I fancy a bit of a lie-in and probably scroll through some LoveFilm choices instead.      You'll regret it when we're on the dance floor, and we're both the only ones not twerking.      Aye Aye, but serious question—what’s Old English got to do with linguistics, anyway? I mean, we're not translating Beowulf for fun when we get outta uni.      Well, you'd be surprised. Knowing where language comes from, and how it's evolved like that—y’know, Old English helps us understand how we got to Modern English. It's kind of a building block for everything in our world now. Like, if you’re a consultant engineer, aren’t you all about structure and how things are built?      I suppose. I never thought of it like that before. I mean, I like details and systems—so maybe it’s not a million miles away. Though I still don’t get your thing with runes and symbols and all.      It’s not just runes, it’s about how people used words back then. Like, they borrowed words from Latin, and sometimes it just changes how we see the world. Now don’t go rolling your eyes at me. I’m just trying to make it sound less boring than it feels.      Fair enough. You just make it sound like we’re rediscovering some lost library of letters instead of skimming over Chaucer in a lecture hall.      Kinda about the same, though. And you can thank me later when you finally get into a chat with some hot Danish guy because you can plug and play some vocab from Viking English.      Should've gone with you to that seminar last week.      Aye, it was a roastie. Dr. Whitlow tried to make everyone pronounce “þ” like a dragon was growling. Some of the first-years were trying not to laugh through their whiney lattes.      I bet. You're like a linguist version of goth rock with your obsessions.      Well, at least I don’t study bridges and pretend it's poetry.      Hey, I could have been in the play with you and performed in full Viking dress with a real rune-stick if I wanted to.      You’d have fainted from the string vest and wool cape weight.

Right, so we've got about two hours to get to Rovinj if we want to hit that market before the big midday rush. I’m so ready for some fresh olive oil and wine — I’ve heard Istria’s the best for that sort of stuff.      I’ve read a bit about it, yeah. The truffle oil and wine tasting thing at that little place near Bale? Sounds lovely. But I think we should take a detour to Banišće. It’s got that little church and some amazing viewpoints. They say the views are just out of this world. You can almost see to Venice on a clear day.      What’s a truffle? Like the animal? My friend at school said they’re like weird mushrooms. And what’s a detour?      [Laughing] A detour’s when you go off the main road to see something extra, and yeah, truffles are kind of like weird mushrooms — really expensive, really tasty. You’ll get to try some when we get there!      I was just thinking, if we detour to Banišće, we might land a bit late for the early food stalls at the market in Rovinj. I say we keep it simple. Drive straight in, grab some lunch, then maybe a sunset walk and dinner somewhere with a view. No dilly-dallying.      You know what, Rhys, I might agree with you. Our youngest here doesn’t need to be in a car forever. And I’ve heard the sourdough bread in Rovinj is to die for. Any chance they still serve that  malvazija  wine in about half the place?      Oh, definitely. I had it at a little family restaurant last year — paired it with some grilled octopus. Absolutely brilliant. You’re not thinking of going for the big seafood platter at Bota 50 Bistrot, are you?      I might have it marked as our top spot on the list. If you had it, I’ll have it. No arguments here.      Okay, so if we stick with the Rovinj plan, can we stop somewhere on the way to go for a walk? Maybe check out some of those olive groves? I just love the way the green of the olive trees blends with the blue of the sky here. So peaceful.      We could take the road through Momjan, maybe even stop at the viewpoint by Motovun for a few snaps. Then we head down into the valley.

So did you lot see the video of Sophie last night? She was practically recording her own reaction when she poked Rebecca and she well she just went full anal on her. Honestly, I've seen less shocking moments on YouTube.      Oh I saw it! It was like a two-minute drama in eeny weeny passive-aggressive tones. Rebecca didn’t even say anything at first—just stared at her with that look like, “What the hell was that?” and then Sophie had the audacity to film her reaction. What’s wrong with her?      Honestly, Sophie's taking TikTok a little far. Like, who  chooses  to film someone's shocked face when you’ve just mocked them? My brain hurts watching it back.      Honestly, I was on the bus the other day and this lad I don’t even know came up and challenged me to a game of chess. I said no and then suddenly this happened. He just flicked his hand over the tray and spilled my drink, then said “Check and mate.” I swear I would’ve hit him if I hadn’t been holding my phone in one hand and I don’t even play.      And you didn’t film it? That was brilliant. I would have rhythmically clapped and said “Good one – very 80s.”      You know what’s the real problem though? All these people who think their lives are so interesting and they need to be on record 24/7. Like, who are these people trying to impress? Future historians?      I had the same with my mates at uni. We split into two: the  performers  and the  observers . I’m an observer all the way. I prefer to take the jokes and document other people doing the fails. Let people fall off pews and handle it unscripted.      True. I watched Tom do this thing at the pub the other week. He tried to juggle three crisps with his elbows cos someone dared him. Not only did he fail drastically, he got a bit of sprite in his eye and then tried to 'handle it like a pro' with this ridiculous man-scream. Still cracking me up.      That's classic go-to-school on Monday-viral video stuff though. Just don’t expect me to chuck in a hashtag.      Nah, Tom already added #CrustaceanDisaster or something to his Snapchat and it's been shared like 50 times now.

Rather skip the queue and just bring my own swill in.      Yeah, like I got a big ol’ flask of tea today, and I smuggled a scone in my bag this morning. You can’t blame a girl for trying to save a bit.      Right on. I brought a sandwich today, and I ain't looking back. Proper chicken mayonnaise with a bit o’ pickle on the side—cheers to lunchtime nostalgia.      You lot are all proper sensible. Me? I run out halfway through the day. Had to fetch chips from down the road, just because I forgot me wallet and the takeaway place only lets you pay by card these days.      Oi, no shame in that, Rob. I nearly fell over trying to microwave a jacket potato the other week—my student was far more interested in how it looked than what it actually tasted like.      Aye, you ever notice how we’re always ordering puff pastry and salads? As if we’re still in uni fresher’s week, lads. I mean, I fancy a full plate of chips as much as the next bloke, but today’s dinner is… watching Netflix with a packet of crisps.      Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion none of us eat proper meals. Me and my flatmate take it in turns to phone in a curry or a kebab every Thursday. Saves the hassle of going out at night.      That sounds good to me. I do wonder what normal people are up to when we're all glued to our keyboards at the library after hours, though.      I reckon they’re eating proper suppers, having cups of cocoa and chatting over what they did at the weekend. Not trying to convince the printer it’s not jammed because the bin’s full for the fourteenth time this week.      Aye, the bin is a landmine. I once dropped a biscuit in there and it went straight past the tissue paper and halfway up the sleeve of a student’s jacket.      Ah, classic Rob. Was it that guy from last week who had the dog with the printer cable in its mouth?      If it was, respect—no one in the history of the universe could’ve blamed that dog.      So, tea break over? Back to the grind, or do we fancy a cheeky cuppa in the staff room? I saw a ‘free biscuit’ sticker on the door earlier.

So do you lot ever actually get through anything with all this Twitter business?      You mean apart from the fact it often takes longer than doing the job properly?      Exactly! It’s like half the library’s built from hashtags and memes at this rate. We’ve got a Twitter page, and now a TikTok one as well, but I reckon it just confuses the kids more. They probably think we’re some kind of disco now.      Honestly, someone once commented on our library’s TikTok account saying “Still not feeling the vibe 🎷” — I had to go back and make sure we hadn’t accidentally posted a picture of a hippo in a cardigan.      Yeah, we tried doing a short clip of the new D&D night last week. The lights turned out a bit too Ed Sheeran and the lighting guy looked like he was about to launch into “Thinking Out Loud”.      That’s not what I’m on about though. We got asked why we weren’t on Snapchat. I told ‘em we had one page, but the last post was from 2014 and it only included two pictures of bookshelves and a duck.      Ducks feature prominently – very important birds in the radical, young, post-internet era of libraries. I reckon the duck deserves to be immortalized in stone. Somewhere near the printers at least.      Honestly though, it’s a bit of a balancing act. On one hand we’re trying to encourage students to engage more with study spaces and services. On the other hand – “Can I just ‘eshare’ the lecture notes from 2017?” Honestly, I’ve never met a student who doesn’t know how to ‘eshare’ but couldn’t find the bin.      And it’s not like they actually read the tweets either. Last week I posted a library event with QR code access, and within five minutes someone else had replied with a photo of a mysterious yellow sprite being held hostage by a pen.      That’s the best kind of librarianship these days. Meme-inspired mania. Next go, we need to figure out how to post a real-time status update when the Wi-Fi goes down. It could go viral.      Yeah, but what if the internet’s the only reason anyone’s there in the first place? I mean, we gave up trying to teach students how to ‘ask a question’ properly and just made a 10-step infographic.

Rather than going the traditional route of buying a serviced office, do you think building something specifically tailored for a hospice would be a wiser long-term investment?      I've been thinking about that. If we can secure the right land, and given our budget for this round of capital investments, it might make sense to design something bespoke. It would allow us to integrate better with the existing health services in the area and give us full control over the layout and environment. The BUPA model of modular, patient-centered design is one we might want to look at.      That's a good point. I’ve also been considering how vital the location is. We need to make sure the hospice is in an area that’s accessible by public transport and close to local health services. Tenbury Hill or Broadwater would be ideal, but I’ve been told the land register shows most of it is currently zoned agricultural. We might need to apply for a change of use.      Yes, and not just that, we’ll need to go through a formal consultation process with the local council. I spoke to the director of public health in Tunbridge Wells this morning — land use in the area is hotly debated, especially as we gear up for the municipal elections. We should make sure our rationale is politically sound and – above all – community-focused.      Absolutely. We’ve already liaised with St. Oswald’s Hospice in nearby Tonbridge. They’re willing to share staff, and there's a strong mutual interest in merging some of the emergency services to reduce duplication. That’s a win-win for us and the local NHS trust. What I want to avoid is underestimating the nursing implications, especially when it comes to people at end of life. We can’t compromise on that.      Agreed. That’s why I’m pushing for a dedicated housing section within the building design to accommodate family, caregivers, and occasional hospice guest staff. A multi-functional space that supports both patient care and emotional well-being. And as for the business case — we need to factor in the costs of an estate agent as well. We can’t afford to wait too long on the land.      I’ve received a preliminary set of costings from three agents. One of them is even recommending that we map out a staging process — acquire a piece of land now, line it up for approval, and then go further into the architectural design phase once we’re certain.

Rather skip the newfit one eh?      Aye, it's not real string like it used to be, this gear. I’m more of a traditionalist these days.      Honestly, I can’t even read cursive sometimes! But this photo—it’s so nice. I don’t remember meeting Aunt Mabel until I was about six. Did she live in Dover?      Aye, just off Beachy Head Road, right by the sea. She had a cot in the garden and nothing was ever the same when the wind got up. Funny bloke your granna was, taking a photo of  every  meal. Look at the date on that one—1986.      August 86—that’s when I was born, actually! You never told me this was my mum’s first baby shower. Wow, was that a hot one! Wait, is that Mrs Jenkinson from next door with a perm in every picture?      That’s right. Mrs Jenkinson was a tough old bird, but she knew how to do a perm—personally, I favored the side part myself, mind.      And then, look at this—this must be the Royal Ascot trip in ‘89. Tony looked so dapper in his hat. He wouldn’t let us watch the races until we had a proper English breakfast.      You know what I love about this? The way he dressed for it was just  so  him—proper toad. I tried to mimic his tie once at an open day and the kid next to me couldn’t stop laughing!      Look, here’s you at school, Temperance. That dress was gold, the day the hall had to be closed for a whole hour because some kid let loose a stink bomb.      I still have nightmares about that! And I didn’t do it!      Aye, well the guilty always say that. Speaking of guilty, I tried to apply for that job at the hospice last week—assistant head care thing. Got a bit of a weird vibe off the interview panel.      That's a proper job, though. You’ve got the experience. Did go off really badly then?      No, it was quiet really. Just felt like they were sussing me out more than what your actual skills were. It was like I was up against someone with a degree and a masters and all I had was this old casebook on antiseptic solutions.      Aye, that’s the problem with all the paperwork nowadays. Used to be about gut and experience, not CBAs and 'professional development' nonsense.

Nah, I swear The Conjuring 2 is utter bollocks. I was watching it with my cousin and she got so scared she hid behind the sofa like a proper baby! Honestly, it didn’t even scare me that much. Not worth the hype, I say.      Okay, but that’s just because you  want  to be tough and say you’re not scared. Classic Doncaster stubbornness! I was petrified last week when I watched  Hereditary . Like,  proper  nightmares for three nights straight. It was so slow and quiet, but when it hit—it  hurt .      Yeah, but that’s not scary—it’s just depressing. That film made me want to go visit my gran and give her a big hug. Real life stuff! I prefer proper jump scares, you know, like the old school slasher stuff— Friday the 13th ,  Halloween . Bucks of blood, a chainsaw... proper action!      Oh come on, you didn’t scream when the killer came out of the wardrobe in  Saw ? I remember being in your flat—there I was in the kitchen, as normal, and  BOOM ! You ran out of the room like the devil was on your back. That was hilarious.      Okay, fair enough, but that’s because you  made me promise not to tell anyone  and then you  laughed at me ! I swear, you’re just out to humiliate me. Honestly, you shouldn’t be a good viewer for horror films. You’re too mean.      I’m being fair! That’s called  camra-aderie . I do like being scared though—there’s something about it, you know? It’s like a rush. My mates and I had this bet last term: whoever got the most scared in a horror film, had to do the washing up for a week. I lost.  Big time .      Oh yeah? Who scared you?      Some girl who just said “never watch that again” and then jumped three feet in the air when the static guy came in with the red light in  The Babadook . She then hid under the duvet with go-cupholders for foam fingers and sipped hot chocolate. I had to do the washing up that week. And the week after.      Ha! So I’m not the only weird one, then. I had my mates over last weekend and we started watching  The Ring . I told ‘em I was gonna record how long they lasted before they screamed... my cousin lasted four minutes and ran out.

Rather skip the newfit one eh.      Yes yes.      What was the price on them.      Erm.      It was £29 or something like that.      Yeah yeah it een £29.99.      Yeah I thought as much.      I think they done one this morning but it was easier to just go to John’s place it was just easier to just pop the set on the outside when he come with his big car.      Yeah.      What’s that you got there on the side that My turkey one.      No no this is the new one from the Wood Dronfield company and I think it turned out alright.      Oh better than breakfast, no doubt.      Yeah in fact it was quite good the turkey was quite good, didn’t have the ham in it.      No no, you don’t need that.      Right.      And then, what, did they give you anything for the stickers?      Yeah, they gave me one of those vouchers for, like,£10-off something.      Oh right, you always use those, don’t you.      Well, someone has to. It’s the only way to keep a grip on what we’re spending. Some things just need to be monitored. You can’t be buying an iPad every week!      Apple do make nice gadgets though.      Oh, I agree. But I’ve already got one. And that was you!      Maybe I’ll treat myself to a new one when I go to Spain next month.      Are you staying in a villa on Airbnb again?      You know me. We had such good times there. Though I do miss pizza.      Well, I’ve got news for you. The local place delivering now.      Oh really go on then I’ll see if I can get a takeaway tomorrow.      It’s between 6-8, but sometimes it takes a while. The latest I’ve known delivery arrive was 8:30.      Oh, well, I’ll talk to the postman if it’s not there by 9.      You’ve done that often.      And always with good results.      It’s not a postal service issue, it’s a food service issue!      Well, I’ve had a bit of an operation, so I can be a bit delicate when it comes to my late-night snacks.      You sure you’re up to bedtime?      I didn’t think I was going to make it into my late nineties, but here I am.      It’s funny, isn’t it?

Rather skip ahead a bit here eh. You remember when we did that thing with her in Chester? The first... What was the name of the place? It was down by the canal, had a really long name.      Yes, the Marsh Trait?      Aye, that een! I thought I’d lost the both of us that day if it wasn’t for that laddie with the spaniel. He just pointed us this way, and suddenly we're seeing ducks and swans like it’s a whole different world.      Oh, the kids loved that. specially saw the baby ducklings. Mary kept saying "Look, Look!" every time one popped out of nowhere.      Aye, you should've seen her face when the swan came real close and just stared at her. I think she turned pale for a second.      Yeah, I still laugh about that. I mean, swans are beautiful, but they can be a wee bit intimidating, can’t they?      That’s for sure. I was half expecting her to try to pet it. She looked like she might!      And the real twist? We ended up in this little café right by the canal. Have you ever known a loo to be called "public cloakroom"?      Oh, I remember that! We had to ask the waitress twice before we even knew where to go.      Honestly, I just said, "Aye, maybe it’s just a fancy way of saying 'bog' in French or something."      Anyroad, the tea was good, the scones were better, and I think we sat there for nearly the best part of an hour just looking at ducks and pretending we weren’t lost.      It felt like we were in one of those old English films. Poetic, tranquil. All that peace after the madness of getting lost.      And you know the funniest thing? I found out later that the canal path was just as long as we thought it was—there’s nowhere special to reach at the end! Just more water and more ducks.      Aye, but the journey was the go, really. It wasn’t about the destination.      Spoken like a true philosopher. Although I did manage to drop my sandwich in the canal at the end. Lost a decent Ham and Pickle.      Well, someone had to feed the ducks, didn’t they?      Or maybe that was the plan all along. The great oat-crumbs heist of Chester.      You keep thinking that, laddie.

Mum, thanks again for taking the time to look at my application. I know you’re busy with work and all, but I really want to make this stand out.      Of course, love. It’s no trouble at all, and I’m proud of you for going after it. This post at the sustainable design firm does look brilliant—and well above entry level, if I’m being honest with you. You’re not applying to just  any  old job, are you?      No, not at all. That’s why it’s a bit nerve-wracking. I’ve applied to some other places too, but this one is the real dream job.      And you’ve got the skills for it. I’ve seen the portfolio you made—even I, who can barely pick architectural lines in a drawing, can tell you’ve got talent. But you better make sure your CV and personal statement show  exactly  what they’re looking for. Let’s read through this, shall we?      Yeah, let’s do that. So here, I’ve highlighted my experience with the regeneration project in Finsbury Park. I designed a community space using repurposed materials. The client was a charity focused on sustainability, so I thought that aligned with the firm’s values.      That’s good, but maybe you should expand a bit more on what you did  specifically . ‘Designed a community space’ sounds good, but what role  exactly  did you play? Did you coordinate with other architects, did you manage the budget? Also, have you considered mentioning your Master’s thesis on green architecture? That’s key, love.      Right, the Master’s part—yes, I sort of left it out. Maybe I thought it was assumed since I’m submitting the portfolio.      No, don’t be shy about it. You earned that degree, and that’s more than a lot of people your age have. Write it in, even if you just say “My academic focus on sustainable architecture has prepared me to contribute academically and practically to your firm’s vision.” That’s powerful.      Okay, I can rephrase that in the personal statement. What about my work experience section? It’s not super long. I had my internships, but I haven’t worked in a big firm yet.      It doesn’t have to be. You’re not after experience— you  are the experience, with your portfolio and education. But maybe you can link the internships to how they taught you the value of teamwork and project deadlines.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You used to be able to get a house in this area when we were young and now it's all bally nonsense with prices. I mean, my son nearly had a fit trying to buy a two-up two-down in Swaffham for a quarter of a million.      A quarter of a million! That’s madness. My George wanted to buy a plot of land up near Wymondham years ago and I told him, “George, what d’you think you’re doing? You’re not going to live in a tent.” But he went ahead and bought the lot anyway. Still haven’t made a penny off it.      It’s like that with everything, isn’t it? The cost of living, the cars – I had to chuck my Dacia after twelve years because the lights gave out. You used to be able to keep something fifteen years if you looked after it. Now they break down after six.      It’s the politics, that’s it. We’re not being looked after properly, not in the places like this. We need more houses, proper transport, and decent healthcare. I’ve read in the papers that housing is still way behind demand and nothing’s being done.      Tell me about it. I spoke to the chap down at the village hall the other day – he said they’re trying to get planning permission for some flats on the old quarry site, but it’s like pulling teeth. They want to put in a supermarket first. All they bloody care about is building places to sell tins and beans, not houses for people.      And where’s the people gone? All the young ones are up in Cambridge or London, living the high life while we’re left here with aching bones and not enough to keep us warm.      That’s right. My grandkids only visit once every six weeks. They passed me a fiver and said, “Here’s some money for the kettle,” and left it at that. Not that I expect them to stay, but you miss them when they’re gone.      It’s the same with mine. My Johnny’s in Brighton and sends a card once a year with the same tenner in it. I suppose it’s something. If it wasn’t for the council dentures, I’d be out of luck, I can tell you.

Rather skip the newfit in the living area to get more people through the door. We need that string first floor available for the kids’ music program this week.      Yeah, we’ve been doing a cash £20 spread the week in as well for storage. We haven’t booked it een beginning of June, but we’ve got the fire   escapes   all clear as well. The guys from the A listing came up last week and said all the details were clean.      That’s good to hear. I was worried when the landlord said he wanted the new fit up to fetch the prior floor ready for . Have you spoken to   Derek the fire department   about the access?      Oh, I did talk to him last week. He says the route back into the building is clear and the   staircase   to the ground floor is wide enough for taller crowds. He just wants us to put up some awareness signs for in-case-of-emergencies.      Right. Well, I’ll pass that along to the project manager when we meet next week. Speaking of, I’ve got that short meeting with the landlord to go over the   conversion budget  , as we’ve got a couple of   tenant complaints   about light from the utility room leaking into the common areas at night. He wasn’t happy because the room was used as the kitchen last time.      That was the issue with the last tenant. He’d put the coffee machine someone at full song. Honestly, I don’t know how they managed to run a   coffee bar   from the utility room.      I know – it’s a   management nightmare  . I’ve blocked out Thursday afternoons to meet the landlords for the next few weeks. I think we need to make   clear that the agreement is laid out  .      Definitely, ‘cos the new tenants for that part will probably want to run a   cookery workshop  , and they’ll probably ask for microwave and   oven access   too. You know how it is.      Let’s not forget space calculations with lunches and maintenance. We also need to   protect the glassed-in area  , since the   baby birds   have started nesting by the gooseneck pond again.      Oh, I remember that happened last spring. We had to box in the area with   motion-sensor lighting   to keep the dogs and cats away.      Exactly, and we don’t want to lose any of the   performance floor area   when we do that again.

So do you not like meatballs?      I love meatballs, it's just like... got to be homemade or nothing. Otherwise they're just sad, processed, grey things in a tin.      I know what you mean—some frozen meatball thing with spaghetti sauce that’s just tomato purée and spices?      Ay! My gran used to make these massive juicy ones with fresh herbs and just the best sauce. I’ve tried to recreate it, but it’s like trying to copy gold and end up with lead.      Oh, I remember meatballs like that—from when I was growing up. My mother used to fold in garlic and pine nuts, and they had the turkey on top. Still makes me feel like I’m back in the kitchen on a Sunday.      I think the world should just take a vote for the best meatball. Norwegians would probably say they've got the best... but in my opinion, the best ever is when you have some good puff pastry wrapped around a spiced meatball and you serve it with a lentil sauce.      I mean if we’re going down that road, I’ve seen stuffed meatballs in Cardiff—like Moroccan ones with lamb and dried fruit, wrapped in pastry. It was a Baptiste café, fairly fancy, and I had to eat it with a fork.      Oh, that sounds amazing. I’m already picturing it. And let’s be honest, someone at this table should just invent a new type of meatball just for the purpose of impressing us all.      I’d be down. Make it a competition. Whoever creates the worst meatball about to win... something.      No, no, no. The worst meatball is not fun. Once I had one that was like, a rock with bits of pork in it. Burgundy baked it for guest speaker visit. Said it was 'rustic'.      But was it edible?      It was edible, just... not digestible for over 72 hours.      Ooh, speaking of digestive adventures—remember the Sainsbury’s meatball pizza I had last week? The ones that come go bad really quickly? My partner had to open a window just to air out the flat after I ate it. Honestly, it tasted like something from the ‘90s.      Ay, and you charge it against the hours you cleaned?      I did. I told them over the phone, “Yeah, this is a meatball problem; I need to rest and recoup.”      Listen, if it’s a meatball emergency, then by all means, charge it as an HR crisis.

So do you reckon we should go to York or Scarborough for the weekend?      Yorkshire... either's fine with me. Been to York more than I'd like, actually. A bit touristy for my taste. Charming as the place is, you can't walk past a gift shop without eeny weeny passive-aggressive vibes.      Aye, I heard it’s a bit like that. Like one of them places where every street sells jam but none of it tastes like you expect. Know what I mean?      Definitely. Maybe Scarborough then? It’s like York without the medieval brooding—still got a castle, but it’s less aggressively medieval. Plus, you get the beach. You’ve never been to the North Sea, have you?      Na, and I hear it’s like a different beast altogether from the Atlantic. All flat and grey, no big waves?      Exactly! Walk the prom, maybe pick up a cod and chips, have a bit of sea air. Or we can go inland and do one of those bookshop cafés—there’s a quirky one in a converted chapel somewhere. I think it serves espresso as well as hysterical country house novels.      Sounds good. I’ve been meaning to catch up on some reading, but all I seem to do is skim through the same articles twice.      Ah, the corporate doomscroll. I mean, it feels productive at first. But also suspiciously not.      Tell me about it. So, is it a proper road trip? Any chance we could swing by  that  place in Durham? The one with the university walkabouts and the belfry that’s taller than the vibes.      Oh, you mean Castle Keep? Yeah, if we’re going to the North, we might as well. Got a couple of mates who live near there. They could sort the overnight if you wanted to split it up.      You’re speaking my language now. Like, I’ll propose doing a short stay in York first, then Scarborough or whatevs.      Perfect. You’re not into hotels anyway. That one time in Manchester when I tried to book us a boutique place and you said "nope" after hearing the word ‘velvet box’—vivid memory.      I mean seriously, why would anyone want to sleep in a velvet box? That’s not a mattress, that’s a poetry metaphor.      Well said. Now—music-wise, I’ve been stuck into this new playlist. Lot of folk, some 80s pop, very little taste, but hey, it’s nostalgic.

Rather skip the queue at the café today.      That was a bit mad, wasn’t it? I thought they’d never let me through. I’ve had three cups of tea this morning and I’m still shivering.      Poor you. It’s been a real shock, hasn’t it, with Ruth’s mum? I know you were close to her.      Yeah, I was. Such a lovely woman, so full of life. It’s not like it was sudden—she was poorly for ages. Didn’t make it any easier, though. Her family’s still coping, I suppose.      Of course, only human. I’ve been doing the turkey shop rounds for them—roast left-overs, mince pies, the lot. D’you take mince pie?      Only if there’s something better for breakfast, no thank you. I’m trying to lose some weight, and my doctor said the antidepressants have been putting on the spare tyre so I need to do more walking and less snacking.      Oh, I’m so sorry. Was it that medication you were on? For your nerves, wasn’t it?      Yeah, the one that makes your eyes water all the time, right? I still cry at the news every night. Ruth’s daughter nearly had a heart attack when she started sobbing at the telly during the weather forecast.      Oh no, that doesn’t sound like her at all. That’s so sad. Some people just don’t know how to grieve.      No, she’s never been the emotional type. I think she felt bad about crying, so the other night she had a row with Ruth’s brother. Going on about not showing enough support and things.      That must’ve complicated things. I always tell her family to just let it all out. Don’t hold it in.      I tried, you know. After I found out about my appointments, I thought I’d get a bit of help with lunches and a new plan from the GP. But the next thing I knew, I was informed I’d need a scan—MRI or go home. I didn’t know what stage I was at.      It’s brutal. I had a bloke in my class last term with renal issues. His doctor made him attend a conference and eat nothing but stew for weeks. I had to send him a card saying I was proud of him. Poor lad looked like he hadn’t had a meal since the 80s.

Right, thanks for putting the plates in the dishwasher, Tom. That was a cracking lasagne — where did you get the recipe from?      D’you mean by you, Aunty Cindy, or me, Dad?      Either — well, the timing was excellent and the béchamel  just  covered it all, so I reckon someone had it all planned out!      I think he got the recipe off a top chef site or something. It looked like someone cooked it in a Michelin star kitchen and called it 'homestyle'!      That’s easy enough for you to say, Uncle Jamie, when the only recipe you can do is toast and boiling an egg!      Oi! That’s not fair, young man. You try boiling an egg and I’ll be the first to buy you a watch — a digital one with countdown timer, no doubt!      Haha, yeah, his cookery style is “throw it in the microwave for eleven minutes and hope for the best.”      Come off it, Jamie — you’ve proudly written off two barbecues as ‘experimental’ and only reallocated the blame to the gas canisters. Doesn’t count!      Fair point — but at least I burn fairly large, and sometimes it’s  exactly  the taste you’re looking for.      If what you’re looking for is your kitchen smelling like charred canvas someone painted with an open flame!      It just goes to show the importance of having someone like Aunty Cindy as backup. Any weekend plans?      Actually, we’ve got about five days off after a busy month. Jamie and I were thinking of heading up to Chamonix for some skiing. Proper frost this year, according to the snow reports.      You planning on taking lesson books or binoculars?      Well, the binoculars probably won’t help once we hit the slopes, but the lesson books could come in handy if you and I are being stubborn again and insist we've 'seen a couple of videos.'      That's where you're wrong — this time I’m going with a proper go-kart map: up if you say left, down if you say right.      Honestly, the three of you on a mountain — it’s like watching someone play chess in a thunderstorm and then expecting it to go quiet after the first hour.      Oh, and where are you off to, Tom?      I’ve been lucky to get a work experience placement in the engineering department of that car plant in Tamworth. Uncle Jamie made a call or two, I guess!

So do you remember this one? I found it when I was digging out the photos for the blog post.      Oh my word! That’s  such  an awful photo of me! Why is it me with the badger in the background?      Well, you were the brave one who  allowed  the badger to get within five feet of you! Most of us just stood there screaming in the trees.      I remember that. It was in the Cotswolds wasn’t it? I think it was the night of the full moon or something.      It  was  during that awful trip with the photography group, right? You know the one that Myra dragged us to because she swore there’d be a documentary team there or something.      Oh right! She turned up with a thermal suit and a giant camera and said it would "enhance the experience". I just wanted to take some pictures of fields and not be the odd one out.      And then the badger just  calmed down  and looked you right in the eye. Like it was judging your life choices.      It probably was! I did buy it a snack. Well, a little nut thing from the local market. Mya Mateo told me badgers love cashew pieces.      Yeah, she also told us they like wine. You know what? We didn’t bring that. Probably why the badger just looked at us like “I’ve had a bad day already.”      Oh you had the one with a red head torch and it scared it off, didn’t you?      I did! I was trying not to look like such a professional, but now looking back I definitely looked like some kind of spy.      You should’ve turned it to the side, like for dramatic effect. Remember that Japanese guy we saw in a documentary once? He used a red light and was holding a camera like a chef holding a cleaver.      That was Takahiro, right? And he always called the badgers  tanuki  by mistake.      Oh  that  was funny. We ended up watching the same go-to YouTube clip of his about seven times while we were waiting for "the big one."      Yeah, I can see why the one about him and the sumo-suit badger conservation conference went viral.      I’ll never forget hearing that he had been in the Japanese camera industry for 18 years and still swore up and down that all cameras came out of Japan.

So did you lot ever take the plunge in Ireland? You said something about skinny dipping in the loch.      Oh God, I almost did. We were by this lake in County Kerry and it was   freezing  , honestly, like a jacuzzi for seals. But it was pitch black and all I could hear was Liam the barista back home saying, “If you drown, I don’t clean that up.” So I just got halfway in and got out.      Liam needs to chill. You didn’t even go for it!      Sounds like you’d frozen to death! Still, better than me. I went once at a festival near Sydney. It was like everyone else was a shark and I was jelly.      I’m terrified I’d turn into a pickled potato in the sea and then spend the rest of my life being eaten by crabs.      Okay, alright, no hard feelings. I hear the real horror is being out in the wild and the zombie apocalypse starting.      Oh, you mean like,  x_-Files style? You don’t turn into a zombie unless you’ve snored too much in the shower…      Well, from what I’ve seen at work, it’s mostly the baristas and customers who slap themselves awake after a ten-hour shift. It’s enough to scare the whole café.      Honestly, I wouldn’t want this world at full volume. If the apocalypse starts, I’m taking your bakery, sourdough holder, and the Wi-Fi.      What, and leave me with my starter culture? No chance. My sourdough is the gold standard.      Honestly, if I had to take one skill into the zombie apocalypse era, it’d be knowing how to make proper Jewish food. Burgers, brisket, latkes—call it nostalgia on a plate.      Oh, I once tried making a recipe from Claudia Roden. My apartment smelt like a Yom Kippur feast and explosion all at the same time.      Was it the chicken shashlik? I had that once in Melbourne— terrific . But I think it was more of a Melbourne-Yiddish fusion.      Honestly, the Yiddish verse of what your food should be. I have a few recipes from my nan and one of them is a poem, like actual lines of poetry to go with the stew or something over the top.      That’s brilliant! I wish I had a recipe that was half joke and half loaf of bread.      Nan’s jokes are the main course.

So did you go on the rollercoasters at Alton Towers then?      Oh yeah, the big one—Nemesis—was still my fave, even after all this time. You ride low over the water and the drop just punches you in the chest. Madness.      I’ve never been one for loops and drops. I reckon I’d have been on a log flume or one of those walk-through things like the Harry Potter ones.      Oh, the Forbidden Journey was alright. Slightly overrated in my opinion. Still, watching you get frozen to your seat as broomsticks whizz past you is something people will still talk about for years. But what’s your take on parks like this though? I mean, do you think they’re still as popular with young people anymore?      Honestly, it’s harder to say. I get it—there’s TikTok and all that virtual stuff now. But the social stuff about it never hides, you know? With friends or even taking your cousins, it’s like a shared memory. Even if it is peanuts and popcorn and people queuing with sore feet.      That’s fair. Although, I’ve noticed how campuses have theme park-like services these days. Fast-tracked buses, luxury halls, you name it. It just means students today are choosing a brand experience.      You know what I find interesting? The way universities, and even business spaces, have shifted in how they manage crowd control. Like, they’ve borrowed from theme parks—app-based boarding passes, timed entry, marshals and all. Made me wonder about border security in airports. You know I did some consultancy work there a while back. Interesting parallels, actually.      Oh really? Going back to data then? I mean, if you think about it, the system at an airport is just processing humans efficiently. All that profiling, scanning, and lane management. You can strip a lot of the fear and politics and just look at it as performance optimisation.      Exactly. But what’s always struck me is the psychology behind it all—how you regulate the flow but also set expectations. You come into an airport and the system is set up so you’re never really stopped dead. If you go wrong, you’re just gently triaged into a side queue with a bloke in high-visibility gear and a clipboard.      Like a ride operator redirecting you to the next available cart. True to life, innit?

Rather skip the newfit and go for a jacket and jeans.      Yeah, I’d got the lightweight waterproof one from Dunelm last week. I wore it on the lake where we tried kayaking at the weekend.      Was it any good? I’ve been meaning to learn to row, but I’m told it’s pretty hard if you don’t know what you’re doing.      Kayaking was fine, honestly. It took a while to get used to steering, and we kept capsizing at first—my cousin nearly went under the bridge. You know my cousin, Helen, from Lakelands? She came to see the baby, only that was the first time we’d met properly in years.      Oh right! I remember her wedding—what a summer that was. She’s the eldest of your sisters, wasn’t she?      Yes, and I mean, returning after all that time… it’s different. She was quite little, even back then. Anyway, the reunion was lovely, but— Mum’s not well, I’m afraid.      Oh no! What’s wrong? I only saw her at the bookshop launch…      Yeah, it got her. Breast cancer – early stages, but fairly aggressive, and now it’s spreading again. The doctors weren’t optimistic this time. We’ve all been trying to make the best of it, but it’s hard. Our brother couldn’t come last week—hospital appointments. He was a bit upset.      That’s awful. I’m really sorry.      Thanks. I spoke to my dad today about arranging a weekend walk for the rest of the family, you know, somewhere peaceful. To just… spend some time together. Not that dramatic, but it felt like the right thing to do.      That sounds like something she’d love. A bit of open air, minimal noise.      I tried to reassure him when he started crying while telling me about her childhood. He’s doing what he always does: lunches delivered, the whole whack. Not that I mind—it's just tiring after a while.      I know what you mean. I’ve been there with mine. Grief is like a separate holiday, really.      A what!?      Yeah, seriously. You think you’re in control, you pack the right bag, but then it rains on you and you end up walking in the dark and not remembering half the journey. I read that somewhere once.      Haha, that's cruel, but probably accurate.      So back to the rowing—I’m thinking of joining the Cambridge rowing club.

Dad, I swear you don't even know what a TikTok is.      Oh I do, I do! Just don't see the point in watching a load of people dance about!      It’s not  just  that. People use it to make proper videos and learn things too, like how to send stuff in   Morse code   on your phone app? I saw that the other day.      Morse code? Like, what was that, Second World War thing?      Didn’t it get used in  Star Wars ? Or is that Star Trek? Anyway, can we go past the Boots on Oxford Road first? I need like  three    pens  ,   stationery  , and a   new     glass water bottle   or Aunty Eileen will be on me about my phone being too far away and me not drinking enough, again.      Haha, yeah she was on you about it last Results Day, remember?      Ugh, that was stressful. I tell you, being on Results Day is up there with giving a speech dressed as a pirate for school play. Or having to open a   Vodafone   box by mistake and getting all the bills.      Don't mention that, still not sure how you got that much into my account. It took me   weeks   to find the right chatbot!      Honestly, just someone at the shop should help. I wish my   phone   just did  everything  without me having to install dodgy   emoji   apps and being told I’ve used all my   data  !      Ah well, you’re not the only one. We were down the other week doing an   Amazon delivery   that got   lost   and it took a week for it to appear on a delivery   Update  .      So true. I bought shoes off a random   eBay   seller once and they turned up way too big. I had to stick them to the side and pretend they were  on sale .      At least your   shoes   didn’t smell like  that    food   you left on the top shelf go bad. I still see it sometimes.      That was in July! I had a   memory   blooper. And what can I do? I can’t take fluency tests on how to shop in   supermarkets   and never choose the right type of   vegetable   or get overcharged at the till.      I know what you mean. Always get hit with “university student discount” claims but it's only for   Student Finance   beneficiaries, and then I’m stuck with   extra  -chargy stuff.      I just wish the whole thing with university could come with free   food shopping   vouchers.

Yo AJ, you ain't even gonna believe what my laptop’s been doing. It shut itself off like... three times in the same day. I’m like  wtf ? I think I might need to upgrade or just buy a new one before I go back to uni.      Nah nah nah, I feel that. My laptop’s been running so slow lately—probably needs a memory clean-up or something. Like serious tho, this stuff isn’t cheap, y'know? Especially not if you're a student grinding through exams. You going back to your uni or staying in London?      Tomorrow bro. I’m going back to Bristol. Y’know, working on that Masters in Computing. Just wish I had more time to plan. I tried applying for this exchange programme in Japan, specifically Tokyo, and I think I got in. Still waiting for the final confirmation.       Tokyo?!  Seriously?! Haha, you and your dreams. Last year you was telling me you wanted to go so bad. What university is it?      It’s some uni in Shibuya I think—Tokyo Institute of Technology. It’s only for a semester, but it would be so good for my work placement in AI. Plus, imagine taking Akira Kurosawa walks through the city and actually understanding the street signs. I’ve been trying to brush up on my Japanese through apps.      You might as well just start speaking fluent. I mean, I remember when you said you’d never be able to pass a chemistry exam—look at you now.      Haha, I still  hate  chemistry. But I did make it through. Just about. I swear those exams were trying to brainwash me out of studying anything else. Anyway, I’m barely surviving the housing crisis too. Maybe I’ll do something like ‘rental deposits offset’ or whatever they call it now. You know? Like a guarantor or a bond?      You need a waiting list just to get an apartment in Bristol. I swear to God, every space comes with '2+ years’ experience’ written underneath it. And no, you don’t get a bonus for being a student with a laptop goin' on the fritz.      Exactly! It’s like they only wanna see job histories with big salaries and zero loans. Bro, you still at that marketing placement? Or are you transitioning roles after uni?      Nah, I just took some time off over summer to work at that creperie in Clapham so I could save up for Japan.

Rather skip the new phone altogether eh?      Well I know it's not like it's a real big leap from one to the other but more than I can afford anyway.      I don't think we do need the latest thing as such. Just things that work well enough is eenough if you ask me.      I reckon it depends on how much of a hassle you’ve got with your current one tho. If it's dying on you every couple of days, worth getting something a bit better.      Didn’t even want to upgrade last time – specially with everything getting more expensive. I mean, I still use my 2014 phone for some bits like apps My turkey still works on it! So eccentric.      I had the same one, Viv, and then I upgraded because the little updates started making it crawl slower every day. Now it doesn’t crash every time I take a photo with a smile in it at least, thanks to Elaine! .      Phones, like me bones, just don’t work like they used to! I remember in the 80s you didn't even need a phone, we just went out to meet people.      That’s so true, Bertie. But with the grandkids and stuff these days, trying to meet online and all that, phone has to be the phone.      And with FaceTime, they can even see someone at the same time!      I tried once. I had a picture with my granddaughter, and it worked, and then the picture split in two – like  blink  and there we all were about five times smaller. I thought I had the touch of the green man or something!      That's the reflection of the front and back cameras. My sister had that first time she FaceTimed my gran too.      Speaking of things working, someone suggested we take a trip down to Buckfast Abbey next month.      Ah Buckfast? I drove through the area with my wife once, the 50s or so. Then it was just a place with lots of gothic details on the outside if you ask me.      Yeah it’s quite beautiful inside. We went a while back on a school trip and it was really nice. Lots of history to it and the abbots had amazing tea after the tour!      Is it still going with the tea part?      I’m not entirely sure, but I’ll check for you.

So did you actually like Belgium? I mean, I know you love the French, but I’ve heard it’s got its own vibe out there.      Oh, it was lovely, darling. Quiet, very clean, and they speak English in places—just not as much as I expected. I had to use my Sat Nav a lot, and   it got me lost twice  . Wandered into a village called something like “Sint-Kruis” and ended up in a church by accident!      Don’t mind him. He got a bit of fun out of watching you panic. But honestly, it was  marvellous . All those little markets, the waffles, and that chocolate—absolutely divine. I’ve still got left-over truffles from the market in Bruges. D’you want one?      Wow, was it as nice as the brochures make it seem? I mean, no queues for food or anything?      Oh, no, it was absolutely hassle-free. I had to queue once for chips, but the woman serving was sweet and gave us extra mayonnaise because she liked my accent. And the toilet blocks in the train stations—proper clean, I’ll have you know. No dodgy little loo doors swinging in your face.      That’s huge. I’m always scared of foreign toilets.      And the food—oh, the food! We had this pan-fried herring with onions and fries. I thought it would be oddly sour, but it was just—  perfection  . Not overwhelmed with oil or salt like in some places.      I must say though, the Sat Nav didn’t always help. I had it on a clipboard, and the phone died once. Got stranded beside some cows near a windmill in Flanders. Had to stop a bloke on a bike—he passed me a biscuit and said,  “If you follow the road with the wind, it always takes you where you need to be.”       That’s a bit poetic for a random Belgian cyclist.      Wasn’t that road  steep , though? I think the hills there are gothic. I cycled about three miles and thought I was in heaven until my legs went gelatin.      You cycled!?      I  rented  a bicycle, yes. From a shop near Antwerp. It was a proper classic: gears, bell, chain, the lot. Pedalled like I was in  Mary Poppins .      I drove. That’s the real adventure. Right, unless you fancy getting stuck in some town where they reverse-park  every single car  and honk at you in perfect unison when you make a wrong turn.

Rather do this than watch yet another rerun of that grumpy old cookery show, eh?      Agreed. Although I’m more of a “stir it up and pray for the best” type when it comes to cooking. You’ve got that restaurant chef vibe, so what’s on the menu tonight?      Just a simple chicken cacciatore with peppers and herbs. A bit of wine, a bit of thyme, and we’re sorted. It’s easy as that. You can even do it in your sleep once you’ve done it ten times.      Impressive! I still can’t tell the difference between oregano and thyme in real life.      Oh, left’s thyme and right’s oregano—don’t worry, I’ve got a system. But I did actually watch a video yesterday on how to plant herbs—turns out thyme’s easy to grow in pots. Maybe I’ll start a desktop garden, you know, for the Instagram aesthetic.      Ah yes, tell me—personally I listen to crop care vlogs with the sound off to drown out human voices.      You watching too much TikTok again?      Ha – no, been on a bit of a Facebook hiatus myself. Got too much of my old flatmate’s wedding updates and someone called Karen from Swansea who keeps tagging me in old photos from 2006. Spooky.      I know the one. I occasionally check out my friends’ lives just to feel like I still  have  a social life. Look, are there any friends I should know about from your past?      Oh, you mean like a Ron Swanson failsafe “just in case” provision? No, I think we’re good. My ex-flame from the 90s isn’t even on here. Probably better that way.      Speaking of, I tried using perfume for the first time today.      Oh yeah? And which grand scent do you plan on confusing the poor digestive system of strangers with next?      It’s a lavender-based one called “After the Rain.” It wasn’t suffocating, so I think I passed.      Lavender, blooming wonderful. Lift your arms and you could be planting a garden in someone’s nose.      I think I’m over-accentuating it though. I sound like I’ve been dragged through a field of daisies in my sleep.      Just make sure you don’t romanticise it too much. You’ll start getting DMs from Manchester-towners saying, “Oi you got that scent from a Movember charity shop

Rather skip the queue bar none eh?      Aye, it's always like that on a Saturday, isn't it? You’d think more people could see a queue when there is one.      Aw, don’t worry, mind you — you can’t rush a proper cup of tea and a decent knob of cake, eh?      My George used to say that a man should never leave a flat cap lying in a puddle, but in Australia, you’d get a reasonable slap if you wore no hat at the beach. Didn’t even want to know what he’d have said about sand.      Oh no, you’re talking about Queensland now, aren’t you? I remember you told me once you met an eccentric rich businessman in Brisbane. He was the one who wore the same suit for weeks.      Blimey, that’s the one! And breakfast, no less. I swear half his bloody staff thought he was a ghost, you know?      Aye, he was the type who would expect you to polish his wingtips if you had the pleasure of meeting him. I never did quite work out whether he wanted grief or warmth, that bloke.      You remember what a nightmare it was trying to get a mortgage over there? I had to convince a bank that I wasn’t some “laid-back flatlander” to get them to trust me with a loan.      Laid-back flatlander? Aye, that’ll be you trying to explain a Sheffield accent to some sour-faced accountant with a degree from wherever it is they get them in Australia!      Look, it’s not all brollys and Steve Irwins — you can do proper business down there. But let me tell you, they take their coffee seriously.      Mind, I think the first time I tried to order a flat white, the barista asked me if I was pregnant.      Ohhh, was that because of how I tried to say “flat”? I could see the confusion. Those poor Southerners — they never know what the 'th' and 'gg' do in a word. I swear you try to tell a Southern Englishman that the 'g' in 'Bristol' is silent and he’ll argue you into next Tuesday.      You don’t say, bloke — I’ve met some of them. I asked one time if they ever had a “jolly good tea” down there and she gave me a right funny look. Know what she said?

So do you watch The Crown? I’ve been going through it again—it's just so riveting, even though I know how much they change the facts for drama. I can't get enough of those costumes and sets though.      Oh I haven’t got round to watching all of it. Got a bit obsessed with  The Last Kingdom  instead. It’s got history nerd written all over it, but with that gritty feel. Much better, in my opinion. Still, I can see how   The Crown   is a guilty pleasure.      Didn’t your mum get into  The Great British Bake Off  this series? I mean, I don’t get the appeal of baking shows, but I have to admit the turkey leg pies looked impressive! Although I think it’s time they moved the show from the shed, don’t you?      Yeah, you’re not wrong there. It looks like breakfast, but somehow it’s this extravagant Anglo-nostalgia throwback. I’ve actually been enjoying a comedy on YouTube more—it's this bunch of uni students doing satirical news. Total laugh, and it’s refreshing to hear some takes I don’t usually come across.      Hmmm, I might have to check that out. I’ve been getting most of my “news” from podcasts lately. This one called  The Infinite Monkey Cage —bbc thing, right?—they talk about science, but through comedy. If I understand one in ten of the words, I’m in heaven.      Oh yeah, that one is great. I used to listen with my students before class. It's a real hit with their sense of humour too! We did a project on it in about late A2—great motivation for listening practice.      Oh yes, you always found clever projects. I remember you brought in that series of TED Talks for us to do debates on. That must’ve been six or seven years ago now. Still, I have no idea where it went. My life seems to consist of eating vegan pasta, tidying my flat, and being overly obsessed with  The Great British Baking Show .      At least your flat doesn’t resemble a bookshelf explosion like mine does. I’m like a student all over again. But really, being a part-time teacher does cut into my reading and watching time. I’m trying to keep up with a few Instagram accounts now—mainly recipes and queer stuff.

Right, who’s ready for a trip to the pool tomorrow? I’ve booked it for half an hour first thing, and I’ll take them both for a bit of cake at the café afterward if they behave!      Caaaaake!      And ice cccre een!      Well, maybe   a   bit of ice cream… not too much before swim goggles start fogging up! Now, Pippa, remember your goggles go   on top   of the rubber ring, not behind your head like last time when you turned into a squinty little goldfish.      I   am   the best fishy!      You are definitely the best   squinty   one. Now, I’m picking up the Oliver from Toni this afternoon—he’s helping me round up all the photos for Pippy’s Blue Peter badge. She needs a total of 12, and I only found three under the sofa.      I have a picture of the   Travelling Circus  ! I saw it, and it had a man with a   lion  !      Oh, that sounds like a good one.
