I wanted goldfish from the gashapon at the shops…      I wanted toys that shoot!      You’re six and six.   Toys that shoot   should happen at a   very   advanced age. And the goldfish are probably too expensive for the   elephant amount   of pennies you have in there.      But Ms Monica always gives me lunches! I   want   to do   something   with money.      Pippa, you can earn goody money on pond life if you tidy your room properly. But only if you leave the licorice out of the box this time—and don’t try to plant it in the planting pots.      That was a   mistake  …      Yes, it was a mistake, and Mumsy found it growing in the carrots. Speaking of which, do you remember the story I told you once about the Chinese who eat   months-old eggs  ?      They’re   scrambled  , aren’t they?      No, no, they’re still   hard-boiled  , and they’re called century eggs! They look like strange moon rocks and taste a bit like… strong stilton, I think.

So did I, but it was weird.      What was?      You know, when we went up for that joint and we had that wine      Yeah?      Well, you were fine. But he was... not on it.      Not on it?      Yeah, I mean I don’t want to make him out too much but, um, he was alright earlier, pulling me closer and everything...      Didn’t it get awkward?      It did, yeah! I mean I don’t expect someone to just, you know, be perfect like that the first time. But I thought... I dunno, you know, I’m not the type to expect too much and I think he turned round and said he’d just been a bit ‘in and out’ lately.      Huh.      Yeah! That’s what he said. Like he was trying to make it sound normal or something.      I mean, maybe I’m short-sighted, but to be honest I think that  could  be a bit…      What then?      Mate… Erectile Dysfunction. I mean, I know you don’t want to call it names or make assumptions, but if you couldn't even get it up and you’re not on anything and he's just someone who, in your words, ‘seemed alright earlier’, yeah, I’d definitely be thinking about something like that.      Ergh! I don’t even want to think about it in about five days time. I mean I just want to forget it happened.      Oh! You know that was you! I mean it is a classic first date kind of blip.      Is it? Cos it felt like total humiliation.      Oh, it wasn’t, no way. I mean he was awkward after. You didn’t  notice , but he was like, trying to find his phone and stuff and then just left without really saying goodbye.      Ugh! I didn’t even go out of my way to be rude or anything. Just said it was nice to meet him.      You’re not to blame. It’s not like you asked for it!      Well, you know, maybe I’m overthinking it. Maybe it was stress or something. I did say to them that I wasn’t the type of person to be pushy.      That's the thing, right? I mean we’re not in that position to want to make it happen, you know? Just, we were on a date and we wanted to see if we had chemistry.      Che-mes-tree?

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh?      What?      The scales lying to us. I put them on this morning, and I lost a stone, and then this morning again it was different. You wouldn’t have thought it would lie to you like that would you?      Well yeah, I think they all do that if you use them in different areas of the floor. A lot of them just measure pressure from your feet, so depending on how far back you are or if you’re balancing or not, the numbers change.      Mm, I saw that online. But even if I made sure I was standing in the same spot, same time of day like that… you know, I’ve lost enough to not need a lie from a machine to make me feel better.      Fair enough. But if you're using Slimming World’s Healthy Extra breakfast, you don’t need to worry about "syns" either. That’s the deal, right?      Yeah, I still check the backs of things though. I do like the 0 calorie syrup, but I always wonder if it’s just as flavourful as the real thing. Honestly, I’ve got a funny feeling it's just sugar in a different colour.      Have you got the cinnamon one?      Yeah, the mint one's quite nice actually. But you have to be careful not to pour too much. And, God forbid, if someone at the house tries it. They won’t like it. They expect the sour or lemon kind.      Oh I know. Any tea I make using that mint one, it’s like a conspiracy about how I’m trying to poison them. But it’s all healthy, innit?      Yeah, that’s the key. I’m saving up for a treat day next Saturday, so for the rest of the week I’m going to be extra strict. I told my calendar it was a roast day, so it set it as a reminder for me on Friday. We’re doing cauliflower cheese and that double peas from the freezer.      That sounds better than the Quorn chicken slices I tried last night. I mean, it was edible, but I wouldn’t say it smelt like real chicken.      You’re not the only one that’s thinking like that, I can tell you. Supermarkets need to up their game with the Quorn stuff. Although, we did get those veg box deliveries last week, and to be fair the quality was better than I expected.

So do you think we could maybe avoid the whole Christopher Nolan thing next time? I mean, I know he’s got the big brain and all, but I just want a holiday where I don’t have to think about anything deeper than “is that beach over there or what?”      Fair point. I liked the idea of somewhere where the   most stressful thing   is figuring out how to order a gelato in Italian. Not where I spend three hours debating the nature of reality between sips of coffee.      Exactly. So I was thinking, maybe the south of Portugal? Get a villa near the beach, just us and the kids, no phones, no deadlines, no meetings in my head. Just… sunshine, sea, and me not having to wake up before 8am for once.      That does sound like a perfect day in your world, doesn’t it?      It does. And while you’re in there dreaming about perfect days, I’m wondering, what even is   your   perfect day? I mean, walking around Wateringbury Fields, maybe reading some sci-fi, or are you secretly a maximalist who wants to spend a day in a smart suit binge-watching something on the sofa with a cup of builders?      You know me too well. I just don’t like to admit it. But don’t get me started on the perfect day idea—I already had a go at describing mine in the coffee shop someone said, "That’s suspiciously not my real life."      Oh yes, the dream holiday versus the holiday you actually   get  —they’re  very  different things. Especially when about half the time is spent trying to remember the   real meaning of “quiet vibes”   versus whatever your kids decided is their new hobby. I mean, yesterday George wanted to build a secret jungle using  all  the cushions in the house.      And Max wanted to become a pirate and was holding everyone hostage. At 7am.      We are not parents anymore. We are professional negotiators and space navigators.      So, if we ever reach that mythical  perfect holiday , with no kids and the sun shining and nobody wanting to get arrested for climbing a tree or whatever – what would you actually do in that day that  you could only do if the world stopped being your normal self ?      Well, writing-wise, I’d love to write something proper—like, a real novel, not just the ‘mom blog’ posts or whatever I tend to string together these days.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's always a mither when we don’t hear back from the group properly. But I suppose it gives folk a chance to think.      Yes, but I'd rather have a bit of a shout than nobody at all. I've already had to change my plans with the birthday arrangements.      Oh aye? When is it this year? I do like a good send-off, don’t I?      Twenty-third, like always. Funny that, when I was younger I used to grumble like mad about it. Now I’ll take any attention I can get, I suppose!      My word, you seem to have aged gracefully then. Well, I’ll come to the party—weather permitting, of course.      Blimey, you’ve been saying that for years, and I’ve never seen you skip a one for the weather yet. I expect the same again this year, even if it's a downpour!      Right you are, you get me in and we’ll be fine in there with a few pints and a few old jokes, like always.      Exactly. I’ve been meaning to show you the postcard – Matey sent it from somewhere in Scotland, it seems. Got some great snap of her standing in front of one of those highlands glaciers.      Aye, those pictures from up North always look grand. Although I’ve not been there in ages – years.      They’d better not be too busy up there being ‘independent’ all the time, as they like to say about the place. Seems a right waste of the good scenery to me.      There’s not much point to any of it, really. The whole lot of it—being clever, arguing over maps and borders. Doesn’t do much for ordinary folk like us at the end of it.      Precisely. I suppose people get too convinced by what they read in the papers. Though I’ve seen enough to know the people there keep on going with their lives no matter the politics.      Then again, if it's all the same goings-on on both sides, maybe it does make sense. But I'm just not in the mood to be making a decision for the lot of them.      That’s the spirit! You and me both. We’ll mind our own gardens and leave the big ideas to the talk shows, eh?      Aye, that sounds like a plan.

Right, so today you two did this wonderful picture of a chair for the Syrian refugee children, didn’t you? What was the idea behind it?      We wanted to show them where they can sit in class. Not like the scruffy chairs in our classroom — our chairs are  proper  chairs!      Yeah! Miss said some kids haven’t got chairs at all. So we drew chairs that are  super  comfy and have a blanket. They can use it to read stories.      That’s such a kind and thoughtful idea. I’m so proud of you both. Did you talk about what kind of chairs to draw?      Yeah, first we did boring folding chairs — you know, the ones you get at the library. But then we thought they should be fun, so we made one with wheels!      I made mine look like a throne. I called it the King’s Chair.      Oh really? So you designed it yourself?      Yeah! I drew gold ones, and it had a red cushion. I told Miss, “If they feel special in the new land, maybe they won’t feel scared.”      That’s brilliant. I love how you both thought of the way it makes someone feel — it’s not just about the chair, it’s about making someone feel welcome.      We also talked about  who  uses the chairs. We made one for a baby, so someone can hold it. And another with a backrest for older kids who want to do schoolwork.      So you worked out different types of chairs for different purposes? That’s amazing for your age. Did you enjoy the drawing part?      We were allowed to use shiny pens! My chair looks like it sparkles. I even drew a rainbow on the side to make it happy.      Miss said they might hang all the chairs up at the school so it looks like something from a fairy tale. I hope they do!      I’m sure they will. You’ve both learned so much from this — not just about chairs, but about being kind and creative. You should be so proud of yourselves.      Miss go me a gold star for being  gentle .      I go two, cos I helped the other boy in my class who couldn’t draw a straight line. I showed him how!      Well those stars are well deserved. It’s so important to talk about what’s happening in the world, and to learn how we can help, even if we’re at home.

So did I tell you yet? Sarah’s pregnant again. I think they’re just jumping straight into having a second after the first was born so quickly. It’s only been like a year and a half, isn’t it?      No, you didn’t. That’s fast. Do we know how far along she is?      I think she announced it at the last group dinner. She’s only about six weeks or so. Honestly, I’m so delighted for them. It’s not like it’s a surprise—they were always going for at least two kids, but still… You know how it is, things like this make you stop and think, don’t they?      Yeah, definitely. It’s strange because I remember when they got married, and now there’s a little one and another on the way. I think it’s amazing. They’ve got it all figured out, better than I do.      Don’t be silly. You and me, we’re not in that race, are we? We’ve got the teaching, the deadlines, the marking—there’s enough on our plates without a tiny human demanding constant attention. Or a couple of tiny humans!      True. Although… sometimes I wonder if we should give it a shot. Not that I’m trying to convert you right now, but sometimes it does cross my mind. You know, the idea of having a baby and changing our dynamic.      I know, and I suppose I do too. But juggling two lectures a week, a research paper due next term, and— laughs —the occasional red wine and Netflix night is enough for now. No need to add anything else to the chaos!      Fair point. And besides, watching Sarah juggle her PhD thesis and being a mum is impressive. She barely left the house during the day last semester—half her lectures had to be moved online because she was expressing and putting baby to bed and getting up again. I admire her strength, really.      I know. I sort of wish the two of us had that kind of drive. Although, trying to find conference funding and writing grants sometimes feels like enough of a challenge. Still, maybe after a few more years of the grind we can go back to the question of if we  want  to slow down.      Hopefully by then we’ll have a better idea of what we actually  want  instead of what we think we’re ‘meant’ to want.

Rather annoying isn't it, how even in the countryside, they glue sticks to everything—the lampposts, the bins, the roads. You’d think they’d give it a rest.      I know. “No littering, No smoking, No dogs,” like the place was burgled on Tuesday and now everything’s got a sign. It’s just madness.      Though I suppose that explains why I haven’t seen one dog all week, unless they're hiding under bed sheets pulling leashes. We’ve walked three miles and seen not a single squirrel, let alone a pup.      Maybe they united and formed a revolutionary alliance, led by a ferret in a waistcoat.      You know, I actually got into a funny argument over this the other day with Oliver at the uni. I jokingly asked why we can’t just stick a sign on the moon saying "No politicians", and he said, “Why not? The Ministry of Silly Walks is already there, you know.”      Good one. He’d say that—always dragging in those surrealism references. Though I have to say, your idea did have a certain bureaucratic charm.      Oh, I wasn't joking. I seriously want a “No sarcastic comments – this is a superstitious area” sign. Just to confirm that we’re not all cursed by black cats, broken mirrors, and rogue shoes.      And toilets that never flush properly. I swear one of the toilets at the university just glares at you.      That’d be a great scene in a comedy show—stand-up about university toilets with bullying plumbing. “Why did I become a university lecturer? Because I wanted to touch the soul of young people. And also because the kettle fails to boil water at least twice a week.”      You do have a gift for the dramatic. Speaking of which, have you heard about that new comedy open mic the student union is running?      Yes, I’ve been persuading a few students to enter as well. Though I’m not sure if trying to get academics into the comedy circuit is the same as trying to get fish to remember a password.      That’s one way to put it. But if you ever go up there, I expect posters line the walls. “Upcoming Event – Dr Lucy Jones: A Fully Educated Snark Machine.”      I’d bring a policeman to emcee just to enforce silence.      And if that fails, bribe the audience with pie and custard.

Dad, I just wanted to go through the whole thing about the van again. You said you'd seen a couple of them on the motorway side now?      Oh yes, over by the old garage in Cheriton. They look like they'd do the job well enough. Big enough for your box set and the furniture from the attic. Not like that little dickybug you had last time!      I think I'll have to get a trailer one, actually. It was easier pulling it with the car when we were moving the flat. Didn’t even need a hire van. You don’t like those things, though, do you? Still, it’s the only way to get the box springs across without Myra complaining.      Yeah well, you know Myra. She’d moan if you brought in a bloomer the size of a phone box, just as quick as if it was too small. You need to measure up, luv. And don’t forget the china cabinet! That thing’s taller than you and twice as heavy. I still don’t like you moving it, you know.      I know, but Aunty Brenda said she and the other grandkids will help. It’s not like I’m doing it on my own. You’re coming too – that’s been settled. I wouldn’t dream of trying to move without you. You’ve got eyes for these things.      Right, and don’t be leaving the screwdrivers in the airing cupboard again. Last time I looked in there, I found half a fishing rod and an out-of-date jar of marmalade. Mind you, I still used the line to mend the fence last spring.      That was you? I thought the holes had just gotten worse from the weather.      Not you! I fixed it. You’d be in trouble if Myra found that lot. She’d tell her twin about it, and that would be me on the receiving end of something bloody sharp.      I miss when we went to the Dorset Steam Fair and I didn’t have to worry about trailers and lunches to keep the whole lot fed. Now it's like planning a military op.      That place is brilliant still. You really need to see if you can go again – at least before the line in the paper becomes a pension. You’ve got that mobile phone, your lot will keep in touch.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be trying to encourage reading, not shut it down. I can't believe they're seriously considering it.      I know, I saw something about it in the  Deerfield Post . Seems like they want to build a new town hall or something on the site. But that place is a bit of a listing, if you ask me. I mean, it's a shame, though—every town should have a library.      Didn’t it get a bit of a facelift like ten years ago? I remember when they repaintig the front and replaced the windows. You know, like that old post office in Southfield? The outside left it looking like it did in the sixties, but on the inside, I think it turned out alright. It used to be a bit of a character when you walked in, you know?      Oh yeah, I remember the oversized clock that used to be on the wall—and the creaky floorboards that almost made you do a pirouette every time you walked across them. But the problem is, libraries cost money to keep running, and as we’ve seen, the municipal budget is stretched quite thin. They probably think it's too expensive to keep open with all the other things they need to finance.      Still, I reckon they could do something with the old building instead of just knocking it down. There are those modern designs where they keep the original facade and build a new structure behind it. I've seen some lovely examples in the south—like in Belford. The outside still looks like the old town, but the inside is about as modern as you can get. That's the way to go, in my opinion.      Definitely. I know some people might argue it’s better for progress to have something new, but I just like the look of an old building. It gives the place character. You can't say something fresh ever adds the same charm. It’s just not the same. We lost that good-looking colliery in Harton陉      That was a bittersweet move, wasn’t it? Gave the town a new shopping area, but the colliery really had that old-time feel. I wonder if anyone has made a stand in the paper yet against this library plan.

Rather skip the new Spotify Wrapped this year.      You just listened to  Bring Me to Life  and some reggaeton, like, 200 times.      Well… it worked for 15 years of insomnia. Why fix it?      Honestly, I don’t think you need   wrapped   to tell you your top genre is a playlist that only plays when your head hits the pillow.      It was a dump of energy. We had to vacuum the car and triple rinse the pots, but the garden is looking good now.      Someone’s still got termites the size of small mammals. I saw one climbing the turkey leg.      That one? That was a napkin rat. Darcy, pick your head up off the steering wheel—Don’t you dare eat that pen!      Look at you, returning to childhood in a car full of clutter and oversized desktop hides, rewatching Netflix and eating expired Army cookies.      At least you didn’t spill coffee on your crop sweater again.      Did I? Huh. I might’ve.      I saw that new show “The Diplomat.” Baptism of fire. I almost became one because the first 10 minutes were subtitled in Ancient French bureaucracy.      Oh, don’t talk about toilets and wine in Parliament.      Just because my tongue wasn’t tied to the wall at school doesn’t mean I don’t crave a bit of  intrigue .      You’re like a conspiracy about geopolitics with walkie-talkies.      Alright, present ideas. Who wants what? Sarah, are you still collecting vintage combs?      Yeah. Burgundy hair clips, ones with diamanté, not that sparkly nonsense.      Do you know how many of those you’ve already got?       Exactly  how many I need.      I told my son to get her a hair band set from a junk shop. Priced the same as a go-kart on pond life if you ask me.      I was thinking about getting into tie-dyeing face masks. Lift your hands if you think I have the flu or 2006 in my DNA.      True to your roots: fearless, avant-garde, and not at all fitting in.      I’d buy one. Totally trendsetting. With a little CBGB vibe.      Or maybe we can just cover it with glitter and you’ll wear it to work and your customers think you’re a DJ.   Speaker_1 :   Before we lose the signal and the goat, who wants snacks? I have chocolate-coated straws and pepperoni crisps.      Deliscious aka like eating the future or a failed experiment.

Right, I just wanted to go through a few things with you about the car insurance, seeing as you’re thinking of taking the car out more often now you're getting your learner’s license.      Yeah, I thought we’d already have to sort things out for motor insurance sooner or later. Got a bit confused when I looked it up online, though. I reckon it depends on how much I drive?      Precisely! Now, I’m the main policyholder, and if you’re gonna be using the car, I'll need to add you as a named driver. Otherwise, you can’t legally drive it even if it’s on my insurance.      Oh, I didn’t know that. So if I don’t get added and I accidently drive it, I could get into trouble?      Aye, that’s an added risk — not just for you, but for me too if I knew and didn’t add you in. Insurance companies usually expect the named drivers to be, well, named. Also, the more driving you do, the more it could increase the premium.      I don’t really want it to cost you more. It’s not like I’m going to be using it every day. I’ll only drive it if it's really necessary?      That’s good because the other option is a provisional policy, but they're often more expensive and have limits on mileage. Besides, you’ll be learning, and the more you get into the car, the more they might read into it. Besides, I can always buy some additional cover for periods of high use if you want.      I hadn’t thought of that. So about how much more is it going to cost to add me?      To be honest, not too bad. Maybe around £200-£300 extra a year, depending on the insurer. But that’s if you’re added as a designated driver. If you’re just a pass-by, it might not cost anything, but then you can't drive it. As long as you stay within the bounds of what the policy allows, we should be fine.      Okay, that sounds doable. So once it's added, can I drive go anywhere?      Not  anywhere . Motor insurance is specific in where you’re covered. For the most part, it’s the UK, but you might need something else if you want to drive in European countries.

Rather skip the curry and just go for a Chinese takeaway, but then the chicken in the korma was... What's the word? It tasted like it had seen better wars.      You’re talking about “off”? Or like “waxy”? I wouldn’t say it was in good condition, if I’m being honest. It was like chewing on wallpaper.      Exactly! It was all rubbery and dry. Why do takeaway places think undercooked chicken is a feature and not a bug?      Oh亲爱的, when it's chicken, undercooked or rubbery, it's just part of the charm. That’s the takeaway version of "I’ve been in poverty and it’s showing."      Haha, fair point, but I still think the risk of salmonella is not worth the experience. Or the mental image of the chicken’s windpipe.      Windpipes, eh? That’s a bit personal, love. You want to get into windpipes and the anatomy of why chicken is never actually like chicken from the shop, maybe we need a podcast.      What would it be called?  “The Curry Chronicles: A Descent into Flavoured Disappointment” ?      Mate, if you could monetise awkward silences and poorly cooked chicken, the podcast would already be a bestseller.      Actually, you know that wholeEquality referendum in Ireland was someone’s chicken curry moment too. Just trying to stay afloat, one oddly sour sauce at a time.      That’s being diplomatic. That was a  revolution . You know, most people about forty or older finally woke up to the idea that the sun doesn’t come up just for them.      Speaking of which, have you managed to run into that stress test thing they talk about in the articles? You know, the one with the questions? Like, “If you lost your job, would you have a mini heart attack or just a strong opinion on the weather?”      Websites like that are the modern-day equivalent of horoscopes. “You’re going to have a productive day where you relearned that the printer is still broken and your manager still hates you.” Not very motivating or useful, really.      Honestly, the only thing that properly tests my stress levels is trying to pronounce “Wexford” on Google Maps while it laughs at you with its best British accent. True to life? No. Fun to overcorrect? Definitely.      You know my stress test is trying to get our toddler to pronounce “podcast” without throwing it in the bin. Toddlers are the human equivalent of poor internet signal.

So do you reckon we’ll get through the cloud cover once we get onto the M62? The pidgeon forecasts are dire today.      I’d say probably not. The satellites are showin’ heavy build-up over the Pennines—looks like rain. But it was sunshine bright eenin’ when I left the house.      I’m tellin’ you, I’ve seen a plane go past the top of the hill, like, ten times. It must be like that journey from Bolton to Leeds, but for aeroplanes.      Careful, son. That’s how people end up asking questions like “What’s the difference between a helicopter and a pigeon?”      Ha! Yeah, but you know what I’m sayin’ Darcy, the way the clouds are lookin’—it feels like we’ve got to break through breakfast, lunch and tea just to get into Manchester airspace.      Don’t listen to her, Liam’s plane. We’re not escalators, we’re like terraces—you just go up one hill and hope the next one lets you down somewhere dry.      But what if we go over the country and the clouds flatten it out then we just go floating over the fields?      Right, now that is a problematic image. Let’s try not to imagine that as we drive past the Nando’s junction.      There’s also this funny thing in one of the books I read—somewhere in山西, I think it was—everyone had to walk up a hill and then the politicians would be at the top analysin’ the weather because it was about cosmic influence or somethin’.      You’re going off a bit, aren’t you? But I know what you mean. The old upland folklore—being on a ‘high’ meant being closer to the will of the gods. Though I reckon they reckoned it was a democratic uplift too—high ground, high authority.      But you had queens and kings on the high ground too.      Aye, the same path really.      Right. Enough of that. Let’s pivot. Mags, your law conversion course—how’s it going?      I had to convert everything from grams to kilograms when I did the assignments. So I’m like fluently bilingual in kgs and grams now.      It’s a pity we don’t have ‘miles prononciation’ translations like that. You know—keeping miles to yourself and letting everyone else convert.      That’s probably how the EU Referendum went, honestly—everyone used ‘miles’ and ‘kilometres’ in the same sentence and we all just looked confused.

So do you just mean like something like gravel or something like that.      No, it’s specifically for candles—like the ones you put down the sides to keep the flame steady. You can get it in craft shops or even the DIY kind of places. It’s all sand-coloured but it’s kind of designed to dry the paint if you use it for that too.      Oh, right, but would that mess up the candle if you use it in a jar? I mean, do people actually use it like that for decoration?      Yeah, I saw a YouTuber do it. She put a couple of pebbles in the bottom of a glass jar and then placed a pillar candle on top. It made it look like a little beach scene or something. Darcy, you used to make fake mini-forests with pebbles and moss, right?      I mean, I did micro-terrariums, not faux beaches, but you know the kind of vibe. It’s actually kind of meditative. I do that when I need to take a break from illustrating. Anyway, what were we talking about before I got distracted by candle aesthetics?      Vegetarianism. Or rather, synthetic meat. Akira was saying she got a chance to try some cultivated meat at this startup event the other day. It was actually not bad. Silky even.      What, they’re serving food at startup events now? I’m not surprised. I tried this lab-made salmon a while back—looked convincing, but tasted a bit like bland chicken. I still prefer real fish, though, as long as it’s sustainably farmed.      Well, I get that. I’ve never been a huge fan of the idea of "lab meat" because, for me, the process just sounds like they took the soul out of eating. But if it saves animals from cruelty and helps the environment, maybe it’s worth trying. I tried some mushroom-based burger once—it was okay.      Right, but isn’t it the same with a lot of meat substitutes now? Some of them are weirdly good, honestly. I tried a steak alternative the other week that looked really fake but tasted like steak. If it hits the right notes, do we even care that it's synthetic anymore?      Yeah, but what about the vitamins? I’ve been reading that a lot of vegans and vegetarians struggle with B12 levels. I started taking a vitamin supplement at the chemist where I work.

Right, I just clicked "buy" on that phone. Cheapest I've seen it anywhere.      You sure it’s not one of them dodgy secondhand ones? Last time I bought online, I got a phone that didn't charge properly.      Nah, I read the reviews, and it even got one from   OldManGamer2001  . Sounds legitimate.      Why not just go to the shop and try it yourself? You don’t have to be the first person to click “Buy” online.      Because, love, it's  6pm . I've been lying here all day doing nothing, and now that Myra’s watching "How I Met Your Mother" for the 1,000th time, I feel vaguely sad in a nostalgic way.      Mm, it doesn’t feel old if you watch it when you're 23 and pretend it’s modern. Roger hides, you remember?      Yeah, and that man still thinks he knows Ted’s mother. I mean—what are the odds? Like, did he read the grief handbook or something?      Anyway, back to phones. Have you got one yet, Akira?      No, I’ve just been using Anna’s old one. It’s from 2014. If I drop it, it crashes and gives me a photo of a butterfly instead of an error message.      That's oddly poetic. You drop it, it dies a little, and then gives you a metaphor for your life slipping away in a flower bed.      You’re dramatic. But okay, point taken. Both of you need new ones. I’ll buy you both the same one and we can unbox them together like it’s a  YouTube  video.      Mm, I’d prefer to unbox a Christmas present from my gran. At least that way I can cry at the ribbon while being genuinely moved.      Ah, yeah, speaking of… Grans invited us over for the big Christmas lunch thing. She’s even got this new course on the "healthy festive goody bag". It's about 80 per cent beetroot and 20 per cent disappointment.      You sure it's not 50-50 beetroot and Santa?      No, I doubt she’s hearing from Northern Ireland at this stage. But either way, we should go. It's a family event; if we don’t show up, the cat will cry. Again.      Okay, but only if we can play board games after. I swear there are 30 copies of  Trivial Pursuit: Christmas Edition  in that kitchen.      And if we win, we get chocolate.

So did you go back to Lincoln for the summer or just do everything online this time?      Oh yeah, I actually went back for a few months! It was nice to see my family and just switch off for a bit. How about you—get to travel anywhere exciting?      I went to Spain with my flatmates. We did this road trip—Madrid, Granada, Seville—and then just chilled in a little surf town on the coast. It was mad how much it poured one day in Seville. You’d never believe it, but the place was flooded in the streets.      Haha, classic. I love that you still do that kind of thing. I still haven’t managed to get to Barcelona. It’s just always felt like the right time never comes, you know?      It will, definitely. I’d say go when it’s chaotic if you want a real experience. Speaking of which, what’s the deal with your job now, then? I keep meaning to ask.      It’s fine, don’t get me wrong—admin side of research, quite a bit to organise. I love the university setting still, but I’m watching other people move into more data-oriented roles. You’re in the coordination side—is it any different?      Totally. I help liaise between researchers and funding bodies, so it’s a bit more strategic and meeting-driven. But I also help in the field sometimes when they're doing phonetic studies. I’m quite lucky to get to do both—job’s very hands-on.      That sounds amazing. I’d love to do more fieldwork, honestly. My sister just went to New Zealand and worked on a Māori language project. She said the communities are so open to researchers who really care.      That’s so cool. I’ve always wanted to visit Aotearoa. I have a friend who did a study on te reo Māori in Cambridge, so when I get a chance, I’m going over. Though I’ve only managed to get as far as Scotland recently.      Was it any good? I did a shoot in Glasgow once for a media project. It was my first time up there and I got so confused by the weather. One minute it’s brutal cold with hail, next it’s gloriously sunny and we’re in shorts.      Sounds like it was a bit of a ride!

Right, I just wanted to say sorry for last night, I know I was a bit moody when we were watching the film.      No worries, you had a hell of a day with lectures and all that. I would have been grumpy too. Just like you gave me a good eeny weeny massage last week to wind down, right?      Yeah, I remember that. It wasn’t just the muscles that were feeling better after, you know what I mean?      Aye, and what was that when you said the bloke in your lecture was asking for essays even though it’s dead week?      Yeah, it was like everyone else thinks university should be exams only. I got so annoyed I just wanted to tell him I’m not even gonna pick up the pen unless the uni gives us an extra week holiday.      Maybe you could just ignore him. Not write the thing, and see if he ever mentions it again, you know?      That would be ideal, wouldn’t it? Might get me some extra credit for creative defiance instead of handing in a week late and ending up with ten per cent.      Exactly, and if it doesn’t work out, I can always give you a foot rub to make you feel better after.      Now don’t go making promises you might not be able to keep, Liam!      Aye, but I always remember. Just because my hands are big and clumsy doesn’t mean I can’t make the thumbs work.      Okay, but no promises about ballet, or romantic speeches in about five minutes about the importance of deadlines.      Alright, I can manage that. No need for that extra schoolteacher drama. But if you do run out of ideas for that assignment, I can give you a few hints.      Like what? Doing absolutely nothing?      Nah, I meant waiting till the last minute while you panic and then copying off of someone whose brain space knows the difference between a metaphor and a haiku.      Okay, serious now. This course is the worst. Next go I really need to see if nursing or social work or something practical makes more sense.      You’ve got time to figure it out, and you know I’m right here for all of it—assignments, massages, hours of pretending to care about your life to make you talk about it.      Aye, I’m the lucky one.

Rather skip the newspaper today. You know, too much talk about people in tents and no electricity. It got to me, honestly.      I know what you mean. It's been on the telly quite a bit, and it’s hard to watch. But it’s also hard not to do something, isn’t it?      My class actually did a small project on it last term. Some of the kids were confused—how come we eat out so often, and someone else is living in a camp? They asked me the silliest, but also the best questions.      I’m proud of you, love. It’s good they’re thinking about it now. My students are too young, I think, to really understand what’s going on.      I used to think the world was a smaller place back in my day. Probably better for breakfast, but worse if you want to help someone a bit further away.      That’s why I’m always saying we could do more locally, you know—charities, food banks—personally I’ve been up for it since we were married.      That’s right, Sue. You made us all lemonade and pasties from the kitchen last Sunday at the Baptism of one of my colleagues’ nephews. You said something like, “the hands don’t lie.”      Bless her, she’s got the principles and the baking skills.      And you know what? It just feels oddly satisfying when you give someone something—especially if they’re struggling. It’s not about solving the world’s problems in a day, but it’s something.      I’m just glad we can have these chats over lunch. Not many folks are willing to talk about the worrying stuff.      My sister’s planning on taking the kids to visit one of the food charities in London at the weekend. I might tag along. Do you think there’s anything I can bring or do there?      I’m sure they’d appreciate it. And honestly, I think it helps to do things together as a family—it keeps you grounded.      That’s a good idea. I remember your mum used to volunteer at the old community centre in Southend, Catherine. She always said the tiniest gestures mattered. Pass the gravy, would you love? The chicken feels a little dry.      I’ll do it now—and I’ll talk to Lisa about planning this visit. Maybe we can even raise a few quid among us for Calais if they accept donations.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, having to glue the tiles in the bathroom yourself when you’d far rather pay some chap with a hammer and more sense than us to do it properly.      Aye, I understand that. I've just been quoted five grand for my bathroom and all I did was mention I wanted a bigger walk-in shower. You'd think they'd come with a wheelchair ramp these days if you're asking that!      I thought it would be reasonable to ask for some help removing the old tiles. Didn’t even want to start ripping things up myself until the bloke said it might take him a week and double the price because of the plumbing.      That's the thing with tradesmen these days, you start asking, and the numbers just keep on climbing. I’ve given up trying to negotiate—either I pay far more than I anticipated or I live with a slightly damp wall and some wonky tiling.      There we are, then. I told the man the same. So now I'm stuck with the job, and I'm thinking of just knocking through the two small rooms and making it bigger. I’ve got a spare room that’s got nothing in it now.      You’re taking the advice Matey showed me the other week. He had the same idea after his bath leaked and nearly caused a disaster in his hallway.      That’s the one, and he's just starting on the kitchen now—removing everything from top to bottom, he said. Funny thing was, Matey is a surgeon, and he thought being able to tile a wall would be simple, but it took nearly about five days to line a single row properly.      Ah yes, I remember—he had to get his wife to fix the tiles while he fixed up the wiring to the extractor, ‘cos he says "I do hands in the body, not on the floor with a sponge!"      Oh, I liked that. So when he started doing the kitchen, he ended up asking a professional to do everything once he’d proved to himself that he was probably the wrong person for the job. Still, I think he’s happy with the result.      Aye, and he does say now that it was worth the money, even if it cost a bit more than he expected.

Right, so the kid’s goin’ mental again, tha’s the third time this week ‘e picked up a metal spoon an’ tried to eat it. D’ye think it’s a phase or a mad thing?      That is kind of weird. Maybe like a developmental thing or something? My friend’s sister had a phase with rocks and stuff when he was little.      Maybe he needs some iron? I read that sometimes kids do odd things like eat metal when they’re lacking something in their diet. Maybe we should check with the doctor?      Tch, I wouldn’t worry yet. Mary ’s nephew used to chew the turkey leg at Christmas until he realized it left a bit of a funny taste on the back of his tongue, and now he won’t even touch a piece of meat for about a week after. Wait, does he even know what curry is?      No, not really. He tried that mulligatawny soup a while ago, and he thought it was one of the most amazing inventions in human history—said it tasted like “exploding banana chips and sunshine and rain.”      Ba-ba-baa      That poor wee thing—he just Baptised his new toy car with a bit of orange juice and some dried mint.      Aye, Silly little rascal. Maybe we should keep the car locked up for a while. Spent half the morning trying to read  "The Science of Horrible History" , with a saucepan full of spaghetti in the other hand and asking me if leeches were in it.      I’m disappointed he didn’t try to touch the spaghetti and taste the vibes from a thousand years of nutrition gone bad.      Honestly, if we didn’t step in, he might've made baked alaska out of his birthday cake, based on the cover picture.      Ah, I had a bit of a plan for the cake today. We were talkin’ about how cool it’d be if he had some special powers for the big day—like being able to glow in the dark or somethin’. Course, he started asking if it go with night deposit boxes and if you could open them with super strength.      I had no idea he was aware of night deposit boxes. Where does he pick all this stuff up?!      Well, he heard the word “deposit” from a customer on the phone, and overheard us talking about a park event near the local library, so he just combined it all into "The Night Glow Deposit Bank of Power."

Rather skip the queue didn't we?      Aye, it's such a busy time with Halloween and all, I wasn’t sure how long we would have to wait.      I don’t think we do this sort of thing as a family enough. We should make it an annual thing.      It was lovely of Margaret to let us in without the kids going a bit melty from too much sugar and sticky fingers all over the door.      She's a softie at heart, she'll do anything for family. Especially when the sweets run out too quick like they did last year.      Allie's been talking about Halloween non-stop for weeks. My turkey still hasn’t recovered from the talk of ghosts and ghouls, to be honest.      I think ghosts are cool. I want to be a witch this year. Mum doesn’t like that idea much.      A witch at Halloween’s perfectly fine, love. You can even do both. One costume for the morning, one for the night.      That’d be a faff though, don’t you think? Time enough when the hob-goblin fancy dressing up properly.      Allie, you got a good mark at school?      Yeah, I got a star certificate today. For English.      Oh, that’s brilliant! What were you writing about?      A story about a haunted village and a girl who found a sword. It was like fantasy or something.      Sounds right up your street being a witch then – all the magic in the world, eh?      I think you’re the only one of us who still lives for a good story. My lot are all about school and whether the housing is fixed up yet.      Burgers and balls for them. All passed on to the teachers and the union.      What about you Terry? You still riding them horses when you get the chance?      Once in a while. Used to take some of the lads from the school to do an outdoor class at a riding centre near Coleshill. Kids love it. Gets them out of the classroom and into something a bit more real.      Imagine that, horses instead of homework.      Some of them you could see the light in their faces. Thought it was magic, like those tales Allie was telling earlier.      Can I come sometime? Only I want to learn how to ride the big horses like in the films.      Only if you come with a helmet on, no arguing.

So do you think we’ll get through all this traffic before we get to the fair? It’s been like... non-stop for twenty minutes now. I’m more than a bit worried we’ll miss the steam train demos again.      Look, love, you can't blame the traffic for everything. I'm just as fed up with it as you are. But if it wasn’t for government not building enough houses, we wouldn’t have so many people from all over coming to see a few steam engines, now would we?      That’s a bit harsh, David. I mean, not everyone can afford to live right next to the fair. I know plenty of people who are still waiting for council housing like I was before I got my flat. The system is broken, not just the roads.      But that's the problem! They don't build enough for the elderly, and they definitely don’t do enough for disability access either. I saw a lady in a wheelchair trying to park five miles away yesterday, you know? She had the blue badge, but the council lot—there was nothing left, and the fair’s got more space for mascot vans than disabled spots.      Honestly, it's insane. I mean, we’ve got Disability Awareness Week in October and then come national holidays – it’s all forgotten. I saw a bloke just pull into a blue badge spot and park his car there as if it was for everyone.      That's why they should enforce the laws more. I work in care, and my clients are constantly having trouble accessing places. You’d think something as simple as a parking badge would give you peace of mind – but no, people are ignorant or just plain rude.      And it's not just disabled people. The elderly can’t get into places either. They don’t know how to get housing, they don’t know their rights. I had to put my mother in a care home because I couldn’t get a place for her locally. She was paying taxes all her working life, and then you’re waiting on a list while the council gives housing to people who’ve been out of the country for ten years.      I remember when you were helping set her up with a support worker. That place was so far out, it was brutal for you both.

So do you really think an allotment is a good idea? I mean, I haven’t even mowed my own lawn in months, let alone tried to grow anything properly!      I was the same at first, honestly. But I kind of frightened myself into it—Deirdre at the charity said she  never  had time for all that and now she’s got tomatoes better than most. She’s only got a plot because she volunteers too much, honestly. But it’s started to get into her.      That makes me laugh. I can see Deirdre trying to talk like a Russian peasant even when she’s planting marigolds. But I do miss being outside more in the evenings. I’ve been working from home so much lately. It would be nice to do something like that, even if I’m just staring at the same-faced basil plant in a pot.      Well, if you’re in, I can drive in with me and split planting the bed! I’ve got the basics covered. There was that guy at the plant centre—Greg?—who gave me a killer tips on raised beds last week. He says it’s way easier for people who live on cluttered terraces in cities. You just layer wood chips and then put your soil on top—he showed me how to prevent the water from pooling, because if you don’t, the roots die in weeks.      Oh, I already foresee a situation where the two of us in sweatpants at 8 a.m. on a Saturday arguing over whether to plant courgettes or carrots first. Also, have you considered the pests? I’m not sure I’m brave enough to face slugs at 6 am with a walkman on.      You’re going to be doing that  if  you want to see anything grow before it gets snowed on in December. My sister had that problem—had no idea her plot was shady half the time. She ended up planting spinach instead of sunflowers, and now she’s laughing about how she thought she ruined her garden.      Right. And also, are we thinking of a shared one or are we going solo? I mean, you’re a manager, so you’re probably the one who can go in with the pond and scare off the squirrels or whatever they do. I’d just water the ground and assume it was blooming something marvellous.

So do you go back to Cambridge on Monday?      Yeah, tomorrow morning. We’ve got that big chemistry test on Tuesday now they’ve moved it forward. I was  not  expecting that.      That’s harsh, innit? They can’t just chuck that on us like that. I mean, one minute we’re chillin’, the next— surprise —exam.      I know, right? Oh well, at least it’s not history. We’ve been stuck doing the same essay for weeks. Honestly, the coursework model’s doing my head in.      I reckon, but at least you don’t have to worry about doing the turkey on Christmas Day, eh?      True, my parents would never dream of letting me near the kitchen. They screamed at my brother for burning a biscuit once.      I cooked a dinner for my Nan last night and she went mad about it! Said I’m turning into my Mum—and I thought she was joking, but no, she  meant  it like it’s some kind of rite of passage or summat.      Tell her I said good on her! You’re such a legend.      Mate, I got the vibe last night, though. You know, while the dinner was on.      You mean what vibe?      There’s something going on with my sister. She’s been trying to hook me up with one of her mates. Some guy from the gym.      Oh no! Like seriously?      I about blocked her off the group chat I was like  nooo  I don't need a date, I just need someone that laughs at my jokes and doesn't want to meet my parents.      Fair enough. Honestly, I wouldn’t say no to a laugh and a biscuits round your place instead. Speaking of, I tried your jam recipe when I was here last.      Right? And...?      It was  amazing . My Nan would’ve set fire to the whole house but  I  bloody loved it.      Haha, seriously? I thought I bricked it, but I suppose it could’ve been worse. You know what your lot do with recipes—just chuck in loads of sugar and call it a day.      It’s survival fuel, innit?      Exactly. Well, I’m not entirely sure what I’m doing yet for Christmas. My Nan’s doing the main, but if I don’t spontaneously get a flat in Cambridge and then want to run away halfway through December before I’m dragged to another dinner…      You  will  come back.

Right, I just got beat at FIFA by my mate in 12 seconds. That’s real string-pulling, innit? I had Ronaldo up front, and I still lost by like a mountain of a goal.      No, I saw what you picked. You had a team full of eeny weenys from the lower league. You handed yourself the losing card.      Aww, come on, Aydan! Why'd you pick him anyway? You watched Ronaldo play in like every match! Put in the best team and be the best!      Alright, alright, but I had to make it fair! I thought, “Aye, let’s do some real tactics,” but then Rich here just scored with his back to goal like it was nothing.      It’s FIFA, I think he turned round and had an automatic shot by the goal. It’s a video game!      Honestly, I’m just sat here looking at the replay and thinking, “What’s happening here? Man, why did he not slide?” I would’ve just gone down for a penalty, innit?      Rich, you’re griefing real hard. Tell me what was your cheat code? Was it rhythm mode, was it “play like Haaland?      No cheatin’! It was just skills. I’ve been practising that turn for weeks. You know what I got from Liam? He said, “It's just someone who found one move and doesn’t let it go.”      That move’s hotter than the summer sun in Manila, let’s be real. Can I try next? I’ve got my goals today about how I’m finally gonna play you properly, Rich.      Go on then, Rad! Let’s see if you can take me down. Quick, pass the controller. My grandma’s got better FIFA reflexes than you right now.      Don’t talk to me like that, innit. I haven’t eaten since breakfast waiting for my shot. I’m gonna pick Mbappé as well, just so you know. No fair.      While you play FIFA, I’m gonna try to revise for that environmental geography quiz we got goin’ on Monday. I’ve got notes about monsoons and I just started smiling at the word “rain.”      You can revise later. We all have that fluency to jump in and take it out. Besides, after this round, we’ll start planning on pizza. Lisa said she’s making the food run.      I’m all for pizza.

Rather skip the new films at the cinema love. I saw one of the posters for it and they’re like... got nothing on some of the old ones I used to go see with my mum      Which one was it love? Was it the one with the motorbikes and aliens or that one with the holidays? I don’t think they’re good but if you like effects they have nice effects.      Not the one with aliens, it was the one with the holidays, interesting name that. We used to go to the cinema when I was a girl but the films now don’t... like, seem like much      Some of the people in the films do make it sound like it’s a bit confusing but you get to like watch a lot of explosions, cars and fighting men in funny clothes      Oh I suppose you do, but the old ones had character. I remember seeing that one about spies. They had some in there who were not being very smart and hides, you didn’t have to think too much to like them      Yeah, those are some of the good ones I think. I sometimes wonder how people remember what’s going on      Mate, I often wonder if people still go because they don’t know what the film is about. I suppose you could say that is part of the fun      Maybe, if the film wasn’t over £10 for one entrance      And at 60 it is a lot mate, I mean, I tried once, but when I saw the price I said “never mind that”, as they say      Yeah and it's not just the price love, it's where you get the tickets. Sometimes you can queue up an hour go in and get your own seat and end up next to two pre-teens and popcorn, no thank you      Oh yes, your legs and you could be bent like a pretzel

So did you watch The Undateables last night?      No, I missed it... got home so late after editing. I’m more of a board game person anyway.      Oh come on, they had this one bloke who wouldn’t talk to anyone unless they played Scrabble with him. Honestly felt like they’d handed me the script.      Sounds like Aneurin would love that. Last week he tried to date someone by quoting  every  Kingsley Amis poem in alphabetical order.      Oh my god, I saw that episode too! The girl just kept eating crisps and staring at him like he was a stressed budgerigar.      So unfair. I mean, surely there’s a show for Welsh Darcy types?      We had an editor once who thought Cats was better than breakfast, and he once tried to propose during a Hovis commercial. People’s lives are so weird.      Anyway, enough of that. I’ve been thinking I should do something a bit more... therapeutic. Maybe I’ll splurge on a spa day this weekend.      Good for you—what, one of those West End deals where you get a bottle of Evian and a fairly stingy facial?      Har har. No, somewhere proper. You know, with a large soaking tub and a woman who isn't distracted by her phone.      Just don’t fall asleep and end up looking like a prawn hotter than the Michelin man. I worked with a girl once who came back with a face like she’d been in a microwave.      Interesting anecdote. Have you had any interviews lately?      Not recently. I’m trying to keep up with both editing freeloaders  and  the new National Language Policy guidelines. Honestly, it’s madness at the moment. They want a standardised Welsh pronunciation guide for spellings like ‘Ll.’ I told one bloke it was impossible. He said, “It’s English with a point.”      Some people. My sister just spends her time folding magazines and arguing with the printer about font goop. I think life is getting more boring every year.      I see you're nostalgic for box sets then.      So much. I popped in  Fleabag  and ended up watching all of  The Great British Bake Off  because I felt guilty over a pronoun debate and needed a carb fix.      Judging by how we're currently sat in someone's flat like it's 2008 and the power’s gone out, I reckon we should do a board game.

Right, I just wanted to bring up the whole washing machine thing. I know it's been a week and it got fixed and everything, but I was talking to my sister, and she said she saw a proper built-in model at £200 cheaper than the one we picked.      Oh come on, Natalie, I don’t think you want to start this now. It’s working, it’s clean, and it’s quiet—what more do you need?      It’s not that it’s not working, it’s just that when you chase the right deals, you  can  get a better one. I’m just saying, if we’d waited another week, we could’ve saved us like two hundred quid. You know how I am with that kind of stuff.      I know, and I respect that, but I didn’t want to wait about a month for it. I just wanted it sorted and to stop everyone piling their laundry up in the bathroom. That looked a bit messy, even for you lot.      Fair enough—points for getting it done. But still, listen—my sister reckons the one we got is still high-end. It does everything fancy, but if something goes wrong—and it’s only been a week—it might be a bit of a lemon.      Let’s just see how it goes. I reckon it’s gonna be fine. Anyway, enough about washing machines. You’ve not even been here two hours, and someone’s already knocking your lifestyle choices. That my manor. So, what did you think of the new movie? The one about the Russian spies being double-crossed?      Oy, I about fell out of my seat the first time the grenade lit up. I had vibes from it. It was good fun, but I think I need more popcorn next time. Maybe even that crisps thing they serve in the new cinema here. Eddie passed out halfway through, and I nearly cried the whole time holding him up.      Ah, poor little madman. We should’ve gone as a group. Let’s plan something with everyone next weekend. I miss the lot of them—plus, let’s face it, I’m not too bad with a group dinner. Meat go bad? I’ll see about that.      You’re on. Just let me know. And don’t forget—afterwards, your lot owes me for all the planning I do to get us all together in one go.

So do you know what’s goin’ on with Volkswagen? I read on the news it’s some scam with their cars and emissions or somethin’.      Yeah, it’s a big one. I think they fixed their cars to cheat emissions tests. People are really mad — environmental groups and all that.      Cheeky if you ask me. Cheating on a test should be a criminal offence, not one that’s ignored because you've got money.      Well you wouldn’t expect the Germans to be runnin’ scams, would you? I thought they were all about quality and precision.      I know right? You can almost hear Herr Volkswagen goin’ “ Ah, the numbers look good this quarter. "      But this whole business of moving up north — if you ask me, the cars are better here. No pothole-riddled streets, no delayed trams — and the people are more honest! No fiddlin’ with the emissions in the Lake District, I can promise you that.      That’s true — I mean, we’re not as stressed up here and the real estate prices are way saner than in London. You wouldn’t get a pittance of a flat here for twice as much as a house in Surrey.      Yeah, I’m telling you, if I ever move from Birkenhead, it’s definitely somewhere like here. I want a proper garden, not a balcony with a dodgy rail.      You’d fit in very well. After 30 years being a maths teacher, I’m used to the quiet life. I about blocked out all conversation for the last decade except talking to teenagers about Pythagoras and differential calculus.      Poor you! I handle audio all day for my job. My ears  demand  silence now.      Well, Hunsonby’s the place to be. It’s peaceful, clean air — and you can’t hide behind a dodgy emissions test here. Either your car runs or it doesn’t.      At least the scandal took the shine off that German reputation a bit. You know, I always thought the Germans go out of their way to be efficient — now I think they just go out of their way to pretend to be efficient.      Makes your head spin, really. If only big companies were held to the same standards as regular folks. Then maybe fewer of these scandals to talk about over dinner.      Exactly. Imagine if VW had to go through the kind of scrutiny we do when we’re rentin’ a cottage up here.

Rather annoying when a barista assumes I'm mental when I ask for a macchiato with no sugar. I got the feeling they thought I was one o' them health nuts who gives up carbohydrates and starts a support group.      That's nothing—get a motorway service station attendant to give eeny weeny  not  a full English and see what they think. I had one of ’em once ask me if I was “one of these vegans” after I said I just wanted some toast and a coffee.      Oh, don't get me started. Yesterday I was at the shop buying a jam sponge and the girl behind the counter looked at me like I’d tried to put a live chicken in the till. “That's quite a lot of sugar for one person,” she says. As if it’s breakfast, not a weekend treat!      Aye, and I pity the poor desktop hides, thinking we’re all dead when we retire. I sold off me computer to one o’ the lads in town, but he looked at me like I’d robbed the Crown Jewels when I said I only wanted a touchscreen on it for the photos. “Do you even know how to use one?” Mate, I built the roads, I think I can manage a bit o’ glass and silicon.      Silly lads. Last time I stayed in a B and B in Norfolk someone said to me, “I don’t know why the council keeps building housing developments on the outskirs—there’s no space and no profits being made!” As if all we need in this world is more ugly boxes with satellite dishes.      Oh, you mean like the one they just built by the cricket ground? I was driving past the other day, and the lorry that was trying to deliver the flour for the local bakery nearly ran into a family with a pet goat. One minute it was a cul-de-sac, next it's a road full of half-made houses and a lost kid holding a yellow duck.      Kids. Kids with ducks. More pert near the path than anywhere else. Still, I suppose it’s best to have the developments somewhere away from the centre. Don’t want to risk upsetting the villagers. I made my share of enemies when I was engineering roads—told one landowner what he could do with his particularly bent planning permission.

So did you lot see that article about evolution and why some people still say it's 'just a theory'? It got me so mad at school. Our biology teacher tried explaining it, but someone said, "Evolution is a theory, like gravity?" And I was like—  what  ?      Yeah, I saw that post on Reddit. It went viral because people kept comparing it to climate change. Like obviously, climate change is just a theory too, but it's not a theory in the same way as evolution. We've got   loads   of proof for both of them.      Honestly, I think it's mostly people trying to stir controversy, or maybe they just don’t understand what the word 'theory' actually means in science. In school, I overheard someone say, "If evolution is true, why is there still racism?" and I just— what even?  That doesn’t make sense, does it?      Haha, yeah, that’s like saying, "If flight is real, why is there still the moon?" They don’t even follow the same logic, lads. I mean, racism is a   societal   issue, and human evolution is a   biological   process. You can't blame one on the other. That post is so cringey though—public school students, still thinking that natural selection means humans are the pinnacle of evolution. We did a whole lesson on why that's wrong.      True, the idea that someone who looks "different" is somehow not evolved just because they have different features—that's not what Darwin said, is it? Or at least, it’s not what the modern theory says. Darwin never would’ve backed about race like that.      No, and it’s mind-blowing what some teachers even   think   is acceptable now. I had this lad in chemistry say that Islam is a ‘problem’ for development in education. My Muslim friend, Ayesha, told him the most calm and logical response ever— completely  shut him down.      She did? What did she say?      She said something like, "You must have thought the Earth was flat too?" and the whole class laughed. But the point is, go back 100 years and some of the so-called 'western education' in Africa and Asia was just a cover for   control   through what they told people was 'enlightenment'.      Yeah, I think those kinds of people just don’t realize that everything we talk about today—science, religion, equality, whatever—was written and built by so many different   cultures  .

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, Doreen? I've got this operation in a week's time and I don’t know whether I’m looking forward to it or dreading it.      Aye, we do hear the word  operation  and our minds race straight to drama and dodgy anaesthetic, don't we? I had that little hip thing done not too long ago, and you’ve no idea how long recovery can take!      I’ve had some infections as it is—my doctor was worried the swelling might need more than just tablets. Still, I'm hoping everything goes relatively smooth.      Oh love, I had one when I was in my late sixties, a bit on the dodgy left leg. I was scared, to be honest, but my dear Frank was right there holding the little lever— think it was a teaspoon at the time —for whatever that’s worth!      Aye, you ever looked at that thing, Doreen, and gone,  ‘Oh, that’s not going into me, is it?!’ —I always said if they land a lorry on my back I'd handle it, but a tiny tin thing sticking you up the arm? Be right out.      Speaking of surgeries, I readsomewhys about acupuncture helping with pain—expensive, but they say it eases the after-effects. You ever heard that, Jean?      I’ve thought about it. My friend tried it after a bad back operation—says it’s the most peaceful hour of her week.       Oh, she’s got friends in all the right places , hasn't she? Me and the gals at the bus stop chat about things like that—you know, how you barely need outings if you're up for company and a cuppa. Friendships keep you young, no doubt.      Aye, it's a shame how quickly folk can drift apart.      Aye, my good sidekick Brian over at the pub mentioned how he hasn’t seen a rugby match since he broke his leg skiing. Says he lost his mojo after that. Course, I told 'im if goin' on your back in the snow does that to you, I'm not sure what I’d do after a mud fight in the garden!      It's funny, isn’t it—how one incident lands you hours of physio and new hobbies. I’ve had to start driving with an automatic since the last time I landed in hospital.

Okay, so today in History class, we were talking about slavery and the American Civil War, and it got me thinking. I thought I’d tell you a bit about it, in case you found it interesting.      What’s slavery, Mummy?      Slavery is when one person is owned by another. It’s very,   very   old and not something that should ever happen. People were forced to work for others without being paid, and they weren’t allowed to make their own choices. Today, we know it's wrong and illegal.      Why did people do it?      In the past, some people thought it was okay to own others because of the colour of their skin. That was especially true in places like the American South. They made black people work on big farms, and they treated them unfairly.      Did the nice people stop it?      Yes! There were a lot of people who fought to end slavery. There was even a big war in America called the Civil War, where the North and South fought because the South didn’t want to stop slavery. After that war, the law in the United States said that slavery was no longer allowed.      But why did they fight?      Oh, it was complicated. The South depended on slave labour for things like cotton and farming, and they thought their way of life would end if slavery stopped. The North didn’t agree, and they also thought it was unfair and cruel. So they had a war to try to settle it.      That sounds sad.      It was. A   lot   of people died because of it, and even after the war, many people from the South were very angry. There were other problems for a very long time that are still affecting people today.      Was it just in America?      No, slavery happened all over the world at different times. Even in parts of Africa, Asia and Europe. Australia had something called the Stolen Generations too, where white people took Aboriginal kids from their families. It was wrong, and it took a long time for people to make it better.      Mummy, can we learn more about that?      Of course, love. There are books and shows that explain it better. And the good thing is, today, your generation is helping to make the world more equal and kind. You can be powerful when you speak up for what’s right.      Can I help?

Right, I just wanted to say how lovely it is to have everything back together again—the whole gang in one place. It's been a long time since we had everyone over!      Aw, it's good to be back. Look at this lot! You wouldn't think it was six of us, would you? I swear the place was half full when we were just three!      Aww, Dad, you’re adorable. I’ve brought some brownies. Just baked them this morning. We can have them with the tea when it’s ready, or now if you’re desperate...       laughs  Brownies, eh? I'm only human. Go ahead, that’s a good sign. Still baking for us like you were when we were kids.      Always was the best baker. Even made my wedding cake, by the way.      You need to publish a book or something. "Brownie’s Best Bakes." That's a good title for a cookbook!      I was just thinking, you know we haven’t properly discussed the last holiday we had together. Remember that disastrous trip to the Lake District?      Oh my God. The one where Granddad “accidentally” booked three double rooms with shared facilities, and none of the rooms were actually next to each other? It was chaos!      And don’t forget the dog. Benji wouldn’t stop barking at the neighbor’s cat. That cat was a prat, honestly.      Ah, it was a holiday to remember. Still, at least no one got food poisoning this time. I did on the last one!      Well, this time let’s just keep things simple. Going to that B&B near the coast sounds perfect. No tents, no dogs, no ‘accidental’ bookings.      Agree. I’m looking forward to it. I was also meaning to ask, have you all been watching that new series on the TV? “In Plain Sight”? It’s a real drama!      Yeah! They screened it last week. The third season was something else. I was on the edge of my seat every episode.      Oh, I haven’t had a chance, but I will. I’ve been glued to the news, to be honest. So much going on in the world.      It is, isn’t it? Between the economy, the weather, and the politics, you’d think someone wrote it for a thriller!      Channel Five? No wonder it's so dramatic. Everything’s a conspiracy these days.      I used to watch it with you before, you know.

Right, who’s putting the plates back in the cupboard? I think the stack of bowls is about to tumble over.      I’m sorted! I did mine already.      Me neither. I’m just… I’m just making a tower.      Right, okay, I’ll do the bigger bits. Watch out for the cup with the spider on—it’s yours, Harry.      That’s my Horrible Histories mug, not Harry’s. Harry doesn’t even like spiders.      Do you think spiders are alive like people or like in  Fantastic Beasts ?      That’s a good question. My opinion is definitely not valid, but I think they are not Technically, they’re arachnids, not magical beings.      Wait, aren’t Muggles not allowed to know that? I thought Dumbledore’s beard was made of Protected magical hairs.      You are not helping. Also, Dumbledore’s beard is real, not magical—though I wouldn’t try to find out.      What did he teach again?      He was a wizard. Headmaster. He taught, like, wizarding. Important wizard stuff.      And he had a phoenix named Fawkes. He sang songs and cried tears that healed people.      That’s so cool. Our history teacher said George Stephenson also did something cool.      Oh, he was the guy with the trains, right? The railroad inventor? Made sure we all had to commute every day?      No, not just trains—he invented the first public railways. He was a proper genius. My sister is doing a school project on him. She says he turned the whole country upside down.      Like how Harry flipped the Sorting Hat when he told it not to put him in Slytherin.      Except he didn’t stick it to Professor McGonagall.      George Stephenson stuck it to the horse and carriage industry. That’s how you know he was a pioneer. He started the industrial revolution go faster.      If Harry Potter met George Stephenson, would he ride a steam engine with a wand in his pocket?      I reckon he would. If it had a moving staircases and exploding pipes, maybe even more than the Hogwarts Express.      That’s ambitious, but fitting.      I’m gonna draw that when I finish my tea. With spider on my mug casting a spell on the steam.      Just don’t let it scare the dishwasher, okay? We’ve already had enough fantasy for one day.      Spoken like a true history teacher. But I mean, honestly, half of history is already quite magical.

So did you beat me in Words With Friends last night or did I get lucky again?      You were lucky, love. I’m just letting you think you’re good at it.      You both are the same. It’s a game. Just enjoy it. Got the lasagna in the oven, so let’s not get too competitive.      I’ve been banned from a supper club over this too much competitiveness, so watch it. It was some sort of private dining thing with wine pairs and everything. Found out during the canapés that someone had paid for everything but forgot to invite the person who booked.      That’s a whole other level of MySpace-era chaos. Still, who invites someone’s lawyer to their dinner party to play it safe, right?      Wait, is no one going to ask me why I dropped this in the sink?      You, ordering croissants from a bakery in North London at 10 PM and then spilling them everywhere in a tumbler? You don’t need a lawyer. You need a therapist.      Fair enough, but I’m a barista. It's in the job description to spill stuff. I almost dropped the milk frother on my head the other day. It was dramatic.      Ooh, you should’ve been on those cooking shows where someone almost drowns in chocolate. That stuff is a genre now.      Just don’t start a documentary series called  Baristas in Crisis: Froth & Foam . I would watch it about five times.      Speaking of which, this lasagna… I made it from a recipe Sarah gave me. Supposed to have layers of  emotion  and not just cheese.      Is that passed down through generations or just bad instructions written on a strip of paper stuck to the fridge with a gingerbread man?      As long as it doesn’t require  pre陉      Pre- what? Permafrost-phase simulation?      Just kidding. I once tried to make gochujang pancakes and had to Google  ‘ginger vs garlic paste’ , and I still ended up with a box of gherkins.      That sounds like it was traumatic and possibly edible in small amounts.      True to life, yes. Look, overcooked, but not inedible. I’m not entirely sure if lasagna needs a tomato-based sauce or if it's just suffering under my impatience.      It’s looking good, honestly. Just sprinkle some basil on it while we all stare at our phones pretending we're on dating sites for bakers.

Rather skip the queue and just bring us our usual, yeah? I’m starving. How’s your week panning out?      Same here, honestly. This place gives such a good sarnie for a cash clinic. My week’s been busy—IT rollout at the centre next week. Got to make sure the printers and scanners don’t decide to crash on the first day.      Aww, poor thing. I know that too well. Every time we upgrade our staffing system, there's always a crash at 4:59 on a Thursday when people are rushing out. You'd think IT people would avoid scheduling system upgrades during dead week, but nooo—there's always a "perfect" time.      Ha! I think it's like a rite of passage for us in IT, isn't it? A system meltdown just to prove everyone was paying attention. How about you? What’s been going on this week?      Me? It’s non-stop cover shifts, you know how it is when the college term heats up. Last week I was covering both the main campus and this one—had one of the support staff call in with a high temperature. Gave me the jitters for a bit. My own work rhythm’s all over the place.      That’s rough. At least you’re getting some cover supervisor experience. I remember when I used to cover in primary schools for a while—messy, but it made me appreciate the people out there who hold things together on the fly. Ever had a chaotic class before?      Oh, plenty. One time I supervised a group of Year 7s after a ballet competition. You try calming about forty excited boys after a girls’ win. It was like watching chaotic sea vibes. Honestly, you could write a documentary about that day.      No way—I bet the binoculars for the balcony view ended up in someone's pocket by sundown. Do you have a kid or anything? That seems like the kind of thing that you’d understand better with your own.      You're spot on—two kids with lunches to keep in check and binoculars to recover. My youngest just started delivering the odd drawing and snack at the end of the school day. I think he’s trying to raise his social circle pre-social media.      That sounds precious, actually. You know what your hobby should be? Flower arranging. I seriously think it’d calm the chaos out of those days, maybe even your brainwaves to help you survive those madness hours over this job.

So do we go left here or right?      Left, left, left! We passed the turnoff like five minutes ago, sweetie. I can already smell the discount socks.      Charming. Look, just keep going straight, Martha. We're not lost, just slightly...  not where we were an hour ago.       Nana, you’ve only been to this shop once in your life, and that was when I was a baby pulling crisps off shelf two. You can’t really be the best map right now.      Right, because when I took  you  shopping, you were the size of a wet nappy and made no decisions of your own. Now you’re a left-right lawyer in the making, ain’t you?
