So, have you made it to that conference you were telling me about? The one on bilingual education in primary schools?

Right, so we've got this thing on tonight, right? That thing you told us about — the  Friendly Feast and Film Fest , or something like that.      Yeah! It’s a little thing we’re putting on with some friends from the co-op — potluck supper, then we watch a movie and talk about the songs in it. It’s just for fun basically.      Sounds cool. What’s the film this week?      It’s  Guardians of the Galaxy . We’ve got the soundtrack covered and everything. I even made a Spotify playlist with some of the best tracks from it. Disney  and  Bowie, baby!      You know I’m in. I’ll bring the cheese board. I got this new vegan cheddar I’m dying to try, and some pickles I bought from the little farm shop in Grantchester.      I’ll do the drinks then — proper Anglo-German mix. Lager and Pilsner, maybe a couple of bottled ciders for the lighter crowd. And I reckon I can help with the tech side, get the tunes and visuals sorted if I can find the right player.      Perfect, that frees me up to… well, basically just work on my little speech about how soundtracks can actually change the meaning of a movie, and how lyrics really pull emotions out of the film.      Oh come on, you're not giving a speech at our little hangout. Our food group just wants to eat and blu-tack memes onto the screen while we cosplay as Rocket Raccoon.      I  can  be a bit serious when I want, thank you very much. I once gave a 20-minute lecture on the phonology of Yoda. To  actual  linguists.      Right, right. Still, I bet the meme board will be better than the actual guest speaker.      Let’s not forget the film trivia competition. I’ve already got a list of 50 questions. Contestants who get 10 right can have a free jab at Simon’s toe nails with a foam sword from my son’s birthday stash. That’ll be  unforgettable .      Oh yeah go on then. But if I win, I’m taking over the karaoke session in the garden after the movie. I’ve got the Queen album already queued up.      Make it 3AM and I’m out. I’ve got a site meeting in Hatfield tomorrow, and I’ve already over-quoted the client to cover this drastic caffeine deficiency.

So did you lot hear the weather’s going mental tomorrow? Like proper gale force winds and horizontal rain. I got to go to some site near Peterborough, and I’m already dreading it.      Uugh, don’t even remind me! I’ve got a meeting in Milton that I’m meant to lead, and if the train’s delayed again, I might just call in sick with a miraculous recovery.      Honestly, I’m just staying in. It was bad enough last week. We had to cancel the shoot for this short film I’m editing—it looked like the sky had been set on fire.      Harsh. I was actually thinking of heading over to London My mate’s got a beta-tester session for this new game we’re working on, but now I’m not sure. And you think the kids are up to it? I mean, I remember you before as a maths teacher, but now you’re off teaching biology and extracurricular science labs.

Rather annoying this new debt collector phoning every other day, isn’t it? I haven’t got a penny to spare and I’m not even registered on the bloody computer properly! Rather a lot today, wasn't it? That case dragged on far longer than expected.      Oh dear, yes, absolutely. I’m more used to straightforward small claims or traffic issues, not this whole hour-long sob story about a broken boiler and unpaid utility bills.      It’s beginning to feel like the court is just an extension of social services now. Almost as if they don’t have enough support in place to help people in these situations before it gets this far.      That’s just it, isn’t it? Funny how things have changed since I started working here over ten years ago. Everything seems more… stretched. I don’t think the system was ever built for this kind of pressure.      I’m not sure it ever tried to be, to be honest. D’you know, I think the world is changing faster than rules and systems can keep up with. I see it in my classes too—young people are growing up thinking about the climate, about sustainability, but not always given the tools to make a real impact.      I do worry about that. I’ve got a grandchild who’s just turned eleven, and he spends more time reading about renewable energy than playing outside, which is nice, but it does make you wonder what the future’s going to look like for them.      It’s huge. One of my students in the French class started a whole project on plastic waste in the Seine and the Thames—comparing what’s being done in Paris and here. That kind of thinking is inspiring, but it also shows what a mess we’ve got to fix.      That’s all very true, but there’s also the question of money, isn’t there? I know it sounds selfish, but with fuel and food prices where they are, it’s easier to think about the day-to-day survival than the long-term future.      Absolutely. And that’s part of the system too, isn’t it? If you can’t afford to travel anywhere, or if you’re waiting hours on overcrowded trains to get to and from work, how are you meant to take part in a wider conversation about the world?      Still, I try to keep travel adventures in the family. Last month, we went to see about a castle near York—that one with the very active stables. I had a go on a horse for the first time in thirty years.

Right, who’s ready for a story time with a little twist of imagination?      Me me me!      Me too!      Alright, alright, let me start. Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Flo who wore bright yellow wellies and liked to bounce on trampolines.      Like a frog!      Exactly! And there was a little boy named Rob who had a dump truck that could dig the biggest moats.      Like the moat around King Arthur’s castle!      Very good, Rob! Now, Flo and Rob were the happiest kids in town, not because they had shiny new bikes or a mountain of sweets, but because they had each other and a very special secret.      What was the secret?      The secret was that they knew a magic word that made the world feel brighter and better every time they said it.      What was the magic word?      The magic word was…  happiness.       But how does that work?      Well, it’s not like a potion or a spell – it’s more like a feeling, and sometimes it comes from doing something nice or sharing your toys.      Like when I shared my lollipop with Georgina?      Oh yes, and she shared a sticker with you right back. That’s a happiness exchange!      What if you  have  lots of money?      A very good question, Anna! Some people think having lots of money makes them happy. But guess what? Even if you are the richest person in the world, if you're not kind to others, you might not feel very happy inside.      Can I have money to buy a digger?      One day, maybe. But while you wait, what can you do to feel rich without money?      Go to the park and play?      Smart thinking! Because the best things in life are free – time with friends and family, playing, building, laughing… even tickle fights!      Time to tickle your tummy, Anna!      Oh noo, don’t start!      Okay, let’s not fall off the sofa – we’ve got a very important job. Tonight, we all need to make a list of the things that make us happy, no matter how small or silly they seem.      I like rain puddles and chocolate.      I like thunderstorms and orange juice on toast.      Magnificent! And remember, happiness isn’t always about having something – it’s often about  doing  something or  feeling  something. So if we all try to be kind and grateful, we’ll never run out of happiness.

Right, I just wanted to go through the request and make sure everything looks okay.      What request are you talking about?      Erm, the one about the articles for the company website. That would be a massive help. I feel bad asking over and over, but at least this way I’m not putting my editor in the firing line. We’d have to get the materials in bulk really. But it’s doable.      Yeah, and we could market it like a ‘sportssaver’ service. Sort of like the  Dragon’s Den  idea—pitch it, promote it, get folk thinking about saving money as well as time.      Precisely. Imagine fitting it in a homemade setup—keeping the costs low and the profits high.      You know, I had a very similar idea for football boots, back in the day when I was teaching.

Okay, I swear some of these girls are mental, honestly. So do you not find it ridiculous that we're raising a child who thinks they can get by on four hours of sleep and diet Coke?      Is that not a given?      It   shouldn’t   be a given! We were  children  who knew what real coffee tasted like at  eleven years old . I   didn't   think about all that madness with a clean fridge and avocado toast.      Well, we're not backward. Times are different. Today’s kids are   more evolved  , what with their activism, their social media brains… they can handle three things at once!      That's not handling it, that's   juggling MySpace   and a   meltdown   at the same time. And I’m not even talking about them, I’m talking about   us  . Living with someone for 20 years and still breakfasts occur mostly if I   accidentally leave a packet in the car  . And ever since we started shopping online, the   fridge   is a glorified  bottle of red and a jar of jam .      Fair point. But as to the bigger human race question, what do we   say   to Aziz when he comes tomorrow about all the “gender expectations” –?      Oh Aziz, the  woke  Moroccan friend with the PhD in sociology and   a pack of smokes under the bed  . Smokes, by the way, which someone recently found in my bottom drawer. That was   not mine  .      He’d better not be in the smoking and being ‘empowered’   only when it suits him   category.      Absolutely not! I'll   give him a taste  . He said to me last month that “modern men shouldn’t be worrying about   gender roles  , but if the bin’s full, they should just do it.”      And?      I told him I wasn’t disappointed that he did it when I was out – just that   no one else followed suit  .      I think it's funny how   he calls it “common sense”   when he’s talking about washing the dishes, as if that’s supposed to override his PhD or something.      Oh, I see it. He’s a bloke who’s read your 200-page postmodern feminist essay but still uses the word “ better ” to describe men because he’s   used to it  . It's like walking into a yoga studio and still        Expecting a treadmill at the back.      Exactly! Right place, wrong expectations. But to be fair, Aziz’s issue is nothing compared to   some of the things   I see in advertising now.

I said I was just being loud with excitement because we read about a crocodile that could run really fast!      Oh no, that sounds fun, but maybe not in the way Mr. Higgly wanted. You should raise your hand and shout your ideas. You know that.      I know, I know.

Yes, and I’m sure the kids were really inspired by the metaphor of the chocolate supply chain being under exponential threat from Easter lilies and sermon poetry.

So did you read the Twitter rant today about the café in Margate? It was full of people pretending like it was the worst meal they’d ever had because the avocado toast was a few seconds after their cappuccino.      Oh I saw it! I mean, honestly, how do they get so vocal about  seconds ? It’s like they paid for a concierge dining experience not a £7 avocado on sourdough.      Honestly, I’ve had far worse in five-star places. We’ve had customers come in and demand refunds for a scone with  three  raisins in it. Like it’s  1984  and the government supply only lets you have four per day.      I swear to God, the internet review culture is the worst. You get a pastry that lacks a cherry or the latte art is slightly off, and suddenly you’re posting a picture with a sarcastic caption and everyone thinks you’re in a food police squad.      And the way they phrase it too. Like, "Don’t open a business if you don’t know what sourdough feels like in your hands." What does that even  mean ?      It’s so toxic, it’s like customer service from the Stone Age. Back in the day you got a sneaky comment, now you get a whole timeline. I’ve had people ask to “deplatform” me because the croissants were too flaky, which I suppose is someone’s version of a burnout.      I feel like it's not even about the food at some point. It’s about being seen. Like, “I had a bad experience because I have standards” as if every review is gold and the business owes you something for showing up.      Yeah, I was baking last night and it took a little longer to proof the bread, so someone put up a star review saying my sourdough was 'aromatically unmet'. Unmet? What does  that  even mean?      Honestly though, it’s gotten to the point where we’re updating our business with a “terms and conditions of being annoyed” sign just so no one tries to lawyer up over a bad latte.      I need to see that. "By entering this building, you agree to not separate out the raisins in the scone or aggressively rate the taste of bitterness."      And also, no Romans, no gluten-free hours, and please try not to type your review on your phone for five minutes before walking out.

Right, who’s ready for dinner?      I’ll just pop the lasagna in. It’s in the oven already—should be ready in ten. Oisin, wash your hands, darling.      I don’t like lasagna.      You haven’t even tasted it yet, Harry. It’s the new tomato and spinach one I made—much healthier than the cheesy one.      Yeah, and I’m not eating vegetables for dinner   again  .      Well, maybe if you tried them when they don’t look like they’ve been frozen three times, you might  not  throw them onto the floor like last week!      My turkey came here!      That’s pasta, silly. I think he meant he’s seen an animal again.      I still can’t believe we have a gerbil in the garden. Harry saw it today again by the shed.      It was the same one, I’m sure of it. Small, brown, fluffy. Like from one of those pet shops.      I think it might’ve escaped. We should trap it and take it to the RSPCA. You can’t keep a wild gerbil in the shed, even if it is adorable.      He tries to follow me when I water the vegetables. I blame the raspberries.      Wait,  raspberries ? In the garden?      Yes, Harry’s been helping me plant some. He wants to grow fruit like his big brother does with veg.      I don’t want to grow fruit! I want to grow chillies and have my own cooking show.      I like chillies. Mummy says they taste like toffsie.       Turkish delight , Oisin. Not toffsie.      Well, I say if it grows, you cook it. I’m not doing all the weeding again just to feed a teenage boy who’d rather eat a chocolate bar and watch the rugby.      That’s not fair. I like eating the food we grow. Mummy, remember when I harvested the tomatoes and made my own pasta sauce? Miss Brooks said I was a chef in training.      Oh, you made such a mess in the kitchen that day though. The sink was pink with tomato sauce for a week!      But he was brilliant at it. He cleaned up after that. You have to give him credit for progress.      Right, dinner's ready. Lasagna, salad from the garden, and fruit compote on the side.      No way—I said no veg.      I had a bumble. Bee came on my leg earlier.      Did it? The new planting spot's attracting pollinators, which is a good sign.

Rather skip the queue at the chemist if I can, do you need any vitamins or anything?      No, no, I’m sorted. I’ve already got my folic acid and vitamin D in. Not like I’m the one who needs it these days.      Right, now  I  do. Not as much as I used to smoke— used  to— but I still have the occasional one in the garden. Still, easier said than done to kick the habit properly.      You lot never chase your own groceries, then. You just fetch everything, don’t you? It’s so thoughtful, really.      It’s no bother at all, love. I’m always passing the shop on the way home, so I pick things up for everyone. Easier in the long run. Less crowding for you ladies.      And then I do the coffee, which I suppose repays the kindness. Only thing I can do, really, besides keep the kettle warm.      I do tell you—personally, I’d take one of those pre-prepared meals from the shop and say goodbye to chopping.      Doesn’t work for me, love. I like to know what I’m putting in the pot, and none of those ready things suit me. I’ve got quite the eye for what looks fresh.      Still, if you carry on like this someone’s going to ask you two to audition for some kind of carer reality show.      I’d say I’m the least likely to maintain a pair of eyebrows in this room, and I do mean that with all seriousness.      Oh, you’re doing a terrible job of maintaining your own shape, then. I mean it, you could do with a trim.      Yes, well, I know. Just haven’t got around to booking it yet. But I think I might have to soon, I’ve been told I’m looking a bit “rough and ready.”      And what do I look like? I’ve got enough silver strands in there you could use them as fishing wire.      Look, I’ll tell you what. If you lot give me a shout on the weekend, I can pop down the salon and get something done while your man Mike’s in at the doctor’s for his blood test.      And maybe we could go out to that new little place that opened over by the station—had them over for dinner once. I think it’s got that proper buttery steak and kidney pie.

Right, thanks, I've got my coffee. That was gentle. I was just reading through that website on baby weaning again, just trying to get more confident about it all. I've found a few good articles, but I still feel like I'm not sure what's the  right  way to do it.      Yeah, I get that. There's so much out there these days—it’s a bit overwhelming. I would love to do it more slowly, but with my job as a primary teacher, it’s hard to be available for every single new step when he starts.      Oh, I know. I mean, I don't work anymore, so I’ve got time, but I still feel like I should be doing everything  just right.  It’s ridiculous! I’m constantly Google-checking if I’m feeding him in the right order. First fruits, then veggies, and then protein, right?      Well, I suppose some people start with iron-rich stuff like meats actually, especially if the baby’s a bit anemic. I remember my sister did that with her twins, and the midwife said it was fine. Anyway, what are you planning to feed him when you start? Have you bought any baby food yet?      No, I want to try and do it myself at first—steaming, pureeing, all that jazz. I’ve got my blender and all the paraphernalia. I’m just waiting for the right moment, maybe the day after someone else in the family offers to watch him so I can have a proper rest. I’m exhausted just from breastfeeding at night!      Oh no! I feel  so  for you. I have about five days off every month with statutory paternity leave, which is lovely, but I still feel guilty about not being there for everything. My partner and I have managed to split things up quite well, but for the first few days after he started solids, I was so nervous I ended up crying one night because I was scared I had given him something he wasn’t supposed to have!      Oh honey, I  definitely  get that. I keep thinking “What if he chokes?” or “What if I get something wrong with the temperatures?” I’ve even got go-to backups on my phone if something breaks or burns or whatever.      It’s funny because we were just arranging for my nan to come over next week.

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich, aren't we? I mean, this walk—the peace, the pheasants, the quiet—what more do you need?      True, and it beats standing in a queue waiting for someone to serve us overpriced gin and tonics again. That bar’s  notorious  for making you queue longer if you wear glasses.      Agh, don’t remind me! Last week, I swear the barman mistook my specs for a membership badge and was like, “Lecture class again, are we?”      Horrible. Anyway, speaking of classes, did you read the student feedback yet? On the seminar? My postgrads seem to love me though. I’m not sure if it’s the content or the fact they pick up I make the world’s best brownies in the handouts.      I’ve read enough to know my students think I sound like a bad audiobook narrator when I read out the sonnets. One even suggested I speak more directly to the ceiling.      Fair. Though I have to say, your teaching notes on landscape and grief are brilliant, by the way. Real emotional depth. Doesn’t surprise me you write like that—I mean, look at this countryside: it’s beautiful, but it does whisper  stories , doesn’t it?      It really does. I love how the hills here seem to hold everything. Our parents always said when they first met in King’s Lynn, the first walk they took was through exactly this kind of scenery. Just a muddy stretch of path and an unspoken promise that nothing bad could ever fully last.      That’s lovely. I wish the students had this place to walk in. Maybe they’d start seeing that learning isn’t just in books. There’s so much to be found here—quiet thought, treacherous puddles, abundance of cows.      Abundance? I think I counted six different farm animals today. You mustn’t bring the students here—there’ll be more lambs mentioned in their essays than historical references.      We’ll just say it’s a learning curve. Puns intended.      I’ll see if you get a higher attendance at the next seminar.      Deal. But while we’re here, can we stop at the farm shop again? I’ve been eyeing the sausages for weeks, and I’m not about to let farm talk remain the only agriculture this walking tour covers.      Oh go on then. But if they run out of the soft goats’ cheese, I’m casting blame on you.

So did you watch The Last of Us on HBO yet? I’ve binged it in two days — like, proper weekend waste.      Yeah, I did. I was a bit late to it, but finally got to it. Was not expecting to cry half the episode through. I mean, I'm an engineer, I don’t cry very much. But that opening episode... man, that’s a hit to the gut.      I know, right? Like, you think it’s just gonna be a post-apocalyptic zombie apocalypse and then you're literally halfway through the first episode and you're like, “Oh no,  this is emotional cinema now .”      Exactly. And that Joel and Ellie dynamic — they’re not even left with each other at the end, and I still love them both. Made me think of the little sister I never had, to be honest.      Heh, I mean, Ellie’s ballsy enough to punch people, so I’d have been into her even if the story was flat. But it’s not— it's great.      Oh, definitely. I think the best thing about it is how human the characters are. Like, they’re not perfect, they’re flawed, and then you just root for them anyway. Mate of mine at work said he tried to watch the first few episodes but had to stop because of the pacing, but once you get into the meat of the story, it flies.      Yeah, I get that. The first few episodes are setting up the world, definitely. Some people like that, some people don’t. It’s not as action-packed straight away, but it builds up nicely.      I think you just have to come into it with the right expectations — like, this isn’t The Walking Dead. It's more like The Road meets superhero-like action. My sister’s planning on rewatching it for the detail — she's into the plot threads and the secondary characters.      Oh, that Kelly stuff — wild. I honestly thought the show was going to end after Joel and Ellie were safe, but no, keep on going with the larger world stuff. Was it weird for you, after the first season?      Actually, really well done. I think the second season expanded the world in a really smart way without losing the emotional core of the characters. You get to see all sides of the society post-collapse — the zealots, the humans in power, those just trying to survive.

Rather lovely walk today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to break through—the peace out here is... well, rather heartening.      Definitely. I've been buried in a mountain of economics papers and funding applications since the start of term, and this is just what I needed. I'm almost jealous of the farming students out here with their hands in the soil instead of in spreadsheets.      Fair enough. Though I must say, I find cash crop research quite interesting—especially as it relates to the local economy here. Didn’t the university get a new grant focusing on sustainable farming methods in East Anglia?      Yes, and I can't fault the theory behind it, but I’m sceptical about its practical outcomes. Funding tends to go to the projects with the flashiest presentations and least risk. They might end up publishing ten papers about the same three crops while breakfasts are still served at this time.      Blooming hell, is it that late already?! I didn’t think I’d lost track of time that badly. I do tell you, being out here surrounded by crop fields instead of lecture halls leaves one with a very human sense of time—or the lack thereof.      Absolutely. Speaking of time—I still can’t believe Mateo signed with Wolves. I mean, it was a long shot, but he actually pulled it off.      Oh, no! When did that happen? He never mentioned anything.      Just last week—well, technically week before, but he’s been playing it low key. Typical him. Probably being told not to speak about it until it’s fully signed off. I daresay he’s the first proper footballing export from this village. Not much else grows around here apart from beans and data.      Well, I’ll have to go see for myself. If he's playing against Portsmouth next week, that’s at 6pm. Any chance you’re going to the game?      I told you, my good self has already bought the tickets. Best seats in the house, right behind the goal—my wife took the liberty. Though I’m still learning Portuguese with the kids, so watching him play in Portugal is on the cards if Wolves let him drift too far south.      You Spanish speakers go on forever about "touch" and all that. But at least you fluency means something when you’re in Iberia!

So do you want me to bring my car or shall we do mine?      We’d be better off with yours cos it’s more compact and I can fit it in the tighter spaces there. I don’t wanna be stuck in the middle of nowhere trying to parallel park my big lump in some dodgy car park.           Aye, that’d be a comedy. A big flashy consulting car trying to park like a top gear challenge.      Oh come on, it’s not  that  big. Just, maybe keep an eye out for those little signs near the motorway exits—those places with the 1.3m height limit? You wouldn’t think you'd fall for that, but I left a golf client back there once because I couldn’t get my car through and I didn’t want to knock the sign off for fear of being chased by the council.      Seriously? You drive in there all posh, and then you finish up stranded in some remote car park? That’s like the real north—village bureaucracy and you get told off for missing a space. I like that.      It wasn’t funny at the time. I ended up booking a hotel room in a town I’d never heard of just to wait for a hire van, and then it rained and the ground was like soft custard. You know what it’s like up there—land of the Angel of the North and the wettest clouds in the UK.      Aye, but that’s the charm—big steel angels and bigger puddles. So, being back in the north brings back some memories, eh?      Definitely. I used to play touch rugby near the Tyne. It was wild. We had this old concrete wall that barely held the housing estate together, and we'd do 10 overpasses just to hit it. One of the lads ended up getting into a real argument with a pigeon over the airspace.      You mad or what?      He said the pigeon interfered with the 'field dynamics' or something. He was a big man, that Tom.      I bet he was. He still goes on about his old football days though, doesn’t he?      You don’t know the half of it. Anyway, all that’s in the past now. Speaking of which, we should check out where those flats are—my client says they’ve got a games room or something over there.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know what I mean. The people on telly always pretending like they got the hots for someone and now they're suing 'em for something or other. It's like, hun, you can do better than that.      Aye, it’s all a bit  far-fetched , if you ask me. I reckon half of them couldn’t tie their own shoelaces if they weren’t being filmed. Still, easier said than done to get a bit of clout these days, I s’pose.      Tch, I like to watch it. I mean, I don’t get it at all, but I do like watching it. My loony cousin Sheila watches it every day. She says it’s more interesting than watching the birds in the garden, and I’ll be the first to say that is  some  competition.      Oh I know! The other day I saw these geese, you ever seen a squad of geese looking for somewhere to shout? One flew straight off the cliff edge over the lake, and the rest of them just glided calmly on, like it was their job. I tell ya, birds today got no respect for personal space.      Tell me about it. My son’s been out feeding them, and now they all follow him around like he’s their new leader. One tried to attack my car. I swear, they don’t even wait for traffic lights any more.      They don’t just migrate, they  annoy  now, don’t they? Back in the ’50s, they came and went like they were on a schedule. I used to make Steve walk us all the way from the bus stop to keep clear of ‘em. Now they just shuffle into town and make themselves at home.      I suppose that’s climate change for you. Geoese gone global, or something. I read in a mag it used to be ‘proper migration’ but now they just wander about waiting for someone to chuck them chips.      And don’t get me started on people leaving chips outside! My boss took the kettle out of the kitchen for a year after it was left on the grass one go. That one pond life nearly suffocated on crisps and custard creams.      You’re blooming right. I had a parrot in the 1970s, and one day I come down and it’s sitting belly up on the floor, and I’m thinking, “What’s happened to them?”

So did you go for the interview at the primary in Sutton Coldfield yet?      I got it sorted last Thursday. You remember Tom from down the road? His wife heads up the subject team there now.      Oh right! The one with the two little ones and the dog that chased everything.      Yeah that’s the one. She said she’d put in a good word for me before I even applied. Still, I had to go through all the formal stuff.      Well what was it like, the interview? You not too nervous like you were back at Lakelands?      A little, but I managed to stop My turkey leg fall off my chicken tin though. I remembered this time! I made the right sandwiches, even!      Oh ha! So did it help having Mhairi back when you were expecting your interview?      Oh absolutely. I had her over for a trial run the night before. We did the whole thing, from walking in to the questions she thought they might ask. She even pretended I faltered halfway through a sentence to see how I handled it.      Sounds like she’s got quite a little career as an acting coach coming up!      She needs it more than me these days. I reckon she’s gonna go freelance next year.      And the job? Did they seem interested?      Yes! I think so. They asked me how I’d manage with the mix of mainstream and SEND in the class and I told them I’d use the techniques from the PGCE and also about how I ran the group play sessions when the nursery lit up like a Christmas tree during storytime.      That was a time! The snow globes in the window and the ‘Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer’ on loop. I remember Kath saying it was a miracle no one spontaneously burst into song during your observation.      She didn’t  say  it out loud but I saw the eye-roll. Anyway, what about you? Still doing your Spanish drop-ins at the after-school club?      I am. I usually see about seven or eight of the same faces each session. I’ve got a boy named Pablo who lives for the films I show. He’s five and wants to be fluently bilingual before he’s eight. I think he watches the whole lot of  El Castellano Profesional  over the weekend.      That’s dedication! I remember one of my ex-boys in sixth form started speaking to me always in English, but then one day he said “Oliver want mushroom on my pizza, but before Oliver speak, needs to speak… properly.”

So do you ever just lie awake at night and think about what’s next? Like, what’s the  plan , right?      All the time. Honestly, I've been over this with my flatmate so much we’re like co-hosting a podcast on  adulting . Do you want a coffee? I’m about to refill my cup.      Please, yes. I miss the day I used to think “next week this project is done and then I’ll relax forever.” But no, it just loops. You ever feel like you’re working your way into the future but not sure what the future is?      Every. Single. Day. I still can’t believe I’m doing the same admin job I had seven years ago. I’m qualified to do, like, five other things. But this place is stable, the insurance is good, and it’s a nice gig if you’re, you know, 25. Not a 45-year-old needing a promotion by 44, or something.      I get it. I mean I do like the satisfaction of knowing I’m controlling the production pipeline and that stuff leaves as it should. But I worry, like, is this going to be where I am in five years? Still just “coordinating” –?      Listen, I had the  exactly  same chat last week with my mum. And you know what she said? She said, “Why are you even comparing yourself to someone else? What’s  your  version of climbing a ladder?” That hit so hard. Some people’s ladders are curved, and some people’s are horizontal. Like,  literally , there is not one version of being successful.      That’s true, but sometimes I feel like I need to make a “bold move.” I’ve been thinking of doing up a side project. My sister’s planning on rebranding her beauty brand and I could probably lend a hand with planning the logistics. Might give me something  else  to do, you know?      That sounds awesome. I mean, doing something creative always feels better than just ticking off tasks from a list. And if it works, you could maybe even run with it. I started a budgeting go-to guide on Instagram and I’ve had  so  many messages from people like “This helped me so much,” it’s blooming weird.      So how have you made it all work, though? Like, where do you find the time?      Ugh, I overcommit and then panic at the end of the week.

So did you talk to him yet, Sophie? Or is he still pretending you don’t exist?      No, no luck. I texted him like ten times yesterday after he ditched us for Lucy. Not only that, he said he’d meet us at the café but was nowhere when I turned up.  Where does he think he is?       Yeah, I saw that. Lucy’s starting to get that  cold shoulder  vibe, but she doesn’t get why you’re clued in. She thinks he’s just “being a bit busy,” whatever that means. Honestly, I’ve had it up to here. I’m done with the “charming” ones who play everyone like a fiddle.      Oh, you haven’t told me half of it, Viv! Wait—has Lucy gone back to him then? I was about to ask you if she was still ignoring me when I said hi.      Yep, you bet. She hides behind, “I didn’t mean to hurt anyone’s feelings,” but I caught her with her hand wrapped around his wrist in the supermarket last week like some sort of  reality TV show  reunion. Honestly, I’ve got a better shot at getting a second date with the postman.      True. He actually still remembers my name, and he’s the one who hands me the parcel every week. Silly really, isn’t it? We talk about homework and the weather, and at least he’s consistent.      That’s oddly romantic. You could write a thesis on it. Or at least a  very chic  social media post.      I’m not doing any of the worrying anymore, though. I had this breakdown last week where I was sat at my desk stressing that I barely have time to revise,  and  to do laundry,  and  manage being single and insecure all at once. It was just too much.      Do you think talking to someone would help? You know, like a proper talk? Not over Likes and DMs but face to face with someone who  gets it ? My uni has these advisors who don’t laugh when you cry during a diagnosis of the entire universe.      Oh yeah, I used mine at Cambridge—no judgements, no cost, and they even brewed strong enough tea to finish your assignment for you. It’s like  therapy 2.0 .      I’ll take it. But right now I just want to swirl this coffee, pretend to be alone, and maybe go back to my flat to watch  something  that doesn’t involve people pretending to be my friend.

Right, who’s having meatballs? You know, I swear mine came out of the oven with string on them last time. Never mind—just shovel it on. I can take it off after.      Not me, thanks, I had chicken at school dinner. But can I have some cheese?      Help yourself, love. Ay, Mark, d’you want a second helping of mash?      Yeah, thanks, Angela. It was a dump of a journey home from work, so I.Fatalfanst need carb therapy.      Did you hear about the hockey match yesterday, Dad? We won 5–3 and Rob went in for like ten minutes of overtime. He scored!      Ten minutes, mate? That’s not even special anymore. I used to play for a team that played for two hours and they still hadn’t called it a draw. Now  that  was a show.      What’s overtime, Dad?      That’s when the game ends and it just carries on until someone scores. Like, I don’t know, a rude way to play human beings for two hours.      Well, while Mark’s out destroying opponents, I’m at home proofreading reports with a pot of tea, because that’s how I roll. I’ve got three more to go tomorrow and one’s a 50-page beauty with spelling errors on every second page. someone enjoy ripping it up.      Ooh, I had a school trip last week—we went to the science museum in Birmingham. Made a robot that could draw shapes, but it kept drawing about half the time. I think it had the hobbles.      Maybe it thought it was doing abstract art.      Maybe it just didn’t like you for cutting up the construction paper.      I did not cut the construction paper.      You tried to stuff it into the printer. We all saw it.      Ah, well, lunches sorted for the next trip then. Now, Mark, I know you said you might come with us to the weekend trip to the go-kart track. If you do, I’m sourcing my own air into the head, no arguments.      Go-karts!? Yeah, you know I’m in. I’ve been kiting roles in spreadsheets for weeks, I’ll take a bit of speed on the road, even if I’m the last to reach the finish line.      Can I come, too? I’ve done three kart races before, once I won, and the guy in second place swore I used nitro boosters.

Rather skip the hotel and just go through the redwoods now? I mean, it's such a clear day... got to see it while we can, don’t you think?      Yeah, honestly, we probably don’t need to book in for another hour or two. We passed a rest stop on the way in, and the signs said the redwoods were only about 20 minutes up the road.      Do you think this is the place where we're meant to turn off? This road is just... nothing. I keep expecting a dragon chase truck or something.      That’s California, isn’t it? A mile of nothing and then out of nowhere, a dragon chase truck and a turkey festival. You never know. Fun fact I read this morning – I think the Coast Redwood is the tallest tree in the world. Some of them are over 300 feet! That doesn’t sound real, does it?      No, that’s mad. I remember we saw some in the National Trust area in the Lake District, but nothing like that. They looked like buildings, some of them. Our guide there used to say they were like ancient skyscrapers.      Funny… watching him now, trotting around in his parka with a bottle of Mateus Rose, mistaking squirrels for bears. You'd think he had a PhD in woodchips by the way he rambled on.      God, yes. I just wanted to hear about the squirrels. He kept saying they were poison.      They're not. But fair enough, the beavers are a bit aggressive if you get too close. Not that I would know... I once got locked out of the ranger office because I tried to feed a beaver and the doors are automated.      You're joking? You fed a beaver?      It was a granola bar. The beaver looked at me like, “What have you done?” Then it stared at the bar like it was a stick. It didn’t like that. I gave up and went back with a sandwich I didn't really want.      You lost a granola bar and a snack! For a beaver!      Sacrifice of the forest or something. You’re just not dressed for that kind of stuff in a big forest. You’ve got to blend in. Wearing flip-flops to a conference sounds casual, but walking into a forest in them is basically a survival crime.      Yeah, but honestly, I’m loving it.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the grilling. That was her best kiev yet.      Oh, she’s just full of surprises lately, isn’t she? I mean, we were all cringing when the bub got backchat on the rugby match with his Gran again.      It wasn’t backchat! I was just correcting her… like, the Lions didn’t lose by 47 in this one, Gran. Not again. It was ten points last time.      Ah, the chase for accuracy continues. Still, looks like you inherited the love of arguments from  both  sides of the family.      You like that one, don’t you? I swear, every time we go visit Granny, the conversation goes from “go on, Eamonn” to history lessons within an hour.      I still can’t figure out whether she’s still a Wallaby fan at heart, thanks to that Aussie boyfriend she had in the seventies.      She told me he left her because of the inappropriate amount of jersey crop tops in the house.      And you believed that version? Try again…      Well, from what I’ve heard, the jersey crop tops were fairly damning, and I think the wallabies moved on.      Speaking of things moving on… what’s the plan for the weekend? Are we going to her place again?      Only if you want to listen to her brag about uploading all the kid’s holiday snaps to Dropbox and then being confused why no one’s  actually  looked at them.      I think she’s trying to beat you at this stage. She said you forgot your phone yesterday because you were too busy telling her about the hedgehogs in your garden.      I was not  telling  her. I was  educating  her. There was a difference.      You must’ve told her about their hearing as well. You know, how they can hear the crinkle of a chocolate wrapper from the shed?      Oh, come on, like you didn’t casually mention that they really like your own-brand biscuits.      I stand by the biscuits. You don’t go further than that without getting near your actual stock.      Alright, alright… moving on.      Unless someone else wants to talk about the number of headaches this week’s had, I’m all ears.      Can we talk about the rugby match next week, though? I heard it’s on at the same time as the film Leon’s got tickets for.      You better pick a side, Daniel, because I’m not driving three different places.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      What's that, then?      That email from work about the leaving do. Blows me away, someone actually remembered to do this for a change.      Yeah, it's been a while since I’ve had one of those. I remember the last one was all Chinese takeaway and someone played slide guitar on their phone. A real highlight.      Oh I don’t remember that one. It was Dan’s leaving do. We had to drag him out for a proper night when he quit.      Right, right. Still, better than just a cake with someone's name on it, eh? This one seems more thoughtful, actually. It's at the local community centre this time – I think the market committee are helping them pick the venue.      Oh, the market’s nice at the weekend. I often pop in when I’m doing my shopping for the week. They usually have some proper interesting stuff, you know, homemade pickles, that sort of thing.      Yeah, and I saw this man selling buckwheat bread the other day. He said it's only made on Fridays. I’ve got a bit of a hankering for it. Want me to pick some up?      Oh, actually, yes. I’ve been trying to cut down on wheat and all that. Silly really, I blame the internet for that. One day I browsed someone’s full low-carb bucket list and now I’m half way down it.      Ah, I see. You can’t be trusted with a social media account when it comes to food. I about considered baking my own sourdough loaf the other week. Twenty-four hours later and I just ended up crying at the stove.      You're not the first to do that, I can tell you. My sister tried making croissants once. Said it was a spiritual journey. Result was a greasy cardboard disaster.      Haha, I'm not even going to try then. But back to the leaving do – we need to bring a gift. Not just the bottle of wine you remember delivering to someone once and it ended up with the cleaner. Not really the best impression if you ask me.      Yeah, let's see. I’ve seen a bloke on eBay selling these vintage cups and saucers, you know, the pastoral set with the cows and sheep. Really nice quality, porcelain type stuff. Just made me think of something proper.

So did you lot actually take the ferry on time or did you get delayed again like last time?      No, no luck this time, actually. Ferry was an hour late. Stuck in Dover because of some cargo ship or something. We missed the train to Lille after getting off.      Liam even got twitchy about missing the train. He wanted to know if a train that left half an hour before the one we were waiting for was going to turn into a ghost or something if we missed it.      Right, right. Let me guess – you two went to Paris again even without the train?      Of course they went to Paris. It’s Paris, Simon. You don’t talk someone out of going to Paris, unless you’re their bank manager and their credit score is already buried six feet under.      It wasn’t  that  irresponsible! We just got a taxi for the night and slept on the train bed in the morning, didn’t we?      Yeah, like you said it looked like a bed, and it was warm, and there was no one in it. Did you tell the story where the guy in the seat behind us grabbed your selfie stick and then walked off?      Oh, I’ve heard that one.      Yeah, she’s gonna be re-telling that for the next three years until Liam tells her he’d rather never go out again. Spent £50 on a taxi just to rush to the station because he thought he saw something suspicious at the hotel.      That’s not suspicious – that’s reckless. Leaving a £200 tip for the hotel staff to check the hallways for shadows. What if you’d found out he was part of a money laundering ring?      He claimed he  did  find out. Said he heard someone whisper about "crypto and transfers" by the lift.      Okay, but let’s be real, Liam’s suspicious about everything. He once thought our Auntie Margaret was dealing in counterfeit lunches. He walked out of her tea shop thinking the scones were fake.      But he was right about the money laundering stuff, if you think about it – at the camping store in Lille. I bought this dodgy box of tent pegs and one of them was made by “EuroBarrel Imports,” and Liam’s eyes went everywhere. He said anyone with that name is dodgy.      Look, I’m not saying Liam isn’t paranoid, but if I were paying for those "tents and weird pegs," I’d be casting a few more sideways glances.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the baby. I can’t believe how fast they grow—what feels like yesterday, she was barely a week old and now she’s talking like she’s going to start school anytime.      Aye, it’s like blink and you miss it. That’s my job, don’t worry. Having you and Aysha nearby helps as well. Though I’ve been meaning to ask, Aysha, how’s the sign language class going? It was quite interesting last time you mentioned it.      Oh it’s brilliant, honestly. I’ve already started using it with some of the kids at school. One of the deaf supply teachers came in for training recently and Myra, our matron, who’s got hearing aids, says she’s finding it useful too. It’s a good way to be inclusive and make sure nobody feels left out.      That sounds amazing. I mean, I can barely sign "hello" and goodbye, but I reckon it’s something I should be learning too. Good for communication at the shop, especially with any customers who are deaf or hard of hearing. I never thought about it like that.      Tell me about it! I reckon it’s something we should all be learning. It’s amazing how many people have some deafness, and not just the obvious ones either. Anyway, have you picked up that new routine for Silas yet, Steve? The one with the baby monitor and the wet bag?      Just about. I’m still not quite sure whether I should be floring the bed with a red flag or a white flag if something goes wrong! But overall, better than trying to do everything at 3 a.m. standing on broken leg.      Steve, your hip replacement is months ago now! I’m surprised it’s still affecting your step. Myra had hers and she was dancing at her granddaughter's birthday by sundown. Come on, a man your age should be twirling the baby around by now.      Ha! Very funny. I’ll have you know I've been doing yoga to keep the circulation going—my doctor says it helps. Though I’m still not convinced this new weather’s helping either.      Ugh, don’t get me started! I open the front door and I swear it could go three ways—storm, frost, or sunshine. You never know what you’ll get.

So did you get the revised version of the Spanish primer from Pedro yet?      Oh, no, I thought he was sending it today, actually. I’ll double-check my inbox after this. I’m just worrying we might not have time to review it before the deadline.      Yeah, deadlines are tight this quarter, aren’t they? We’ve got all the grammar guides to clean up before the ethics committee review next week too. I’m still going over the differences between Latin American versus European Spanish usage—such a nightmare.      Oh, trust me, I’ve been to seminars on it! In fact, I was involved in the last debate on regionalised accent marks and punctuation.      Oh, really? Interesting. I think I missed that one—it sounds important, though. I’ll definitely read your notes if you’ve got them.      You guys are working on Spanish, huh? I’m just slowly getting used to the British English style guide, to be honest. I mean, why do we still capitalise “I” so often and ignore some of the continental spelling rules?      Haha, tell me about it. As a publishing assistant, I’ve spent hours fixing hyphenated compound words that no one else even notices. But I guess it’s part of the charm, right?      Definitely. And it’s not just spelling—sentence structure, word choice, even the formality levels vary depending on which part of the UK you’re targeting. It’s one reason we do so many dialectal checks at the pre-edit stage.      That’s true. Working in publishing feels a bit like being a walk-in thesaurus half the time.      Exactly. Another thing I worry about is the new project on bilingual education policy in Latin America—have you guys read over the draft response from the Chilean publisher yet? They were pretty specific about their preferences.      Oh, I tried, but some sections were a bit confusing. There was a mix of English and Spanish footnotes, and the formatting wasn't consistent. I flagged the document with red text, but you’ll have to run with it.      Thanks for doing that, Sofia. It does help so much when documents are line-marked. I had to clean up a similar one last week—thankfully, you don’t have to fluently read six languages to do it all!      It’s a relief we can rely on each other, honestly. We’re all over different parts of the world’s languages and education systems, but somehow we manage to keep the books remotely readable.

Right, I just wanted to go through the visa stuff again. I’ve had an email from the embassy and it says the processing time is longer than normal because more people are applying post-pandemic. I told them we were going with a registered charity, but they just said to include that in our documents. Got eeny idea when ours will clear?      Yeah, I read something on their website a week ago—they’re saying up to ten weeks now. That’s a bit longer than we’d planned, ain’t it? We need to hit the rally on the sixteenth, don’t we?      Yeah, even if it’s late processed, as long as we get the visa before the first of November, we’ll be okay. I’m just not sure if mine flew over or if I filled the form in too carelessly.      Blimey, you’ve got to be tactical when you fill those in. I mean, I did mine in two goes. First, I looked up every fiddly part online and dotted my Is and crossed my Ts. You need to do that, otherwise they’ll send it back and we’ll be stuck.      I did do that for the application, but I didn’t check my passport photo. Have you got one yet?      No, I was going to take one at home today. Let me sort of make sure there’s no shadows and use a plain white wall like they said. What’d they say in your case?      They said my photo wasn’t clear enough—my face was outta focus, and I had a hat on. Typical!      Look, it’s because most people about to leave the country rush the photos. I had the same problem once—kept getting a rejection for my holiday to Spain because I blinked! I had to get a professional one in Boots. My sister nearly died of laughter when I told her.      I might do that. I can’t cope with redoing the application again. How about the Gumtree ad for the dorm trailer we mentioned? I just posted one, but it’s only had one query.      Yeah, let me put one up too. I had a bit of a brainstorm the other night—added a bit of personality to the ad. Told people how much space it’s got, how clean we kept it, and even added what your cat’s opinion was.

Okay, thanks a million for helping me out last night, Sarah. I was seriously cringing when that happened with my arm.      It wasn’t a problem at all, honestly. I’m just glad we got you to A&E before things got worse. You wouldn’t have been much company if you’d broken it properly!           Oh my god, A&E? Like serious stuff? Why wasn’t I told about this earlier?      Well, you were asleep by the time we got back. It was after midnight. You don’t like to miss a second of beauty sleep, do you, Elsie?      You wound me. I look fine, thanks! So what actually happened?      I was trying to do some push-ups I think I turned my wrist wrong or something, and the pain was unreal. I couldn’t even lift up this tea bag without wincing.      The nurse thought it might have been a hairline fracture. They did an X-ray and said it’s just badly sprained, though. So no cast, which is a relief. But still, no more lifting, no more dodgy push-ups for a while.      That’s so typical of you, Anna. Competitive about literally everything. I mean, even gym class was a warzone with you.      You know what I blame? Liam! He made a comment about how many push-ups I could do and I had to prove him wrong. Rude.      Liam again? I swear, if I bump into him once more I’m gonna scream. He’s like a mosquito about to bite your neck—he just won’t leave.      Honestly, I’ve seen him at the library twice this week! I’m avoiding it now. Maybe I’ll start using a different study room just to avoid that boy.      I’m with you there. He’s not got all the charm of a gingerbread man, bless him. Honestly, Elsie, you and I are the saner ones here.      Well, I do have Lorenzo now. That's progress, anyway.      Oh my god, go on then! What's he like?      You’re going in, aren't you. Quick update, Anna—Lorenzo is from Italy, he doesn’t take flu seriously, and he’s decided we should go to Florence for Easter even though we still have two modules to finish.      Sounds… chaotic. But I’m not entirely surprised. I like him already.      You’ll meet him soon, I promise. He’s coming up for the weekend to meet us all.

So did you enjoy the party last night love? Your grans would’ve had her fill of stories by now.      Yeah it was alright, I suppose. Erm, I dunno, it felt a bit long to be honest.      Oh, you were sat in that corner all the time, I noticed. It was like your grandad tried to rope in every cousin with a funny memory. Even your uncle Derek turned up! I don’t think anyone saw him for a while.      Oh was that the one who tried to sing "Windmills of My Mind" like three times?      That’s the one! I swear he still thinks he’s like a crooner from the fifties. Funniest bit is when your gran told him to shut up, and he said, “Oh, relax, I’m just giving it my best shot!” She nearly fell off her seat laughing.      I didn’t hear that, I was just messing about on my phone. I don’t mean to be rude, but it felt like I was just there to eat cake and listen to people I don’t really know.      It’s not that they’re strangers, love—it’s just that we’ve been out of touch with so many of the Baptists and Cartwrights, and now it’s all back in one room. But it’s not often your grans have a big party. They’re both at that age now where you want to make the memories before they—well—pass on.      I know. I just don’t think I’m used to big family stuff like that. I mean, we’ve got uncles and cousins about everywhere, and suddenly I’m supposed to know their names and remember who had the kid with the black and white cat?      It’s cruel, really, but that’s family, innit. Your uncle Sid was even trying to get you to speak to Maxine’s daughter. She told him he was embarrassing.      Oh bless him, did he crack out the “how about a player of my age?” line?      More or less. She just rolled her eyes and walked off.      Haha, classic. Look, I get it, it’s a nice idea. But next time, can I just pop by for the cake box and then go? Proper promise to still come. I just can’t handle 30 odd relatives in one go.      It’s your family, love. They’ll understand—eventually.

So do you think we’ll get through all right or is it going to be like last time when we got stuck in the middle of nowhere with a massive traffic jam?      I dunno, it’s probably quieter this time o’ year, mind you — motorway can still be a bit dodgy if there’s an accident. But I reckon we’ll be fine. Just as long as you keep your eyes on the road and not your phone this time, yeah?      I ain’t doin’ nothing with me phone, Dad! I just want to watch  Jurassic Park  again but I had it on my iPad and I left it at the house, and now we’re in the car and I’m sad because I love those dinosaurs.      Well, I got the DVD in the boot I think. If you’re good the whole way, we can pop it on when we stop for lunch.      Woo-hoo, thanks Dad! You’re the best! Er, so do we stop at that place near Crewe again with the big chocolate bar?      Dunno if it’s still open, love. That old Boots might’ve become something else. They’re always changing shops, like Amazon putting in their own – it’s mad, really. But I think there’s a decent coffee shop near there somethin’ to do with Holland and Barrett. Bit pricy though.      I just want a full bottle of fizzy water. The manor houses shop one always gives me tummy aches, is it because of the ingredients? Cos I had a funny tummy in the middle o’ the night last week... after eating all that chocolate the night before.      Serves you right! You were telling me you’ve got this Irritable Bowel Syndrome or whatever and you go and scoff four whole bars o’ chocolate like it’s nothing. Kid, you'll learn one day.      It wasn’t  fair , I had a biscuit as well... and that sprite.      Oh right, because that helps. Anyway, the good news is you don’t get tummy aches in the car so much goin’ on holiday unless you eat s    again.      Alright, I will be good. Cross me heart and hope to die. Cos you know I have to get fit to go to Japan one day, like those anime people?      Japan? Why Japan?      Cos they like LATIN and anime and they’ve got big moomins there?

Rather annoying isn't it when the printer just gives up halfway through. I was just in the middle of preparing a transcription and now it's telling me there's a paper jam, but I've checked and there's nothing there.      That's the modern age for you. Ten minutes of figuring it out and then it just dies. I had the same with my photocopier at work last week — a paper jam turned into a flatbed error and now I’m waiting for a repair call. It's not like it used to be when you could take the back off and just give the gears a tap.      Technology these days is made so no one can fix it themselves, don’t you think? When I was a head mistress, we used to get the boys in the technical class to do the basics around the school — replaced lightbulbs, mended windows, you name it. Now everything is sealed and doesn’t want to be opened!      Exactly! And the cost of the printers nowadays hides how much the ink costs. I got the cheapest one I could find, thinking I’d save, but now I spend more on the ink than if I’d bought one with a high-yield cartridge. Honestly, I might have to switch to using proper paper again and write it out by hand. It’s slower, but at least I know it won’t jam.      Aye, I did that once when I first started up. Paper and pen every job — slower, yes, but someone at the end of the day could say they’d seen the work done. Now I buy all my bits from the tool shop in Cardiff. It’s cheaper in the long run if you plan ahead. You can’t do half a job with a broken drill bit the same way you can’t finish a document with no toner.      I find myself thinking more about the tools I used as a teacher. A blackboard and chalk — no power needed, no glitches. And if you made a mistake, you just rubbed it out and tried again. These days, when I try to use the smartboard in the church hall, I nearly have to read the manual to write the date!      Tell me about it. I had a day last week where the system crashed so much that I had to handwrite correspondence.

Right, so today is Mother’s Day weekend, and I was thinking we could do something special — just like a proper weekend rather than one of those normal ones where you both lose your socks and then find them under the sofa later. What do you think?      Can we have pancakes for breakfast again? Mummy makes  amazing  pancakes.      But not as good as Daddy’s.      Oh yeah? Well I don’t make pancakes with  banana and Nutella  as a topping, thank you very much. That’s called a recipe disaster.      No, it’s not! It’s a masterpiece! Besides, the pancakes are still pancakes.      Okay, fine, but only if it’s not on this Mother’s Day. I want to feel a bit more respected.      Like you’re not respected every day?      I’m respected… most days. Alright — so morning plan: pancakes, no banana and Nutella, then we’ll go to Forest School. I’ve booked that extra session with the puddle walk and the bug hunting. You’ll get muddy — probably.      Yay! Puddles!      I hate puddles.      You can’t hate puddles, they’re  precipitation !      That’s quite advanced for you, Lulu. If I’d known you were going to quote  precipitation  someone at the dinner table, I might have made more of an effort with the sour milk.      I didn’t even say  precipitation . I said  precipitation . You said it about five times.      No, no — that’s the point. You  emit  the idea of water falling from the sky and it becomes a  precipitation  of nonsense. Which is just like raining idioms.      Can we use idioms in our Mother’s Day cards?      Absolutely! You can write “I hope you have a  piece of the cake  day” or “I’m  over the moon  about being your mummy”. Even if you  don't have a clue  what the words mean, that’s fine.      I’m going to write, “Mummy, I hope you always go with the flow” — what does that mean?      It means I never have to shout at you again. Well, maybe not  never , but let’s say, “not very often”.      I’m making you something special. It’s going to be a  two-in-one card  with a mini present inside.      Ah, the kind that’s got glitter, and a scribbled picture of me with six arms and a hat made out of dinosaurs?      Yes!      That’s exactly the kind of Mother’s Day present a person dreams of.

Rather skip the newfit isn't it.      That's it, yeah. We had to take our mister out of the newfit and I think it's probably gone over to a care home in Cannock.      Right. Poor things gone through so much. Has he got cancer?      Mm he had bowel cancer and then they thought they'd got rid of it but now the side effects and the pain... Oh it's just not fair, is it. We've been through so much and now the chase of trying to keep him safe and not getting infections.      Aye, it's the worst, you can do all the right things and you still fall over, you still get ill. It doesn't matter how much you look after yourself.      Yeah and then with the mental health side of things... He's getting anxious and confused sometimes. It's breaking my heart. The doctors don't want to give too much strong medication, even though it's so obvious he's struggling.      That's a real killer, isn't it. I know with my mother, it wasn't grief so much as the fact that she was on her own, and then it started eating her up. She lost weight – no food, no sleep, no chekin'.      Yeah, she don’t got any children did she?      No, no children and her sisters was all older. Poor lass. Just not knowing what to do with herself. I think she was scared something’d happen and nobody’d notice.      That’s awful. You know, most people about our age... we think it’s our mammys and daddies but it’s starting to creep up on us. I was doing some screening and it turns out I’ve got to have a colonoscopy. I’ve been put on high alert because of my dad. He had it as well.      Mm, I did mine when I was thirty-six. It was straightforward and I came out of it thinking, "Right, I need to start watching my diet more". Since then I’ve lost ten stone.      That is something goin' on then! I’ve tried cutting down on red meat and adding more veg, but I still feel like I’ve got that "middle bit", if you know what I mean. The kids don’t help though, they’d rather eat takeaways than even stir-fried veg.      Yeah, the food at them catering colleges isn’t the healthiest either.

Rather skip uni today but I’ve got a request for a student. I was supposed to write a report on... What was it, some vowel shift in Welsh English?      Oh right, you mean that paper about how certain vowel sounds have contracted in places like Ceredigion and Powys. Got it? I thought  I  was supposed to read that one to you yesterday.      Aye, but I think I got side-tracked by your dad’s chicken casserole. Still, it’s a good paper. I got some pretty fascinating insights when I asked the students in my linguistics class to talk about how they grew up using dialect. Some of the younger ones don’t use "oi" that often anymore, you know, especially if they left the area for uni.      D’you think it’s because they’re trying to sound "normal"? You’ve heard how some of the lads from Ponty use a bit of Hiberno-English when they’re speaking to people from, say, London or the South?      It’s not just Ponty, luv. I’ve noticed the same in Bedford with quite a few students. It’s subtle, but when they mix in some RP vowels, it’s like they’re trying to fit in. Though I suppose it’s not unique to Wales, and certainly not to the UK as a whole.      Speaking of which, I was reading this article about universities in South Korea, and the way they frame education in language classes—like they treat it like a survival skill. I mean, Japanese lessons in secondary schools is one thing, but in Korea it’s intense. Men and women even get different levels of training in about how to address each other in formal contexts.      It’s fascinating stuff. Maybe that’s part of the reason why I find syntax so interesting. You ever notice that the older lecturers at Lewes University always use certain words like "suchlike" and "whyn't" in their sentences, as if it's a personal brand? It's almost like spoon-feeding dialect into academic settings.      Oh, I’ve seen that. Dr. Perks? Wasn’t he telling us in the last seminar that "regarding the matter in goin’ on" wasn't invalid or anything, but just predated the modern linguistic preference for constraining clauses?      Aye, and he said it with such pride. Honestly, I think he’s trying to sound like one of those BBC linguistics documentaries to give it authenticity.

Okay, who brought extra cheese? I'm not mad, I'm just  selective .      I did! Thought it was implied. Blimey, I've been in the North for three years and I still can’t read between the lines!      You lot up north use single  drops of sauce  on pizza. I think it's a survival thing up there.      Fair dos! Proper pizza isn’t about slathering sauce, it's about reasonable expectations. We’ve all got to meet in the middle.      Honestly, I like to think of it like  choosing a degree module —if you don’t do some research you end up with a soggy mess you’re not sure how you got into.      So, anyway, I think the world is ending. It either  is  or it definitely will when the flooding comes back and this house collapses like a soggy doughnut.      Oh, don’t exaggerate so much. One time the kitchen was like Waterworld and that was a  sink  flooding, not the Sean Bean of land masses.      But it still washed away my essay on  Cloud Atlas . I rewrote it in Bedlinog at my nan’s house with a net connection like, 0.5kbps. I almost died of loneliness and grammar errors.      You don’t say. I mean, I’ve only ever cried in Lectures 1: Ancient Greece, but that's oddly therapeutic.      I just spent three hours looking at module assessments for next term and it's like they've all been written in Old Norse. I don’t even know what the  option on gendered pronouns in 19th-century cricket data  is.      You’re not the only one. I just signed up for “The Ethics of Controversial Late-Night TV”. I'm told it involves Jack Whitehall talking about witches and them giving him passing marks.      I’m doing  political philosophy . It’s basically just a fancy way of Googling if Marx is allowed to be  that serious  with a bowler hat.      Speaking of, anyone seen  Charlie Simpson  performing lately? Is it just me, or does he randomly box punches in the air at one point? It's like he’s in a 3AM seminar and it’s gone wrong.      Oh right, we saw that! He was so animated I thought he was about to tell the audience something  reassuringly  true.      And then it cuts to him spontaneously side-eying the camera like it used to be part of an old argument.

So did I not see the meeting memo on the software upgrade or what?      Yeah... I don’t think they sent it yet. I asked my assistant this morning, and she said there was some confusion about who to send it to.      Honestly, it’s so annoying when things like that get lost in the system. I tried to log in this morning, and half the tools were down. I spent twenty minutes debugging a problem I didn’t even cause.      Yeah, I had the same thing. Funny thing is, I called the help desk and they said everything’s working fine. So I made them talk me through the login process, only to find out the system had changed itself overnight.      Oh no, did they auto-deploy the beta without telling anyone?      Looks like it. I was just about to message you when I noticed the new look. God, they’ve taken out the old dashboard, changed the colour scheme, and reorganised all the tabs.      I mean, it  does  look better, in a really modern way, but honestly, as someone who spends eight hours a day in that interface, it’s so frustrating when it changes without a warning. I swear half my personality is that system at this point.      Totally. I remember when I first started learning to use it two years ago. I had no idea what half the buttons did and spent ages just figuring out the basics. Now I’ve got my own shortcuts and key combinations that no one else probably even knows about.      For real. Like I’ve got a keybind for flipping between the data parsing tool and the anomaly scanner. I can do the whole workflow in under二十 seconds if I’m not distracted.      You handle it like a superhero in that thing. But honestly, the worst part is when they mess around with what you’ve already mastered. I remember one update where they removed the timeline view, and I had to drag little boxes manually for a week to reassemble what I wanted to see.      Yeah, that was brutal. I took the easy way out and set up a macro with a script I found online. It runs every hour on the hour if you don’t mind the odd pop-up.      Oh god, did I miss something?      No, it’s just me cleaning up the interface after every forced update.

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather.      Aye, it’s been like a proper nutter all week. One day it’s baking, next it’s like we’re in a rainforest.      I know what you mean, Dad. It was sunshine bright and early this morning, and now it’s drizzling again. Makes me think about all the poor choices I’ve made wearing trousers when I should’ve worn shorts.      Imagine what it’s like for the older folks. My aunt Phyllis called me in, said the damp has got her back like a branding iron.      Oh, the damp, don’t go on about that. My knees are playing up again, and my left foot feels like it’s swollen to the size of a lemon, bless it.      It must be about the old age then, mustn’t it. I notice my hands won’t stay in repose anymore, they’re always a bit fidgety, always tingling a little. I reckon it’s the price you pay when you get on a bit.      Right, as if you’re not only paying with old age—you’ve got to be worrying about your blood pressure and cholesterol now. You’re bound to see your doctor more often than you see your grandchildren these days.      Now don’t go making them depressed at tea-time, Selina. It’s not been so bad for me, actually. Spent a week in King’s Lynn just a month back for some specialist tests. Turns out I’d better watch my diet and take more walks through the park.      You know I about blocked artery years ago? My doctor nearly put me on medication, but I took it as a sign and started eating better. Not that I gave up meat altogether—just went easy on the pies, for example.      Aye, cut down on the pies. You try telling a man that, love.      You mustn’t start on him, Tony. I know what you’re like when you've had a mince pie with your tea.      Honestly, I find this entire conversation a bit bleak. Let’s talk about something cheering—like football.      Oh, not the football again, Darce. That team of yours has already had 12 points deducted for debt this season. You think you’re watching football, you’re really watching financial statements.      Very funny, very funny. At least they're still in the game, unlike yours—they got relegated and they were the only team in the region remotely worth watching, in my opinion.

Okay, thanks a million for meeting up. I needed this. Work has been absolute hell this week.      Don't worry, I'm glad we did. I've been buried in sales figures and client meetings. When do we ever get time to just chat properly anymore?      I know, I feel like I'm either at the office or at home designing websites. No in-between. Agh, but enough about that—how's the wedding going? Is it all planned or is it a train wreck like the last one?      Oh trust me, it’s like three miniature weddings baked into one—our preferences, my sister’s, and the venue staff trying to sound posh and failing. Honestly, I’m just happy it’s not back in Wegberg, Leonie, even if that was the only place you had a stable phone signal for dress appointments.      I’m just trying to remember not to drive in there and burn the whole thing down when we argue over the wedding cakes. Also, the colour scheme is still hot pink and lime green, yes?      I mean if we’re going to do this, why not be deadly? Look, though, I’ve been meaning to ask, are you all coming to the dinner at my nan’s next weekend? I know it’s informal, but she’s been cooking like her hair’s on fire all week. Silly woman thinks it’s the last supper.      Who wouldn’t miss your nan’s roast? She still insists on making her oddly sour Yorkshire pudding with nutmeg, by the way. What even is that?      I’ve never tasted it and I’m honestly never going to. But yes, I’ll be there. It’s a cooking mission, and not one I’m signed up for.      I’ll be there, but only if someone brings wine that’s not passed its expiry. My health depends on it.      Speaking of wine, someone brought it up when I was out with Casey last night—how are you two doing?       sigh  Well, I took the bull by the horns and told him I wasn’t stopping working just to be a goody-two-shoes life partner. So now he’s got a cold shoulder line in, and I’m left with the boxset binging and questionable investments in virtual pet rabbits.      Oh no, not virtual rabbits. That’s a step too far from tattoos to farm games.

Rather skip the newfit and go through the request button.      Yeah they said like you got to go through this thing. Otherwise they won’t pay you.      It is rather complicated with all that computer stuff I mean what would I do with all that I don’t want to use it I mean I’m just an old lady I sit at home read all day not on a computer.      Yeah this is a computer. Oh but I watched a programme about someone that had one of these and she got like this new chase when she bought the new tablet and she saw like three times more money in her bank.      Yeah only if you know someone like that My turkey still walks around with a tin though left over money you know. I had one like that in my young days and I think it turned into a piece of scrap now.      I would never be that clever with computers no matter what in my whole life I would ever want to have one of them.      Yeah I mean that’s why I do it, get it done and out of the way I never thought about it as much as you and dad do, old ways.      You have to remember when we got married we didn’t even have a television at first I mean and now it's all this newfangled stuff.      Yeah I use mine for games and mail and messages and the odd online shop.      Well I wouldn’t know what a message button did I’d probably buy something and not know how to stop it and then get chased through the door like I had done in the past because of a catalogue.      That's right the delivery man once had to chase a woman into the garden because her husband was trying to stop him delivering it.      Yeah I mean I just like the ones with high scores and all that. I play them on the tablet before I go to work it passes the time.      My sons insist I have one and that they can call me but I always tell 'em I’m not one of the tech-savvy folk like you and dad.      That's because go out of my way to be like that I got mine at the shop in town and the man that runs it showed me how to use it and what your buttons do you know.

Rather skip to the front of the queue.      That's alright, no rush. I got the time, same as you now I suppose. I used to be the one rushing about, getting things done. Not quite so much these days.      No, but it's good to catch up, isn't it? Having tea on a rainy Saturday afternoon—there's something very retro about that. Almost like one of those Channel 4 dramas where everyone drinks builders tea and talks about their mortgages.      Ah yes, well when I was still running things up north, the only tea I ever had was when I was stuck in boardroom meetings, and that was mostly lukewarm and swigged out of melamine mugs.      I bet you had a special mug for the boardroom. Something engraved with your company’s initials. Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt.      No, I didn’t go in for mugs or breakfasts.
