Kept it simple. Worked early—set the tone, you know? Always believed in starting the day properly if you wanted your staff to respect you and the business. Bit of routine, bit of discipline.      That sounds very… seventies – very estate boss with a briefcase and clip-on tie.      Now don’t go making me sound like a lost cause. I might’ve had that look, but I also had someone who could speak four languages. And not badly either. It helped when we had clients coming out of the woodwork—Dubai, Jakarta, here, there.      Ooh, I did teach Indonesian for a while. Decent language, but tricky to keep up with. I’ve switched more to Spanish now that I’m teaching more in the local school up here in Hitchin. Makes for easier holidays—I can still survive in Barcelona if I need to.      You mentioned holidays—still trying to get to Germany for your little study break? We had to do that when I was managing. Always had to send someone off to keep the whole production line ticking.      Yes, something around March, if I can get the leave go through. I usually take the kids or my brother along. Keeps them out of trouble, and I can teach them a bit of basic language while I’m at it.      Good call. You never know when language knowledge comes in handy. You might find yourself ordering a beer in Berlin and overcompensate by chatting them up in broken German.

So did you go out for Valentine’s weekend? Or did you glue yourself to your books again?      I’ll have you know I did more than  glue  myself to my books! I went out… with two of my cousins and we had a slap-up meal in that little Italian place on the High Street, the one with the garlic steak. I reckon it was more Valentine’s than most people.      Fair enough! At least you had edible roses instead of your ex. I just sat at home watching  When Harry Met Sally  for the fifteenth time.      Oh, classic! Still, better than my week before, when the takeaway garlic bread got stuck in the microwave door and I had to reschedule my dinner to Tuesday. It was tragic.      Oliver should’ve brought round bubble tea or something. But no, he was far too busy working on his breakfast recipe—cereal bars made of leftover pasta.      I pity the man who hides feta in his spare change jar. Are you over him now?      A hundred per cent. I’ve even written him two letters saying I’m over him and I only sent one by accident. He probably thinks I’m still living in his postcode, but hey—I’ve moved on.      I know I would’ve just ghosted him. Let’s be real, no one needs a man who’s better at making lists than people.      True. So what about Friday night? What are you doing this week? Trying to hang out at the cinema?      Oh, I thought we might split a pizza and  try  to watch that new Apple movie everyone says is “philosophical.” But honestly, I’m just there for the popcorn. Maybe we could meet up beforehand and then get a coffee afterwards?      Yeah, that sounds way better than hiding from my flatmate who insists on giving me  looks  every time I eat a bag of Maltesers. I tried to tell her Maltesers aren’t an emotional response, but… middle-aged women never listen.      No wonder you’re single. Some people still talk like you  chose  this lifestyle.      I did! I chose it about seven breaks ago.      Okay, but seriously, do we go to the one on campus or your nearest town’s cinema? I’ve noticed the 3D one’s been playing every horror film since 2009.      Perks of growing up in London: everything’s 10 minutes away.

So did you order yet? I was just checking the menu. This looks like it's going to be  way  better than the same old bap from my lunchtime takeaway desk superstall.      Yeah, I got the pad Thai with extra tofu — you can have half if you want. And I got a side of spring rolls for the table.      You're a godsend. I’m still trying to decide between the chicken pho or the ramen. Honestly, both look amazing.      Go for the ramen. The pho’s got a lot of ginger, and I’m still not used to that spice level. Though honestly, do you ever miss that Mynter Square bakery cappuccino and rugelach combo?      Every single day. I think the world is missing out on assembling proper croissants properly. Wait… on a more serious note… have you read this article in  The Guardian  today about housing in London? They’re saying property developers are using the EU excluded migration crisis as a smokescreen to blame low housing supply on "foreign demand".      Oh yeah, I did. That’s wild. It’s like watching municipal politics circle the drain in first gear. You want to build –?      Housing – but it’s easier to throw a tantrum about “dark foreign money” than fix the council tax system or streamline planning laws. It’s so classist, honestly. As if low-income housing crisis is somehow a result of racism, not austerity.      Exactly. And now the real estate politicians are replying like,  “Oh, there’s not nearly enough affordable housing,”  while the same people are talking about building luxury apartments for vibes and a Netflix special budget. It’s so performative.      It’s like the system is  designed  to keep people rent-stressed and disempowered. I remember when the Whitechapel land was all set to have a housing development for council waiting lists, but then the market got a whiff of "investor" space and next thing you know, it’s "stayed in the area".      Welcome to capitalism! The system is set up so developers get capital gains if they wait until housing demand increases naturally, while the rest of us are left with rent hikes, bloated deposits, and your actual architectural blueprints are just planning permission for 300 one-bedroom flats where those 23 people could have been living more affordably.      Which is why I hate that they always bring up “growth” like it’s this neutral, kind thing.

So nurseries today, they’ve got these whole systems, do they not? I mean, they’re like... proper organisations rather than just childminders like when I were younger. I've been over to a few to have a look, and they have rules about what you can bring in and how much notice they want for holidays.      Yeah, I reckon it depends where you are. The one I’ve got my eye on just outside of Sutton has got a playgroup thing and they do some sort of activities. We’ve been invited to a taster session in a few weeks.      Right, well, if you can get a spot, that’s the main thing. I’ve heard bits about how the waiting list can be years sometimes. I left mine on one when I was still working, and I swear they kept adding people in the queue without telling us!      Ugh, I don’t even want to think about that! I’d be losing my mind, you know?      You’d be justified too. And I reckon once she’s in one, it’s a bit easier for you—going back to work, all that. But still, grief when she’s having her weaning properly and not used to being away from you all day.      Mate, I don’t know, I think it will be hard. I imagine her crying the first day and me crying through the car window or something. I don’t fancy the job of being the villain someone who drops her off and walks off.      I know, but what you’ll find is she’ll get over it and be fine. That’s what mine did. You’re there most of the time at home now, but you can’t do the job lot forever. Work and rest for you and some time for yourself is necessary.      Maybe. I do need to get back on the balls for my PhD after the summer, so that’s part of the reason. But I was thinking, once the nursery’s sorted, you know... maybe a quick trip. France or Spain somewhere. Maybe even doing a short bit of work online to keep the money ticking over.      That sounds like a good idea. We went to the Algarve for a bit when mine started school and it was brilliant. Not much else to do in the day, so we just relaxed, ate bad chips and read.

Right, I just wanted to bring up the whole phone bill thing. I know it's been a week and all, but I’m still confused about the £12 I got charged by EE after using my phone on holiday.      Was it the same as last time with the data roaming? Got warned about that when I had to call them for my son’s phone.      Oh yeah, that was a proper scandal last summer! My sister got hit with like a hundred quid for pulling her phone out of her pocket in France. She didn’t even use it that much.      It’s a bit dodgy, honestly. I’ve got the same plan and I’ve had to put a pin code on my SIM to stop it auto-surviving when I’m abroad. It’s annoying, but it beats paying extra every time you flick a switch.      Exactly! And when I called the number on the bill, no one was in until next day, and the phone kept dropping out, to be honest. I was trying to speak to real person like I was with Thames Valley Police last week when I gave my written statement.      Giving a statement? For what? Nothing dodgy going on?      Oh, it’s not that dramatic — just about a road accident I witnessed last Friday. The police were trying to get accounts from everyone around. I did mine in the phone first, then later went in and did it in writing.      Oh no, weren’t you trying to go into work that week?      Yeah, hence the reason I had to give it through the police so I could be clear when they came to speak about the company’s insurance side. I’m the main contact person at this stage.      That’s quite an extra you’re having to handle. You up for it? I mean, I’d be baked if I was in your shoes.      Honestly, a bit. I was meant to be working with the team all morning, waiting on them to come. But it’s not that bad as long as you keep notes and hand over a clear timeline of events.      That sounds proper lawyer stuff. You need to make the points clear or go in with someone to help if you’re not used to it.      I reckon it's like explaining a bloomin’ recipe to your nan.

So did you watch  Spartacus  last night? I was telling people in my class about it—basically the whole show is just one big Roman history crash course, murder, rebellion, and a bunch of fighting in sandals.      Oh yeah, I caught the first few episodes again on catch-up. I mean, it’s wild, right? Makes me think about all the real Romans I’ve probably stepped on when I was walking around the garden back home.      Haha, you’re gardening on the bones of ancient history! Do you want to make a Roman-style meatball like they had back then? I made some last night with lentils, garlic, chickpeas and a bit of olive oil. I’ve even got a mortar and pestle now—from a market in Bedford.      Oh, you? You spend your cash on fancy kitchen bits while I’ve got calluses from actually working this land. Honestly though, I’ll give it a go. I remember we used to have something like that when I was growing up, but that was more for spices and coriander, not meatballs.      Here’s the thing though—I started reading up more on Roman food and it turns out, they actually liked their food pretty spicy. Not too different from what we do these days, except they had more  garum  and far fewer flat white orders to go with it.      Garum? What, is that like this super-dusty anchovy sauce?      Pretty much. Imagine a fishy nut sauce—sounds weird, but apparently delicious. Anyways, speaking of spices, your grandmother gave me a bag of about five herbs and told me not to lose the red one. She says it’s for cooking or for “the teas you take when you’re laid out like a lasagne.”      That must be the cinnamon—or maybe cardamom. She always mixes it into everything. I remember she once rubbed turmeric on my ears to get them to stop “glowing like a fire engine.”      Ah, classic grandmothers. I’ve tried to do the same but with no success.      Anyway, man, I heard goings on with your life are wild. You got married? Did I even know that?      You did—vaguely. It was a quiet thing. Just me, her, and her Greek aunt who insists on holding all my hands like we’re both about to die.      C’mon! What about a big party? The kind with music and meat on the barbeque and people suffering from sea lice because they swam in the wrong sea and then want a kebab at 2am?

So did you get an email about the English test yet? I’ve been stressing out all week about it.      Yeah, I did! It’s next Tuesday, isn’t it? I was doing past papers over the weekend and the vocab questions are such a nightmare.      Right? I  hate  the ‘synonyms and antonyms’ section — it’s so annoying because half the words I don’t even know! I got to like question ten and thought “this is it, I’m done for.”      Oh, don’t say that! You’ll totally pass. Did you go to the after-school revision session last week? I only grabbed ten minutes in like the last five minutes before I had to leave.      I didn’t go at all. I was helping my mum get the house ready for an open plan — we’re trying to sell. But honestly, if I’d been there, maybe I’d be a bit less confused about the conditional tenses, right?      Yeah, those were brutal. I still can’t get my head around the difference between the second and third conditional. Want to revise together before the test on Monday?      Yeah, that’d be good. Want to come over after –?      Yeah, I’ll bring my notes. Also, weren’t you telling me about the wind band at school? I heard one of the teachers say the orchestra is going to do that joint music festival thing with the school in Ely?      Oh yeah! They’re doing a concert in the church and it’s supposed to be super fancy. I’ve been practising my flutesuper intensely. My dad’s even started talking about booking flights to watch me. Honestly, he goes from zero to emotionally supportive in seconds when I’m near a musical instrument.      Haha, he’s your proud parent 2.0. I told him the year before last when I was in the choir, and he’s been waiting for me to stick with something ever since. I’m in the art club now trying to draw portraits. It’s harder than it looks!      I did a portrait once for art class and the teacher go me a B for life improvements and a B+.      Wait, no, that’s like the highest praise ever. You were one of the only people who managed to get the nose right, apparently.      Ugh, don’t remind me. I still have nightmares over shading mistakes.

Right, thanks for coming in today, love. Thought we could talk about that holiday—the one we kept pining over last year, Barcelona. You remember?      Yeah, I dunno, Gran. It all sounds nice and all, but I’ve got exams coming up. And I don’t want to mess my GCSEs up just for a holiday. Plus, I’m not sure how much a plane ticket would cost.      Hold on, Tim, you don’t need to know the exact cost! Just enjoy the thought of it. Didn’t your Nan teach you how to dream before you worry about the price?      That’s right. You’re only young once, and you’ll have a proper holiday with your gran who actually left the house this morning! I’m not missing this, Viv, I’m doing it!      I’m not arguing with you! I just, um… if I do go, won’t I be missing revision time?      Oh, don’t you be so serious. One week, Tim, that’s it. We’ll get reading guides and listen to the occasional podcast if we land a rude teacher. You’ll be fine, love. Besides, education isn’t just books.      That’s what I kept saying when I was teaching. Sometimes, you’ve got to get out of the classroom and learn the world.      You know what I found interesting, though? My teacher’s sister works at someone’s music festival. She said Ed Sheeran might be playing one night. I wonder what he’s like up close.      Er, Ed Sheeran? I’ve seen him once in about 2008. Bloke from the bar said he was “the one with the lack of larynx.” Not that I’d know. Haven’t heard a note.      You can’t just rubbish him, Gwen. He’s a global superstar. Proper brand, man.      Yeah, he’s got all the hashtags and stuff. Likes to use #goals and #focus with his songs. Grans, are you even on social media?      I’ve got Facebook! I posted a picture of that really smelly fish I had for tea last week. Gave my friends a right laugh, I’ll tell you.      Oh yes, you made all the news feeds proud with that kippers one. I think you gained five new followers because of it!      So does this mean we can be tourists and still do a little bit of studying? Like, if we hit a café and I write my notes, can Gran order me a chocolate croissant?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh Harry? That car in front’s practically trying to get squashed in first gear every time. Never mind driving—how do they even pass their test these days?      Aye, we do see the odd one—some people wouldn't know a carburettor if it bit 'em. But I'm more worried 'bout people eating now—half of 'em look like they’re too heavy to get in a car, let alone drive it. It's a mess.      Oh, don’t be so negative, Harry. That new vegan bakery opened up in the village, you know. People are trying to eat healthier now, thank goodness.      My lectures are full of students with jelly-leg syndrome. One tried to lift a textbook and had to sit down, he was so out of breath. Half the class is allergic to gluten and the other half doesn’t touch dairy. I swear, everyone has a microbe these days they’d rather not share.      Aye, I had to stop smoking for that cough I got last year, otherwise I wouldn’t have been up half the night with it.      It’s not just the smoking—everybody’s always short of breath these days, from what I see. My partner works in healthcare, and she says young people these days are more likely to end up needing an op than their parents ever did at their age.      That’s because they’re born with someone older in one hand and a phone in the other. It just messes with the genes—everyone’s walking around with aches and pains and being overweight. Can you imagine when your grandmother had us? She nearly did cartwheels after a hip replacement.      Aye, and I remember you being the one who couldn’t plug in a toaster if it didn’t have pictures step-by-step, Lucy. You called me twice that week after you tried to cut the plug off with a pair of gardening shears.      That was you, waiting till I could see the plug! I had that toaster in pieces for weeks. Took me 'til I found someone with a soldering iron and a brain.      You're like a couple of old Victorian gothic novels on your own if you start boring about toasters and loosened dentures, but I will say this—my dad had a bypass at your age, Harry. It really makes you think about why we’re all still out here driving off-roads in belly flops to third gear.

So did you get the tutorial sheet uploaded on to Moodle before you left the office this morning?      Yeah, I think so. I’m 90% sure I did. Let me check quickly on my laptop when we get home… No, wait, I remember now—it’s up. Got it all sorted at about half past eight this morning. Sent a confirmation email to the module leader just to be safe. A lot of people would panic if this stuff isn’t there on time.      Oh, good. I was worried for a second you’d missed it again.      Not this time! I’ve been trying so hard not to leave the last-minute deadline stuff to the wire like I used to. Although I must say, I left the weeknotes just overlong this time. You know how it is—three paragraphs per week? Half the students probably just skim the first one.      You’re not wrong. Honestly, I simplified mine this term, just five bullet points and a link to the reading. Students have enough to digest, and that way I get to tell them exactly what is essential without them glazing over in the middle.      I wish I’d thought of that. I spend hours writing them and then no one reads them. I’m thinking of adding a pop quiz just to make sure they’ve seen  something .      Haha, you and quizzes. If I do one, I make it fun, though. Like this week I put in a multiple-choice question:  "What is the capital of the UK?"  with flippant options like   "Manchester," "Hogwarts," and "Cambridge."   Guess what most people chose?      "Hogwarts," obviously. You’re trying to make light of your fails at engagement, aren’t you?      Maybe. I do take this stuff seriously though. There’s something about teaching computing that’s different. It’s not like the arts—this is technical, it’s very black and white. If your code crashes, it crashes, and you  have  to debug it. Except when the system itself crashes on Moodle and half the class can’t even reach the login page.      Oh man, I got goaded on my forum post about that. Some students think Moodle is "broken" every time they see a pop-up update box.      It’s like the joke goes—"Moodle 3.0 released"—"What’s new?"—"IT ISN’T WORKING ANYMORE!" Honestly, over half the time I’m just troubleshooting the LMS instead of my actual job.

So did you sleep at all last night?      A few hours, scattered in between flights and the kids woken by jetlag at different times. You know how it goes.      Not quite how I would describe a holiday! But at least the timing was good for one of the holidays, I guess.      True. We wanted to see if a week away would help settle Olivia’s sleep schedule a bit, but somehow we all ended up as insomniacs. We’ve been feeding her at 2 am, when it’s still 9pm in Norwich. It’s like being trapped in a time zone error.      You know, I always think you look older after these trips. You left with a clean shave and now you look like you’ve been living in a post-apocalyptic world for a month.      Thank you. Very kind of you. I feel it, though — in my bones. I keep expecting to hear that flight attendant ordering puff pastry and wine again. Good lord, I thought I was over aeroplane coffee but I must’ve had six cups in two days.      And how was the baby? Did she like watching other infants circle the terminal in little baby strollers?      She liked it, and hated it all at once. Some babies stared her down like rivals, others cooed at her like fans. The other parents were the worst — all these proud someone’s baby doing a TikTok dance. Olivia just laid there, judging everyone.      Judging them or just deep in thought about the cosmic meaning of flight paths and parenting culture?      Possibly both.      Have you had any time to actually enjoy your holiday or are you regretfully logging the flights as research for a lecture now?      I watched one episode of  Parks and Rec  and read 10 pages of a paper on bilingualism in very young children. I miss when holidays meant doing nothing.      That’s what we always tell ourselves. One holiday to “switch off,” and somehow we come back with more reflection points than a philosophy essay.      It’s true. But if you ask me, the one good thing is Olivia started smiling at 4 am. Who knew jetlag could be the one thing that unlocked her personality.      She’s been smiling at you since she was born — it’s just been a bit more hidden from over-tired parents.      You’re so kind. I’ll return the compliment when you come to the baby's CBeebies casting call.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, me being German and all, but I've been living here in Liverpool for well over twenty years now. Still find I can't say enough about how different things are across the water with the politics and the oil mess—get on well with the place, but it's all a bit  beyond  me, really. Still, it's not as grim as it used to be, is it? Not like in the old days, what with all the Wahabi nonsense pulling the strings. Know what I mean?      Yeah, mate, I know what you're saying. It's mostly  managed  from here, isn't it, still? You know, like that old turkey, Reagan, back in his day left the mess for us to pick up now. And what with the push and pull in the world now, oil's still the main muscle behind it all. I've worked with loads of Iraqis over here, some in hard cases, needing visas and all that, especially after the war broke out—and I tell you, it's  not  easy getting permission to get out, or in, really. I've done quite a few translations for people who only made it out as war refugees.      That’s a right struggle. I mean, my Mateha from university, she got her cousin out just before things really kicked off. He was in Baghdad and got offered a place here on a student visa, but the process—good God. Took what, almost two years to get the paperwork sorted. Now he's here doing a bit of teaching—piece of work, he's a fluent English speaker and all. Can't speak  for  the Prime Minister, though, mind.      Hah, yeah, I get that. I’ve interpreted for some folks who were pretty outspoken about the government up there. Still, I try not to get  too  involved. My sister’s in Kirkuk, working on health stuff, and she says it's not safe for anyone under thirty-five to hang about for long unless they’re armed. She had to  move house  twice last year because of the 'community issues'—you know the type, the ones who like to  sort things out  by fire and steel. Yeah, go there on holiday? Not if you like  sleeping at night .      You're serious? That's bad. I read a bit in the paper about the rise in violence up North, but I didn’t think it was that bad.

Rather skip the newfit and go to the gym tomorrow, do you reckon?      Oh, dear, I often say the dining room isn’t properly utilised these days. A bit of telly in there with a nice spread would make it feel homely again.      That would be a nice touch. It’s all right here if you just wanted to have evenings with a bit of quiet conversation, but I think the telly would bring it to life. Imagine a roast lamb or something. We could even pop the dogs in the garden during the commercials.      Right, but truth be told, I can barely afford to keep the fridge full at the moment with the new rent the landlord slapped on us. I swear, he’s milking us more than the cows back in Dungavallen. I think he turned round and sold the house for about 20k more when it was practically falling apart.      Oh, he’s not the first! That’s what happens when property is so in demand. I remember when I was headmistress, the school had to move out of the old building because the land was snapped up by developers and sold for twice what they paid. Come on, they did an acoustic set and a cover of that Sparks song – I nearly fell off the barstool in tears.      Oh yeah? They’re been getting brave with their covers lately. Last time they did some The Cure and even went into some Queen!      Yeah, I know. I reckon Sam, the lead singer, just jumps into the tunes that are stuck in his head that week. Kinda endearing, though. Kinda terrifying as well though, when he does "Heaven is a Place on Earth" in a leather jacket at 11pm.      True. I miss that. Punk rock and questionable pop covers? Silly British nights.      So what did you do all week while I was living the rockstar life?      I got out the paint, finally. You know I started this abstract thing in September – all bold reds and greens? Well I did a whole set of smaller ones to sell on Instagram.      No way! Did you?      Yeah! And a couple went out to some uni kids. One of the girls from Geo., actually. Said it made her feel at home.      That’s amazing. You’ve got to sell your stuff at the next gig, mate. Indie Razors’ merch stall is always trying to find new stuff to sell – I’ll suggest it to them.      Really? That’d be awesome! Then go talk to my cousins’ baby while I’m doing so.      Deal. You know what else? I signed up for the zip-wiling at the farm just north of Donny. Thought I’d live out my cheap thrill phase while I’m still broke.      Oh hell, why not? I’m still counting how many cupcake profits I need to do that.      Listen, if you get too busy babysitting, I’ll take the baby and go do it with me. We’ll just drop it off in the zip-line cart for the ride.

Okay, so the red outbreak is spreading everywhere. I don’t think we’re handling it fast enough. We really need to focus on this city before it gets out of control!      I agree, we probably overextended ourselves last turn. We saved three cities but now the cure for red is on hold and there’s more than one outbreak already. We’re at 12—get that?—and that only takes one more to lose!      If only we had a player controlling the ambulance! Instead, we’re stuck with this chef trying to save the world with chopsticks. Get the med kit!      That’s your idea of a joke? You’re the one that set this up. You picked the board game.      And I still say if we played this and I won, the accolades would be in both my job and this! Domino breakfast, anyone?      Haha, funny. But honestly, we need to decide roles properly this round. Cas—and that’s not your full name, by the way—you’re the director of policy changes. Robin takes meds. I’ll be logistics. And Adam, you’re the curator of cards. Try not to drop any during outbreaks.      Excellent. Looking back at my thirty years in charity, I’ve learned the secret to success is delegation and tea. It’s not just any tea, it’s herbal—strong and sensible!      I just don’t get how this is a cooperative game. When I work at the support centre, everyone works together, but it’s still someone’s fault if something goes wrong. Is someone always in charge here?      That’s the beauty of the game, Helen. You have to work as a team and make decisions together. There’s no blaming the housing officer if we run out of treat actions, for example.      On that note, I just used my only treat action to save Dublin instead of Birmingham.      You madman! We needed to clear Birmingham  first  to get out of Yellow!      At least the team took the bull by the horns and prioritised Dublin. Now we can work backward.      If I had a quid for every metaphor in this game...      You’re all missing something important. Pass me the board. I have a theory.      We’re hours into the game and now he’s got a theory?      Bear with me. If you look at the outbreaks so far—they’re all on the grid points where the outbreaks started in previous games.

Right, so today is CBeebies day, and I thought we could have a little baking session in the morning. What do you two think?      Can we make fairy cakes?      Of course we can! And I got those cupcake cases with the rainbow colors. They’re just like the  In the Night Garden  ones. And if we use food coloring, they’ll look like something out of a CBeebies story too.      I watched   Ping’s Party Time Today!   last night. They had cake and dancing in the garden.      Yeah, I like Ping! And Maisie. I want to dress up like her!      My, look at that imagination! So, what’s Ping’s favorite color, do you remember?      I think it’s blue. Or maybe green?      Wait, it was blue! I saw her in a blue dress in the episode!      Well, you two are both right—and wrong. One time she wore green, and one time she wore blue. But I think blue is special for her. Like a lucky color. Did you know that on   World Book Day  , they sometimes read books that have characters in blue?      My teacher read one with a blue dragon!      Mine read one with a blue cat! It talked like a phone.      Oh! That must have been  Paw Patrol . Oh no, that’s not a CBeebies character, but it’s definitely an imaginative one. Speaking of imaginative, how about we add a ‘sayings’ board today? Something like "Today is a Happy Day!" or "Time for Fun!" to hang on the fridge?      Can I write it?      Of course, if we run out of markers, we can use the wet paintbrush and colored card. Just like in that  Mention  episode where they paint something on the pottery.      I want to help!      Great. Now, after we’re done baking and crafting, I thought maybe we could do a CBeebies pantomime night in the living room.      Can go as Jasmine?      I want to be the Genie!      Well, you’re both in luck—I already found some fairy lights to string up, and if we turn off the main lights and just use the fairy lights and table lamp, it’ll be just like the magic lamp scene in the show!      Like  Singalongaaurus !      Exactly! And maybe, if it’s nice enough, we can take a family walk to the park in the afternoon, and before it gets too cold, pick out some flowers for   Mother’s Day  .

So do you ever just wish you could just up and leave everything behind and just go? Like real go—basically to another continent or something?      Not really, no. I mean, where would we go? We wouldn’t have a home, a job, or friends. I like stability, even if it  is  a bit routine.      I get what you're saying though. A change of scenery would do wonders for my social life. And my mental health. Honestly, sometimes it feels like we all just orbit the same bar every Thursday night.      That’s the problem with living in a city—everything’s so close, and people are always around. It’s like you’re never really alone, but you’re also not really getting out of your bubble.      But moving for the sake of moving? That’s chaotic. What about jobs? How do we get work in a new country? I’d hate to have to start at the bottom again, especially in journalism.      Well, I might actually consider it. I’ve been thinking about teaching English abroad—Thailand, maybe Spain. You don’t need as much paperwork as you think for something like that. Plus, I could always remote-teach part-time from wherever I land.      That’s fairly radical, but I respect the thought process. I’ve been offered an engineering gig in Norway next year. Temporary, sure, but it’s a massive shift from what I’m used to. Spent my whole life in the north of England, and suddenly I’m a Brit with a Norwegian winter to survive.      Really? That sounds wild! What about the culture clash? I mean, I’m not a fan of standing on the subway clinging to a pole looking at a screen all day. Going into that intentional silence and minimalism sounds exhausting after London.      I say do it! Just do it for a year. You’ll learn more about yourself in one year of living abroad than you would in ten years here. And when you come back, you’ll have a  story  to tell at every dinner party.      Fair point. I do miss going out there for proper hikes where I can actually see the sky. Yeah, go on, I’ll tell you what—let’s go on a camping trip this weekend, just the three of us. That might be the closest thing to “relocating” we can manage.

So did you manage to pick up those books I needed from the shop yet?      Yeah, I got them this morning. I grabbed a few extra ones too, just in case we wanted to linger a bit with the discussion this month.      That’s very thoughtful of you, dear. I’ve been meaning to say, your little son, James, is getting so adorable. He’s constantly bringing stuff to me at work now—stickers, drawings, even a small dinosaur he proudly said was a "rexiter"—I assume he meant T-rex.      Oh, I adore his imagination. He started asking me yesterday why the fridge eats only when we open it. It took me a while to explain electricity in a child’s version. Ten minutes later, he told me the fridge is a very sad robot because it can't go out in the world.      That actually reminds me of something. When I was in elementary school, I had the hardest time understanding how day and night worked. I was convinced the sun was directly above the world and it just got tired of going around. My teacher laughed and showed me a globe. It still didn’t make sense to me until I moved in with my grandparents during a heatwave in France. That was the most amazing – waking up every day to croissants, sunshine, and long evenings.      Oh, I can see why you're so fond of France! I always say they have the food figured out. Nothing like a good roast chicken with crispy skin and just the right amount of lemon— oring’d out?  Or is that a British thing?      No, I think that’s a universal gold standard. Speaking of cuisine, I had this amazing ravioli last weekend at Sarah’s place. I asked her if it was from a cookery book she found online. Turns out she learned it from an Italian exchange student she met when she was in university. She told me stories about living in Rome, and how you just can’t take your shoes off everywhere unless you’re in a house. Even if it’s a weird, dusty museum café—you leave the shoes on.      I find languages absolutely fascinating! I’ve been learning a bit of Japanese online—just basics. I’m slowly building up courage to try ordering in Japanese when I go to the sushi place near my office.

So did you go anywhere nice on your trip, Grandma? I’ve only just seen your photo on Facebook. It looks beautiful wherever it is.      Oh, aye, we went to a little village in the Scottish Highlands called Plockton. It’s on the coast—Dee’s old een! There’s a bay with a sandy beach and these little white houses with red roofs. You should a seen that sunrise from the window—absolute winner.      Was it peaceful up there or was it busy?      Oh, it was quiet, lad. Not a soul around most of the time. Just the birds and the sea. We had the cottage all to ourselves. Alice and me had the loveliest walks, especially down to the tide pool. Ten minutes, half the Post Office, twenty minutes, and I’m lost. But Alice had the map, thank the Lord.      What about the food? Did you try any local dishes?      Oh we fared well, love. There was this little restaurant,  The Creel , do you ken—personally owned, run by these young lads who said they’ve moved back to the village to escape the city life. They made us venison pie and West Highland salmon. You ever had venison?      No, but it sounds good. Bet it’s a lot better than the staff canteen at work. I’m still dreaming about the fish finger sandwich they served in the staff kitchen last week.      Hair? It tastes like squirrel, I’m telling you. Also, they served us tea in these tiny tea cups—had to make a second pot every five minutes.      We went on a boat trip one day, too. There were a few others from the village. One man had binoculars and kept shouting, “She’s comin’ up over the rise! She’s coming up over the rise!” The rest of us looked like it was a land invasion. He was talking about a whale, turns out. I told him the only whale I was seeing was the one behind the bar trying to catch his breath.      That sounds like a good laugh. Did you take the dog?      Oh no, the pond wasn’t big enough for Roxy. But Alice had to leave the gate open once. We were out for the evening and the little beast had herself a nice wander through the garden, down to the stream, and back. Found her by the steps, grinning like a loon, covered in mud.

Rather skip the queue and just bring my own swiss grater.      The first... What was the question?      I think it's probably fixed where we are where we live.      Be as frightened as well.      Right and there's more more of them than there used to be.      I've been taught not to use one before so this is a conscious choice.      That sounds a bit odd.      Yeah when I was younger I was really into... like, miniature model ships you'd made them.      That's cool.      I haven't done anything like that for a while.      D'you know how I think he turned?      Yeah.      He turned up to a dinner with a micro in his back pocket, you ever looked in that, you'd see spiders.      He was like Watergate with a dinner jacket on.      You don't think he was still trying to impress people, like still trying to make something of it?      That's what I thought – trying to get back in with the old crowd because they were his support network.      It's the phone.      That sounds exactly like what he's doing.      And trying to manipulate a bit of sympathy out of the school with all the kid related things.      What kid related things?      I don't know... absent a dad syndrome.      It's the phone.      Not that I've met it.      My sister had that problem with someone from her parent's generation.      Yeah the whole... you mentioned being nice to the teachers, being accurate about your performance at school.      Yeah.      And lunches and stuff like that – "Can I do the meats?" – you remember that?      That's classic go-to stuff.      Yeah so I think he's just in the same loop.      You'd think your actual kid would be your focus though.      That's where those jokes fall apart.      For him, he's still trying to be someone he was.      I think so.      Right, okay, let it go.      To be honest I used to find it quite amusing before it became, quite frankly, just sad.      The bit I could never get was when he'd refer to people as "pillars of our community" and just keep listing stuff like that practically in their faces.      That really grates.      It's the phone. Women in the office.      Back in the day he was the one who brought light to the dimmest corners of the town.      He was a project manager with a flower in his lapel.

So do you not find it funny that we're all sitting here saying we know her address by heart when like... we don’t even know what Reg is short for?      I dunno, probably Reginald. Why do you sound like that?      Because I’ve met her family and there’s no Reginald anywhere! Her sister’s named Julie and her dad’s called Graham.      Fair enough. Honestly, I’ve only ever known her as Reg, so that’s what I’ll stick with. Isn’t that the whole point of nicknames?      Aye, I couldn’t agree more. I used to call my cousin "Banger" and everyone knew what I meant. You don’t get to choose your nickname, luv, the universe does.      I think it’s because Reg was an admin in the military and they’re big on call signs and shit. Now she’s returning to Saudi in two weeks and we’re all trying to act casual, even though I’ve never been that far north, let alone to the desert.      I’ve never even been out of the UK.      And yet, here we are having this emotional dinner. I mean, it’s only a job transfer. Not like she’s moving to another planet.      You trying to tell me that her flat in Riyadh ain’t like a whole new climate zone? Last time I heard, the toilets flush the other way. And the skyline’s so high you can read headlines in the sky.      Yeah, but at least she won’t have to be navigated by us anymore! We’ve spent the last two years about to fall off the M1 because Reg kept talking to us while we had our SatNav on.      I still blame the SatNav. It said "Continue to the roundabout," and I took it literally. I ended up doing twelve laps of the stupid thing.      Oh my god, I remember that! Everyone else waiting at the café while you circled like some sort of professional tourist.      Honestly, I think the SatNav was trying to play a prank on you. You looked so confused.      I was confused! But it was Reg who kept saying, “Look, look left! There’s a green bench with a box of cakes on it!” and all I could see was the roundabout.      That’s where those cakes went?      Do you think she took them over to Saudi Arabia or…?

Rather stunning place, isn't it? You can’t really do this back home in New Zealand — not like this, at least. The organization of the gardens here is next level.      It is beautiful. I can see why the Swedes are so proud of their green spaces. Back in Dorset, we liked the countryside, but they take gardening here to an art form — every leaf is a statement. A bit too clean for me, honestly. I prefer a bit of chaos.      Well, nothing says chaos like Croydon during the spring clean. Still, I agree with you, Helen. There's something incredibly calming about a well-kept garden, don’t you think? Being surrounded by greenery definitely helps with my general anxiety levels.      I’d say the same, but for me, it’s more about the mental reset. With the business — it’s breakfast, bedtime, board meetings, and everyone has a micro-choice to make. I need five minutes in a space where the only decision is whether a sunflower is getting too close to the wall.      Oh, I know that feeling — even as a teacher, you end up managing a million tiny human dramas in a single day. I used to burn out from the emotional labour. Now I find it helps to take my own advice, literally.      What do you mean?      I teach students about emotional awareness and self-regulation. Then I walk into my own home and expect my husband to just  feel  what I need. Turns out you have to spell it out. I started journaling through my feelings and even  schedule  a weekly “self-check about how I’m doing.” Ridiculous, right?      Honestly, that sounds like good practice for any entrepreneur. I’m guilty of ignoring my own fatigue to the point where I start cutting corners on basic hygiene. Toothpaste on a spoon — I’m not joking.      Oh no! I tried cutting down on showering once when I was grading 300 papers in 48 hours. Mistake. Bad idea. Smelled like old bread and regret.      You're both a couple of imps go at it on your own, but have you ever considered building a wellness routine? I triage self-care like a communications strategy now — non-negotiables, like early bedtimes, fluency water intake, and one hour of forced isolation with no screens.      Sounds like a solid plan. I’ve tried yoga mornings, but I’m not entirely sure if I did it right.

So do you ever find it funny when voice recognition software gets confused by accents? I tried using it the other day, and it thought I was speaking Welsh because of my Kentish drawl.      Oh yes, that’s happened to me before. When I used to use the phone for voice dictation, it thought I was from the West Country or something. I swear I said  consultant  and it came up with  constant ! Such a pain.      It’s all about where you're from, isn’t it? My sister lives in Liverpool, and the other day I heard her on a Zoom call. I thought, "How much has she changed?" Then I realized her accent was like that the whole time, I just wasn’t used to hearing it properly. Probably sounds the same to her as it ever did.      Yeah, you get used to the way you talk. I still remember when my uncle moved in with us after living in London for years, and the first time we talked, I said “Yeah, I’ll come over later,” and he nearly fell off his chair—my accent must’ve been really different to what he was used to.      That’s the way with accents, innit? You don’t hear them the same way others do. My Mate Laura from Brighton says I sound like I’ve just rolled in off a farm.      Speaking of which, I was thinking the other day about how your whole childhood is kind of molded by your accent and your environment. I still remember climbing the plum tree at the end of the garden and getting told off for making a mess. It’s strange how those little things stay with you, isn’t it?      Yeah, I remember the same sort of thing—cracking thimbles, climbing fences, pretending that the bushes were castles. And the sound of my dad’s bike chain squeaking every time he came back from work. I miss that.      Oh, your dad was always bringing home something weird from his bike, wasn’t he? That time he had a mysterious yellow sprite of some sort... He probably just wanted to keep the whole whanau laughing, really. My parents never let us near a bike by the way. They believed in go-karts on pond life if you ask me.      Yeah, go-karts were a big no-no in our house too.

So do you know how to make a baked Alaska, Miss Sarah? I was watching it on YouTube and it looked proper complicated.      Oh, I know how to make one, love! It is a bit fiddly, but I used to make one every year at Christmas for my mum and dad. You layer sponge, ice cream, and then frosting, and then you torch the sugar on the top. It’s like a Christmas in a dessert.      Torch it? Like with a blowtorch or somethin’? Didn’t your fingers get burnt?      Most of the time! I used to get a little singed, yeah. But it was worth it.      So what made you learn to do that? Did you like cookin’ when you was little?      Actually, no. I was quite the breakfast person—cereal and toast happened. But after I went to university and got into catering as a career, you learn to make a bit of everything. I became a Programme Director for one of the big culinary colleges, and we used to specialise in baking quite a lot.      Wow, sounds fancy. Did you always know you wanted to do that sort of job?      No, not really. I started off in catering, but the more I got into it, the more interested I got in the training side of things. People always say they don’t like someone who talks about work too much, but my stories are mostly just about oddly sourdough-tasting pizzas and awkward group projects in the kitchen.      I bet people are weird when they’re about to make food. My mates are always arguing over who’s slicing the cheese properly. I once put parmesan into mac ‘n’ cheese and it just didn’t work out.      Oh, parmesan can be too much for that. You want to go for something a bit milder—cheddar, maybe, or a little bit of mozzarella. It gives you that gooey feel.      That’s the kind of thing I’m thinking about when I’m trying to get into a Halloween party. I told my mates I goin’ as a cheese platter.      Oh really? That’s a brilliant idea. You could be the "proper cheese one"—you know the one who gets made fun of but everyone still wants to stand next to so they can grab a nibble.      Sounds good to me. But I was also thinking maybe go as my history teacher, Miss Rigby.

Rather than going back up North again, I thought I'd just stay the night here in Swansea. The drive’s far too long, and with the wind today, I’m not risking it.      Good choice! You can finally have a decent lie-in for once. Or at least try to. Do you want a cup of tea or one of those fancy breakfast coffees I’ve been making?      Tea would be lovely, thanks. Still can’t get used to the coffee habit you’ve got! Back in Leeds, I stick strictly to builder’s, but I suppose being Welsh has its complications.      Aww, don’t knock it, it’s warm, it’s black, and it definitely wakes you up enough to not post anything you might regret later on Twitter. You remember my brother-in-law’s infamous live tweet? Half the county of Carmarthenshire saw it.      Oh God, no! I only ever live-tweet when I’m in Japan, and even then I have to double-check my grammar. One bloke nearly took it out of context once, and I had to write him two letters in Japanese as an apology. I only passed university by the skin of my teeth—thankfully, my Japanese letter was pretty humble.      Well, I’m not surprised, because you were busy learning to fly a plane in your spare time as well as lecturing. I still can’t believe you’ve been doing flying lessons in your forties. That’s more than me trying to keep a garden alive.      Yeah, well it’s a bit of an obsession now. Can’t wait to take you up in the spring when the weather’s better. I’ll show you the best views of the River Towy from 4000 feet. Proper scenic.      No pressure then! I just hope I don’t wet myself if it gets bumpy. On the bright side, maybe a scenic flight will help you decide where to go after New York. I know you were planning a trip.      That’s right—New York next month. I’ve got a week booked to do some research work at a university near Central Park. It’ll be the first time away in a while, but it’s going to be brilliant. I think I might even tick off a few museums. Smithsonian’s on my list, if I can get past the Metropolitan first.

Right, I just played "unspecified" and I think that’s the longest word I’ve played in Scrabble in weeks. Someone check the dictionary for me, will they?      That's probably not in the official dictionary. No one even knows what it means properly. But it sounds very academic, which is exactly  your  style, Liam.      Yeah, I just figured I should lean into my degree in English and use words that are longer than my arm. Besides, it’s got two e’s, an S, and a Y, so it's a sneaky-high-point word.      I don't even know the real Oxford definition, but I like how you think you're being clever with it. You left out the ‘what’ though, right? You're saying “unspecified what”.      It's a valid move if you’re tactical. I just needed to block this diagonal. Honestly though, I think “unspecified” should become an official term, given how many times the government uses it.      I do like the way we're taking spelling so seriously. I never thought I’d see the day. I only passed English by the skin of my teeth in A Levels.      Tell me about it. My A Levels were mostly about trying not to burn the kitchen down while my mum said, “Ben, you did better than average at secondary school, didn’t you?”      Honestly, I just got full Ucas offers by accident. I was a chef, remember? I thought I was hotter than the grill.      But look at you now —  student  and fully into academics.      I prefer "professional kitchen experimenter".      Anyway, moving on. Sarah, are you still reading that series of children's books about that girl with a time-turner?      No, not really. I’m into something a bit older now. I just finished a very intense non-fiction about the history of the Chelsea Flower Show. Turns out, that horticulture pageant has been going on since 1862.      The flower show? I once had a date that started with a trip go there. I got lost in the tunnel of horticultural features and came out in the orchid greenhouses. She was blooming furious.      I can see that. You’re one to talk about being late, Liam. You missed your orientation lecture on purpose just to get over here and meet us at the coffee shop.      I did not  miss  the lecture. I  delayed it  strategically so I could make an entrance.

I don’t know, Doris, I just sat down, and already the cat’s jumping on the table like it owns the place. And I swear, that one down the road blasts their telly at ten in the morning like nobody’s watching. Oh, come on now, it’s peaceful compared to when the van parked outside with the lads doing that bit of “My Way” every morning with a kazoo. That was the last straw for me. A kazoo! Honestly, someone should invent a law against the misuse of kazoos. Although, I suppose it’s not as bad as the time old Mrs. Partridge tried to reverse her car and ended up in another person’s garden like it was a parking meter. Still, enough talk of chaos—had a good morning? Aye, and I’ll tell you why. I got a phone bill the other day. Wait for it—this lady at the post office goes, “Oh, this is from India, Mr. hides, you didn’t know?” And I look at her like she’s speaking Martian and says, “Excuse me, listen—these are reverse charge calls landlines as well as mobiles. You can’t just leave a line open!” Reverse charge, right. So is that one of those things where you ring somewhere, and they take the money out of your account without you saying yes? Sounds like a postcode robbery to me. That’s exactly what it is! They just kept ringing and ringing—must’ve been a man in Jamaica just playing the piano on the phone while I’d be stuck with the bill. It’s bad enough with the energy prices these days, let alone extra charges about nowhere. You’re the talking of prices, I had to throw out my soup last night. The tin was dented, and it had a use-by date that was older than my granddaughter. I’ve got to start checking those labels again. For a moment, I thought it was a time capsule. Well, you know what they say—time is money, and in this day and age, we’re trying not to spend a penny more than we have to. Still, it's not all bad news. You know, I found a tenner in the bin the other day, rolled up like it was waiting for me. Thought it was a gift from above. Tenner in your bin?

Rather skip the newfit app eh?      Well I was just trying it out this morning... got a bit too enthusiastic with the circuit training, and I think I saw stars after仰卧起坐 for 50 repetitions.      Lmao. Ten would’ve been good eenough if you ask me. You shouldn’t trust these apps if you don’t know what they're asking you to do.      Honestly I don’t use it but I watched what you did and it looked painful! You’re supposed to be on holiday aren’t you? Letting things simmer on the stove, not on your knees.      Well the idea was to try and get in some fitness while you're here. I did manage to sneak in a run last night, albeit around the village, but it was good.      Blimey, you’ve really got into it. When did you turn into this gym-obsessed version of yourself?      I thought I'd start looking after myself a bit more once I became a teacher—set a good example, get into healthy eating, all the rest of it. It's not like I've got the energy anymore for fancy dinners every night anyway—it's just... work rhythm, then home rhythm.      I get that. I’ve tried, but really, trying to cook the cheapest meals on a budget and making them taste good for the kids—well that’s a job in itself.      Spoken like a true teacher. You lot are the ones who run the country on what you're paid, if you ask me.      A crude but fair point. Still, it’s about balance. I’ve been trying to make the most of what we’ve had here. The fresh bread and the local cheese that Andy bought—ah, it is a holiday, in that way.      Yes, that was a nice touch. And that soup? The leek one you told us was inspired by the new recipe book you got?      Not really inspired—more of a "I had to use up the leeks before they went off" situation. So do you want me to go through this with you? I think it might help if I explain it like I got to my tutor when I was stuck on the first one.      Yeah, that’d be good. I’ve read the brief like ten times and I still can’t make sense of half of it. I mean, the word ‘synthesise’ is basically in all caps like it’s trying to slap me.      Haha, yeah, it does that. But basically, it’s just asking you to tie everything together. Didn’t your module use the term  integrate  like three times in one paragraph?      That’s the one. Yeah, I managed to underline the word like four times but I still don’t know what it means in this context.      Okay, I’ll break it down. First, you’ve got the introduction part. You’re supposed to present your main argument upfront. Not a general thing like “climate change is bad,” but something like, “The shift in consumer habits post-2010 directly correlates with increased carbon emissions in manufacturing sectors.” That’s the kind of short, strong hook that gets you credit early.      Right, got it. So it’s not a general observation but a precise angle.      Exactly. Then in the body, you need to back that up with three main points—ideally primary sources. If possible, one from a journal article, one from a business report, and one from a policy paper. That way, you show you’ve done a decent range of reading.      What if I can’t find a policy paper?      Don’t panic. Your university library has all these things. Go into their online database—there’s a link for “policy reports and white papers.” I found one on the Department for Environment in like two minutes.      Oh yeah, I passed that by. I just thought it was a student blog or something.      Nah, you just haven’t clicked “Advanced Search” yet. Anyway, after the academicky bit comes the critical analysis. That’s the part the tutor loves the most. You basically say, “Here’s what these sources agree on…” Then go, “Here’s what they don’t agree on or what they’re missing.”      And then the conclusion?      Yeah, you just sum up what you said but don’t bring in new information. Restate your original argument and maybe suggest a gap in the studies or where more research is needed.

So did you go to A&E?      Yeah, had to. I walked in like... ten hours ago, honestly. It was packed, and I ended up on a trolley in a corridor for nearly three hours. You’d think one of the Seven Wonders had fallen over outside the front doors.      That’s honestly nothing short of criminal. I had a broken finger once, and still got seen in under an hour at our local one. I’m not saying ours’s perfect, but ten hours to crack a rib? Someone needs their head examined in A&E triage.      Right? The waiting room was full of kids with broken legs, elderly people with chest pain, and me, the oversized twat who fell down the stairs. I mean, not like I  broke  bones or anything, but still!      I’m sorry your pain wasn’t taken seriously early. Did they at least give you something for the pain before getting to a doctor? You’re not exactly the A&E your GP recommends you to.      True, though I do have a 100% success rate with broken fingers, sprained ankles and overcooked kidneys. Which, by modern standards, is near expert level.
