I remember the tales of your Royal Grammar School, Horace.      Well, it weren’t that bad. Not at first. I was one of the senior teachers, y’know. They respected me. But then— health inspections . That was the end of it.      Still, mind the tea Harold.       You  are the one waving a about with the milk jug like it’s a damn Renaissance sword.      I resent that! I know that I shouldn’t take the handle off the jug while pouring— but —      But you do it all the same. Just like yesterday. I remember you nearly flooded the hallway trying to relive your ‘glory days’.       Glory days ? That was trying to catch the  train  from Norwich. Not tea-phase simulation.      You were trying to catch the train because you were late on your own  simulated  tea-phase.      It’s not a phase— it’s a lifestyle change !      I’ll tell you this: one morning I was down at the market garden, helping Eva with the feed for the chickens and lambs, when I stopped and said to her— ‘Eva,’ I said, ‘I think I may be onto something with the tea, pure-brewed and strong. Might be the way to go.’       Eva said precisely what I would’ve said— ‘Harold, it's not that complicated, love. Just drink what you like and don’t burn our roof tiles with steam.’

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know the one near the train station. Felt like a university bar with the seats and everything.      Not a bad thing if you're a student, but probably not quite our scene, is it?      Aye, it een't the place if you're lookin' fer good conversation and decent pint. Proper pub needs a bit of dirt on the walls. Not the plastic seats and laminated menus.      Fair point. We've had our fair share of plastic seats in London, but the worst was the one with the three-legged table. Spilled half my beer before I'd even taken a drink!      My brother still claims the best pint in the county’s in this backstreet pub in King's Lynn. It’s tiny and the owner’s the only one who knows where the loos are.      Remind me of the Anglo Indian place I used to live next to. Only opened on Sundays, you had to shout the order from the street over the bhangra music.      Speaking of places—did I tell you we’re taking the kids to this family-friendly hotel on the coast? It’s got a CRB-checked staff and a little workshop where they make recycled bottle art?      Right cheery that sounds. Not used to the idea of staff being checked and bottles being given a new life. I blame the universities for that—now even the supermarkets want someone with a degree to operate the tills.      Well at least they’re getting the kids thinking creatively. I remember my dad once repurposed an old bike chain as coat pegs.      Creativity’s a good thing, especially with kids. I teach a module on creative pedagogy—I’m trying to convince the department it should be mandatory in primary schools.      What about protests? I saw a big one in Norwich last week about education funding. A professor was shouting about student fees being a ‘shadow tax on dreams.’      Oh that’ll be Dr. Monica Bellamy. She’s been on ITV talking about the same thing. Sorely needs a good hairdresser and a quieter man behind the wheel.      She’s not wrong though. Education funding is a mess, but that’s probably a conversation for another time—and with the bottle of red you opened.      Drink and protest, it’s the usual weekend combo. Just don’t forget to drive carefully back.

Oh my god, you’re back! You’ve been gone ages. I was starting to think you’d forgotten about us and our chaotic flat.      I know, I know! It felt longer than it was. I honestly couldn’t have gone without being completely over it. But it was nice—do you know my sister finally got married?      No way! Is she not the one with the A-level maths degree and the side hustle as a personal trainer?      That’s the one! And yes, she got married on the Amalfi Coast. I was the bridesmaid. It was beautiful. I mean, I was a bit tired the whole time because I was stressed about work emails catching up on my phone, but still—it was good.      I would’ve DMed you a dozen times every day if I were you. I’d be checking for gigabytes of breakfast photos and whatever. But I’m glad you had some time off at least. Work ever getting to you, or are you just a bit too empathetic for your own good?      Honestly? Yeah, it is getting to me. Sometimes I come home from work and I just feel like I’ve been emotionally drained… watching people fight for their mental health when all I want is to curl up with a book and a pot of Horlicks.      I feel you. I did my own kind of emotional burnout this month—project after project, no clear boundaries, and someone at work kept calling me “elegant” in a way that felt oddly patronising. I’m still not sure if they were trying to compliment me or make me feel fragile.      Sounds like about five of our colleagues rolled into one. But okay, what did you get up to while I was gone? Did you meet any ex-boyfriends and have a dramatic fling in my absence?      Haha, no. I had lunch with Aimee, actually. Remember her? She got the promotion last year.      The one with the impossible to reach flat and that sprite of a dog that always chews your keys?      That’s the one. We went veggie after I had a snack attack the previous night—sampled everything on the menu, ended up ordering a side of paprika fries just in case. She was telling me about her dad—apparently, he’s retiring and wants to backpack through Tuscany with his best mate from work.

I spoke to Anna yesterday. She’s not doing too well. Her oncologist says the chemo is starting to take its toll, but she’s determined to press on. She asked me how we were, which was sweet of her. You wouldn’t have thought she’d be thinking about anyone else with how tough it’s all been.      That’s Anna for you—still as selfless as ever. I hope things start to look up soon. I mean, I know it’s not going to be quick or easy, but it’s hard to watch someone you care about go through that. She’s too young for all this.      I know. It’s shocking, really. On the positive side, she still laughs a lot, still jokes around. It makes things more bearable for the rest of us, I think.      It must be hard for James too. I saw him at the village market this week. He looked exhausted. He mentioned he’s planning to move out of the bungalow soon—it’s not working for them now, what with the terraces and lack of a garden.      Yes, I’ve seen their listing. I think the agent called it "a characterful property," but it’s quite a dark house. You can’t really see anything from the front because it’s built into the hill. Still, I imagine people might be interested if they’re looking for something unusually shaped and not bothered about natural light.      Who knows. I heard the planning office is looking into a proposal to build some new housing on the edge of the woods near the church. If they go through with it, prices might dip in the short term as people get nervous about developments.      That’s something to watch. I mentioned it to Jane at the coffee shop the other day, and she said she’d moved her offer up on a house over on the High Street. She’s desperate to be here by the end of summer. I think she mentioned the kids needing to get into a primary school catchment area.      Right. That’s the pressure of it all with people starting a new phase of life. I suppose the village is growing more and more each year. Pity it sometimes feels like it's getting harder to get a place that's  right  rather than just  available .      True. I can see why Anna and James might be conflicted.

You’d think a place called "The Royale" would at least have a bit of class, eh? But no, the bloody shower in my ensuite is like a waterfall I can’t control.      Aye, we’ve had the same in our halls. One minute you’re boiling, the next you’re shivering like it’s mid-December again. Someone needs to sort the pressure out, or I swear I’m just gonna install a kettle next to the shower.      Haha, you and me both. I got so numb last night when I tried to take a shower after my shift, I had to make do with a flannel and cold water just to avoid another frostbite-style recovery. My knees still ache.      Oh, don’t get me started on the building itself, let alone the showers. I’m just trying not to trip over the dodgy flooring in breakfast, and that’s just me having coffee with a smile in my face. It’s like they took a shopping list to the spare parts store and went nuts.      Numb, numb, numb. That place takes numb to a whole new level. And don’t get me started on the noise factor—every time someone flushes, the rhythm of the toilet gives way to a session of Mate’s Mate with the pipes, and I barely had any sleep last night. I reckon the pipes are trying to start their own punk band.      Mate, they should just give someone a full-time job—someone with a toolbox, a sense of peace, and preferably an ambition hotter than the shower. It shouldn’t be this difficult to enjoy a decent shower after a 12-hour shift or about five lectures.      And the smell, I mean—juggling what passes for “neutral"" cleaning products with barely a hint of disinfectant leaves my nose doing chin-ups. Burgundy baked beans, guest speaker dust, and what I’m calling “the man who brought his gym bag inside with him” fragrance. I once tried to air out my duvet while my roomie was holed up doing a speed-write marathon with his computer on the bed—you can guess how well that worked.      You're like a man with a masterclass in room sabotage. Honestly, sometimes I think about taking one of those posters off the walls that say “report any issues” and just pin it to your face with a sewing needle.

So do you remember that trip we took to Antwerp, Dad? I was just reading about it in my holiday planning and I thought of you. Remember how we got lost in the Christmas market and ended up in this little café? And we had those waffles that were so good, like the biggest I’ve ever seen?      Oh yeah, that was the year before I retired. You were a bit younger, hadn’t hit your teens yet. I don’t remember being lost, just me trying not to embarrass you by stopping to take pictures of every tram that passed. But the waffles were good, I suppose.      I was with you both the whole way, you know. You made me try turkey on Christmas Eve because you saw it on the menu and insisted it was "authentic". I still can’t get the taste out of my head. But I was thinking the other day – we’re British, why are we so obsessed with "authentic" when we barely cook properly ourselves?      Grandpa, you’re harsh. I like your attempts though. I do. I mean, we’d never had glühwein before, and I’ve still got a little warmth in my heart for that Dutch lady who taught me how to pronounce it properly. “Glühwein – it’s not ‘glunknown’.”      “You weren’t saying it right,” as if you spoke Dutch. Still, you picked it up quick. Like those rhyming couplets in one of your books. That university course of yours – did they still do that with the rhymes?      Yeah, they still used rhymes to help remember grammar stuff. I did a whole project on English linguistic rhyming in the 1700s. Apparently, they thought it made people easier to teach. Doesn’t sound too different from how you two teach me stuff over dinner. "This is how you spell it," "This is how you pronounce it," "Don't say that at the market."      I did stick up for you when some of the locals gave you funny looks trying to find the right museum. English people do have a reputation, no matter where you are. Then again, I think the real issue was the language barrier. They didn’t know our accents, so they thought we were tourists in the wrong city.      Oh, what can I say? We are the masters of misunderstanding. I was in a street market in Germany last year and asked for a "Buchteln", and the guy gave me a confused look and said "is that a type of dog?"

So did you watch the news last night love? That business with the equality vote in Ireland, they passed it you know?      Yeah I heard about it! Erm, does that mean people can marry whoever they want to?      More or less. It means same-sex couples can now get married, yeah. It’s a big deal over there.      Oh. So that means if I wanted to marry one of my budz, I could?      Oh you! You’d be moving to Ireland first! But yes, technically.      Not budz! One!  laughs  I was talking about the one who only eats crisps and pasta.      Oh you mean Terry? The one who wears your older brother’s socks as if they’re brand new?      Blimey, you’ve got to stop embarrassing me, Mum!       giggles  Well Terry’s got style, I’ll give you that. But back to the vote. It was all that—voters saying yes, yes, yes in the papers. I mean, don’t you think it’s time we did more of that as a country?      I don’t know. I mean it’s good for couples though, right? I wouldn’t mind it if other people wanted to get married and stuff. But why’s it so important?      Because it’s about equality, sweetheart. They wanted to have the same rights as everyone else. Like a family, like a wedding, like being able to sign up for a birthday party as a couple!      Erm, how would a same-sex couple even have a birthday party?      Oh come on, they can have cake and presents like anyone else! Unless Terry turns up with his unopened socks and that’s just a  very  awkward moment for guest of honours.       laughs  Terry’d probably assume he was the guest of honour.      He did once. Last year at your uncle’s birthday. He turned up in a 'Top Dog' T-shirt and was shouting he was 50 for  weeks .      That was Dad goin’ on for ages about it.      You’re just picking on him because he thinks he’s a bloomin’ knight in your eyes. Now listen, have you made that speech for your school’s equality week?’      It’s not a speech it’s a ‘presentation’ and why would I need a speech?      Because you said you were going to talk about it. You mentioned it to your teacher last week, remember?      Oh yeah, I just said it before I thought about it.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd have proper lathes in the house when you're retired and have all this spare time on your hands. I’ve had this one nearly twenty years now, it’s probably older than some of the lads at the club.      Oh I saw the tools spread out on the table the other day and nearly had a heart attack. You don’t clean that up before I come in, Arthur! I don’t want to find a lathe chuck in the bread bin one of these mornings.      Well, if you want things done to a standard, you’ve got to use the right tools, Moira. I supply the tools for schools and colleges you know, still keep up with new developments though not so much in lathes, more the safety regulations these days.      Oh I don’t mind the tools, it’s what they’re doing with them that worries me. Arthur nearly burned the house down last week, thanks to that poor little fella in the spare room.      He was taking a nap, that's all! Came out with singed fur and two looks about him. The microwave's not suitable for hamster naps, if you ask me.      You got a hamster in the microwave? Are you planning to make hamster scallops or something?      It was an accident! The phone’s on the table and the emergency number’s been knocked off the microwave door. Arthur put the hamster in to warm it up a bit, thought it was a toaster—piece of toast is what he says he was looking for!      Look, it’s not rocket science, is it? That critter was just having a little kip on the heating hob and Arthur switched the failsafe off. Not that I’d tell him, of course. He’s quite proud.      Proud? He’s passed out on the sofa now, with a glass of his sherry and the microwave door left ajar. I found little Arty junior wandering about the hallway looking like he’s seen things he shouldn’t.      At least he’s got some life going on, you know, after retiring. Not like some of the folks I go out with on the days I still bother going to work. Sitting in the dent in the pavement, wondering what day it is.      Oh, you still at the school, then, George?

Rather annoying isn’t it, paying for plastic bags at the supermarket. I know it's for a good cause, but still feels like they’re bleeding us dry more than we agreed to.      It is a bit over the top sometimes, but I suppose it's helping. We haven’t bought a single one in months, and we’ve got one of those reusable cloth ones that's as thick as a book.      Ay, that's the way to be. When I was a headmistress, we always taught the children to take care of the planet. It's the least we can do now, even if it feels like just a drop in a very large ocean.      You sound like Myra, my mum, you know. She’s always going on about how the planet would survive better if we all used handkerchiefs and went back to washing up by hand.      Well, if that keeps happened, I suppose I could throw in a teaspoon of non-detergent dish soap to the spare sink and do the Good Housekeeping Month once a year.      Haha, now there's a thought. A good laugh to go with grief. Speaking of old ways, there was something on the news last night about a woman from Scotland who wrote her whole – what’s the word I’m looking for – her letters  mirror-wise  the whole her whole life.      You mean mirror-writing? Like what Escher used to do? Like what someone with dyslexia might do?      Aye, that's the one. They’d never noticed until she handed over a will she'd written – all back to front, couldn't read a line of it unless you held it up to the mirror.      That must’ve been quite the drama. I can see some lawyer trying to figure out whether it's a secret code, like a Da Vinci Code kind of thing.      And there you go. Thought you’d mentioned bloody politics already.      Well, speaking of drama, did you catch that story about the cat in America? He’s the first to be elected to public office in Texas, or so it said.      No way! I need to see go viral photos on that. I can’t believe a cat got a vote, even in America.      That bloke in America, your President Trump, what was happening with him? I hear he’s still trying to claim those polls are unfair even though he's already been voted out twice.

Right, I just wanted to bring up something I’ve noticed. I know you both love your games, but it feels like you're not reading nearly as much as you used to. I know Minecraft is super fun and I get that Ninjago is your thing, Adrian, but spending so much time on these games might not be the best use of your time.      But Minecraft is like making a whole world! I built a castle last night that had a moat and everything. It was awesome.      I'm not saying don’t enjoy it — it's brilliant that you’re being creative and using your imagination. I just worry that it’s taking over your free time, and reading is something that’s going to help you keep getting better at school and life in general. What do you think, Blake?      I think it's cool. I built a jungle with a lava pit! And I even made a dragon that guards the treasure. It was in my world last night.      Blake, that’s amazing! But what if you spent some of that time reading or doing something a bit different? Like maybe reading about how people build real castles or read a book with dragons in it?      But books are boring. I’d rather just build it myself.      I understand, and I know reading’s not as exciting as building your own world. But reading gives you the same feeling — it’s like you’re creating in your mind. Like, someone wrote the story of a castle with a dragon, and you just thought up yours. Both are made-up worlds, just different versions.      Can I read  Ninjago  comics then? I like seeing what the characters are like.      Absolutely! That could be a good start. Let’s try that. I can even help you find some books that have Minecraft-like worlds or adventures. There are ones where you can solve puzzles or build things too.      What about  My Life as a Teenage Robot ? I read one of those once and it was cool.      Oh, that’s a great one! There are also some graphic novels that you can get where the stories are like games — visual and action-packed. They’re usually really popular with kids who love video games.      Can I read it with you, Lizzie?      Of course! We can even make it a reading club, where every week you try something new and then tell me what you thought.

Right, thanks for coming in today, love. I’ve missed having the house full again, even if it’s just for an hour or so. Coffee’s just ready.      Thanks, Mum, we were just telling each other about our week—Ellie’s uni trip to York was brilliant apparently?      It was! We went to this museum near the castle that had a Roman exhibit. I never thought I’d be this excited about pottery shards, but I was!      Oh, was it the one on the outside of the city? The big one? I went to that when I was your age. Found a Roman coin once, accidentally kicked it under some paving stone and Mycroft still reminds me of it.      Mycroft? Is that your brother? He still here?      No, he’s in Middlesbrough. He moved there when he started work. Construction or something—building basements, planting wires, you know, the usual son’s escape from the mump.      That’s, like, the opposite of me. I can’t even land a part-time job without grief.      Oh, don’t be silly. You’re in the best place. University is a cycle of: “I’m broke and worried” and “I’ve broken the cheapest pair of jeans I own.”      She already said that at brunch. Twice. Honestly, this is going to be my new retirement plan: read books and listen to my daughter sour about her life while I serve tea.      Don’t listen to her, Ellie. Work’s been great for about five minutes. Anna’s the new head of the store near the civic centre. Got a bonus for “best stock turnover.” Not that I’d know it if I wasn’t in there. My idea of retail is the local farm shop.      I’m actually planning a day trip soon. York was so nice, I was thinking about maybe going to Manchester. We could come back as a group. Auntie Zoe mentioned staying over with her and a couple of the cousins.      Oh, that’s a nice idea. Zoe’s good for that go-to-place on the edge of the world kind of thing. But make sure you bring a jumper, it’s always colder up North than it should be.      I can fill in on the way home after work. We could all go together—like a proper family kind of thing for a change. Might do Mums good.

So did you watch The Last of Us weekend? That first episode was bonkers.      Yeah, I binged it after the match on Saturday. My mate stared at me the whole time like, “Why are we watching this?” I was like, “Survival horror, it’s real vibes, mate.”      Honestly, I think it’s so easy to make a show with that budget now. Like,  The Crown  or whatever, but this one was wild. I think it’s why we all got so into it at the pub when we played the board game last week.      Yeah, I still can’t stop thinking about that scene where Ellie kills the infected lady.      Man, that’s one of the benefits of the show being based on a game, right? The whole world is already built. I was about to try the first game when my dad was like, “You’d like Hades more,” and he’s not wrong.      I tried the game once, but I’m more of a Quests kind of person. I’d rather just be dropped in a fantasy land with a sword and a few quests than fight zombies.      GIRL. Quests are just the modern-day school DT – “Design a mission” and stuff like that.      Yeah, but don’t get me started on DT. I still can’t believe Liam got made a prefect and he once set someone’s chicken casserole on fire.      I know, right? And now he’s got a red badge pinned to his blazer like it’s  actually  a big deal. I about wet myself when he pulled it out of the oven the first time.      At least he’s consistent. Still barely passes English.      He just writes like he’s texted the essay. All caps, no commas. I’m surprised they don’t strip him of the badge for plagiarism.      Speaking of which, did you guys catch what that teacher said to Ms. Patel? Racist comments or not, that’s just wrong.      I did. She told him he “looked American go to America.” But he was born in Slough – his mum runs the bakers in Wembley.      And what were we taught at school? “Let’s be colour-blind and judge by ability.” Yeah, well, maybe we should be better at recognising it.      At least the catering staff at school are great. The lasagna at lunch last week was  chef’s kiss .      I know. They make a mean chicken tikka wrap too.

So did you watch  17 Again  last night? I think it was on BBC Three or something. It was alright, I guess.      I did watch it! I thought it was kind of funny. Not the best film ever, but Simon Pegg is always good at being sarcastic and all that. Did you like the part where he puts on the braces and the fake acne?      Oh my god, yeah! That was so funny. And he used so much gel in his hair. We watched it in the living room and me and my little brother were laughing the whole time. Although, I think my brother just liked the bit with the party and the supply teacher getting totally stressed.      Haha, I watched it with my sister and she kept saying "Oh my God, he’s so annoying" every five minutes! But then she actually got into the bit where he buys breakfast, and then doesn’t pay for it. Hilarious.      Yeah! That’s the best part. But anyway, what’s up with your physics teacher? I heard Mr. Ellis had a massive rant at the start of the lesson about someone leaving their calculator on his desk.      Oh yeah, that was so funny. Well, he got really sarcastic and said “Finally, someone’s trying to warm up my cold classroom!” Everyone cracked up. But seriously, I did NOT like the whole lesson today. I got so confused with that whole homework question about Newton’s laws.      I struggled with that one too. I just guessed at the answer and put the letters in a random order. I still don’t know if I got it right. Honestly, most of the time I don’t even know what he’s talking about when he says “resultant force” or “action-reaction.” I think I need to ask someone after English next week to go over it.      Yeah, you should. Did you speak to Max about it? I think she was sitting with us last time and looked way more confident when he started explaining it. She even did like that calculator thing with her fingers when trying to draw the forces.      Yeah, Max is weird like that, but she’s good like that sometimes. Oh, go on then, tell me about your form tutor again – I think I saw you in separate houses last week. Mine’s a total nightmare sometimes.      Mine is Miss Hall.

So do you lot reckon we’ve got a chance of anyone going to Transylvania this summer? I know it’s got the gothic vibe and stuff, but honestly, I’d murder for a break where we don’t hear about sunbeds and beach clubs for a week.      I mean, I'm in if there's somewhere to bake an actual      cake instead of scones or muffins every day. Slap me in a town with a castle and a patisserie, and I'll be floating.      Oh come on, Beth, the muffins you make are like edible miniature picnics. I’ve sold them as “artisan” in the café. Kids in pink wellies buy them by the tray! Besides, if you want to expand your horizons, I’m running a special this summer:   _The InternationalBake-Off:_   Romanian Mărțișor, Thai coconut rolls... I’m thinking of adding some Australian pavlova, thanks to Tom.        Oh mate, that’s humble of you, Beth.   But tell you what—pavlova takes three days of baking, a week to let it grief   , and a bag of passion fruit the size of a West Ham squad. You want me baking for Mateusz's new café, you’ll have to slap a deposit up front. I’m not taking orders for emotional baggage and phone calls at 3 a.m. anymore.      Haha, fair one. But seriously, regarding Translyvania – have we got a group going? Just need to weigh up laser eye surgery and being able to see the   _Transylvanian hills_  , or about five metres in front of my face.      You’re looking at a no-brainer!   _She laughs._   I mean, if you're going to go all jungle gym for eyes, do it for something epic. A road trip with Beth and Max baking on the side—now that’s a Netflix show. I’ll write it myself when I’m not deep-frying muffins.      Don’t ignore the gossip machine too much, Charlie—my cousin took the laser eye thing and came back with a hatred for Romanian vending machines. Supposed go bad on her day three if you don’t deactivate them first.      Yep, I’ll be needing a bloke who’s already had all of that. I’m planning to hire a navigation wizard and someone who knows where the off switches are      on foreign tech or I’m walking into the middle of the Carpathians alone. I can see it now—my voice on a podcast titled  "Lost in Transylvania: One Englishman and a Dog Named Bratwurst".

Right, so the photoshoot is on Saturday at 10. I just wanted to make sure everyone’s ready. You two, put your pyjamas on and we can take some fun poses. Maybe a little dance move? Not the one you did during the children's party with the muddy obstacle course though—do you remember that? I swear the trampoline was   not   part of the course… until you guys found it.      Yeah! I got covered in mud but then I   didn’t   go in the puddle again after the aerial hoop! Muuurph! That was squishy!      I  promised  me no more aerial hoop, only if we wore our helmets and Myla didn’t drop me! So, not today, okay?      You fell off, silly. I told you the little pigs had mud in it.      Okay, okay—let’s not go into mud stories for now. We need to be the  fancy  version of us for the pictures. Maybe listen to some music that helps you dance?      I listen to Alice in Wonderland music. Like the one with the Queen and the croquet with flamingos!      I like it too, but I only want to wear my princess dress-up hat. I don’t want it to get muddy again.  Wheep . Mummy, what did you use to make the tea leaves in the pot? It looked like coffee.      It   was   coffee unfortunately, but just imagine it was a special kind made from the mushrooms in Wonderland. Now let’s be calm and smile for the camera. If you’re good, we can listen to your Alice in Wonderland CD while the photos come out. Deal?      Deal! But are we going to make a real tea party after the photos?      Only if someone offers me a “very nice” snack. Biscuits, maybe a Cadbury’s something, as long as there’s no swearing about who gets the last one.      I’ll propose a system—blindfold and pick one! No whining either.      That sounds  unfair , but Mummy can be the judge!      If I see or  hear  anyone trying to cheat, I’ll use the full force of the ‘unmuddy your pyjamas’ threat. Alright, everyone in position! Hands in the air, pretend you're holding flamingos… like in the croquet game!      Like the croquet with the Queen shouting and the jabberwocky underneath!      I want to be the Jabberwocky! With wings and a woolly hat!      Maybe before the weekend, we can pick out some合适的 costumes—just don’t bring home a tea-cake for inspiration again, okay?

Rather skip the school dinner and go to McDonald's, couldn't do it.      Oh I got to go to parents' evening now poor girl.      Oh right, what are they like? Not too bad are they?      They were alright, but it's all about holidays and activities now. It was like   "How many times did your child come with a clean uniform this year?"        That's right, but she was quite good, you know. She's been doing quite well in her subjects.      She looks after these little children.      A bit much, but the teachers are still human. I've had that My turkey still cooked, but I watched it left and right.      I've been cooking too, and I think I turned my oven to an oven, but the chicken is better than breakfast, no doubt.      Hiiii.      Good morning, love, didn't expect to see you up yet.      I do tell you, being old and missing all the impacts of the technology is a real insight. Did you tell her, by the way, she got her results tomorrow.      Tell her she's done – Mate it's got a sting, and I know.      Yeah, she's gonna be excited.      What results?      There you go, someone who knows!      Yeah, she's just done her end of school term exams.      What did you get?      We'll wait for the results, love. I'm not a bad parent.      I had to teach a lesson where they had to know that frost forms when the wind goes down a pipe.      You're smarter than you look.      Hey, what's for dinner?      Pizza and chocolate roulade, you know your favourites.      Mmm that sounds nice.      Pizza and a roulade? That's not healthy, but it's festive, I suppose.      Yeah, go on then I'm up if you need me.      Is it just pizza and roulade or something else?      Cos you could have something else.      No it's fine, I just like knowing what's on the menu.      Yeah, we like to know everything.      Fair enough.      My kind of thing, all the details.      Just make sure to keep the conversation going she’s just got to be.      Just has to be, yes. I don’t ever want her to feel that she's not.      That she's okay.      Yeah. That she's okay. That she's got people around her if she needs them.      That's right.

Rather skip the breakfast bar and go for a swig of tea.      You like that, don’t you? Just a tea and a biscuit before a game.      Aye, can’t be arsed with anything else on a weekday morning.      Thought I’d make a start on the garden while he settles in with the board. The strawberry patch needs a bit of weeding before the next heatwave, I swear it’s going to go to seed if we don’t keep it under control.      Do you think the weather’s clearing up for good this week? I’ve been watching the forecast and it’s still dodgy for the south-east.      The weather here’s like Brexit, you never know what you’re gonna get next.      That’s an astute comment, James.      You need to worry about cricket or garden in South Korea. I hear the weather there is brutal, even in July.      Korea, eh? I do like the way they handle education. Far better than our two-tier system. Still, with inflation and tuition fees escalating, I expect there’ll be riots before the year’s out.      Yeah – but it’s got me thinking, I actually had a mate back in my teens who got deported because of that whole thing with the council housing and fake documents back in the eighties. He never did anything wrong, but one letter and he was gone.      That’s rough. Though I’d rather have a fair system over a politicians’ backsie any day.      I did listen to a conversation once between two bumblebees – don’t mind me. I’ve always found animal communication fascinating. Not that I’d tell any of the boys in my group. My job’s got me looking into things like morphophonemics and all that.      You told us you were an English teacher, not a mad bee cultist.      Actually, phonetics is a vital part of language acquisition. I think it helps students grasp accents and nuances. My students adore it, even if they roll their eyes sometimes.      But let’s get our heads back on straight, lad. You sure you want that green tea with the box breakfast granola? Lift your legs and you’ll be planting tomatoes in no time.      I’d sooner feed the belly than the garden right now. Got a meeting over at the call centre at ten.      The call centre? Always forget you’re in customer services.

So do you ever find it strange working in TEFL in such a different cultural setup? I mean, like... teaching in Poland versus back home?      Honestly, it’s wild sometimes! I mean, the students here can be super respectful and eager to learn — but they’re also much more formal than the ones I taught in Manchester. It took me a while to get used to all the “pan” and “pani” stuff! I had this one guy who wouldn’t stop calling me “Miss Rachel” it was just so British in the worst way!      Oh, I know what you mean. I had a similar experience when I taught in Germany. It’s like they’re almost trying too hard to be polite. Although I must say, the food’s a lot better here, to be fair.      I’ll give you that! Living in Tarnow is nice — it’s got that small-town charm without being too remote. You drive in every day?      Yeah, I drive in from the outskirts. I’ve actually just passed the MOT shop over there, so maybe I need to drop in next week. Honestly, I’ve been putting it off for ages.      Make sure to do it before the rhythm of the services gives way. I remember my Mate Joel had his fairly mot last year, it was a riot. The inspector nearly kicked the car out for making mortal sin at high speed.      That sounds like something he would do. Honestly, I’m also suspicious of my brake lights. It just feels oddly silent when I hit the pedal.      If you're not sure, better safe than sorry. You know, most people about here are quite cautious about the inspections. I had one of my Polish students who said if you don’t pass your MOT, the police will take the car away unceremoniously.      Unromantic stuff. But I can’t complain. The views at least are scenic. Speaking of, how do you cope with the politics here? I’ve heard there’s a crack down on universities and teachers' unions of late.      Yeah, it's been fairly depressing if you're not prepared for it. I mean, it's not the end of the world every day, but it's suffocating for so many people.      I can only imagine. That brings me on to what your younger self must have thought when planning to live abroad.

So did you go?      Go where? To the open day at Oxford? No—what, and miss the rugby sevens weekend at Twickenham? You saw the draw, right?      Yeah, I read somewhere that it was on the same weekend as the Human Sciences open day. I  really  wanted to go, but I couldn’t book a later slot.      Man, if I were doing this human sciences, art, or whatever degree thing, I’d go. But me? Maths? Nah. I just chase the rugby season.      Yeah, I get it. But still, I talked to someone at the department and they said it’s like a mix of biology, psychology, anthropology—you get to sample a bit of everything. It’s for people who don’t pick one discipline yet.      Sounds like my uni bro at Cambridge. He does natural sciences and has to do all those lab modules in his first year. And no, he hides, you know, he says he isn’t doing biology full-time, but I saw him buried in a book on human evolution one time.      Still, I think human sciences could be good. I’ve got a bit of time before I decide, but I got an offer from Lady Margaret Hall. I got fairly high in my predicted grades for maths and chem. They weren’t expecting me to get into anything else, but I guess it went okay.      Mate, you got into Oxford. That’s huge! That’s like a big flex at the bar. You can just ignore the kid talking about his three A grades and their YouTube DJ hobby.      Haha, about that—your cousin Alex mentioned you’re having a bar pass this Saturday. Not much of a bar pass if you are drunk before you even open the handle, right?      Nah, hang on. There’s guest speeches after. I did actually book a hotel for a few of us. My mate Tom said he brought a cake, which is wild because I told him not to. He  insisted . Also, mentioned you two were coming, so the whole team’s waiting to cheer you on.      Man, are you gonna man up and toast go out of my pond life if you don’t get into Oxford? You’re on the hook for that.      Deal. And what your team’s bar pass is missing is  me  helping you pick roles in the kitchen.

Rather skip the new tax increases eh?      I’m trying to get my head around it all, Dad. I teach French and Spanish at the college, but I don’t earn nearly as much as I used to when we were in the same bracket as you were.      Aye, things change, luv. Back when I was working at the tax office in Woburn, everyone had to file by 31st May and it was much easier to track. Now it’s spreadsheets and software you never knew existed. But governments never run when it rains.      Right, but it feels like they tax us for everything now. What’s the point if we’re just giving it all back?      Well, it’s not just taking, see. The government uses it to build schools, hospitals, the lot. Back in the 80s, Margaret Thatcher changed the whole system. Look, she’s still a bit of a controversial character, but the way she pushed for lower taxes on property and higher taxes on companies? That built a different kind of economy.      But isn’t it unfair if we’re not earning that much and we’re paying as much as someone earning double?      That’s where the Progressive tax system comes in – the more you earn, the more you pay. That’s not new. When I worked in accounts, that’s what we always advised people to understand: the tax bands.      So someone earning £30k doesn’t pay the same rate as someone earning £60k?      Exactly. The basic rate stays at 20%. It’s when you start climbing those higher brackets that it gets a bit steep. But it still means the government can afford to keep streets lit and the bin men coming.      And the new universal credit? That just feels like a burden. If you lose your job, it takes ages for them to sort it out. It’s not giving people stability.      Aye, I’ve read about that too. It was meant to cut out bureaucracy, but with any big change like that, there’s always some growing pains. The government’s got a budget to work with and sometimes their hands are tied because of the cost of living and interest rates.      Is it possible they’re not planning for the long term?      That’s what I’m thinking. You’ve got to manage the books like any business, innit?

So did I tell you about the stress levels at work lately? It's been insane—the project I’m managing is due next month, and no one is on the same page!      No, I haven’t heard. You’ve been managing a project at work?      Yeah, I sort of took it on by default, really. Someone else was supposed to do it, but they’ve been off sick. I know I’m just a graduate, but apparently, I was the next reasonable person.      Oh dear! Do you get support? I mean, you can’t possibly sort it out on your own.      In theory, yes—but in practice? My boss keeps saying “trust your instincts” and “you’ll be fine,” and I’m like, “Thanks, very reassuring!”      Sounds like classic management speak. I remember when I was in charge of exams in the school; I used to live for the last five days before we finished, even though I had absolutely no idea what I was doing half the time.      I can’t even imagine! You did all that as part of your job?      Oh yeah—it wasn't glamorous. I remember one year we had staffing issues, and I had to proctor three different papers on the same day in three different subjects. I nearly had a heart attack trying to remember who was where.      That’s wild. I just have to make sure everyone in my team is submitting the right documents on time. It feels out of control!      It comes down to communication, really. When people are unclear, it causes about half the problems. I used to make the teachers draw up a list of key dates and what they needed from us admins. It helped so much. Why don’t you do something similar?      That’s not a bad idea. I’ve been just sending out emails and getting ignored. If I asked them to submit a mini-timeline or something, maybe people would actually take it seriously.      Exactly! And don’t be afraid to ask for small things first. Once they start giving you a bit of information, it’s easier to push for the rest. I remember once I told our head of year I needed a schedule line in the password reminder system. He looked at me like I was mad—but after a week of me pestering, it was done and everyone’s life was easier.

Rather skip the new beer and bring us a red, would you love?      Yeah, got any white left? Just a small one, actually. Not sure what I fancied yet.      I'll have the same as you, Ruth. But maybe make it a half? I've got to drive back today, and I haven't had my medicine yet.      Oh, don’t worry about that. I’m barely going to touch it.      You and your wine. You always say that when it's the good stuff. Careful, you'll end up like me—house full of bottles and half a supply of antacids in the cupboard.      Ha! Yeah, but you’ve got the taste for the Cellar Door, Dad. I stick to the bog standard merlot most of the time.      Merlot? Now that’s not a wine—eh, that’s more of a desktop paint, ha! Still, better than that sweet stuff I see on the supermarket aisles now. Might as well just call it fruit squash.      Oh, Ruth and I went to that fancy place in Durham a couple of weeks ago. The owner was from Spain—I think. Anyway, he told us that the real trick with wine is to pair it with your mood, not the food.      Oh yeah? And what’s the mood been lately? Because from what someone said in an email last week, sounds like it's been "existential crisis" week with you two.      Hey! Don’t listen to all that. Yeah, there've been a few crises—mainly about the goldfish. Barney the Goldie finally bit the dust a week ago. That poor little thing was like a child to me.      My, my! What happened to him? Poisonous tap water? A depressed fish?      No, apparently it was a heart attack. I mean, he was old—actually, 12. That’s 84 in fish years.      Okay, but surely 12 isn’t that old for a goldie? Maybe he was into go-karts on the lake?      Ha ha very funny. Goldfish, like us—midlife crisis by the age of your 20s.      Oh, leave it out. And now I’ve had to go and get a new one. Lisa from the hairdressers gave me a baby fish that looks like it’s been fed oatmeal and butter. Totally unnatural.      You're giving fish makeovers now?      It’s just, you know, it’s a long story… Anyway, we’re off-topic.

So did you go to the conference in London last week, Sarah?      Yeah, I did. It was supposed to be a weekend conference, but I ended up staying Monday as well because there was an extra workshop on integrating tech into the classroom. You would’ve liked some of it — there was a bit about using gamification to teach literature.      Oh, sounds interesting. I miss those kinds of things when I’m teaching overseas. I’m teaching in Seville now, and while there are lots of nice private schools, the funding for professional development isn’t really there.      That’s a shame. I mean, I know it’s different for people in state schools too — funding’s always an issue. But I’ve been luckier. My school prioritises continuing education, especially for their English teachers, which is why they paid for me to go.      How was it? I’ve been wanting to go to one for a while, but between planning, grading and getting enough holiday, it’s not always easy to make the time.      It was good, but honestly, I left feeling slightly exhausted. There was quite a bit to take in and only so much coffee could help. But I met a few people who do international teaching too, so it was nice to have someone to complain to about curriculum differences, time zones and trying to get the kids to do their homework.      Oh, I could relate to every single one of those. Our kids here don’t even get the concept of a read-and-respond paragraph. I had a lesson earlier this week where half the class spent the time looking at their shoes and trying not to speak in English.      I feel you. And you can only do so much with “role-play” if no one wants to engage. I’m trying new ways to handle it too — like mixing in some meme culture they actually care about. It’s surprising how much grammar practice you can get from them arguing over the meaning of something on TikTok.      That’s brilliant! I stick too much to textbooks and end up being the only one excited about the 'British Romantic Poets' unit. I do wonder, though, how do you even find time to plan around the conferences and still go every year?      Well, I write a proposal at the end of each term outlining what I want to gain from attending and what I can bring back.

Rather skip the gym and just go for scenic walks when I’m here. It’s beautiful countryside through here. I got to admit, I haven’t touched a treadmill since I turned forty.      You’re lucky. Not all of us have the kind of scenery to motivate us to walk twenty miles a day! I tried a fitness app last week, but by the time I got to the third level, I couldn’t be bothered any more. I ended up just doing squats in my leggings while watching some cheesy rom-com. You can laugh, I don’t mind.      I saw the same one last night!  Obvious Child , with Judd Apatow and Jenny Slate. Brilliant film. Anyway, speaking of cheesy rom-coms, I’ve been reading more lately to keep my brain from going too soft. I just finished this little novel— The Song of Achilles , very slow and poetic, but really moving.      I’m reading a bit, too. Just started  Where the Crawdads Sing . I know, I know, everyone’s read it, but I get around to it eventually. Sometimes I feel like the only thing I’ve read this year is teaching manuals and syllabi.      You work too hard then. You’re still teaching at the language school in Manchester?      Part-time, yeah. I’m actually doing quite a bit of volunteering through the council as well—helping out at youth centres, doing some basic literacy work with asylum seekers. It doesn’t pay a lot, but it’s oddly satisfying. You ever think about doing anything like that?      I did a few years back in Cambridge, helping out in a community kitchen. That felt like something. But now, well, I’m more of a semi-retired person now. I do occasional EFL classes if someone emails me, but to be honest, I prefer reading and playing board games with my godchildren.      Sounds like a dream. You know, I once thought I’d be someone who had everything figured out by forty, but here I am, thirty-something and still trying to find the right balance between work and the things I love. Like, for example, learning how not to get lost on the way to go swimming in the pond outside Rzeszow.      Is it far? I was just looking at the map earlier—and I might have misread the turn at the cow flu ranch. You know the one where the gates say “Wielki Skot”?

Rather skip the new moonlight cycle. You know what, let’s go hurroo tomorrow. The first... What's the word she uses—     Hmm?     Creator cycle is thrown into physics. You know, like when things start to repeat. But it was in that eeny weeny passive voice thingy with the Moon      Moon cycle?     Aye, but I think that this one isn’t so interested in seeing the moon cycle; she’s more obsessed with seeing the pyramids and stuff. Do you want to go with us?     PyObject. Lakelands?     Y’know, we can add like that My turkey pyramids trek thingy. Fun stuff. It’s supposed to be loads of fun, although I dunno how I’ll be with little kids running around in sun dress climates and giggle-sneezy babies shrieking at me while everyone goes “Oh look at the egyptians and their desktop hides, look at them tombs!”     Well, I mean, it’s not like we can take a trip up to Cork and not land a week to ourselves. I’ve been deadly since November. Between the doctor appointments and the toddler trotting around, it’s been nonstop. Even Baptiste stopped coming over to play with her because he’s busy working.     All that “depression at home” stuff. Aye, I understand. It’s daft what someone who once laughed for ten minutes at a conspiracy about a comet colliding with Earth can now cry at something as simple as a cartoon turtle. It’s like telomeres dying right along with her smiley face. I mean, I know she’s not a man—but still, watching someone get worn down like that by life…      I know. But it’s not like we’re the only ones. Everyone’s baked. My sister’s working at Nordstrom, she just shows me a picture of a shlimmer wooden mannequin and says, “Get your Archeologist stick out.”     Right. And every time you take a breath, the whole damn planet gets older, and you want to be like,  “Wait, am I the one accelerating time or is it my parents?”  It’s like… you don’t expect to line up in a queue between a group of Vikings and Time chờirs at your 40th birthday.     Oh gosh, I’m scared to imagine anyone even suggesting that life expectancy might start falling. I mean, I’ve been working at home this year   from the sofa so much I probably already qualify for "old people."

So do you lot reckon we should bring the new baby chair to the restaurant?      No, don’t bring it in. That place isn’t exactly known for their baby facilities. Best leave it home and see how we do.      Maybe we can just pop in and get a coffee or something quick. It’s one o’clock and I reckon the baby will have a nap before that.      Yeah I don’t want to eat out again unless it’s like once a month you know. I don’t like the prices when it’s kids involved.      That’s mostly cos when you bring a baby you’ve got double the stuff to buy and like that My turkey still cost me ten quid though last time we tried.      I know, I used the vouchers I saved and it was still dear for just a hot drink.      I just happened to see a new coffee maker at the shop last week. M hides, you remember them near the bus stop?      Ah yeah, that big one with the white shopfront. I don’t think your mother would’ve let you get one of them when you were little.      Well it was like fifty pounds which is not bad really. Plus with the deal, you get free beans for a month.      That’s sweet. Maybe we should all go together and pick one while we’re out. Our coffee here at home always tastes so suspicious. Like my brew is just hot water most of the time.      Cos you buy the cheapest lot at the supermarkets. No wonder it’s weak as a daisy.      I know! But it’s on offer most weeks and what can I do?      I reckon if we all went in to the shop, they’d do us a better deal.      And maybe we can pick it up on the way back from the restaurant? Provided we don’t eat out today. We could pop into M hides and then to the market for some fruit trees.      Oh I do love going to the market. I got these nice plants last time, sunflowers and goji berries on the edge of the garden.      Yeah I like the fruit trees. We could plant one by the front window. It’d be like nice to have something growing up there and see it in full bloom.      True, but we need to think about the budget.

Rather skip the new German History books. You know what, they talk about.      Yeah.      Just went on today, and I can't say I found it particularly interesting.      I know, I kind of skipped over them. But it was interesting when I read the World War II chapters last night.      My goodness, yes they're a bit ambitious, listing every little policy shift in every year.      It was quite interesting, actually. We had to do a presentation for history class, so I read the chapter on the Enlightenment and the spread of ideas. I mean, can you believe that Voltaire was taken seriously back then? It’s like the influencers of today, but with books and pamphlets.      Oh I dare say Voltaire was very popular in his day.      Yeah, and they’re even breakfasting with him now at this conference. They did some in-depth analysis on his effect on revolution in Germany, which was pretty cool. Also, the chapter on Angela Merkel was surprisingly good.      Angela Merkel? Well I always thought she was quite a calm person for someone in such a deadly job.      Yeah, it said something about how her humble background really helped her – that she came from a simple, provincial kind of life.      Doesn't surprise me, as calm as you can be when you're stepping out every morning and you're never in a rush.      And not everyone was a rush to run up to the wall with flares and fury.      Exactly, I mean I don't think people are fully aware of what about Berlin Wall meant to a lot of people.      It was really a generational and psychological barrier. I mean you barely left the housing estate if you were in East Germany. Everything had to be approved. Even guest mail.      And now they'll go anywhere they want. Travel all over the world.      I sort of wonder about my grandad and how he would’ve seen it. He was born in 1945 so he never lived with the separation you remember, after the war it was split the Wall came up go.      It's a wonder how anyone could live in line in separate countries that had such a close relationship.      Yeah. It's all so historical now, but I think it’s important to remember those days, don’t you?      Oh, I think so. They say history repeats itself, I suppose.

Right, thanks a million for helping me move in today. I would’ve been stuck in the hallway with a box of mugs forever without you.      No problem, I’d have dragged you out of your £200,000 bachelor pad if you’d been stuck in it on your own! Honestly, I’m just impressed you managed to get this place so quickly. You don’t often hear of a one-bedroom flat in this area going so fast.      I know, it was crazy. The agent said people drive past it every day but nobody stays long enough to get the key. Maybe it’s because the nursery’s next door.      Yeah, that’s what you said. You’ve already got kids hanging around the balcony pretending you’re the boss of their building. But hey, I think it’s sweet. Living near a nursery definitely means you’re better for breakfast, no doubt about that.      Oh absolutely. I’ve already looked up what’s on sale at the local farm shop. I’m determined to cook like a grown-up here, not just survive on shop-bought lasagna and pre-prepared risotto.      Tell that to the leftover Thai we grabbed last night.      Okay, fair point. But I’m trying, and I’ve already ticked off connecting the broadband. Now I just need to sort the phone line and the council tax and everything will be perfect.      Oh yes, and the recycling. You’d better rush to get that bin on the right day before the council sends a letter and then the politicians send out a press release about your lack of civic responsibility.      I’ll be living the dream, blinking at bin lorry diagrams and cross-referencing local by-laws. Speaking of, have you managed to switch your mobile over yet, or are you still hiding fromodafone’s evil SMS campaigns about switching providers?      I was going to ask you to come with me to my local branch today. We could rebel together as we fill out forms. And also, you do remember we need to buy a bin lopper? We’ve no idea where the old one is.      Of course, bin lopper—the manly antecedent to the microwave ladle. I’ll pick one up on the way back from the hardware store. But also, you know how I said I might grow a few herbs? I was thinking of just planting them in old jam jars to start with.

So do you remember the time we got lost in that little town outside Cambridge and ended up in that weird pizzeria and ate cold chips with balsamic dressing?      Oh my gosh, I was half-impressed and half-horrified—half for you for getting us there in one go, and half because I thought the chips were going to make me sick. But hey, that’s a funny memory.      Yeah! I mean, I don’t think I’d go back there for food now, but it was a good night. We literally had no clue where we were—we just went to whatever had lights open at 9 p.m.      Still, I miss that time. It was definitely madness living with you and the rest in that flat. I’m glad I’m not living with someone anymore who eats half the food off my plate in the middle of the night.      Oh I hated that. Honestly, I used to live with my brother and he’d hides my bread to “teach me a lesson” over something I said—so I know the feeling.      Okay I can relate. Was your brother like this from when you were a kid?      Yeah—and it got worse in university. He left me no spoons twice. I had to use a fork for soup for a week. I thought I was going to die.      Oh wow. Mine didn’t do that, thank God. Our parents always said we were too messy. I think my mom still regrets not teaching us to do the dishes properly.      I can imagine. Anyway, enough about mess! So, are you still living in about five square feet of a flat?      Oh I have more space now. My company pays for decent accommodation for the placement year and it actually does mean I can step outside and not hit a wall. But no guest bedrooms, obviously.      Well, as long as you have fresh air and a clean flat, I’m happy for you. My place is alright too—new flat after being in a shared space for the first year of the job. I’ve got my own kettle and toaster for once, something I truly took for granted.      That sounds lovely. I’ve been working on a building project lately, just started, but I’m genuinely enjoying it. It’s outdoor cafes and community centres. It’s nice to work on something with a bit of heart in it.

Rather skip the queue bar here eh?      Aye, it's mad busy for a Thursday. You sorted with a pint?      Just had a lager, gotta keep it simple. You don’t see too many lagers being ordered in this part of the world, do you? Always pints of dry or something fancy like Camden Town.      Yeah, I’ve been here a few times now and every time I say, “Gimme a lager,” someone looks at me like I just insulted the Queen. Here in Cambridge, they take their beer seriously.      Lakelands is where you go for the real serious drink, not some posh pub off the market. You living somewhere near the colleges?      Yeah, I’m in a house in Eynesbury. Pretty quiet place—most of the PhDs down here have been there too long to care about much else besides their research and the bar at the end of the week.      I bet. I’m not bad, still in Sunderland though—only here for a couple of weeks. Gave one of the research talks a week or so back and got roped in as a guest on another panel. Doesn’t cover the airfare from Tyne and Wear, but it’s a chance to see the old college town again.      Cambridge or don’t go? Fair enough. You know what it’s like—once your brain starts fermenting in this kind of place, it’s hard to switch back to normal life.      Oh you know, I miss a decent kebab and being able to walk across the road when I feel like it. Not about stopping at crossings every time. You can just wobbly across the road looking for a light, and some local is like, “Oi, you’re not a student, are you?”      Aye, I had that. Tried to waddle across the High Street holding two pints and three sandwiches, and some Cambridge missus stares at me like I’m from Mars.      That’s probably the first time a lass from Sunderland has ever rendered an oxford-educated PhD speechless.      Maybe. I’ve go to say I usually settle for more of a denim and beanie look these days. Living out of a suitcase with a box of books isn’t what your average philosopher’s supposed to look like, though.      Well, you look the part. You ever been to Northern clubs? I mean, over this way, everyone’s decked out like they’re going to a formal dinner at a library or something.

No, she meant it like it was a tragic love story! Like, “He left me for the cold, empty fridge before me. A fridge full of… sour milk.”

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You think they'd have decent commentary by now, seeing as it's a final and all.      Haha, I know, I nearly fell asleep during that first 20 minutes with the sound off. But at least it keeps the place calm if we’re not shouting at the telly every time they take a corner.      Yeah, I’ve been trying not to wake the baby every time I see a save or a free-kick. She's been up three times last night, poor thing. Didn’t even get to test out her new onesie like I planned.      Oh, did someone knit her a new one? That’s brilliant. My gran still says I’ve got the most beautiful knitting fingers you’ve ever seen. I reckon she'd have made a dozen by now if she'd been here.      Probably! She doesn’t miss a prime knit sale in Argos or anything in Jo’s website, you know. Anyway, I’m ordering another spare swaddle from the internet. I told her I was going to, if only for the Olympics. She takes one look at the telly, goes for the knitting needles.      Honestly, watching football during the Olympics is a little surreal. You’re like, who even won the bobsled last night, because all I saw was a kid with her hands in the air going  I don't know what to do .      Honestly, I just watched the highlights. But I’ve got to admit, the athletes are amazing. I can’t even finish my half a mile in the park without being out of breath – and I’m not even doing it for gold, just survival.      Haha, yeah, I had to stop a couple of times the other day when I walked past the baby’s park. No one mentioned that parenting is like a full-time obstacle course. Running, chasing, lifting, folding – and all without a medal at the end.      I tried to name her something with a bit of flair to make up for that. "Aurora", you know? Fits a little angel with golden eyes.      That’s a beauty. You're like a modern-day poet with baby names. I still can't believe you're settling for one name and not six in separate languages, like they do in some blooming countries.      You joke, but I seriously considered Elara-Faith-Rose.

Right, I just wanted to bring up the request that gramma’s promising.      We saw the Queen and James.      No I mean going to the Palace where we saw the Queen.      Was that the one at Windsor?      Yes een, and there’s entry fees even for the Royal family I reckon. But I wanted to see if you’d like to go when we’re next in London and see if we can stretch to it as a family day out. We can even pop to the shops at the Crown when we get there.      But is it even open now?      I think it only opens for certain bits like the state visit areas. You know, like the drawing rooms and the stuff where they entertain important guests.      I think the Palace is called Buckingham Palace in the cartoon.      Is it Bucks-okee?      Yeah, sorta. But it says Windsor on the map.      Good ones, we can argue about the names when we get there, or we can take one of those audio tours.      And then can we see the Royal Gardens?      Absolutely, then we can have a bite at the Crown estate café with the real Royal Fruits.      What Royal Fruits?      Silly, the ones with the crest on them. Like they gave in the Prince Harry Spaghetti incident.      Were they blue?      Only in the cartoon.      But what if we want to  be  royalty or even a politician?      Well you can start small, like joining the council or standing as a local representative.      I’d be better than a Prime Minister.      Yeah, I could be a teacher like mummy, but better and have my own palace.      Sounds ambitious. I tried being Queen for a day once.      What did you do?      I told a couple of the mums at the parent-teacher thing you had to stand around with a crown and the kids believed it go.      Why don’t we go to see diving at the Olympic Stadium?      That big one on the edge of London?      The one and only, and it’s quite amazing those divers, swooping like super heros.      But they’re not real super heros like in the cartoon I watched with the bees.      What cartoon was that?      The Bee Movie, the one with the bee who used to say bees don’t actually bee. But he was speaking.      Ah, the Barry B. movie. Was that with the Queen?

Rather skip the queue and take a seat, I think. Cheeky, but it saves time when you’ve got the aching knees from the tip today. Blows my mind what folk chuck over there, by the way. Not only old fridges and broken children’s rocking horses—what were you doing chucking all that plastic  binnage  in the bin-liner, Mark?      A whole life in a bag, love. Proper human memoirs. Oh, and a sock, interestingly. One sock. Found it near the microwave. Didn’t even want to touch it. Gloves on, like I was sorting out a  crime scene . Bit much for the afternoon, don’t you think?      Touch wood, I’m not heading for the tip until next week. I’ve got Oliver on my hands and I think he turned my garden centre trowel into a sword for a Tudor project he was doing at school. He won’t put it down. Blooming planting’s not happening until he re-invents Henry the Eighth in the flower beds.      Can I have a Mars bar? Pleeeeease?      Here’s a thought—outhouse, old-school garden parties, and watching men fight with trowels. Mark gives “stumping at the tip” a new meaning, wouldn’t you say, Mark? Bet you could write somethin’ poetic out of all that  binnage . Mark, you could put it in a chapbook. “Plastic Tales from the Thorn: A Waste Walker’s Journey”.      Only if the blurb says, “Inspired by tea-stained socks and the ghost of a Prime Minister waving in about five recycle sacks.”      Oh come on, this place is full of history. My father knew old Fred Birtle who ran the Thirsk Market back in the 1960s. Fred told him once that he’d seen people sell baby strollers there. Unbelievable, really. These days it’s all about auction websites and getting your telly to clear as soon as it’s 12 years old.      Aye, I remember the good folk of Kendal delivering something amazing with trolleys the size of buses goin’ on the fairs. Not now. Just got me and Mark chuckin’ out old-toys and plastic box sets that never went on your shelf.      I lost a conker in the bin yesterday. It was really good. Dad says I’ve got to talk about that ‘clearing out’ business at the tip like I’m some  event manager .      Event manager? Right, that's a title for folk who make sure the stale pasties and the dirty oven mitts get noticed and disposed of in glory.

Rather skip the Museum this weekend eh?      Aye, it's always busy at Christmas... got to pick up some gear for the party at my sister’s too.      Yeah, plus I don’t fancy standing in the queue outside again for them cars. Parked in that eeny weeny lot last week and got twitched by a pigeon.      Oh aye, I had to park nearly ten minutes from my job last week. They’re charging   £8   to park now! It’s ridiculous. You’d think outside of the city centre it’d be easier... like, literally two streets away and still dead.      Aye, and I managed to get Myra a Christmas gift, but I had to go all the way over to Bold Street for it. She’s picky about what she likes now. You thinking of getting Fin a gift yet?      Not yet, been busy with a trial in placement at the clinic. Only just clocked how fast the weeks are flying by. I might pop into John Lewis—settle for a nice scarf or something sturdy. She doesn’t go in for all the flashier stuff.      Tell you what, I’ve been thinking... we should seriously consider moving out of this flat at some point. This place is alright, but I barely see the kitchen for all the boxes and books. Mate of mine offered me their spare room down in Widnes for a while if we fancied a change. Could be cheaper rent too.      Widnes sounds oddly appealing at the minute. Just need to weigh up the commute for both of us. You're starting that MA in Teaching in January right?      Yeah, submitted the application last week. Interview is in mid-December. Been stressing about it because I’m trying to juggle it with the English classes I teach. My head’s full of lesson plans and guest speaker topics at the moment.      You’ll do fine. Just give them the talking points we rehearsed. You’re a pro at this, even if you do overcomplicate sentences sometimes.      Gringe! I do   not   overcomplicate things. I’m a teacher, course I talk proper!      Aye, you talk  proper  at your job, but in conversation you still say “get the box” instead of “pick up the box”.      That's just how we speak in Birkenhead! And don’t forget, I’ve got a cockerel and a cat at the flat at the minute.

So did you watch The Rings of Power weekend? I stayed up way too late watching it and I’m  still  tired today.      No I haven’t had time! With assignments and all, plus my group project’s a bit of a nightmare at the minute. But I’ve been watching eeny weeny bits of it on YouTube, like just the big scenes.      You’ve missed all the slow-building stuff! Honestly though, it was easier watching than reading Middle-earth, you know. Tolkien’s books are like… okay when you're in the mood.      Right, I tried  The Hobbit  once and got bored half-way through. Still, I managed like three episodes of the show before I fell asleep though. I’m not sure if I’m into the fantasy genre anymore, I used to love it when I was younger with all the Disney movies and stuff.      I know! I still love  Frozen . Like, I know it’s cheesy but I can still sing those songs in my sleep. I would  die  to meet Idina Menzel.      I never thought about meeting Frozen characters but credit to the real ones for still being nice. I mean, I tried following Idina Menzel on Instagram once.      Oh my god, did she respond?      No, obviously, but I still follow her. I’m one of thousands! Though, I mean, I just wanted to see what her lifestyle is like. You know? It’s wild how much the internet gives you access to people now.      I know, but I don’t even know what most people do with their lives anymore! My cousin just started talking about tattoos and I had no idea she was into that! She got an owl on her ankle and it looks amazing, honestly.      Oh yeah! My sister’s thinking about getting a snake somewhere. I told her the only way she's getting one is if she gets it at the café when I’m working so I can tell her not to shift to get out of the pain.      Ahaha, do you let your customers skip washing up after getting one then?      Nooo, that’s if they don’t get a tattoo! You’re still in, no excuses. Honestly, the busiest day last week was what your mum used to call “the worst flu” hitting the café and everyone ordering takeaway.      Oh no! I had it Friday, stayed in bed all weekend except to go out for pizza.

Right, I just texted your gran to say we’ll do that thing on Sunday—the garden tour in Cork. What do you think, Oisin? We’ll see the pretty flowers, yeah?      No, I mean—why are you texting my gran? She’s on Facetime now, isn’t she?      Oh, actually… she’s on with your Aunty Karen.      No, but she promised me ten minutes of Call of Duty!      Didn’t your mum get the new tablet? That’s like three times more gaming!      That’s not the point.      Pikachu! Pikachu!      Oh, look, he’s figured out the world’s most exciting game is just holding a toy to his face.      Shouldn’t you be in bed at his age, Mega Millions?      Alright, I’ll tell you what—after dinner, I’ll let you two struggle your way through that Ramen tournament. If you win, we go on a proper Pokémon run to the game shop, yeah?      Real ones, not that €5 fake swag from the bargain bin.      Pikachu! Pikachu!      There he is, someone who agrees.      So, have you thought about doing a buy-sell-buy-trade at some point? I mean, being here in Cork and all, we could do Oisin a Pokémon about-you.      Don’t be a prat. We’ve gone over that. We barely have space for his unmentionables in slippers, let alone for 152 little lizards.      151, technically. And one Dragonite.      Dragonite could come out to clear up this mess. Let’s not tempt it.      Daddy Pig!      Ugh, not the animated version of go-karting man-via-sphincter. Show respect, bruh.      Who’s this one? Thought you were into tighter stuff?      True, but sometimes you just want something over this slim-fitting silence of fitting like string. You know? The gym’s not exactly conditioning me.      And your guitar? It’s been in the corner for six weeks, looking sadder than my mum after your dad’s last rant about her wine budget.      The night's young. Maybe I'll give it a plug-in and jam to counter the vibe of Oisin's Pikachu domination.      Please, don’t. The only harmonics I need are from the overload of baby food and the microwaved "lemon_cheers_with_better_backticks" of my leftover risotto.      Mmmm-maaa!      That means "Outside!" Come on, bit of fresh air then we’ll siwalk for an ice cream cone. He needs more strength than holding up a Pikachu.

Rather skip the new sock drawer eh?      Well they are just crumpled up like mince pies in there anyway.      I know, I've been in this cupboard since we moved in and honestly I don't know what half of it is. But it was in that box, and there  was  a sock that didn’t quite match.      Oh aye, I should never have bought that one from the 99p shop. It was some sort of merino fiber and it was bright green and slimy in the wash.      I like to think it was mostly  you  that was slimy the last night we wore them both in that fancy dress turkey do. You remember? The one where someone accidently brought a real live dove for their centerpiece?      Awww don't remind me of that poor bird. Made quite an impression, fluttering about and knocking over everyone's gravy boats!      But getting back to this, didn’t we have the Bako set over here too?      Aye, in this box—there it is! Faded leaves as ever. Did you know that we’ve still got pieces in here that are still stuck together from when we put them in? The glue – Mate’s been in there forty years and still holds!      I remember building quite the castle out of it! You know what it looked like? Like that medieval toilets they had in the castles in Kent. Strictly for royalty to sit and pee and look out over the moat.      Or as I thought it was at the time,  our  own fully fortified biscuit tin stronghold. I was the Queen of Sugarplums and you had this job looking after the bridges.      Not that I was very good at it! Those bits always fell over, like Burgundy baked Alaska falling apart in high winds.      Well, the biscuits did fall, but the  castle  stood! Ah, we had such imagination. We had to, as we were just kids of divorced parents with two separate lunches to keep in order!      And no less memorable than those afternoons tending our little 'gardening set'. Remember the pond life? We used to think real snails were going to come out of that green plastic bog.      And your insistence that you could grow proper tomatoes in it!      Well, those plastic ones never aged like the real thing. But it was the process that counted, right? Or at least the string beans—remember my cunning plan to make fake tomato ketchup by stewing red crayon slices?

Rather annoying isn't it, the amount of swarms of mosquitoes we've had this summer. I know it's got to do with the wet weather, but honestly, I can't cover up much more than I am doing already. Not to mention they're not even being deterred by the DEET I’ve slathered on my arms!      I know what you mean. It’s like they’ve all formed a committee to target us. I was nearly devoured last night when I was trying to dump the bin. We need to start doing the mosquito proofing outside when it gets dark. You know, those little zappers with the light. I’ve seen them in the hardware shop, only a few quid.      Oh, I saw one left on a shelf last week, half-eaten by what I can only assume were the same little demons. I did actually watch a programme about them – turns out, they’re more attracted to people who exhale more carbon dioxide. And I, ever the unfit one, probably puff out enough to make a small volcano explode.      Fair point, luv. I think I’ve got it in me somewhere to jog to work, but only for dramatic effect. Imagine the look on the other commuters’ faces if I stumble past them glowing bright red at the park. Plus, I’ve got a gig Friday night at that new jazz bar off the High Street. You’re coming, yeah?      If I don’t, they may just have someone smuggle me in via the crowd. I’d never miss your gig. I do wonder what the other band is going to sound like though. Any word from the promoter?      Only that they’re some kind of “retro funk fusion” thing. Promoter says “they blend 70s soul with cabaret sensibilities and a hint of electronica.” Sounds like someone’s just listed genres for the sake of words. But hey, if they play B-flat at least I know it won't ruin my set.      I’ll be passing on your good word to our friends over at the uni. Even if they ignore the gig, a couple of them are always looking for an excuse not to be stuck in the car during peak traffic.      Traffic really has got worse since that new housing development went up, hasn’t it? I’m lucky I don’t go further than the main campus.
