So did you get an interview today?      Yeah, I did! They messaged first thing in the morning, so I went straight on my computer and filled it in.      Which company was it?      It's one of those big accountancy firms in Reading. I met the girl at one of the careers fairs at uni. She said they were on the lookout for fresh grads.      Cool. You'll probably get a call back soon. You always do well in those sorts of things.      I hope so. I just wish I had even half your confidence. You seem to breeze through auditions and stuff like it's no big deal.      Nah, I just try not to stress. I mean, I get nervous, especially if it’s a big event. But I’ve learned to breathe properly. Helps when you’ve been training your body since you were a kid in sport.      That’s true. I always say the most exhausting thing I do all day is scrolling through job boards.      Haha, I know what you mean. But still, you’ve got to take the opportunities when they come. You’ve got a degree in something people actually want. Not like my golf qualification. No one wants to pay me to hit a ball around a course.      Don’t be silly. If I could swing like you at ten, I wouldn’t be buried under forty-three apps for prospective employers.      That’s because I got out there and played at a young age. I didn’t wait till university to try something new. You know, most people I meet at tournaments have PhDs or bizzarre qualifications. I had to work out what I was good at by doing it.      I remember when we went to that play in Manchester. I thought I was going to pass out from embarrassment. I was trying to write it up for something on my course.      You were fine. We both were. At least until we got to the bar and you spilled your drink all over someone from the cast.      Still remember that guy saying ‘vodka and thespians never go hand in hand.’      And you said ‘nope, just vodka and me don’t go hand in hand.’ Classic Kizzy.      I miss that play. Thought it was absolutely magical.      It was alright. Just made me want to hit a ball into the abyss of the theatre floor. You know my kind of stress relief.

Right, thanks a million for helping us out with the grils. I know her crèche is on a Sunday and Claire here she’s having one of her anti-social weekends again, sure she’d rather lie in bed until sun-down.      Don’t worry, James, it was my pleasure and besides, it’s nice to see her making some good little friends. She's actually been trying to do A,B,Cs by herself now, so this is a step forward for her. It was quite adorable, truth be told.      Yeah, she even tried to sing with us last night... like, very creatively. I mean, "hot," "cloud," and "dinner" were in there somewhere.      Yeah, she tried to recite the alphabet like it was a movie script. I think A turned into ‘Adventure’ and B was ‘Batman,’ then C was, um… Claire?!      That’s my Claire, full of opinions and creativity, even at three. Well, I suppose once she hits four, we’ll get into her truly challenging phase, like spelling and maybe dabbling in algebra.      Caa... Bu... Da...?      Oh no, here we go again, trying to act like she’s fluent in the filmography of Christopher Nolan.      If she keeps this up, maybe we’ll let her attend film club. She might just end up directing the next Oscar winner.      I’m just hoping she’d at least be able to sit through a film without turning it into a musical ballet.      Well, I think she's inspired. Last week, she had this whole set-up with her toys and some clouds made of paper. Supposedly it was a ‘dinner movie’ with a ‘very important ending.’      And I told her the clouds looked a bit like my microwave. At least someone knows how to appreciate performance art.      Right. Well as long as we've covered the lunches, bedtime and alphabet recitals. Now if only we could arrange for her to sleep past seven and learn that the dinner is intended go in her mouth, life would be perfect.      I think we’ll stick with the dream team of three-year-olds and IT managers. It’s a winning combo. Even if it means cleaning up cloud confetti every other night.      True to that. For now, I’m just grateful we've at least made it to a homemade mac ‘n’ cheese dinner without her throwing the clouds out the window.

Right, I swear I locked the door last night, but do you think someone just walked in through the front... or was it the back door?      Honestly, I've been thinking about that since we woke up. We wouldn’t have heard anyone walking around — it’s a two-storey house and all the windows are closed tight. It was like   5°C   last night — no one’s going in through the front door halfway through the night! I mean, unless they had a key...      Well, no one has the key. Didn’t even want to give it to the cleaner... Not after last summer. So if someone did break in, we need to file a report before we leave.      Oh, you’re not serious. It’s just a holiday home, right? D’you think it’s worth the hassle? We spend most of the time arguing about who put the breakfast on the fire or if this happened. Honestly... I’m just glad the kids didn’t wake up to any of it.      Mummy, why was Daddy snoring so much?      Because he went to bed with your pyjamas and didn’t even real... Oh, we’ll talk about it later, love. Go on then, off you go. Back to your drawing of the house with the extra room.      Can I have a kitchen in there as well? Silly question, right? No, I’m serious, can I?      Why not. If we’re arguing about the house, we might as well build you each a dream extension. So Florence wants a double bedroom and a room where she can ballet dance in because it’s about five square feet. Tom wants a bouncy castle wall and a climbing frame.      Stop copying her. Not that I mind the dancing, but we are in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom, semi-rustic holiday home — not a London mansion. Though...      Oh, I know. I was just about to say, I did stick the key back in the drawer after I gave it to you. And I’m 90% sure the door was locked. I even set the timer on my phone.      Then go and check the hallway light if you’re so sure you locked it.      I will. But in the meantime, let’s finish your drawings. Tom, I’m planning to fill your imaginary room with one gigantic lava lamp and 500 books, all to do with dinosaurs.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, having to talk about grant proposals in between real coffees... What's the point of having Italian coffee unless you actually  drink  it?      Aye, cannae argue with that—  Llyfrau yn fyw ar y een  , mind you, I meant to say, 'Books on the go', not 'Llyfrau yn fyw ar y een'—      No, no, go on, I think it’s a fine saying anyway. "Books on the run"—a bit of a misrendering, but still.      Well, as long as the department still lets us write in Welsh on the grant forms, I’m all for eccentricities.      Oh, yes, they do, and I think it helps us stand out. Had a German reviewer laugh at it last month, but then he funded us anyway.      Blooming charmer, then. You sorted the funding for the qubit project yet?      Nearer, yes. But I’ve had to write three versions—academic, arts council and water company. Forgive me, but there was something in the guidance that suggested we should mention the Hadron Collider.      Oh, right, because it's  exactly  the same as quantum computing—      If we tell them we're using similar principles, they seem to give someone at CERN a warm glow. All they want is to fund something that gives a  glance  of particle physics.      I see—I see  exactly . Meanwhile, at home, I've been trying to decorate the living room without the help of a decorator. It's like solving a quantum mechanics problem with a plug and a chair.      Ah yes, ‘cos nothing says "poised academic" like putting a chair on the floor with a red bow round it.      Cynical, but fair. My daughter says it looks as if I've redecorated in space. 'Cos of the shiny spots from the mismatched lights.      You know, it's a room with atmosphere—  environmental   atmosphere. I could see a commission for one of those posters on the wall. I had a student last week who wrote about quantum particles emerging from virtual environmental voids.      You mean after putting a tea towel on the wall like it was a manifesto?      Precisely. A modern art installation. You could go all conceptual with that room. "The Entanglement of Water and Mica"—title alone could get you a grant for curtain design.      I’ll scribble it down then, just in case. Speaking of water—did you ever sort out that water company who kept cutting off your line?

Right, I just wanted to get through the sorting of LEGO before we go to bed—the characters need to go back in their boxes, or they're going to be all mixed up again by tomorrow. It’s a mad hatter’s box of bits and pieces in there as it is.      But I want the magical wands from the castle for my   Voldemort collection  .      That’s only from  Harry Potter , so this goes back here. Oh, and what   Easter chocolate   do we need to be moving before it melts in the bottom of the toy box again?      Can I go to the cinema with you next week to see the new  Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles  movie?      Ugh, boys and their turtles.      Hey, I think Leonardo has swirly eyes like you, Phoebe! Wait… does he?      Not quite, Leo, and no, you’re not going to the cinema to see   turtles  . You’re nine now, so you need to start watching more  grown-up  things—like  The Simpsons.  You both like that, don’t you?      Only watching it during  Simpsons  night at Bedtime Stories Club – but it’s better than my last school trip because they had  hot dogs .      Ugh, gross. I want to go back to   Granny’s house   next weekend. She put in new wallpaper in the kitchen. It looks like blue sky with white clouds. It made me want to have a cartoon tea party and be an actual  knight .      I did offer her help with the   renovations  , but she wouldn’t have it. "I’ve lived here since you were born," she said. "It’s  my  house, and I like things the way they are—or nearly do." Said she's still waiting for me to sort the meter box and the dodgy light switch.      I sort things out. I had a  proper  plan of whose LEGO space weapons were whose. I sorted them by colour and character and then whose castle exploded first.      That’s the best way to go—  systematic sorting   like Granny does with her jam jars.      Hopefully, you'll apply that same discipline to your   homework   and not just your LEGO. Speaking of which, girls, we’d better start wrapping up or we won’t be making it to the  Harry Potter  sleepover next weekend at Aunty Claire’s. I’ve been told to make sure they come  well-sorted  and ready for magic, casting spells and chocolate frogs.

Oh my God, you're back! You've been gone ages. I was starting to think you’d joined a cult or something!      Haha! Longer than I intended, honestly. Got stuck in Leeds with a train delay, and then my nan picked me up and wouldn’t stop talking about her cat’s passive-aggressive phase. I didn’t know cats could be passive-aggressive.      Oh no! That sounds  exactly  like your nan. Imagine me, pulling that off. "Don’t be ridiculous, Sprockett, it’s not  my  fault you can’t sit on the table."      That’s harsh, but fair. Sprockett  did  knock my mug off the table and left paw prints in my tea. So, who won the World Cup while I was away? Did someone finally beat Australia in cricket?      Australia won again, obviously. Like everyone knew it was in Australia and they’d be the finals. No drama, no surprise. England was a bit hot, but still nothing to write home about.      Yawn. I never get into cricket. Did anything interesting happen? Did anyone get married? Die? Find a new ex-boyfriend?      No marriages – but Laura  did  break up with Mitchell because he stole her Netflix password. Again. And don’t even start with the whole  who  I’m dating now!      Oh someone  is  dating someone. Spill it! Is it the one from the magazine launch with the ridiculous handwriting? The one who couldn’t spell  ‘prioritise’ ?      I blocked that one after he tried to gift me Renaissance Faire entry as an apology. "Soulstice! Magical energy!" Not my thing. But no, the new one is… Ethan. Works in finance. Poetic soul trapped in an Excel spreadsheet.      Okay. Finance blokes are all scientists of spreadsheets. But you like him?      He  is  being nice, which always wins me over. He brought me English truffles last week – like the  real  kind, not truffle薯片. That was a go-to-place hug.      Okay, respect. Truffles tick the box. You know I tried to get my brother to stop eating all his meals in the car. The man eats on the stairs, in the hallway, heck, I even caught him eating a sandwich on the Xbox.      On the Xbox? I’m not entirely surprised. I think he's got a new ringtone now. It's the sound of me sighing.      So, work? You still having that meeting with the team on Movember? C’mon, you can’t cancel again.

Right then, John, don't be slouching in that armchair like it's your last day on Earth. You've got a job to do today, don’t you?      Aw, Grandpa… can’t I just have ten more minutes?      Haha, eeny meeny miney moe, you got picked! Ay, John's all growed up a bit but still got the same cheek as when he was a toddler. Still thinks he can charm us into letting him do nothing.      Oh aye, he always was a chip off the old block, that one. Mary, when he was a baby he once tried to drink paint. "If it’s red, it must be juice!" So he said. Well, not in so many words, obviously!      Oh, don’t go sparking that again, Jack. Poor John nearly had breakfast with a doctor if I recall.      Oh come on, you’re not still mad about that?! It’s not like I liked it, I was  six !      Well, listen老爷 — I mean John — your job today is to help me and Joan clear out the attic. It’s a proper mess up there, and we all know what happened last time – Matey here got a sneaky and ended up buried in a huge pile of old newspapers and donkey rugs.      I was ten! And I found the secret tin of old photos. The one with Nana in a flapper dress? It was amazing.      Oh, don’t mind the mess, love. The attic’s like a treasure trove, really. We nearly did open a museum up there the other week – had the hall full of dusty vibes and a chair that was falling apart.      Right, but listen up, John. Before you go ‘treasure hunting’ again, your grandpa and I need that space cleared for the charity donation box. If you see anything worth keeping, pop it in the little red box. We’ll talk about it over Sunday tea.      Is that the red one by the door with “Estate Sale” written on it in marker?      That’s the goody bin, yes! Got your mum’s old poetry books in there, your grandpa’s old pair of socks he wore in the seventies, your great-aunt’s saxophone that made the whole family howl one night at the tea shop, and… well, let’s not list it all or you’ll be walking up there with a suitcase.      Fair enough. Can I get a job in the next life as a treasure hunter, by the way?

Right, so today we're going to talk about a very special place, okay? Do you know where Great Ormond Street is, darling?      I think it's a hospital?      Exactly! You're so clever. It's a hospital for children in London. Some of the characters from  Peter Pan  were first written about by a doctor who worked there — Sir James Barrie.      Who's Peter Pan?      Oh, he's a magical little boy who never grows up! He lives in a place called Neverland.      Is it like a fairyland?      Even better! In Neverland, there are fairies, like Tinker Bell, pirates, and mermaids. And boys can go to sleep in their beds at night and fly off in the morning to Neverland with Peter!      Wait… does he really fly?      Well, not with airplanes or anything — he uses fairy dust! You sprinkle a little bit over yourself and  poof , you can fly.      Can I get some fairy dust?      Maybe one day when you're feeling properly magical. But right now, it’s all from the movies. Let’s talk about the ones we saw recently, okay? The one with Johnny Depp as Captain Hook — don’t you remember?      Ooh, the one with the hook hand!      That’s Captain Hook! He’s the bad guy who wants to catch Peter Pan.      Yes, and then there’s another film called  Pan  which is a bit older and shows how Peter Pan became the leader of the Lost Boys.      I liked the one where they had to fight the pirates.      And the one with Tinker Bell, where she helps Peter?      Exactly. Tinker Bell is one of the most famous fairies in all of fiction. She helps Peter build his little house in the treetops and she flies around sprite-like doing magical things.      I saw a show about Tinker Bell once… there were loads of lights and colours!      That sounds like  Tinker Bell and the Lost Heir  — it was a really special show they do at Great Ormond Street Hospital. They use lights and puppets and music to tell the story.      Are we going to see it?      Maybe next time we’re in London, if we can get tickets! It’s a very magical way to celebrate the hospital and help kids who are staying there.      Can I be Peter Pan?      You could be Peter Pan, or Tinker Bell, or Captain Hook… just as long as you're adventurous!

Rather annoying driving up from Taunton on a Sunday morning. I blame the internet traffic, even when it’s got nothing to do with it. Still, at least we’re getting there.      It’s funny to think we used to live in that little house near Exeter — do you remember? The place with the creaky floorboards and the garden that looked more like a swamp after a rainy day.      Oh I do, I swear we used to find frogs in the sitting room! And Mark was so proud of that old outside light he fixed with garden wire and what looked like three different kinds of batteries.      You know, that place was our first proper home after I left the last job in Southampton. Probably the only place I ever liked with less than one sad relative living in it. Living with everyone was far too much for me.      I miss some of the drive in the mornings. I know it was 45 minutes to the school each way, but I actually liked the silence—especially when it was raining and the world just slowed down. I don’t get quite the same kind of time anymore.      Funny you should mention that. I’ve been asleep from about 8 most days – Mate’s been looking after the cat and the post and all that. I miss my tea time.      You know what I miss? When we used to live in the old cottage by the lagoon. It was such a calm spot. It felt like we had a bit of everything — the sea nearby, the forest for walks and not too many noisy neighbours.      I did like that place. I think you picked the best one of the lot. Not much bigger than a boot, but it had charm. I’d take it over the flat in Taunton any day.      Speaking of places — did you get the Christmas plans sorted yet? You told me you were thinking of a house-warming party for when you sort out the flat in Exeter. I’ll come of course—though only with lunches delivered ahead of time, I’ve got enough lesson plans as it is.      Of course you will. But it’s more of a thank you-do for helping Mark line the walls without nails. He’s done a blooming good job, your lot. It’ll be something like Christmas and a small conference all in one.

Rather a lot of people taking a rest today, aren't they? I was just down by the sheds and saw quite the bunch of folk sitting about on the benches. I suppose it's the heat, eh?      Aye, the sun’s as hot as a kitchen range today. Me old een don’t like heat as much as they used to. Still, better to sit and chat than be aching by the evening, if you know what I mean. So, are you one of the volunteers pulling in to help with the track works? Bit of a posh-looking woman for the sort of work I’d imagine, mind you.      I used to run a gallery and antique shop in Frome well into my sixties. Still love a bit of restoring and restoring people’s bits and bobs, if you catch me drift. The track work? Well, you do for the village and all. Helps when you’ve been gone a while and want to feel useful in your old age, you know?      Aye, I get that. I spent thirty years manning accommodation for a big society down in Birmingham. Used to be in charge of landings as they called em—outhouses, hostels, flats. These days, I’m nearer to a domestic gardener than a manager, if I'm lucky.      Well, I imagine the skills come in handy. It’s not all daisies and shrubberies, is it? Though I’d say the people skills helped most in your job—placing folk in the right places and all. I had a customer once who had the fury of ten red-coated guards and she wanted a Ming vase  refurbished . You try calming about forty pounds of pure indignation.      Oh I had me own share of rowdy types. One woman I put in a self-contained flat near Wolverhampton—didn’t like ‘cos the lav didn’t flush well. Complained for six weeks straight. Took a whole bottle of something ‘espresso’ to get her smiling again. You mustn’t stick about to such as her. Though I’ve seen worse. My late wife—God rest her soul—was quite the character. Used to tell me I was a ‘village green man with a clipboard goonie’.      Well, you don’t expect her to be smiling when her lav’s refusing to do its job properly. But your wife sounds like the sort who knew how to manage a man and a home, both.

So do you know what’s on the agenda for tomorrow, Nan? I know it’s supposed to be like a proper countryside tour, but I’m not sure yet. I’ve asked a few times, but I can never follow half of what he says over the phone—some posh twerp with a RP accent and all the vowels stretched out like chewing gum.      Oh, don't be so dramatic, Rose. It’s Stephen, your old uncle’s son, right? And yes, he is a bit of a stiff upper lip type, but he doesn’t mean it, poor dear. Anyway, what I heard is that it will mostly be walking—historic sites, gardens and such, and a little picnic in the middle of the day. You’ll love it, I’m sure. Green fields, birds, the occasional sheep. He even mentioned a local vineyard for the wine tasting in the afternoon!      A vineyard in Devon? That’s not a bit out of place? I didn’t think people grew vines in the UK besides the odd patch in Cornwall. Or maybe that’s just one of those organic farm tourism scams?      You don’t know as much as you think. They’ve been doing it in England for years, love. The climate’s changed a bit, and the South – especially down here – has become quite warm, relatively speaking. There’s a fair few vineyards in the area now. Seems like a nice surprise to me.      Well, if this is true, then I’ll certainly try not to knock a glass over and spill it on one of his ridiculous walking jackets. So, what else? Any tea stops or something? I don’t do "glamping” about with no kettle.      Oh, of course. Both mornings and afternoons—he even said there would be scones and digestive biscuits. No clotted cream, mind, but that’s just Stephen for you. All about the dry crumpet and no nonsense. I’ll bring something fresh, though. Perhaps I’ll make you a little cake or something while you're gone—tomorrow after lunch. It’s always been your special day, hasn't it?      That's you trying to butter me up by giving me the 'memory lane goody bag' routine again, isn’t it?      Is it working? You’ll be the judge when you come back. But seriously, you should be proud—you made it to the conference and decided to take a holiday after all.

So did you watch the Euros last night? That match between England and the Netherlands was cracker.      No, I couldn't make it—I was at a meeting. But I heard it was intense. Did Kane score again?      Yeah, he did. Got two of them. Proper show. I’m just sore I didn’t get to see it all on TV with my cousin. Akeem was over earlier, too. His uncle brought round a load of jerk chicken and rice. You haven’t tasted it like that before. Didn’t even need the hot sauce.      Akeem’s still bringing his cousins over every week, then? Still working on that project in the city, is he?      Yeah, he’s on the verge of moving up, he says. If he gets that promotion, he’ll be earning a fortune. He’s always talking about investing or expanding this Caribbean restaurant he’s got in his head. I keep telling him to just get some proper accounts done first so people know he’s serious.      Haha, yeah, sounds familiar. I remember talking with your uncle about starting something similar back when I first moved over. Good thing I stuck with what I knew. Ten years of managing hotels is no small thing.      Nah, it really ain’t. You’ve done good, man. You know what? Earlier, I checked my bank and there’s that transfer from my sister in Bristol.      Oh yeah? That the one for the laptop you needed?      Yeah, and some extra cash she sent for the flat. She’s been helping out since I started uni. She’s a saint, really.      She’s a good’un. Makes you wonder why she’s barely left the house. You up for going to the market this weekend for some baked macaroni or something? I know you’ve been missing the good stuff.      Hell yeah, that sounds brilliant. You know I could stick to one meal and not touch anything else. Even if it’s just lunches, I miss the whistles and the gossip and the smiles when you remember a relative from ten years back.      That’s the life, mate. If you ask me, family is the only bonus of living between continents.      Speak your truth. Shawna called me about her brother, too—got a job at that bar down the road. You should meet him sometime. He’s got a hell of a passion for cricket, even though I’m not entirely sure he knows the rules yet.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the side doors, do you?      Well if you got the ticket, they can’t really stop you love. Not at their age anyway. They’d probably fall over before they tried to stop you.      Oh come on, don’t be like that Margot. I’m with you, Stan. Tickets are tickets.      Aye Aye, but I’m more interested in the top of the thing. It was quite a reasonable road journey wasn’t it, Reg? Not like the motorway, but still, under the hour.      Yeah, made a bit of a stop at the pub near Wellesbourne for a bit of turkey and mash. Excellent pie. You’d like it, Stan – proper East Midlands fare.      I’ll be the judge of that. I was raised on Norfolk pie – it doesn’t come cheaper than that!      Oh Stan, don’t be so picky. You ate the puff pastry and the tin. Good for you.      Well, I had some of it, Margot. Not all of it. But still, I tell you, since I got this bad leg, I’ve got to take it easy. No more running about after the buses or chasing trains. I’m still limping off the medication today.      Mate, you’ve been saying that for years. Last time you said that, you were chasing after a milk float in Costessey. Just because it was a bit slow for your liking.      Reg, mind your tongue. It’s not his fault the world’s gone all mechanical now. He likes about Yorkshire as much as he does about standing on the moon.      I’ve been there! Going to that place with the big hills and the rocks up York way. Not just a ‘moon’ story like some people.      Aye, me granddad took me on the bus as a kid. I tried to do a little bit there myself – stayed at one of them yellow youth hostels. No space heaters, but we were young and didn’t care.      Still, I did a nice travel course once on the School of Life. They said that life improvements start with a journey – metaphorically.      Oh I don’t know, I think sometimes it’s your legs that make the improvement. Or stop it!      Well, you’ve got us with the Skype now to keep you company. Still better than sitting at home on your own every evening counting the pills, Stan.

So did you manage to sort out those flights to Barcelona? I’ve been trying for hours and it’s like a proper game of wits with the booking system.      Erm, yeah, I thought I did. I booked two economy flights for us on the 10th, but it’s all depending on if the weather is bad on the 9th. My cousin wanted to come with us but obviously Aneurin’s got that meeting and I’m not going to let her travel without a reasonable contingency plan!      Oh right, your cousin’s the one with the dodgy ankles, is it? I mean, I don’t blame you at all, don’t want her in an airport at 5am because of some dodgy weather forecast. But yeah, I’m good for the 10th and I’ll be back for work on the 18th. Got a big breakfast meeting with a client that week.      Oh don’t remind me of meetings! I mean, not that I have one, but I had to give that man in the office coffee, and he immediately started spelling out the impacts of short-term scheduling errors as if I were human capital.      Oh please, we’ve all had that one. The “I want to build a culture of transparency” kind of guy. Honestly, just give him a schedule and a spreadsheet and don’t let him near the phone for a week.      Haha, you’re someone who could just walk in and say: “We are chaotic, and we are proud of it.” Just slap that flag on the noticeboard and be done with it.      Erm, I did once. My line manager was lovely, but she still gave me this “are-you-sure-that-was-professional” look afterwards. I mean it was a  small  print.      Oh, you’re evil. Anyway, let’s forget the workplace horrors. I’m just glad you came over. This chilli looks amazing, by the way. We had to rush as soon as we got off work but it’s been a good evening.      Yeah, it’s been brilliant. I’ve got this travel snack box started—healthy-ish go-to stuff I usually forget about. It’s got trail mix, some dried fruit, and licorice. Sue’s box might have chips and Doritos, but you know how she is.      Yeah, I remember those days, don’t I? True to say, I still have a jar of walking-on-a-bridge-of-cookies in the cupboards just in case.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You used to be able to get a decent bag of sugar for a couple of quid, and now it’s nearly five. I can't be having that.      I feel you, Dad. I’ve been doing a bit of comparison shopping recently. I found a place online where it's a bit cheaper, but the delivery costs are all over the place.      If you're too old to understand online, you just go to the shop like I do and complain to the manager. That's the only way to get the blooming things to listen.      Oh I complain, love. I told them I’d go to the competition across the road, and they dropped the price by ten pence. Tenpence, mind you! D'you think that’s going to help? Half the price of a pack of sausages.      It’s all so frustrating for older people who live on fixed incomes. I try to help Dad online sometimes, but I know he prefers to handle things in person.      That’s just the way I like it. Got as much respect for human beings as you’ve got time for. These shops, they treat you like a little boy who needs to be patted on the head with a sneer and a half-witted smile.      All that “customer service” rhetoric. It's just a front for shoddiness and bad coffee. Who in their right mind offers two types of biscuits in a chipped tin and calls it an experience?      I think the price of everything is tied to the weather in some way. Everything seems about to fall off the back of a lorry these days.      That's true! Going out there in the cold, worrying about whether the wind’s going to take your coat off for you. If I was your age, I’d probably be up at 6 a.m. shoveling all that muck off the drive.      Not to mention the state of our bloody phone bills! Used to be a fiver and it was done. Now it's more than that for calling a relative halfway across the street!      Yeah, mobile companies are getting away with murder. I think I'm going to switch providers again. It always ends up being the same story, though. Buy you in with a discount, then raise the bill and charge you for every tickle of data.

Okay, so we've got this list we're making of our five favourite things for the ‘flatmate mood board’ and I’m stuck on the holiday section. Anyone wanna help me out?      Aye, we do this every week, mind you — well, the food one’s always easy, right? But yeah, holidays are tough 'cos I reckon it depends on your mood.      I think I’d have to say a seaside holiday in County Clare. Just me, my book, and some good coffee from the little shop in Lahinch. The waves crashing in the background... like, I dunno,  chill .      That sounds lovely, but I’m more of a midweek outdoor vibe. I’d pick a national park somewhere, like the Brecon Beacons, and just hike every day. Wildflowers, rivers, and fresh air. Real raw.      I agree with Sorcha — rugged up in the mountains, hiking is my idea of a good time. But when I want to  not  be outdoors? Then it’s definitely a city break in Barcelona. Got some friends there, so it’s like half-party and half-seeing old-school places.      Wait, speaking of food, what's your ideal holiday meal?      Let's just say if I was choosing a dish to eat every day on holiday, it’s a plate of padron peppers with sherry vinegar and some crusty bread — full-on Spanish vibes.      That sounds oddly sour-dog with floring-chilli factor. Not my cup of tea, I’m more about  home-cooking . You know, about five eggs scrambled with a slab of brie and roasted tomatoes — I’d be happy cooking that every morning.      I’m with Nia on the breakfast front. My idea of a perfect day is toast with nut butter and banana, tea that’s strong enough to wash a plate in, and my cat purring on my lap.      Ha, good one. I’d say eggs, but fried in a pan with a little bit of digestive biscuit crushed up with the egg whites — a bit of sweetness and crunch!      So on the animal front, our “favourite pets” question is still in the air. I’m team dog, big time. A big one, like a border collie — I’d be cleaning up stairs and chasing poops for weeks, but yeah, it’s a life worth living.      I’m team cat. I’m not entirely sure I could handle a dog’s energy.

So did you finish that art essay yet?      Not even close. I kept thinking I had heaps of time, but it’s already due next week! How’s yours coming along?      Not bad, honestly, I kind of enjoyed it. I went with a piece about aging—like, how people’s perception of themselves changes as they get older. I wanted to focus on a woman in her sixties starting to paint again after a long time. It felt kind of meaningful, you know?      Yeah, that sounds cool. I was struggling with what to do. I like the idea of blending art and age, but I don’t know where to start.      Start by thinking about what you imagine the future’s like. Ten, twenty, thirty years from now. Like, how do you picture yourself? Or even your grandmum or something.      I guess I just picture everyone still doing their thing, but more tired. Like, older but not, I dunno, less interesting. My nan still plays computer games sometimes—Crossword, maybe Candy Crush? She says it keeps her brain sharp.      Oh, real deadly stuff. Imagine her in a nursing home battling it out over Trivial Pursuit.      Imagine! I mean, I think it’s important to stay interested in stuff as you get older, right? Like, not just hobbies—just having a sense of purpose, even if it feels small.      Yeah. I was thinking about that when I did my essay—how art, or even just creativity, can give people something to hold onto. I guess it’s not just for people about to die or anything. It’s just part of the human experience.      True. I mean, that’s why I’m even doing this degree, partly. I don’t want to stop being creative. I don’t want to wake up when I’m 70 and go, “Oh bloody hell, I used to like art, but I haven’t touched a brush since 2017.”      Exactly! You keep the spark alive. So, do you play games? Because I know you’re not into art that much—maybe that’s your escape?      If by “not much” you mean I don’t enjoy art like you do, yeah. I love games. It’s like another version of planning or problem-solving. Like, strategy in League of Legends or something. Just figuring it out, right? Same with life.      Or writing an essay. Or trying to convince yourself that you’ve done enough revision.

So do you want me to get started on sorting the veggies for the stir-fry or would you rather do it?      Nah, go ahead I’ll get the rice going. Beans or brown rice today?      Beanz! C’mon, it’s been three days—brown rice deserves a place on the menu!      Look, I don’t clean the whole house every day just to have this conversation again, right?      Fair point. We can flip a coin. Heads—beans. Tails—rice. Tails—we talk about your love life.      Harsh. I am still waiting for some kind of fate-altering love, unlike you with your eccentric left-swiper.      Okay, first, he was a   left-swiper   because you added a comment that his cat looked like breakfast, and then he blocked me. Second, I am in no rush. I have five friends who will fawn over me for the rest of my life.      That’s if your bookshelf doesn’t start uprooting people with your energy.      Hey! I might’ve read  The 36-Hour Day  from cover to cover. That does not make me a menace.      True, but the time you nearly picked up Mrs Bell next door under the impression she was one of your Tinder matches—      —was one incident and she was not my type.      Right— “old and adorable”  as you put it. Okay, so where  are  we going for your birthday again? Clubbing? Cabins? Camping?      Honestly? I’ve been thinking maybe just cabby up to somewhere quiet and have a long walk with wine and some decent company. Burgers and bad movies at your place?      Only if the movies include a romantic comedy with  zero  relatable plotlines. You need a reality check.      Right. And you always end up liking the  craziest  characters in the films. The guy who sends a hundred emails and turns up the next day with go-karts on his own?      Okay, Mark was not the norm, I’ll give you that. But sometimes people are your people.      Sure, but he still turned up to my workplace with a birthday cake that was slightly to scale of the Eiffel Tower. That’s not a guy fitting in. That’s a guy setting goals.      I respect the commitment, I’ll say that.      Look, the moral here is, I swear you are as bad with men as I am. You just aren’t ready to admit it.      Oi, I've dated two lectures in the last six months and they’re both quite well.

Rather than going through the seminar outline again, I suppose we should talk about the speaker consent form first. We’d agreed to distribute it to all participants this week, don’t we need their signatures before we start?      Yes, agreed. I had a few queries from the students who’ve booked in on the event list, mostly about the use of their personal info and how the recordings will be used after. I’ve sent a revised version to the admin office to double-check, but it should be fine.      Good. Leeds has got very strict guidelines these days, don’t they? I remember getting frozen out last year for mentioning a participant’s name in a short Facebook post after the seminar. It wasn’t sensitive at all, but the Legal Team got involved.      I had the same issue, Viv! I used a quote from the seminar in an internal newsletter, and the admin highlighted it for "unauthorised disclosure." Now I always double-check for opt-outs and blur any faces in screenshots.      Let's make sure the form includes details on that—tape recording, any transcripts, anonymisation of quotes, and usage in publications or internal reports. We might need to clarify that unless someone object, we will be using material during the seminar and in our follow-up report.      Agreed. I’ll add that it will  only  be shared within the university and not posted publicly without consent. Should I include a ‘tick box’ for those who don’t want their work featured in discussions or illustrations during the session?      Yes, definitely. Some students are very private about their contributions and don’t like their work being used even in a closed context. We can have about five or six walk-ins on the day, so the form needs to be clear and not too long—heaven forbid another seminar that takes forty minutes just to get a reminder email out to the 12 guests who didn’t show up.      Laughs. Let’s move on to the content structure quickly. Sarah, I loved your section on regional communication styles. We could run into time overruns there if people ask detailed questions. Do you plan a Q&A after your introductory part, or is it designed for reflection via the group activities?      I go straight into the case study after the intro, using real trade examples—Germany to China, Spain to Japan.

Rather annoying day today, wasn't it? That meeting dragged on far longer than it needed to.      I know, it was like they thought we all had an infinite amount of time! And I was trying to get some stuff done before the weekend.      Me too. I had to cancel my lunch plans with the postdocs just to stay and finish all the admin on the paper. Honestly, I think policy changes in this department are designed to see how much tea we can drink while sitting in one meeting.      It reminds me of the first week I got here. I thought, "Okay, this is going to be short and sweet, right?" Then I ended up in the meeting from 9 until 4 and left so hungry I ate three fried eggs from the canteen and a dumpling in the first 10 minutes of getting home.      Oh yeah, I remember that. You told me in your accent that dumpling was "the best thing you'd ever eaten in the last 38 years". It was so over the top, I had to check if you'd written it in your notes.      It was deadly serious. I’ve never tasted anything so golden, so rhythmical, so humble and yet so proud – it was a dumpling, not least, because it was trying hard.      You’re lucky you don't get credit for being insulted at your own sense of taste in food.      I would take it. It counts for something. I think what really bugs me is that meeting after meeting, and still no clarity on the funding for our new project. We’ve been about it for months now.      Exactly! We were told mid-year it would be sorted. Now it’s nearly December and I’m still explaining to students who are investing their time, “No, the funding isn't certain yet. Sorry about that.” And they just nod as if they expect it. Do they expect this? Do they think we all live like this?      I think being academically British comes with a nuanced understanding that “horses for courses” can also mean, “Hey, you’re not in charge of the money.” It's noble really, in a tragic sort of way.      Yeah, but enough about work. How’s the house coming on? I saw some of the latest photos you sent. That corner of the kitchen looks absolutely pokey.      True, but we made some space for the sofa bed.

So did you try the meatballs I made last night? I followed the recipe from our nan’s cookery book, and I think she’d be proud.      Yeah, they were actually really good! I didn’t expect that from a batch of leftovers. You really nailed it.      Thanks, I’m glad you liked them. I was just thinking—this book is a bit of a treasure, but I wish more people were into cooking like this. I’ve noticed some of my students have never seen a chopping board before.      That’s crazy. I mean, I grew up around food. Nan and Pop always made everything from scratch, and now people just rely on apps and microwave meals. I’ve even heard talk at work about automated kitchens replacing chefs.      Oh no, not another world dominated by robots. I was already worried about them taking over breakfast, but now dinner? I mean, can a robot make a decent Sunday roast?      Honestly, I don’t see the appeal. I’d rather help Mum with the garden, get some herbs growing, maybe even start that urban farming thing she’s always on about. It’s better for the planet plus we’d be saving on food waste.      True, and it’s not often I see curriculum pushing for that kind of skill these days. I’ve been trying to get my year 8’s to do some practical cooking, but it’s like they’ve never peeled a potato in their lives. Let alone trying to explain a dowry system when we do an arranged marriage project—there are blank stares and some strange questions.      Yeah, there’s a gap about how we prepare kids for the real world. I still remember visiting your job shadow day in sixth form and not knowing how to write an actual cover letter. You should write a book— How to Run a Life  or something.      A bit dramatic, but the system is holding some kids back. There used to be more practical work experience opportunities, but a lot of industries seem  closed off  now.      Yeah, it’s funny how things change. Once it was just rail and steel around here, and now the biggest employer is go-kart centres and cafes.      True, but even in the private industries, they could do more to support apprenticeships. Maybe if we had more people planting seeds in the younger generation, like our grandparents did, those jobs wouldn’t dry up as fast.

Rather annoying that the pasta’s still not cooked. Thought six minutes would be enough.      Well, I’ll take no notice of that, shall I? Just stared at the clock for a whole minute before starting it. You know the rules.      Yeah, yeah. I just wanted to talk about the email I got this morning. From my sister.      Oh, not too dramatic, I hope. Last week she was going on about how her new yoga instructor is a reformed gang member from the East End.      No, not that dramatic. It was more . . . bittersweet, I suppose. She said my dad rang and they had one of his “off days.”      Oh. I’m sorry to hear that. He was very sad in the last visit. I remember how he forgot the cat’s name. Poor George—Charlie now?      Yeah, and he’s started calling my stepmother, “My ex-wife.” And then he smiles like he’s shared a conspiracy with the rest of us.      I know. It’s heart-breaking. But grief and dementia, it complicates everything. At least he still remembers me, I think.      Mate. I often wonder if he still remembers that time we went up to the pub and nearly set off the fire alarm with the tea.      That was a good one. You said it was an emergency—your tea was getting cold. It just spilled over because the kettle was hotter than the fire alarm threshold or something.      That’s your version, love. He nearly flammable-danced off the ceiling. But the thing is, he’s still trying. To be part of the family. To remember.      And that’s what matters. That’s more than many people can say.      I suppose. I’ve also been thinking about how all of this changes the dynamic at home. You know, when one parent’s gone and the other’s being gently taken from us.      It’s the same with your mum. Even though she’s still around, it’s like the house is slowly gothic-ing on us.      Gothic-ing? Is that a new phrase? You need to go further with that. Publish it your next academic paper. “Homes in Late Life: A Gothic Interpretation of Domestic Atmosphere.”      I’ll talk to the editor over tea. Speaking of, do you want that basil pesto? The store-bought one or shall we try my weird chilli-garlic mash?      Pesto’s fine.

Rather skip the newfit and go to the seashore. A few people think it would be a pitty, but I always preferred the old one.      Oh, you mean the old seafront? Not quite as pretty, I'd say. But yes, the footpaths were good and all the little fish and chips shops with the proper vinegar and mushy peas. Proper meals they were.      Ay, that's all changed now. Not since I started going there in '81. All the shops gone. Turned into more of a hotel area. You don’t get the same sort of atmosphere these days—too posh, in my opinion.      It’s a bit too clean, you know. When I was young, there was always someone selling lucky charms on the seafront. If you turned your back for a second, they’d try to pin something on you—costumes and bric-a-brac for tourists.      Mmm, you didn’t have to worry about that when I was your age—there was no one, apart from the occasional sailor looking for something to wear with his sailor hat to impress the lassies back home.      I suppose things do change, but I find it sad when the memories of a place just disappear, like houses these days. I’ve seen too many people move out of their family homes and have to rely on the council or some charity to find a new place. They just don’t have the money.      That’s the sour truth of it all. Not just houses, but the way life comes down on you like a house of cards when there’s a bit about money. My cousin lost the entire bungalow she had all her life—everything from a house full of books to her grandfather’s old clock. She couldn't even take the bits that mattered most, ‘cos they took it for fines. All over some rent arrears.      Bless her. Sounds like a bit of a struggle. You’d think the system would give people a bit of leeway. Even if they couldn’t pay, a little more time—some consideration, you know?      You're right. But the way things go nowadays, it’s all about rules and charges. Just the other day, I had to pay a fee because I borrowed a book from the library and returned it a week late. That book cost me 30p, mind you, and now I’m paying 50 quid?

So did you go into Boots last week? I needed a new glue for my fake lashes and they had that one with the white tip—remember the one you recommended?      Oh yes! The one that doesn’t run or dry out the skin. It says "smudge-proof" on the packet and it really does last. I’ve been using it for over a month now.      That’s exactly what I needed. I tried this other brand last week and it was  horrible . Looked great in the ad, smelled like boot leather and flaked halfway through the day. My friend saw me and asked if I’d  plastered  them on!      Ha, that’s not the first time I’ve heard that. I think it’s one of those cases where the brand sounds fancy, but the product is not. I’m just glad you switched back to the old one. Your lashes look natural—maybe I need a new pair after I run out.      You could always borrow mine if you want to try them. I’ve got that peachy one with subtle shimmer—personally I think it takes years off if you do your eyes to match. Paired with a good manicure, of course.      Oh, speaking of—I’ve been neglecting my nails completely with all this work and stuff. I had a huge backlog of Royal Mail parcels to process and now my hands look like I’ve been picking through bin bags.      You work too hard. Why don’t you book a mani-pedi one afternoon? I know this really cute nail bar near me. It’s got a tea room and they do  amazing  OPI colors.      That does sound perfect. I just haven’t had time to get out much lately. My sister is coming round this weekend and I promised her a day out in Torquay, so maybe I can squeeze in a beauty bit before that.      Torquay is a great place for it. We could meet there too if you want—some shopping, maybe even a bit of lunch at one of those cafes by the sea. I heard the new bistro by the marina has  amazing  vegan options.      Yeah, go on then. It’ll be nice to get out and do something other than line up stamping machines and postcards in box number four. I might even get a hat to match the new nails.

So did you go up to the World Museum last week? I was promising me mam I would take 'er when we was in Liverpool one day. Otherwise she’d have my balls for not taking 'er yet.      Aye, went up there last Thursday. Got stuck in traffic trying to park een the car park, of course. It was like   5 quid   for an hour of parking. You’ve got to be joking me.      No bleedin' way! That’s worse than the one at the   Mersey Retail Park  . Although, I still say that car park’s like a Russian riddle—ain’t no way me finding the right exit in less than ten mins.      Aye, I swear the left’s on the right there or somethin’. D’you know, I think the world museum’s got an app now to tell you where the car parks is—cost me an extra quid for a subscription in advance. Blooming mad!      No way man. Should have told me I woulda shared it. I could’ve got me mam in and out for less!      Here’s the thing though, once we got in, it was   worth it  . We did a little workshop on local history. My mam was into it, I was, like, barely paying attention but she was into it. She picked up a   calendar for the museum gift shop   and said it’s for the mantel.      That’s a good buy. I was thinking of getting one for me flat. Bit Christmas-y looking at it now, though. Hey, what about you and   that future plan   of yours? I about forgot you were applying for the   Master's in Social Work  , yeah?      Oh aye, that. Got an interview next week. I was invited in to do a day at   Liverpool Cathedral  ’s outreach program. Said they want people with empathy, motivation, initiative—loads of bloody buzzwords.      Aye, I get it. You good at   answering academicky questions   with lunches of sandwiches and biscuits? That’s how I do it in teaching interviews—  bribery by snack  .      That works man. I’ll take notes. Just don’t expect me to bring in licorice. I tried that once—  everyone left due to allergic reactions.        You and your bloody licorice. I swear I’ll not trust anything with more than three syllables from you now.      Fair point. You know my dog’s got a   new chew toy  , by the way.

So did you talk to him last night?      No, it’s been so hard... I don’t want to start something now because he’s already got a life with the kids, and I don’t see how we can make this work in the long run.      I understand that. But I meant more about the idea of saying he’s not the dad… not with a capital D, but just to me. I mean, I’m so emotionally attached, but what about practically?      I don’t know. I just want to keep it calm and not upset the kids more than they already are. I don’t want them to think I don’t like their dad or that they have to take sides. I’m just left in the middle of everything, and I feel like I can’t pick and I can’t choose.      Yeah, it’s hard when you’re not actually the parent in law, or even in the picture long-term. I mean, we talked about this before—about the whole idea of step-parenting and what that really means. I get that some people are just really hands-on and some aren’t. But you’re not even in the same category as a step-parent—it’s different because you’re not in it for life.      True. I’m still figuring out if I’m independent enough or if I’m trying too hard to be something I’m not. I don’t want to be the angry woman who's just someone else in their lives. But I also can’t ignore the fact that I care a lot—more than I ever imagined.      I think independence is more about knowing when to step in and about knowing your place. You don’t have to control the situation, but you should be there for them and not feel sorry for yourself. I mean, it’s a tough one. You have your own life to manage, and your own feelings toward their dad, their mom, and them. You can’t expect any of them to adjust fully to that.      That’s really good advice. I just feel like I’m always trying to find the right balance. If I do too much, it looks like I’m replacing something. If I do too little, I look like I don’t care. I want to be a real friend to them, not just the “me-to-be” person.

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode about Margaret’s breakdown was just cringey as hell.      Oh God, I did. I can't say I found it particularly realistic, though. Margaret with a breakdown over the Queen not being frightened by motor cars? Come on. She’s not exactly subtle, is she?      Ay! But I wanted to see it cos I’ve been listing stuff on Pinterest for my birthday this year, weirdly. I thought I'd go vintage glamour. Know what I mean? Like, Margaret style, even if she was a bit unhinged.      Lakelands? Classic Margaret, then. You know, I’ve been trying to get Myra and Simon to come up for my birthday. It’s back in September, if I survive the rest of this year.      Blimey, aren’t you working yourself hard? What with the PhD and this research gig, you’d be lucky to have time for five minutes in the pub, let alone planning a party.      It helps that I do both, luv. I’m researching crop impacts in East Africa, but as a side hustle I also do stats for uni modules. Otherwise I’d have no idea how to pay for all this “vintage glamour”?      Haha, yeah, but imagine the Pinterest board. “Margaret’s Little Black Dress” next to a diagram of rainfall projections. You’d be the most tragic PhD student someone’s ever seen.      That's the plan. I've already got Myra helping—she's been Pinteresting up a storm. Made a whole board for decorations, and there’s a theme about cosmic birthday cakes. I think she’s just trying to avoid watching The Crown.      That sounds brilliant. I know Myra and Simon moved out to Cheltenham last month. Burgers and badgers, luv. I miss them. I’m trying to get them round for something soon, but it’s always someone being too busy or too tired. We’re such good friends and such bad at doing anything fun.      It’s the classic "friendship-phase of work". Still, maybe after my birthday we’ll drag the lot of us go out? I know Myra misses our pub quiz nights.      Oh yeah, I was always the one who kept everyone from losing due to my general knowledge. “Wimbledon” question? I knew the answer was “championships” even when it was just “Wimby” on the screen.      True story. You were my secret weapon back at the uni quiz nights.

Rather skip the newfitting eh?      Aye, just stick with the old pendants we got in here. They're working fine, eh? Not like we've got time to fiddle with them. Not with us looking at houses all week.      I don’t een want to spend a fortune on a new one, but I reckon something nicer wouldn't go amiss. Maybe something with a bit of style? Something from that booth-style lot we saw on eBay last week?      Oh, the one with the brass chase-lights? That looked a right show-off lot to me. Still, if you fancy it, I ain't grumbling. Just don’t want us spending what’s left of the house-search budget on fancy tongs for the ceiling, innit?      Easier said than done, love. It's not about the money — it’s about, you know, thinking ahead. When we move into a new place, I’d like it to feel like ours right away. Can’t have the old ones from the estate taking over the whole vibe, can we?      Aye, well said. But let's not get started on redecorating the next house before we’ve even got one on paper. How many have we looked at?      Far too many. That one on Rightmove with the balcony nearly had me, but then the phone’s been dodgy and the kitchen’s worse. The one in Whitehaven had a garden and everything!      Aye, gardens are a luxury. Mind you, the one near Penrith had a double garage. That’s where I drew the line — because most people about would live in the garage trying to flog their cars.      Honestly, half of them look like they were built in the last housing crisis. Still, I like the idea of a bigger place. Something quiet, no kids about — just us. And maybe a decent Wi-Fi signal for when I’m transcribing.      You’d need your telly to work as well. Though I’ve seen worse. There was that one with the “feature wall” made of red paint and regret.      Ugh! Don’t even remind me. But I suppose it’s all trial and error. I think I’ll just tick off the ones I genuinely like and send you the links.      So we don’t get lost in the madness? Sounds good. As long as the next house has new light fitting space, we can have a proper debate.

So did you talk to the manager about the request for more support at the care home, Jane?      I did yes. I’m just not sure it’ll do any good. He said he understands, but with the budget they have and the staff shortages... well, you know how it is.      It’s the same everywhere. I’ve just applied for another job with a domiciliary care company too. I’m doing this one, part-time, but I’m not sure how much it’s going to last.      That’s the problem with underfunded services like this. We’re juggling too much. I work 12-hour shifts, and some days I come home and still have to feed my cat and pay the bills. Ten minutes, Jane – I need to check on the milk I left on the stove.      Cats are better than breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been thinking of getting one too, but my son keeps reminding me I have no time to look after anything. But he’s at university now, so maybe I could manage, don’t you think?      A cat would probably be better company than some of my co-workers. Honestly, sometimes I feel like we’re in a soap opera. One of them – Angela – keeps coming in late, and now she’s spreading stories that she gets migraines during shifts. I don’t know what’s worse – the migraine or the lies.      God, people are exhausting. At least you’re not alone with that one. I’ve got nurses who ignore the call bell just to finish smoking a cigarette outside. Can you believe that? I spoke to my manager about about it, and he said the same thing – “understood, Jane” – and nothing changes.      That’s the worrying part. These jobs are emotionally draining. My sister’s planning to retrain in education. Says she doesn’t want to work in care forever. I get where she’s coming from.      You know, I considered being a nurse as well. My GCSE results were good enough, but I just didn’t think I could handle the exams. I’d be terrified of something going wrong and feeling responsible. That pressure must go with the job.      It does, and it really does. It’s not just about the qualifications; it’s about what your head and heart can handle. I used to cope really well, but after two colleagues left so suddenly...

So did I tell you about this new sleep study they did? Apparently, people who get good sleep in the early hours—like between 10 and 12—tend to be more emotionally resilient during the day.      That does kind of make sense, doesn’t it? I always feel like if I sleep past 12, I’m just running on caffeine and desperation by morning.      I think it's got to do with the sleep cycles aligning with what some researchers are calling the 'natural cortisol rhythm.' You know, the whole circadian clock.      Right, I’ve heard of that—our body’s internal clock and all that. Still, I managed about three hours of sleep last night after you kept me up brainstorming this new business idea.      Apologies for that. I just got so excited thinking about the eco-tourism camp we’re planning—off-grid, solar-powered, no phones allowed in the evenings. It’s the complete escape from modern life.      That does sound like paradise, but I worry about people getting lost. I mean, not literally, I suppose, but emotionally. We might be supplying the tent, but someone might go in expecting to find themselves.      That’s the point, isn’t it? No Google Maps, no noise, just starry skies and the crackling of a fire. We want people to reconnect with what it’s like to wander and find their own way.      But what if they don’t like it? I remember when we went camping out in the Lake District a few years back, and you got so turned around in the village near Kendal you ended up about five miles off course eating a chocolate bar from the pocket of a stranger.       chuckles  That was you! I only looked lost so you’d show up. My idea of finding the route into a city is usually involving landmarks, not technology.      Unreliable sources, I know. I tried using you for directions once, and we ended up in a car park behind a launderette for three hours.      At least the chickens took an interest in us.      Ugh, the chickens. That goody-two-shoes farmer chick kept trying to get you to adopt one. You actually almost did, I think.      Only because your insistence on following the “natural order” overwhelmed me. But seriously, we had that incident with the pilot in New Zealand last year, right? Remember that flight over the Southern Alps?

So did you lot see that video of the ginger hamster going mental in the ball?      No, what? Like a normal hamster or one of those funny-coloured ones with a little face?      I saw it! It was like the cutest chaos. The thing was running  so fast  and twitching like it was on something. Classic ginger madness, am I right?      Why’s it ginger? Aren’t they all kind of brown or grey?      Not this one, though, no. Proper fiery red fur, like someone dipped it in Lakelands tomato sauce.      Yeah, and the video had the best caption: “When you’re a ginger and the world is spinning too slow.”      Ha! That’s the truth. Living with ginger people is harder than you think. I live with my sister and this happened last week—she accidentally ate my hair, thanks to the dye job I did to cover up the roots.      You mean you ate her hair—personally?      No, not as in I  ate  it, like, metaphorically. I mean, she  ate it . She put it in her sandwich or some weird thing. True story.      Oh my God, that is the worst thing to ever happen. Silly gingers.      It’s the curse, someone said. That’s why we’re all conspiracy theorists and have weird dietary habits.      Fair enough. So, have you got a ginger at the minute, Loretta?      Nope. My previous hamster, Bertie, had this ginger vibes going on. But he escaped during lockdown. Not sure if it was freedom-seeking or running away from my hair smell, but he never came back.      Did you search?      I got my whole flat dehumidified, just in case there was a crack or something. Nothing. He’s out there somewhere, probably with a bandana and a whiske-burger.      That’s a nice image. A streetwise hamster goon with a ginger afro and a motorbike.      Imagine him trying to explain himself in court: “Officer, your honour, I was just puffing on a kush kush and following the vibes of the universe!”      Is it just me or does this make us all want to get a ginger hamster now?      I was about to say the same thing. Imagine getting one, naming it Darwin, and letting it loose to evolve into a ginger super-bunger before it evolves into a ginger super-die-bunger.      Irresponsible pet parenting: the ginger edition.      I once had a guinea pig called Jimmy.

Right Aaron’s taking New York again. You know what he’s like – always playing it safe with his pawns, and then woh!—he just blasts everyone. Honestly, I've told him ten times “Risk isn’t about playing it safe, it’s about risk!” But nooo, he’s always een-augk  awkwardly mispronounces  “Estonia” as "Eastonia." I’ve taught him worse things—like how to conjugate Spanish verbs, but geography... not quite pulling it off.      Oh come on, it’s called fun. You don’t have to stress about it. I mean, I still say "Khing Khaz" when people ask about Genghis Khan, and I’ve met enough people to know it’s supposed to be "Gen-ee-chee Kawn." I think he turned history into a bit of a farce really. Based on breakfast, no doubt. Curry this early in the morning? The man must have had mad energy.      Honestly, the man was probably over-medicated with Chinese herbs and ate ten-quarters of chocolate for breakfast. I’ve always said if you’re going to invade countries, you need real strength—and that’s happiness, good music, and proper alcohol. Well, from what I’ve seen at my son’s mates’ parties, anyway.      Oh come on, you don’t go to them for the alcohol. You go for the company! Though, let’s be fair, someone at every one of those parties ends up asking me a question like,  “Can you give me a kid?”  And I’m like… no, I’m a teacher! Look, if there’s one thing about being young, it’s the belief that the world can be changed in an afternoon. "We can legally not have another child if you want!" I tell them.  “But that’s just a ‘morning after’ kind of decision,”  they say.      I remember when I was younger I thought talking to someone once meant we were going to get married. As if you had that much faith in doctors and in people with lunches to spare.      Anyway, back to the board. You’re not putting your troops on Sweden by mistake, are you, James? I’ve seen you get so confused trying to read the map, I’m wondering if we should send you an update version. Maybe one with big letters and smells like Christmas?      I’m confused alright, but I’m not scared to say it. I’ve got over thirty years of teaching and I still say I’m not entirely sure if I got that right.

So do you ever just lie awake at night and think, “Have I made a massive mistake coming up to Lancs to go to university?”      Every single night.      Right? I feel like I’ve gone from being at home, like literally two streets away from the sea and now I’m sat in a flat with   57 people   in the building and most of them probably don’t even like me.      Oh come on,   James   likes you. We’ve all seen the way he looks at you when he walks past with his coffee. Secret admirer.      Bull  shit  , the only reason he pretends to like me is because you told him I liked   Harry Styles  .      I did not, I told him you said   Harry Styles screamed   if you played  Fine Line  at full volume when you were 14.      And he believed me. That is 100% not happening. Also, he once said he’d rather date Waterstones than me, and I quote, “cause the shelves don’t make me cry as much.”      Harsh but probably fair. Anyway, it’s not all about boyfriends. What about the future?      Ugh, that makes me stressed. I thought I’d figure out life when I got here, but I’m still no closer to knowing what the hell I’m doing. Who am I gonna be in 10 years?      I dunno, maybe the Prime Minister. Or a   full-time influencer   selling CBD smoothies in Bali.      You’re a   law student  , though. You’re supposed to be all "sparkle and grow your own beets" and then end up as a barrister in £500 suits.      I passed 500 and I still looked like I’d just raided my mum’s charity shop. Law is just a waiting game. Honestly, I’m just holding out for a miracle or a sustained vaccine business with my nan’s face mask enterprise. That happened last year.      Right? Remember when she started sewing masks in her living room with your grandma from Bolton and everyone thought they were pre-ordering   emoji pillow covers   by mistake.      And your dad still hasn’t stopped pestering me for free legal advice because he’s convinced he can “sue someone for selling me dodgy sausages from the corner shop in Falmouth.”      You just need to adopt a baby, Clar, then you’ll finally be purposeful enough to be a solicitor.      Oh yeah, I can see that: me, a 21-year-old lawyer, giving birth on the solicitor's toilet.

So do you get how we’ve gotta do this social issues project for the AQA Global Perspectives exam?      Ugh, I’m so confused. My teacher said it’s about comparing systems and how people live. What do they even want us to do?      We eened to pick a topic and then look at it from different angles. My group did poverty in urban areas. I was gonna do Slough, since this is where I’m from.      Oh, nice. I was thinking maybe do something on consumerism, or like how big companies exploit workers. My cousin works in a factory and says they get paid peanuts to make clothes for supermarkets.      Yeah, I’ve heard about that stuff. It makes you think, right? I mean, we all pick up a hoodie or a bottle of water and don’t think about where it came from. But someone out there probably worked 12 hours for less than a tenner.      Exactly. I told my nan the other day, and she said, “Well, you get what you pay for.” And I’m like, no, that’s not fair. It’s not like they asked to live like that.      Nah, man. It’s just capitalism doing its thing. I read an article that said some kids in Kenya or India have to work just to eat. Like, we’ve got free schools and universities, and we grumble about exam stress.      I know. Makes me wish I did more to help. My friends and I talked about doing a fundraiser for a community project in Margate where I used to live.      That’s a good idea. Have you thought of doing it for here? I know some places round Slough that are trying to support families who live off benefits. You could do something like collecting food or just like volunteering at a shelter.      Maybe. But it’d help if I wasn’t stuck with Foundation tier maths too. You ever get the feeling the system’s stacked against us?      Every damn day. I mean, my dad left when I was young, and my mum does three jobs and still can’t get by. I work part-time at Greggs to help her.      I don’t see how they expect us to concentrate on school when the cost of living’s so high. I mean, me and my broz live together in a flat, just to cut rent.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh? You know what, I was out recording my voice for that website like... What was it, Thursday? And this poor girl down the road comes by with a cup of tea and is like, “Are you speaking the Queen’s English again?” Just like that, as if it’s a joke or something!      Oh I reckon people just don’t have time for a proper sentence these days, do they? If this was back in my day, people would come by and introduce themselves. Not interrupt and make sarcastic comments. Didn’t even get the full story!      I said it was  just  for a podcast. What’s wrong with that? It wasn’t like Myra was doing a Shakespeare recital! She’s got this back problem, see – the physio told her not to be in the garden doing all that heavy digging, but there she is! She doesn’t listen to anyone.      I used to live next door to her as a kid, you know. She had the most beautiful flower beds, but that man of hers, Mr Hedgesperson, he dug up the whole garden two weeks after they moved in and planted like six different types of asparagus. Her joints must have taken it!      You’re telling me – I swear every time I see her she limps more. But she’s the one who walks past me and starts lecturing me about my trousers. ‘Lose a bit of weight and the old legs won’t give in so quickly,’ she said. As if I’ve been  wearing  them all day!      I thought it was chic! I mean, your trousers are fine, aren’t they? I’m the one trying to lose the ten stone I gained over the last decade.      Oh that again. I’ve tried it all – the grapefruit in the morning, ‘Positive energy only’ stuff, even that one where you cut up your clothes into a raft and float on it while saying mantras. I tried it once for a day – sank after an hour and ended up in a Tesco carpark.      That’s what I’ve been doing the past two weeks! I get up, have three slices of toast with marmalade and then run up-and-down our house. Just two steps.      And how's that working out for you?      Well… I have gained flu.      Oh pooh. I tried pilates for a bit – three slots in and I ended up in bed with ice packs and a bag of noodles.

Rather skip the newfit incursions.      Yeah.      We can either rewind and rewatch them or just make more tea I think tea's probably the least bad.      Chai or the oolong you picked up?      Erm the oolong we can both twitch and get warmed if it's not too strong.      Yeah I think that's best this one isn't feeling quite right.      Right. We can just watch the one from yesterday.      Mm right.      Still mostly shots of dead fish and mangy foxes.      Mm.      There's a bit with a squirrel pretending to be a badger.      I think he turned round.      Yeah and then he almost fell down the hole.      Haha yeah he did his ginger bottom went over the edge.      Yeah and then he just sat on the cliff edge and looked like he didn't know what to do next I mean if that land belonged to the squirrel kingdom and the other creatures he would've just banned the others for risking it.      So is that the new one?      Yeah, it's the new series. They're filming in quite a few different places this time.      Mm that's cool.      Oh and they also got a new narrator unfortunately.      Oh no what does he sound like.      Bit posh but like in the wrong posh way.      Ah.      Like the kind of posh that makes you feel like they're rolling their eyes at you and the environment.      Oh no that's not good.      No. I was actually quite tempted to open a tab and just watch something else instead.      I know waiting till the new one finishes to start fresh and then just being like what were they trying with that one.      Yeah he's going to be hard to get used to.      Yeah.      But if you like the visuals and the action bits at least it’s not that bad.      Mm what your dad was saying about how you can get lost in conservation and then one day poachers start thriving and then people forget that they're even worth it.      Yeah I think he was half-right. You can go all in to protecting something for so long and then it's just seen as always protected.      Yeah or people stop caring.      Yeah before.      They were like rare things now they’re like novelty things oh look that one that's on a coin or something.      Yeah you see that a lot.

Okay, so we've got the weekend off, and I was thinking we could just do nothing. But like...  real  nothing. Just chill, no gadgets, no stress.      You’re mad. “Doing nothing” is not a plan! I wouldn’t last two minutes without watching something. I brought  The Crown  with me, just in case.      Oh yeah? I only watched one episode last week and now I’m dying to know what happened with Prince Charles and Camilla. Who’s team Camilla here?      I’m with you on the drama, but I prefer my TV  not  real life. Drop the crown, let’s do something bonkers like one of those horror films that you swear is fake but is 100% real. You know, the ones where the guy lights the house on fire with a cigarette by accident and forgets it.      God, no! I only ever watch films if they’re  proper  good, not some weird reality stunt gone wrong. I like dramas that actually  feel  like you're living in them. Like  The Baby  or  Shame ... you know the real deep ones.      GIRL. We’re in a student flat. Let’s just watch something with popcorn and not make ourselves cry because someone’s ex cheated while the film is on.      I just want to watch one of the  Harry Potter  films. It’s my birthday tomorrow and I’m feeling nostalgic.      Nostalgia is premium, luv. If it’s nostalgia we’re about, I vote  Back to the Future ! That’s the real deal. Marty McFly, Doc Brown, time travel… you can’t get better than that.      That’s for little kids. What about  The Matrix ? Demo that up? Let’s go full deep state. ‘The world is a flat simulation, you know little beetle,’ or whatever.      Let’s not go full Neil with it. I just watched that and now I’m convinced my toast isn’t  actually  burning.      Yeah, go easy on the deep stuff if you don’t want to lose your sanity. What about  Barbie ? I heard it’s deep, it’s trippy, and it’s basically about consumerism and gender politics wrapped up in neon pink.      Oh, I’ve seen it. It’s overrated if you ask me. But it  was  really funny when I got to the part where Barbie questions the patriarchy and accidentally insults my friend who’s a Ken-lookalike.      Yeah, that’s the part where Ken walks out, right?

So do you not remember when we were in Paris and me and Mia practically hurled our food into the first bin we saw cos it was so bad? I paid 20 quid for a salad that looked like it was probably left out for three days and then Mia spilled half of her coffee on her trousers and I'm like,  this weekend is one long mistake.       Classic Parisian cuisine. I’ve only been once but I think that was my takeaway from it. If you go to some of those little cafés you just have to hope for the best. But, come on, a salad? That’s not even a lettuce leaf. That’s like a metaphor.      You know, I had the turkey and mash at my hotel. Simple food’s best when you’re tired and far from home, don’t you think?      Honestly, I was far from home but not tired. Just slightly emotionally detached at this point. Mia ended up in a café with me, and I remember we saw this guy looking kind of ill and we were like,  ‘him or us?’  and then we both just ordered teas and I think that was the end of it for food-wise. For two days, we just drank tea and ate pastries. I gained about ten pounds.      I’m sorry I missed it. I had to work on Sunday. One of the staff had taken ill and I was filling in.
