I ended up stepping on a tile in the staff room that was someone’s SpaghettiO stain. Just splatted my shoes. Rude.      Oh, is it gone now?      Not really. I had to take them off at home about five times to walk around the house just to dry the holes out. It was like a mission.      So you barely left the house, Mia had a gallic meltdown and I had to put up with dodgy food and questionable company. Parents, I have no idea why I do these things.      Well, you’ve had a bit of a crack-up weekend as far as weekends of doing something nice go. Do you plan on going again anytime soon?      Defo not for a year. I like Paris, but I can go there when I don’t feel like I’m about to pass out.      I had a friend go with her gran to Nice last year and they said the food was actually  relatively  safe there, if you go for the local stuff and not the touristy joints.

Hey Rach! How've you been? You look like you had a long one.      Oh, hey James! Just bailed out of work early, so I've got time to grab a flat white before class. You know how I like being fashionably tired.      Right, right, I understand the struggle. I just got back from Chichester last night after a training day with some other EL instructors. Such a pain, honestly.      Oh no, do they make you teach the same content every time? I can’t imagine how dull that must get.      Honestly? It’s worse. We were talking about how we can incorporate more local dialects into classroom material, especially for the Malaysian students we get. They pick up English fast, but some of their sentence structures make me nostalgic for basic grammar rules.      Wait, British National Corpus training? I mean, no shortage of data there. When’s the last time you thought, “Today’s sentence is so perfect for a passive voice example”?       [Laughs]  Every other day! I swear if one more student asks whether they’re  allowed  to use the passive in their essay, I’ll just hand over a printout of “The Passive Voice – A Real-Life Story” with my personal diary entries.      Would not be surprised if you already did. You know what I found interesting this week? My store’s new supervisor just got into a massive argument with the system because it auto-categorized her brother’s cosplay DC t-shirt as “inappropriate for a retail setting.” It was hilarious.      Oh, come on, did she actually try to dress as Batman for the Renaissance Faire and then get penalized?      Worse. She barely left the house. She was so invested in the outfit, her Twitter followers baked her a GeoCities-style apology cake.      Okay, now I want to meet her.      You will, eventually. Speaking of, you and that TEFL dream of yours? Still thinking about taking a sabbatical to do your master’s next year?      Ugh, the proposal is still in the bin on my laptop from February. I’m so overwhelmed trying to balance teaching hours, student loans, and avoiding the idea of ever teaching high school due to passive-aggressive teenagers.      You’re not helping. I’m considering taking some linguistics courses to help me talk better to my over-entitled Croydon interns.      I can already imagine it: “No, I won’t put the 80s pop playlist on demand.

Right, so the first thing we need to do is measure out the rice. You get a mug, like... this one, and fill it up level with your fingers. See how I do it? That's about one person's portion. If you want to feed yourself and a friend, you just make two mugs' worth.      Yeah, I reckon I could do that. Easy enough. So what do we do with it next?      Right, you pour it into the pan. Then you give it a quick rinse under the tap. It washes off some of the starch, so it doesn’t make the rice clumpy. Look—just keep pouring and pouring until the water runs clear.      Oh, got it. So that’s how you make it fluffy, right? I thought you just dropped the rice in and called it a day.      Well, if you want soft and nice... you’ve got to do the rinse. Now, once it’s rinsed, you drain it into a sieve, or just tip it over the side of the pan, and then—      What about the water? Do we use tap water, or is it something else?      Tap water’s fine. We just add it in with the rice, and then it all boils together. Usually the ratio is one part rice to two parts water. So if we have one mug of rice, we’d put two mugs of water in.      So like, just measure the water the same way you did the rice?      Exactly. That’s the trick to it. Some people use a measuring jug, but mugs are easier round the house, especially when you’re trying to be quick.      Got it. So it’s like rice, water, heat... done.      And then you simmer it gently. Let it cook on a low heat for about 15 minutes with the lid on. Don’t rush it or stick the heat too high and it’ll either burn or stay crunchy.      What if the water all boils off?      Don’t worry—just check the rice go soft. You usually don’t need to add more once it’s boiling. Unless it’s really dry, but we’ll see how it goes.      Alright. So I can make rice by myself now, then?      It’s a start. Once you’ve got rice down, we can try making a curry. Now  that’s  where things get interesting.      Curry?

Right, I just wanted to say sorry for not coming in for training today. I had a real bad stomach... got the norovirus from somewhere, I reckon. I’ve been lying on the sofa with a blanket for 24 hours and only have toast and tea in me.      Oh no! That’s  not  good. You need to stay off it for at least two days, I reckon. A lot worse than just having one too many lagers, anyway. You alright now?      Yeah, just tired. Still doesn’t chase when I get up, but I feel... like I’ve been baked in the oven and then left to cool. I’ve only got a few bits of posh turkey left in the fridge, but I left it in case anyone else gets the bug off me.     I think I may have had it too earlier this week. I had breakfast, then 10 minutes later I was sprinting in the loo, you know?      You lot are so thick. One time, I shared a Waterstone’s coffee, and for a full week I thought I’d never taste anything properly again. You’re human sponges for germs.      Mate, it’s only from the way we live. My nan’s been barking at me and Mitchell because we eat on the same plate and all dance in the kitchen barefoot. Silly old cow. We’re young! We survive on instant mashed potatoes and someone else’s leftovers!      That’s the absolute truth. I mean, what’s the point of going to uni if you can’t split a Margherita pizza with someone and then make out in about five minutes?      Exactly! Anyway, while I was vibes on sofa doing nothing, I decided to catch up on some shows. Watched a  full season  of that new ‘Revolutionary Moments’ history doco. Man, it was wild. Like, the amount of shenanigans those scientists had to go through before you could even flash a pennylight while you had a cup of tea.      Oh yeah, I watched it with my younger cousins last week. My 14-year-old cousin nearly fainted when the bloke in go-knuts started snorting gunpowder to prove a theory.      I’m not even watching it, blokes. I’ve had to study for my biology exam. I seriously think I might fail, mind you. I’ve never been good at remembering the bits like how the proteins work.

So did you go for the walk today?      No, it was a bit pissing down again. I’m starting to think it rains down here just to tease me into getting fit!      Haha, I know what you mean. I tried to make my dog walk twice and it poured both times. It’s ridiculous. But at least I’m getting out of the house a bit.      That’s the key, really. I’ve been sitting in this flat so long I'm starting to forget what the sun looks like. I used to love walking in the park, but now even the thought of lacing up my shoes feels like a chore.      I get that. I’ve been thinking about starting a group walk thing, maybe with some friends or even some of the people in the area who came to my last event. Maybe something friendly, like breakfast, a walk, and then tea. Something a bit fun to make it social.      That’s a good idea. I might actually sign up for that. I do miss the company of people who aren’t just my telly or my cat. But I’ve been struggling for ages with ... you know, just watching life passing by. I used to be pretty active. I remember – back in my day, I was in the Army for a while. Went into Afghanistan. Now I’m just ... retired and stuck in a flat.      That’s incredible, I had no idea. What happened with the work stuff?      It was all a bit long-term injury. Back and shoulder from being in the field too much, too fast, too often. I did okay at first after retiring but then just the ... the boredom, I guess. And not having a routine. I know that sounds silly.      No, it’s not silly. Having a routine is huge. I started doing events work after university and it gave me a purpose, a structure. Do you think you’d be interested in helping out with events or volunteering? There are a few groups around Cambridge doing community stuff.      I’d probably do anything if the kettle wasn’t boiling and I wasn’t sat by myself eating the same telly goop every night. If you could get me up and moving, even once a week, I’d be a happy man.      Well, you just spoke to the right person! I’m running a team-building event for a local charity in a couple of weeks.

Right, lads—clear up’s on you tonight. I’ve had one too many squints at that spreadsheet, and I’m not juggling the dishes as nicely as I used to.      Come on, don’t start. Look at this—  Liam   just sent me a video on Instagram of him  bungee jumping  with   his girlfriend  . Teenagers today have more adventure than I do in my entire life.      She’s a model, innit? Look at her! My girlfriend’s aunt makes blankets. Didn’t even get a like.      You’ve got a girlfriend  now ?      Yeah, sort of. We like each other’s mugs. Still working on the left or the right hand thing, though.      Always was the shy one. You need to take risks, son. Bungee jumping doesn’t count until you propose mid-air. That’s what Liam did.      You lot are mental. You try bungee jumping and I reckon your facial hair will decide it doesn’t want to be there anymore— mid-jump . Like a panic brush mustache.      At least he didn’t have a Hitler look at the age of twelve. I saw a photo?      Oh no, that was  not  a good photo. Someone had taken that out of context at a history fair. ‘Balloon Hitler’ isn't a look, just someone being silly.      Yeah, but it made the local paper. You were hotter before the moustache, though.      I was  hot  when I started the moustache. It was a marketing move. Now it just means I keep lathering off a little more each day.      I’m growing mine out as a side bet. My mate said if I manage to keep it for a month, he’ll lend me his tennis racket. I’m holding out for wooden decks and laces.      I could lend you my racket— if  you help me clear up.      Make it three rackets and I’ll lend you mine too. You’re not winning that bet, son. Must go—texted Liam back about the jump. He’s got a camping trip line in the works, and it involves a ‘facial hair detox’.      Alright, lads, help me with these plates first. No tennis rackets until the table’s cleared—and no photos of  any  type of mustache on social until this lot’s done. I’ve been proofing for a living, not people’s weird Instagram reels.      So, we’re not going to talk about how Liam’s got thirty-seven followers before he even played a full match?

Rather skip the new furniture till we get our sorting done, do you?      Yeah, I don’t want to spend money now unless it’s  absolutely  necessary.      I don’t blame you, love. You never know what you’re getting from these places now—half the time the thing looks good on the website and turns up broken in your back garden. I once bought a sideboard once that needed more wood than I had in the garden shed.      We’ve had the tip full for weeks now. I can’t keep taking things up to it like this.      I know, we need to get rid of the box files like you said, Nana. I’m just waiting for someone to help me sort through the old letters and whatnot.      Oh, don’t let it get to you, luv. When I was your age I used to volunteer at the beaver scout Christmas party, and I remember one fella turning up with a hamster that he claimed was going to help us with the table decorations—personally I think he just wanted someone to keep him company.      That sounds like someone from my primary school. Mr. Franklin used to claim he got “the most amazing support” from his students. He once tried to take photos of his beard while the class was doing finger-painting.      Bless him, he had that look, didn’t he? Like he was waiting for someone to say: “Oh, Mr Franklin, we’re all  so  impressed with your beard!”      I still remember the  time  when Anon’s pal about her family. That day the washing machine broke down and she had this fella from a house next door washing all her clothes in the sink. I don’t even know if he knew how to work a soap box.      I did something similar once at uni. My roommate had a surfboard as a doorstop, and I once tried to wash my duvet while my flatmate was out. Let’s just say it ended with me shouting a couple of expletives I’d never used in my life and a pile of damp fabric like a mannequin wearing goon socks on a lake.      You kids these days sure are interesting, I’ll give you that. Time was when I had to look after older people, I used to see all sorts—like the fella who kept thinking he had belly buttons on both legs.

So did I! The gym was packed on Saturday, even at ten in the morning. I think everyone and their dog decided to lose some weight after Christmas.      That does sound about right. I was at Tesco and they had Easter eggs already! I wouldn't be surprised if we had a White Easter in a year’s time with the way things are going.      I saw that too! I swear they put them out just to remind us we're gaining five pounds while waiting for it. Speaking of which, how are you sleeping? Still using that hot-water bottle under the bed?       laughs  I wouldn’t sleep at all without it now. That and my wellies before bed. You’ve met my grandad’s ghost, haven’t you?      Always. I think he turned your radiators off again too while we were at the weekend. I couldn’t feel the heat in the house after I went to bed.      Oh, didn’t you hear the shout? I had to chase that man out with the watering can—personally I think he takes pride in short-circuiting things.      Honestly, we’ve got to replace that wiring. The house is falling apart. You’ve no idea – Mateo stopped at the curb last night, because the porch light shorted out and hit the curb sensor somehow.      Bless him! And I suppose the builders have all gone on someone’s chicken Tikka holiday.      Pretty much. I’ve got quotes costing as much as a second mortgage and some of them look at me like I speak Martian when I mention the "waterproofing strip" or "damp-proof course".      Maybe it’s time you got someone in that actually knows what they’re doing. You could ask my step-cousin Lucy. She works with construction stuff. Though I heard she once tiled a bathroom with wallpaper.       giggles  Ah, but that was a “design choice.” Still, anything that doesn’t explode or short-circuit the entire house is a bonus at this point.       giggles  Now, moving on—how are you dealing with the whole work situation? How does it feel to have been made redundant in the middle of your dream job?      Honestly, it’s surreal. I’ve been crying at least twice a day since I found out. I never expected that, especially after three years of doing that restructuring project.      It’s understandable. I remember when I got made redundant for "being too kind to the kids," it felt like I did something wrong.

Right, who’s ready for dinner?      I am! Did we get that string spaghetti with the tomato and cheese one?      I think it's the one where we added garlic to it… Not quite sure. Was I even supposed to put garlic in?      Yeah, you  said  it tasted better with it. I don’t know— you  made it last time.       laughs  Well, this time I’m going to dump everything in and hope for the best. Chiara, come in when you're ready, love.      Mama! Chi Chi— giggle —no, no!      My turkey, you’re going to fall over if you run like that! Dinner’s nearly ready.      I think he just screamed “Chi Chi no, no!” and then fell back when he tried to turn a corner.      Oh don’t, you’ll encourage him. You, young man— kneels to speak to child —Chi Chi no, no—person is not edible, okay?      Want to teach him Japanese tonight?      Are you mad? I tried last time and then he got “chi no pika-pika!” out of me, and now it just means chicken nuggets. I think he’s learning that “chi” means chicken.      Maybe we should just teach him how someone speaks in Japanese. Maybe show him a bit of a video?      Okay, but only if it's cartoon-related. Otherwise it’s just going to turn into your ballet video again and he’ll be trying to spin like a ballerina the next week.      I  love  ballet. You said that you loved the tutu…      That was a  very  different lesson. Anyway, after dinner, what are we going to do today? I was thinking maybe a trip to the park? Or do you want to stay in and stick with  Stick with Mick  again?      Do I  have  to do Mick again today? Wasn’t there a  stick  around this morning?      There was a  stick , yes. It was broken into two because Chiara tried to catapult it out the window with a box.      Oh right, because she said it was for “Minion” roles in her pretend tea shop.      Minion? Lionion?      …What?      I think he just said “lionion!” Again, I’m not helping.      Chiara—try not to say lionion at the supermarket or we will be buying lion-shaped onions.      I think I might try some guitar practice while Chiara does that. Maybe you could come with me? I mean, if Chiara doesn’t take over the ukulele again…      Fine, but only if you let me rest for 20 minutes after dinner.

Right, so the new one we're watching is called  "Fish Hook."  You seen it before?      Nah, never heard of it. I assume it's one of them American films where everyone ends up with a tattoo and likes burgers.      Hey, don’t knock burgers. I liked the burger at that place down by the docks last week. Proper thick beef patty with that extra gherkin sauce.      Oh yeah,  Kingfish’s ? Yeah, me and the lads went there last night. It was alright, but the meat looked like it was dipped in teleportation glue.      Aye, well some places like that think you're paying for the vibe. Fun atmosphere’s one thing, but I ain’t eating mystery protein. Speaking of which, what’s the plan for your dental appointment again?      What, the one I’ve been dreading since I was four? Bloke’s gonna poke my mouth, say I need fillings and then I’ll bleed like I’ve lost a fight with a kebab.      Aye, well least he can’t change your accent for you. I tried having my teeth straightened once, and it did nothing but cost me a fortune and gave me a face like a startled badger.      Fair enough. Now don’t go making me nervous. You know what I hate more than the dentist? Writing those lesson plans at work. Spent three hours yesterday making a lesson on  Harry Potter  that had a  les  and a  lesson . Student corrected me and it wasn’t even a university student.      Aye, I hear ya. I had the same problem when I was teaching vibes for a gigging blog. One time I used the word "vibe" twelve times in one article. My editor had to put me on restriction.      Aye, maybe you should write a book instead. Ever thought about it? Proper novel, not just songs or articles?      I did. It’s called  “Urban Dusk and the Ghost of My First Audiobook” . Six pages in, abandoned it. My dog read the rest.      Ha! You know what, real talk, I read a book called  The Dog's Tale  once, written from the perspective of some smug border collie. I seriously asked the author if they were okay.      It's a pity we can't write from the perspective of the food at the dentist's. Imagine the conversations my sandwich would have at lunch. "Sir, I'm bleeding, and it's not because I was cut on the knife."

So did you get the job? I’ve been dying to ask. I know it’s been a week and you got the email, so have you accepted it yet?      Oh, yes! I did accept. I started last Monday, and it’s at a lovely little primary school just outside of Tamworth. It’s been absolutely exhausting, but in a good way.      Oh I’m so proud of you. I know how much effort you put into your training and your interviews. How are the kids?      Oh, they're a right mix, Mummy – you get everything, from the really sweet little ones who love storytelling, to the ones who’d rather tear the classroom apart if they could. But I’ve met some amazing staff too, and the headteacher is really supportive.      I’m glad. You always had an instinct for working with children. Remember when I brought you to that charity community centre when you were 13 and you’d be the one helping out, even ordering the older kids about? They listened to you too, which was surprising.      Yeah I remember! You used to say to me,  “Make sure they’re washed up properly and not just pretending to wash.”  I think I left that job with – what? – ten fairly clean, and one that just flicked water back at me.      You know what I mean though. You’ve always had that kind of natural authority with people. But also the patience. That’s a big one for teaching.      Also, it’s a bit of a commute, so I’m thinking I need to move out of Litchfield soon. I’ve been looking at a couple of places near the school. Not much out there, but maybe part-time renting to see if I can handle it long-term.      You could always look into Sutton Coldfield if you’re not keen on driving all the way. I’d love to have you back again. I’ve missed you, especially since I did all the Christening stuff and that meant being up at 7:30 to keep the cake from collapsing.      Oh you remember delivering the Easter cake by mistake! The baby was meant go in the christening gown, and I turned up with two pounds of sponge and a smiling bunny on it. Sue’s boxers were on her head your whole life you know.      Yeah, I think those trousers are never going to be the same again.

So, how’s the grandad treating you these days? Still glueing himself to the armchair with a cup of tea and the cricket on?      Oh, don’t start. He’s fine, thank you very much. Busy trying to teach our youngest to play darts. I don’t want to know where he found the darts, but good grief he’s got a dachshund scared witless every time it sneezes in the room.      Imagine a dachshund dodging darts. I hope it doesn’t chase the ambulance when the fire alarm goes off.      Ha! Honestly, I just let him get on with it. You know me—I’m the turkey on Christmas Day, stuffing my head in the sand. What about you? How’s the language teaching life treating you?      It’s okay, but honestly? I’m thinking about starting a Spanish-English translation business. I’ve taken in so many GCSE kids over the years that I can translate wedding invitations and divorce papers in my sleep.      That’s brilliant—personally, I’d be halfway through tears or a property squabble by the end of the first sentence. You’ve got a proper head for it. And what about the staff? Still as much of a drama as primary school?      You have no idea. I’ve got a colleague who swears the photocopier is out to get her every Thursday. She’s convinced it’s someone at the business end of the school trying to break her. Honestly, I think she should open a witch-hunting class.      Sounds intense. I missed the drama in secondary teaching because most of my days are spent tiptoeing round the broken heating and watching kids argue over whether a clipboard counts as a catapult. But hey, I’ve got a new student this year—his hair is a whole unit on itself. I tell him every morning, “Eat a biscuit, leave the biscuits in your pockets, and  do not  meet your sister on a rainy day.”      Oh ho, what’s he done now?      Well, he once proudly took the kettle out of the socket, stuck a banana in it, and called it “an art project.” His own mother says he’s got her eyes and his dad’s head, but that combination’s just a box of surprises.      Sounds like someone who needs fluency in conservation and physics, not just language. On the brighter side, have you tried that new lipstick

So do you lot actually know what you're doing when you do the Seder plate? I've seen like... ten spoons, some gherkins, and what I can only assume is a giant rock dipped in chocolate.      Look, it’s traditional — you dip the charoset in chocolate, and the chocolate is meant to represent the sweet redemption of the Israelites. It’s not a rock; it’s a symbol. And the gherkins are maror; it’s the bitter herbs, supposed to remind us of the bitterness of slavery. Funny how people still want to complain about being bitter in 2025.      Honestly, the symbolism is lovely, but do you have to  dip a vegetable in chocolate ? I left London for Paris last month, and I still had to explain it to my French in-laws. Half of them thought it was a dessert course. Wait, does no one actually enjoy this bitter greens?      When’s the last time you had bitter greens that weren’t wrapped in a tortilla? Or drowned in aioli? I tell you, maror is a whole vibe. I tried making my own matzah once and ended up with what looked like a rejected crumpet from  Mad Max . Be grateful we’re not baking at the table tonight — at least not unless you want it to burn again like last year.      Speaking of which, thanks for the panic fire drill with the shakshuka. Our smoke alarms still have PTSD. Honestly, I’d rather just order room service and pretend we’re on holiday in New York — have either of you been? I’m thinking a decent museum day, maybe a Broadway show...      I went with my boulangerie friends last year. There’s a little deli not too far from the Flatiron District that makes the best pastrami on rye, like, ever. If you ever want to skip the Seder plate and just open a bag of pretzels and greasy pastrami, I will be your Passover tour guide. As long as we can still sing  Dayenu  in the middle of a deli counter.      That's where  Ortolan  comes in! The French version of go-to-resto snobbery. It’s a tiny bird, blindfolded before you eat it, because apparently the surprise of the flavor is what your upper-middle-class mouth desires. I mean seriously, why blindfold someone before serving them chicken with a side of bellyache?      Oh, overcooked kidneys and cod-liver oil were  so  last century.

So did you watch The Crown last night? I only just caught up on the last few episodes. Honestly, I got so invested, I forgot to answer my phone for about ten minutes.      Oh, yes, I did! That one where the Queen says she wouldn't have been a good mother during the war—it really struck me. It was so haunting. I watched it with a cup of tea and my granddaughter was in the next room knitting one of those cute baby blankets. She learned from me, which is nice. Knitting and crocheting really keep me grounded when things get busy with work.      Honestly, I’m still not a fan of streaming the whole series at once. I prefer my books—real, physical ones with pages you can smell. It’s just more personal to me. You can’t feel the texture of an eBook the same way. But I’ll admit, sometimes they’re easier when you're rushing between meetings.      I completely agree with you, Clara. There’s something about turning the pages and the weight of a real book in your hands. I do both, though—some I listen to on audiobooks while driving.      And then there are the book-to-film adaptations. I saw the new Pride and Prejudice reboot last weekend—terrible! They changed too much and none of the characters felt like Darcy and Elizabeth anymore. All that emotional nuance just gone. I understand modern twists, but that one missed the mark.      Oh, I saw that! I wasn’t a fan either. I prefer the original 1995 BBC series. It was so beautifully filmed and the cast was perfect. Jane Austen’s books are such a gift to adapt, but the films still can’t quite capture the full story like the pages do.      I know! The books give so much to the reader, like the inner thoughts and the wit. Films can only show the surface. I remember reading the book before I saw the movie and it left me so much more satisfied.      Speaking of books and time, have you seen Monica’s latest knitting? She made a whole sweater based on a character from a book. Her daughter’s learning to knit it too! It’s so endearing watching them get creative together. It's like a real family tradition.      That’s fantastic. I’ve been meaning to get back into crocheting myself—it’s been years!

Rather annoying isn’t it? I swear these new phone settings do everything they can just to trip you up. I got the Samsung, same as you, I think?      Yeah, me too. I was wondering how to set up the Wi-Fi—half the time it just decides it’s not on Wi-Fi at  all , even when it bloody   is  .      Oh aye, I had the same just before. Gave up and just used mobile data. It’s not like it’s costing me nothing anyway, being abroad. Didn’t even want to test how big a shock my mobile would’ve had if I  had  been in the UK and forgot to switch off data roaming.      Ooh, I remembered to switch it off this time! I had one phone bill in Italy, last year, after I turned my phone on thinking I was at home and forget to disable roaming. Charged me more than a fiver a meg in the end. Absolutely criminal!      Aye, that’s a harsh one. So glad that EU rules sorted it out, otherwise we’d be properly skint. I never thought about it as much with my early Nokia phones, mind. You just switched on—everything worked, no faff about with networks or languages or anything.      I know! My first Nokia was like a companion. You didn’t need to update it, you couldn’t even  break  it. These phones are so clever, but at the same time... weaker in a way. You’d drop a Nokia down the well and it’d probably still ring at the bottom.      Made a decent paperweight too, if you lost your keys about. I always thought the old Nokia “ringtone” was the best—midnight — what was that even   called   again?      “Mighty Love”... or “Revolution”? I always got confused between the two. But that  beep  when it was sent was bloody essential—had to know someone got your message when you were out wandering the fells as a kid.      Aye. No need to wonder what signal strength was if the phone rang, you  knew . Now it’s like the Network Fairy comes in every hour and decides whether you get antena or not. Gave my phone a whack just now because I thought it’d lost reception.      Same! I tap mine if it randomly goes silent during a video call. It’s like we’re conditioned now to treat it like some kind of over-sensitive servant.

Right Aaron, today we need to talk about your birthday party. Are we deciding on the guest list yet?      Yeah, I’m thinking of inviting all my gym friends and Aiden from school. But… can we do a topic like “wild animals”? I want the games to be about animals, and maybe a movie like  The Wild  or something.      Oh aye, I love your passion for animals! Why don’t we send out a few invitations by Monday, just to be safe?      Deal. But can we get red pandas as a theme? They’re like the best. They’re like cats with fur and fire, only cuter.      Haha, red pandas it is. And what about food? We could do animal-shaped sandwiches, maybe some cupcakes in red and brown. Or if you’d prefer, we could have something breakfast-themed—like pancakes and fruit since everyone has energy for partying at the beginning.      Pancake station sounds so cool. And I want to play board games—maybe  Catan  or  Candy Land  for the younger ones.      Hmmm,  Candy Land  is always fun. But don’t forget the humble “what animal are you” game: everyone answers questions, and you guess the animal based off their answers.      Oh yeah! That was the best one we ever did. And we could show people how someone got full on my iPad. Just not my mom, she gets bad vibes.      Fair enough. So while we talk games, I need to mention something about ballet, or is it gymnastics now? I think it's gymnastics from talking to Mrs. Norris.      Yeah, it’s gymnastics! I really like it. We do flips and do tricky moves like cartwheels and stuff. It’s like being a cat that just landed on its feet.      Oh, I loved cats too. You know, your brother Casey had such a beautiful yellow tabby. Even if it liked to chew on the new laptop cables—my patience took the brunt of it.      Haha, Yeah, go Mico! But he had more fur than teeth so he was always slipping off the chair. Anyway, Mico’s box might be in the shed.      Miaow!      Well, you heard the cat! But anyway, to get back: I’ve been over this so much—your best friend needs a birthday present, so what should it be?      Let me see. A plush? Or maybe a CD of Japanese songs? Like, not English songs, just compilations before anime.

So do you lot actually do anything for Christmas at all, or do you just chuck it out the window like it’s the waste-bin Thursday?      I mean, we do our thing, yeah. But it’s not quite like here, I guess. We used to have a big feast in Manila on Christmas Eve—something like  Noche Buena . But we celebrated more on the 24th than the 25th. Got side dishes like  lechon , pork stew, some interesting rice dishes. We’d have the family together and just eat for hours, but the next day was more... like, whatever. Still mostly just eating.      Oh, now that sounds quite like us older folk’s time. When I was young, we’d have the mince pies made from scratch, the plum pudding, and I’ll be good and honest—my dear darling’s dad used to make it breakfast, lunch and tea during December! He still did for years after. People’d be knocking at the door, thinking it’s mad. He was the kind of chap who thought Christmas was one long pudding sandwich.      Yeah, I remember that well. Here in Bognor when I was a lad, there was something of a tradition for the rhythm of it all. You had the pheasant parade: Royal Albert Hall, cheques, cards, and the clock tower. But the main thing? Always the same: tea at 5, carols at 6, and then dinner at someone’s house. But also suspiciously often my mum tried to sneak in some turkey at breakfast— just to get it over with .      That’s  hilarious . Our parents nearly about had a fit last year trying to make the Christmas liturgy match the Pakistani aunt and stuff. There was some confusion over when to open the presents and whether it should be on the 24th  or  the 25th. Also, someone brought pakoras at 6 a.m. alongside the mince pies. It’s like, you can’t half do your traditions anymore—      Right? And also, trying to explain to a new friend from the Philippines why we do things like  carols by candlelight . They thought it was a burning man goth event on pond life if you don’t get real festive candles.      Oh, don’t go on, Manila lad. You lot are still way more diverse than we were! I remember when we first had someone from Nigeria come to our class for Christmas dinner.

So did you watch the new series of  Shadow Court  yet? I know it's supposed to be like... challenging, but I’m loving it.      Not yet, I’ve been a bit swamped at work. They’ve had some kind of system rollout, and all hell’s broken loose. I swear, if I hear the word ‘cloud migration’ one more time I’m going to scream. You’ve only got so much patience before you throw your keyboard.      Oh,  Shadow Court ! I'm halfway through the first series. It reminds me of the old  No Trace  days but more... layered, if that makes sense. Have you read the book yet, Claire? It’s well worth a look if you enjoy that kind of thing.      I’ve got the Kindle on my list. I think I'll queue up the books in order while I wait for the next series, though. You need to read them first or you miss half the references, apparently.      Honestly, I tried reading a thriller once over the weekend and I was over it by page 30. These days I stick to short stories. You know, something you can finish in a couple of hours without losing your train of thought.      That’s understandable. Work – or lack of – has me with more time these days, so long books are my new hobby. But enough about books and shows. I heard you two had a cookout weekend, huh? How was that?      Oh God, it was chaotic but fun. We tried making homemade burgers and the smoke alarm didn’t like it one bit. Made Margot swear more than she normally does, and I about dropped the kettle after she yelled "Turn the oven  off !"      And what else? Drink? Music? The usual?      You bet. My sister brought over her new treacle tart recipe. It was actually really good. I told her she should start a food blog. She just rolled her eyes, but I can tell she’s loving the compliments.      That’s nice. I've been meaning to try writing recipes down. Not as an official thing, just for my nieces. They’re always asking me to make go-to dinners on the weekend if their parents are working late.      Imagine that, being a chef in your spare time. I’m lucky if I make toast without burning it. Speaking of toast, though, we had that cheap bread last week and I was convinced there was a foreign body hidden in there somewhere.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know, that thing that sticks out of the wall — the p... p... plug socket or whatever it is they call it now.      Yes, dear, it  can  be a bit of a pest if you're not careful. My George always used to fiddle with the extension leads, you know. But he always kept things in order.      What’s up, Charles? Fallen over again?      No, not that it’s not me. It's the fault of the outside light, or the garden sockets rather — I went to plug in the fairy lights last night, and now the whole thing’s sparking!      My word, you haven’t disturbed anything though have you, Charles?      You know I haven’t. I just gave the little lever a nudge, and the thing gave a bit of a pop and then... well, nothing! No light in the back garden, no kettle, and that's the kettle’s done it again isn't it?      Let me tell you—personally, I’ve never trusted these short, flimsy leads. You remember when I opened that fancy garden gear shop on the high street, we always sold the proper heavy-duty ones. People just wouldn’t listen, they wanted the cheeps because they were bright green and had a funny logo on them.      Oh, I blame the young generation. Nothing's made to last these days — plug one thing in and the whole system goes a bit haywire.      Just need to find a proper electrician and be done with it. I had one come round last year and nearly about cost me a fortune he was so fussy! But what did I get out of it? Not much! Still, that kettle plug barely held and it cracked clean in two.      That's the problem, Charles. All that modern rubbish. They make it too cheap. I remember when you got those vintage lamps brought in from Germany, the little ones with the stick switches—      Oh yes, those were the days. No need to whack switches or anything, just a flick and you were good.      I had a set go in my sitting room once, you know — brought them over personally from my cousins in Hamburg. Lasted thirty years.      And your cousin was a proper craftsman, I’ll give him that. Back in the day those plugs, those sockets — they were made like stone. Whereas now, you plug in the kettle and the whole circuit melts.

Right, so the print run for  The Last Twenty Minutes of Horace  just finished, and the first copies are on the desk by the coffee machine. I thought I’d let everyone know before we start wrapping this part up. Do we do a read-through or—?       Aye , let’s read it over before we send the final PDFs off. I’ve only skimmed the last chapter so far, but it felt like a big shift in tone. That ending—it just  landed  differently for me.      I agree. The whole book is pretty heavy at times, but that final chapter almost made me think of a lullaby. The rhythm left me a bit breathless, to be honest.      I think it worked. The way the editor slowed the pacing down at the end… it felt like Horace was finally  letting go  of all his trauma. But I’m wondering, did the author’s notes mention anything about why they included those moth images?      There’s a quote from her in the back about moths as metaphors for memory—how they circle things rhythmically, like we do with painful experiences. She called it “revisiting in flight.”      That’s a beautiful metaphor. I’ve heard similar ideas from ecocritics. Moths aren’t just pests—they’re symbols of a delicate struggle between light and darkness. Some readers might miss that nuance, though. Maybe we should include a brief commentary in future editions, or make it a PDF insert for academic readers?      Could be. I’ve already got some folks asking if the “insect” mentioned near the start—page 47, where that little girl saves the beetle—is connected to the moths at the end. Are they the same species? Is the kid trying to preserve something fragile about herself?      Let’s not overcomplicate it. She  saves  the insect—protects it in her pocket, even after the bullying and the fall. That act of care is really the core of the book. If the moths at the end echo that, it becomes a loop. She remembers how it felt to save one life, and that memory becomes her anchor.      And maybe Horace, in those final twenty minutes, is trying to save himself. That silence at the end… it’s almost like he’s gathering the strength to move forward, kind of like the girl with the beetle.      Beautifully said. So, on the topic of moving forward—how many attendees are we expecting at the launch party next Thursday?

Okay, I swear I'm going to fail maths tomorrow. I've literally done nothing.      What, again?! Ugh, I’m so ready to fail too, like, intentionally. I mean, why even bother trying?      Right? Just hand in a blank paper and say, “Ta-da, I’m a genius.”      But my mum’s making me revise. She brought colour-coded revision cards and everything.      Oh no, not the flashcards. Please just let me die quietly. My sister tried flashcards, and now she has maths nightmares. She woke up screaming about quadratic equations.      No way?! That’s horrific. I had that one teacher, Mr. Price, who said if you failed GCSEs, you’d end up in a cardboard box and sad. Fair enough? But then he added, “Unless you’re into Domino’s, then maybe not.” I mean, still valid.      Classic Mr. Price. I saw him at the shops the other day. I immediately ran out like I was being chased by a maths problem I couldn’t solve. I’m not even exaggerating.      You’ve still got time to bow out gracefully tomorrow. Leave it in, put your name on it, and say it was “a gift to the universe”.      Let’s do it together. We’ll be the Silly Sisters of Simultaneous Equations.      Wait, don’t you have a Physics test first? That one with the electricity?      Yeah, and I haven’t even opened the textbook. I just watched all  Back to the Future  movies in about five days to “research motivation energy sources” and still haven’t grasped Ohm’s Law.      Ohm’s who? I’m just praying the exam doesn’t ask,  “Calculate the emotional stress of a high-achieving friend on the brink of a maths-related breakdown.”  That one would be impossible.      I’d fail it. But unfairly, because I’m emotionally  so  there.      At least we’ve got PE next week. Even if we fail the whole term, we can just run around in goody shoes on the track like it's  I Dream of Jeannie  and not care.      That might be the only thing keeping us alive. So, post-surgery, post-exams, what are you doing for your birthday?      I don’t even have a birthday this year. I’m just gonna pretend I’m born in July so I can have a theme park day and chemical fun.      I did that last year.

Rather skip the starter and just go for the main, really. This place does an amazing lasagne.      Ah love a good spicy one. I prefer mine with a decent chunk of garlic and cheese thrown in. You alright, love? You’ve barely picked at your salad.      Yeah, I’m fine. Just had a bit of a migraine this morning. Nasty. Made me feel like I wasn’t in my own head.      That bad, eh? My sister had one the other day and she said it was like the world was rocking back and forth like a boat. Still, at least you could get to work and not fall into a ditch on the way? My turkey still hasn’t finished cooking.      Oh, the turkey again? D’you not learn the last time you tried to take an oven apart to fix the ‘inconsistent browning’? You nearly burned the curtains down after trying to repurpose the ventilation tray as a desktop fan, you daft man.      He was trying to give it a bit of personality, Mum. Not every one of us puts up a banana tree and calls it a welcome home gift.      Well, I’m not paying for the utility bill from the banana tree. Plus, I’m not sure how it ended up trying to sprout in the flat.      You know what it is? It’s that whole, “this is just someone being creative” mindset. Let me tell you, a plum yogurt and oddly sour grated lemon peel does not equate to creativity in the kitchen.      I don’t know how you two have let me live this independently for the past three years without pestering me every time I cook a lasagne and not ask you to taste it.      Maybe because you do most of the planning for the development stuff at your job. I mean, that and the fact that the only time you mentioned being ill was when you fell over at the office waiting for a lift and crack your wrist holding your latte as though it were a sword.      Ah the “coffee warrior” as you like calling yourself. Then you spent the next two days cradling that cup on your desk like it was a broken animal.      It was brutal. And the worst thing was, I had a video call with the German branch that I had to face with a wrist in a sling. They all think I’m some type of clumsy professional now.

Rather skip the newfit incision. You know what, I think I was just trying to be polite. I got the results from Thursday’s scan this morning, and I’ve got something called a hernia there where it was. Not quite as dramatic as I thought—  Lori   says it’s probably nothing I should stress over, but I’m still twitching about it. You know how I get.      Oh, bless you love. Of course you are. You're not the type to not think it’s a big deal. I got one when me cousin nearly pegged me with a car on my way to the Lakeside Cleaners—barrel roll, landed the fence, only broke my left pointer finger and My turkey leg. You’d have been in hospital for a week just persuading the surgeon I was fit for discharge.      Oh for heaven's sake, you’ve got to stop bragging about near-fatal things this early. Honestly, I only mentioned it because I wanted to explain why I’ve been ordering puff cakes and qiaodashi over the last few days instead of getting out, and being inappropriate in front of the kids.      You’re grief is real, love. Listen, if you need someone to circle trot through Westgate services just to make you laugh for 45 mins, I’m still limberging from that burst pipe at my daughter's flat last week, but I’ll do it.      God, thank you. Our teenagers aren’t helping. Emily—my eldest—has just been given detention for oddly sour chemistry between her and Miss Johnson at school. Or as she calls it, “the passive aggressive education lady in a Prime clash dress” about five times a conversation.      She’s watching Jane Austen and cooking lasagna and calling it “detox.” I’d give it to her up front.      Oh she baked you lasagna didn’t she? She probably did. She told me the day before she was docked an hour of Foundation Studies, which is when I sort of said, “You know what? Maybe being academically passive aggressive with your teacher  is  your digestive tract.” She ran out in tears.      Teens these days, all sensitive skin goenvironmental on your life if you don’t validate their emotional preemies at line pace, but that’s aside. You’re arranging the visit to Dorset, right? You were going to take the family down to see Dan’s dad— you know —Andrew, the one who had the colitis.

So did you get the tutorial sorted for tomorrow? Or are they still moving the sessions around?      No, it's all sorted now. They moved it forward an hour, but I got a message this morning. Not sure why they keep changing the schedule at the last minute—it’s so frustrating when you’re trying to plan your week.      Yeah, I know how that goes. I’ve been working at the bar nearly every night this week, and it’s a pain when I get home and it’s light out and I feel like I should be working when I should be sleeping. You'd think uni would sort it out properly.      That must be rough. How many hours have you been working? You don’t get too tired to hold your shifts, do you?      It’s been about five or six nights a week—most of it’s just behind the bar, breakfasts and evenings. I’ve been doing tips afternoons too at the weekends. Honestly, I thought being a bartender would be more sociable, but I just feel like I’m glued to the same spot for hours on end. Got one regular though, quite a character. Calls me  “Madam Bartender”  for some reason.      Haha, “Madam Bartender”? That’s got a bit of a posh ring to it. I imagine he’s the kind of guy who orders a G&T and tries to discuss existentialism with the olive, huh?      Exactly. He’s got a way of making me feel like I should definitely buy him a drink—just because he says the world’s being unfair. Can’t say I disagree, but there’s only so many Gin and Tonics I can fund out the good of my own pockets.      At least you know people are paying attention to you. I’m up here in the library and, like, the only response I get is if someone needs a pencil. I’m surrounded by books and silence. Sometimes I think I might have forgotten how to speak properly.      You just need to go to the bar with me one night and do your  “I’m studying molecular pharmacology but let’s talk about  The Office”  schtick. I guarantee you’ll go viral on the uni chat group.      Ha, I’d be terrified. I’d probably trip over a beer keg and end up face-down in the floor.

So did you lot actually take your summer holidays or what? I’ve been swamped in books since May and it feels like I’ve been in the library for a year already!      I went to Scarborough. Not the beach this time, more like a proper holiday. Went with a few old friends—had a  right  laugh. Sat on the deckchair, basically did absolutely nothing apart from eat chip butties and argue with the telly!      Chip butties?! You’re gonna be one of them Leeds types now, aren’t you?      Careful, you're in Greater Manchester now—watch it! Besides, the real debate was about whether "spinders" is a real word. Still haven’t found out.      Oh I went to Dublin, bless me. The whole family came up—Donna, my daughter, is nearly 14 now and she’s getting  very  opinionated in her old age, you know. Kept telling me to “relax,” like I was running the place!      Nothing like a teenager in your space. I’m dreading it as it is. My little sister, who still remembers my face, is starting secondary school next year and then it’s “what do you want to be when you grow up, Dean?” because obviously librarians are mysterious people.      You can always tell her you’re a secret wizard who shushes people for a living. That always works for me.      Aye, I told Mary—my Donna—she should be a librarian. It’s calm, no stress,  no bullying teenagers .      Oh, right,  those  are the holidays I’ve been taking! Going to that place with barely a chair and way too many people in sweatpants.      What about you, sir? Any glorious time off? Or just coding something confusing for students again?      Actually, I  did  take a trip—Spain. And by Spain I mean “hurried away with the wife and kids for four days of amazing beach and arguing about the sunbeds.” But it was lovely. Got sunburned, laughed at the kids, and ate far too many tapas.      Tapas, eh? So I’m guessing you didn’t read any books while you were there?      True to life. I  did  bring a book, but it got used as a prop—every time someone wanted to rest their mojito, I had to make space.      Oh aye, that’s the kind of holiday I’d like. Being a sunbed referee and mojito organizer. Not bad for an old babe.

Rather skip the half-time take-away this weekend, ay? I’ve had one too many ketchup-covered pints after the match, let me tell you.      Fair enough. Beans on toast is starting to sound quite noble compared to what we usually end up with. But it was my shout on Friday and I  insisted  on the 'two-liner'—still don't know why I said that.       laughs  You said, “if she can get a reasonable two-liner, nothing was stopping us from going for it.” And I said, “No meatballs, please.” And then they  insisted  meatballs were the only way to go.      Yeah, I’ve never seen so much cheese on one plate in my life. I’m half convinced they pickled the meatballs first and then gave them a sun tan.      You know what I hated most? They didn’t give you a side of crisps as an option, you had to have the meatballs and chips  and  the crisps and the dips, and it was like a full meal written in two words.      It’s like fast food has moved on and we didn't. We should be out there sampling burgers with edible spoons and lemon-herb water, not fighting for our dignity in some neon-lit fry-up.      You know what I blame? Football culture. Give a group of people a couple hours in an amber fizzy brew and they suddenly consider themselves professional critics.      Also, half of us can’t even be trusted ordering food without a  script . You remember when Tom nearly ordered a ‘spicy chilli crunch banger’ last month? I had to stop him. Who even knows what that  is ?      Maybe we’re the problem, not the menu. If we stopped watching football at 5pm on a Saturday, we might not be so desperate to eat at 6.30.      Fair point. Though I’ll say this—I’d rather wait two hours for a proper meal than ruin my Saturday with soggy chip butties and ketchup burns around my collar.      Mm, me too. So next match, takeaway? But maybe… just a separate room? You don’t want to witness the carnage when your research manager’s latest fast-food failure hits the plate.       chuckles  Deal. Just remind me to bring wine. Anything to help me survive the food silence after that.      Arranged. Now get back to your PhD and leave the menu writing to the chefs, yeah?

Rather skip the new films at the cinema.      That's it, they don't make proper films anymore, not like the oldies.  Lawrence of Arabia , now  that's  a film. Not all that nonsense about corpses and children frightened by motor cars nowadays.      Yeah, I don't think they'd make  Lawrence of Arabia  today. It’s too ambitious, takes too long to get anywhere!      Oh, well, patience is a virtue! You young folk like everything fast. Didn’t even want to sit still for a full hour like we did! Still,  Back to the Future  is the real blockbuster now, isn’t it? Everyone Myron still talks about that!      Ten out of ten if you ask Oliver. He still watches it every single weekend. Drives us mental, but we try to put up with it. He doesn’t much care about cricket or motorbikes, his world is Marty McFly and shopping arcades.      That’s something, I suppose. At least he’s got some passions. My work sometimes makes me feel like a robot. I spend all day managing spreadsheets and people, then I come home and just want silence.      Ha! Mate, I often just wanted silence and a cup of tea when I was your age! Now don’t go making me feel old again.      Oh, you carry on, Ethel. We’re all old. Just not quite as old as you. I had a proper laugh last week, though—picked up a new bike for Ernie.      Ooh, a bike? What’s he doing with that? He used to crash his bike down our garden every weekend when he was ten.      Don't listen to him, that was just a ‘phase’—I told you.      It’s not a fancy one, just something he asked for. Nothing like the bikes you boys had back in your day. This one’s electric. He’s doing a lot of shopping with it, says it saves money on the bus and the petrol.      Smart move. I told my team at work that we need to invest more in eco-friendly transport for our teams—no one listens, they’re too worried about the bottom line.      Aye, you’ve made it to the big leagues, haven’t you? Project Manager—me belly, I used to wish I had that sound in my job when I was younger!      Nah, I wouldn’t say "made it." Just trying to keep the project trains on the track, really!

Right, who’s having pancakes today? You know it’s Pancake Day, right, you two?      I don’t like pancakes. They go all sticky on my tongue.      Not if you spread the jam  after  you’ve eaten the first bite. Got it?      I don’t want jam. I want chocolate sauce.      Not unless you finish your side salad first, young man. Green Knowe was all about respecting food. Remember that story?      But that was about  ghosts . I like ghosts more than lettuce.      Well, I had to read it to you twice last night before you fall asleep, so you’re not missing the lesson. Eat the lettuce, then you can have chocolate sauce and I’ll read the ghost bit again.      Do we get to go to the Science Museum again? Mum said on Monday she thought we’d be going this weekend.      Yes, we might. I’ve got to check with Nana, though. She’s got some kind of orchestra thing at the Festival Hall. You know how she loves her concerts.      I saw Paris on a Geography poster. Can we go there for the weekend?      Paris is  hundreds  of miles away, don’t be silly. But we  can  go to the beach at Hunstanton if you want. We’ll pack a picnic and maybe see a seagull steal your sandwiches again.      Mom, why do the kids in our class not always eat lunch?      I don’t know, sweetheart. Sometimes people just can’t afford to buy food. Not everyone has what we have.      So they’re poor?      Yeah. And we need to be nice to them. Just because someone doesn’t have as much as us doesn’t mean they’re  less  important.      Like in the short story you read us last week. The boy who lived with his grandma and walked to school in the rain?      Exactly. So no throwing food around the dinner table, go on. I don’t want your pancakes ending up on the ceiling again.      But I don’t  want  pancakes.      Well, I am not starting this conversation again after I’ve made three separate batches just because one of you two is fussy or ‘bored’ of food. Now wash your hands. You haven’t been near the bathroom yet today, have you?      I brushed my teeth already.      Good girl. You two aren’t little boys in the Green Knowe story, you’re growing up.

Okay, thanks a million for this. You know I haven't had decent take out in ages.      No problem love. I ordered more than I can eat anyway.      Same. I only cooked a bit of macaroni for dinner. Thought it was high time I splurgged a bit.      Ay, I’m all in on this. I’ve only had a bag of crisps since Friday.      Let me dump my boots. Who’s had the sweet and sour chicken? Looks like it’s the most squashed one... like someone sat on it!      That’s mine, yeah. You know the delivery lady Myra, she definitely dropped it. She left it on the doormat and ran off like the hounds of hell were after her.      Honestly, she’s better at breakfast deliveries—like when I ordered eggs and bacon last week and she came back with a roasted chicken!      Haha, typical Myra. I once got a pizza with a Bob the Builder themed box inside—somebody put in a joke!      Hilarious. Reminds me when my friend Jack tried to take a photo of the “pizza Bob” and it looked like he was trying to film a death threat.      Oh don’t get me started on phone calls. I got one from Liam at work the other day. Our co-worker at the cricket match—remember him? He sent a photo of his oddly sour chicken wrapped with a funeral wreath. It was eulogizing “the great spice incident of 2021”.      That Liam’s a maniac.      Honestly though, this takeout is better than most of the food I get at student digs. I have a housemate who insists the only spice that should exist is salt. Everything else is “weed on the plate”.      Ew. I once had a housemate cook me an omelet and then sprite as well.      I think it was digestive enzymes. Some health supplement he’d read about in a tabloid.      I bet he read that it was supposed to “boost your cricket stamina” or some nonsense.      That bloke could’ve been your cricket team’s captain at the very least!      Well, those days are gone for me. I’ve been on the bench for five years now. Only play at the pub.      I got invited to a screening the other day. They want to reshoot  The Godfather  from the perspective of the neighbour’s cat.      Yeah?      Says it’s going to be called  The Godcat .

Rather skip the new house and go back to the old one. I still miss it, honestly. The garden... those summers in the back with the kids playing, watering the herbs with their little plastic watering cans.      Aye, the gardens in those old houses were like patchwork quilts—do you remember when Eleanor brought over the trug full of lemons from her trip to Cornwall? She said they were "organic by definition because the farmers sang to them." Barmy, she was, but you did keep one of the plants, didn’t you?      Still under the window, needs repotting again, honestly—Managed to get it through the harsh winter only thanks to Alice and her heated propagator. She’s living up to being the greenest thumb of the family.      Speaking of gardens, have you seen how Dr. Partridge now uses a driverless lawnmower? Claims it recognises the edging like a laser-guided criminal. I said to him last week, “Arthur, if that thing decides it’s overworked and walks off with the hydrangeas—personally, I won’t be sad.”      Hah! And then there’s the roads—every time I go into Wellington by car, feels like I'm in a bottle of Baptism of Fire. I asked young Mitchell from the newsagents the other day, “Do they not teach you how to drive anymore?” He looks at me and says, “Grandad, it’s all apps now. You press the steering wheel to accelerate.” Preposterous.      Though, at least with the scan as you go at Tesco, no more awkward ballet with the trolley in about five aisles while someone's behind you. I still haven’t forgiven them for the whole rice krispie cake fiasco. My sister Sukey nearly had a cardiac arrest when that bag of ingredients cost over £20. “And you passed it by?” she asked. “In the £2 aisle? What were you trying to do, start a war?”      As for Google and that tax thing with HMRC—if you've got to keep the big companies honest, I say do it loudly. Still remember when the Coombs moved in next door with their vast gothic pile on the edge of the fields. They built it up as a country manor but, between us, the box rooms were about the size of our utility. But at least it made for a good story when the insurance adjuster came to inspect after the roof gave way to a heavy snowfall.

Right, who’s ready for Chinese New Year? I’ve bought glue sticks and glitter—the dragon’s going to be  epic , don’t you worry.      I like dragons. Are we allowed to write Chinese with the glitter pen, Mummy?      Of course, darling. Just use the template I made so it doesn’t look too wonky. And don’t eat the glitter—this is not edible.      I drew a spaceship instead. It says “Phobos journey” in Chinese. I read about the planets in school, and Mars has two moons.      Oh, that’s brilliant. I love your imagination, love. You’ve been doing amazing work at school, haven’t you? The teacher said you’ve been explaining the solar system to the whole class!      Awww, he’s making fun of my dragon. He better not when it comes to life and eats him!      That spaceship’s going to pick him up, you’ll see. It’s got lasers and everything.      Well, if your dragon is as fierce as the one in  Barbie and the Great Adventure , it’ll be deadly smart as well. Remember when we watched that last year? Barbie was amazing on the dragon. Pretty epic?      Yeah, but it was  weird  the way her hair didn’t move when she fought the dragon. Like, how?      Well, in real life hair definitely moves. But in cartoons, they just draw it static for simplicity. Funny thing—Barbie has better dragon-fighting skills than most politicians!      Can we watch it again? I did loads of piano after school today, so I earned the extra watching-time.      Not today—you know the rules. One movie max this week. But if you’re good with your drumming tomorrow, we’ll see. How about I order some Chinese food? Let’s go for sweet and sour chicken, general tso’s, and some dumplings?      Yes! Mei Likes sprite as well, but not too much because of the teeth.      Exactly. Sprite, water, and something green with it. Now, how about you go and help me make your dragon more fierce while I heat up the microwave? You can glue on some green foil for the scales.      I’m going to add red stars for the spaceship navigation. And maybe some violin stars for when I’m doing belly dancing on the hoop next week. Miss Perks said I’m getting better at balancing!      Oh I know, love. I was so proud when you did that twist last week.

So do you guys ever just get stuck in a conversation about how everything looks better in the photo than in real life or what?      Oh, 100%. Especially when you Airbnb a place that looks amazing in the pictures and then you get there and half the things in it aren't real or don’t work properly. I had one flat in Naples where the shower basically ran on Italian time — like you had to wait ten minutes just to get a trickle of warm water.      Haha, same! My brother was doing a trip to Sicily last year and the internet was dead — he had to literally walk around with a laptop and a portable charger trying to find a café that had decent connectivity. It was a nightmare. I told him to just relax and take the slow food path, but he was in a rush for something I think he called 'data.'      Yeah, Aussies are all about the Wi-Fi. Like, no matter where in the world we are, the first thing we do is look for free Wi-Fi and the second is find something hot to drink. Doesn’t even have to be coffee, just warm liquid in a cup.      Fair point. But let me ask — have you guys been to that rooftop bar Trastevere? The one with the view of the Forum? I saw it on Insta and thought, “That’s where we’re finishing the night.” But now I’m not sure if we’ve already seen the best of the city just by looking at it on a screen.      Honestly, I think the point of travel is to see things with your own eyes and be surprised. Like, I had a colleague who went to Sorrento and fell in love with the coast just from talking to a local who described it. Never once looked up anything online. Said she trusted her gut and it paid off.      That’s amazing. I like planning stuff out — like knowing what's nearby and how far to walk. But I also know my café relied heavily on repeat customers, so waiting till I get a vibe from the area and then going with the flow... it’s a weird balance sometimes.      Yeah, I work in a café in Sydney, so travel like that is basically my away go-to. I usually let the place talk to me.

So did I! The hen do’s coming up and I’m still panicking about it. I know we all got the Pinterest boards going, but I’m just not sure we’ve covered everything      Honestly, I feel the same, but we’ve got a  fantastic  team. Ali and I sorted out the venue and the menu, and Rosie is handling the decor. You’re just baking a cake and making some cupcakes. Not rocket science!      I  know , but someone once told me you should never eat the cake you bake for your own hen do because you won’t like the taste anymore. I haven’t made a practice batch yet. What if I burn it?      Just bring the cupcakes! The cake can wait. Honestly, you need to calm yourself down, Viv. You’re the only one who’s freaking out about it, and we all trust you.      I mean, Viv, I’m not a baker, but the way you talk, you’d think you’re the Great British Bake Off Finalist. Just make sure it doesn’t have rhubarb in it — I can’t stand rhubarb.      Honestly, I’ve been experimenting with mini vanilla cupcakes and little sugar flowers. I might even try adding some lavender into one batch. I know Elsie swears by lavender shortbread.      Oh, that sounds  amazing . And we’ve already booked the craft station for people to make hair accessories and mason jars with labels. Elsie is bringing her glue gun and glitter with her. Also, I arranged a DJ to come and do some DJ sets — nothing too wild, just chill tunes and about five Spotify playlists.      She’s also bringing her vibes. Elsie can make even shuffle sound like a festival. I’m just hoping she doesn’t play that ABBA medley for the whole night.      Well, I’m just happy the whole gang is coming. Do you think Esther’s sister is going to make it from Cardiff?      I think she’s getting the train with her girlfriend. Should be here by mid-afternoon. And Esther said she’s delivering a cake too, just in case your lavender one go MIA on us.      Honestly, I love our group. It’s like we’ve done a team-building session for what your actual hen do could be. I mean, craft station, champagne, live violin, tea breaks, maybe even belly dancing if Elsie is drunk enough.

Passport. You sure you've got it? Yeah, it's in my rucksack. I got the email from the hotel about the room booking this morning, so I've been pacing about since then. You'll have to stop being such a nervous wreck every time we travel. I'm the one who gets the migraines from all your panicking. Easy for you to say, you never lose your luggage. I remember the time in Prague when I left my coat in the bar. We had to go back the next day just for it, and the bloke at the front desk looked at me like I'd made it all up. That was your fault for folding up the turkey leg and hiding it in your coat like it was contraband. D'you think I should take the patch? Or take an herbal tablet? Wait, you're not ill, you just got over a bit of a tummy bug last week. You're not going to do it again so don't waste money. I know, I know. But I still feel a bit queasy. Like every time I go overseas I expect to wake up with a stomach bug and a fever. Be grateful you don’t get flight sick like I do. I was last in Lisbon and the journey was so rough the seat cushions nearly flew off. You're lucky to still be able to fly. I wouldn't want to get on a plane for a week. It's bad enough doing it on your own. Also, have you seen the way the hotel website lists the amenities? No mention of a kettle, and I about died last time we stayed in a b&b that said it had “tea and coffee” and they meant leaves and water. Don't worry, I mentioned to the booking agent that we’d need tea stuff. She said they'd sort it. I just told her the truth about your tea obsession, said it could be a national emergency if you didn't get a decent brew first thing. And what if they've misheard me and gone with "emergency chocolate supply" instead? You’re not funny. Look, all I'm saying is I need to be prepared. I’m going to write a note in the margin of the booking confirmation. Just in case. Pass me the spatula. If you keep worrying about what might or might not happen, you're never going to finish your dinner—and I need someone to taste this overcooked chicken.

Rather skip the new stamps haven't I.      You can get it through the post you know dear.      Yes I could, but I've found where we used to get them before. You remember that bookshop in Margate on the seafront?      Margate Library used to print one every year. Full of dusty books and self-serving seniors.      Not the best place to socialise, but it used to be quite interesting. They had one of the first computer terminals for the public outside of universities or the Post Office.      Still does. Last I heard, it's the oldest in the country.      Oh, I’ve met some eccentric characters volunteering there. Ten-year-olds to nineties-old Dads, all fascinated by old computers.      They’ve got one of those breakfast clubs now for kids learning to code. Reminds me of when we used to make record covers in school, you remember?      Oh yes, that art project with the jiffy bags and paint. My absolute finest hour in secondary school. I’ve still got it somewhere in a box.      I tried to get a calendar fob made from it once – very 80s vibe, and none of the other residents wanted to know.      You and Silly String are iconic together, don’t worry. Anyway, what's this about birthdays? I noticed the two of you kept arguing over the age on the cards.      Just a bit of friendly banter, as always. You told your granddaughter she was 70 about five times last week.      Well, I had to be convincing. She was very insistent that she was barely 10.      My, time has flown. I always tell her that computing used to be so much more interesting when the only screens were telephone switches and dot-matrix printouts.      We had to clear out over 70 of them before they sold the warehouse to a new café enterprise. They're all going to the computing museum in Leeds.      That's brilliant news. They need stuff like that more than ever.      I was thinking, between us we could box up the rest of what we have. The old PSU, the big tape machine, and even one of those BBC Micros I never got to use properly. Do you think you could get over this weekend? We can drive everything down together.      I’d love that. It’s so nice to be passing something on that’s not just coat hangers or woolen jumpers.

So do you like it here yet, Dad? Or is it still feeling like someone else’s house?      Aye, it’s starting to feel like home, I suppose. It’s a bit different from the flat we had in Southend, mind you — this is more spread out. Got a proper garden now, didn’t think I’d get used to that.      Oh aye, I love your garden! That old fella next door gave you a couple of rhubarb plants to plant, didn’t he? Bit of a legend, that Stan. He told me how he used to work on the railways back in the 60s. Stories out the back!      My word, he did! I swear the man’s lived here since the Stone Age. But yes, them rhubarbs are in the patch by the fence — I’m already dreading the stalks coming through in the spring.      Well, if they grow, you’ll have enough to make jam to last you a few years. Good for giving to the grandchildren.      Aye, speaking of the grandkids, did your mother say whether they’re coming over for Christmas? I might buy in a couple of books for them — been meaning to get “The Railway Stories for Young Locomotives” or something like that.      I reckon she did say something about them coming down for a couple of days, maybe bring your sister along too. Our walking group said there are some nice footpaths not far from here — maybe suggest we do a family walk?      Walking group? You still go out with that lot?      Every Saturday about ten o’clock! Lotta bobbies talking about their greenhouses and cats. Nancy’s got this Danish sister who visits and brings these enormous meatballs. You’d like her — quite the character.      Aye, I remember her. Brought some kind of berry soup once that was bloody nice. Not used to that way of cooking yet, I must admit. Feels a bit odd being in Devon after living so long with sea winds off the Thames Estuary.      You’ll get used to it. Plus, you’ve got the train goin’ on to Exeter and all — got work at the depot, didn’t you?      That I have, thank God — keeps me out of trouble. I was seriously starting to think about moving into full-time gardening after all those years of management. But no, talk about a change over! I’m working at the signal box now.

You do know half the point of living in a house is that we can just order our food through Amazon and never talk to another human being again, right?      I've heard that joke a thousand times, Adam. You're not allowed to say things like that unless you’re actually doing it. I saw you eating a normal sandwich last night.      Okay, fair point. But I still think I should be working from home so this  could  be me. I watched a clip online where a bloke runs his own tech business and doesn't chase the bus or anything. Just sits in a hoodie, sipping herbal tea and responding to emails. All the time.      You like that one, don’t you? I watched it too. It’s just not real, is it? He probably spends the rest of the day patching up his phone in the bin or something.      He doesn’t need a phone! Haha—just a laptop, you know, desktop one, massive keys, no screen glow in the night. I’d be like that. Just me, a screen, and a wireless mouse I occasionally tap with a finger as if I were choosing the next president.      Sounds like fun. But don’t you get bored? I mean, look at me: I’m trying to study, barely watch telly, and the only thing exciting in my week is when the phone rings and I panic it’s a missed assignment reminder.      Well, I’m also trying to not die of boredom. I thought I’d do an online course or something, but they all seem to want you to be a certified something  else . Like "Certified Apple Support Genius" or "Master in Decaf Extraction". Not sure how I’d use either.      You could learn to fix the boiler. That’s up there in value. My mum’s tried every time to explain it. All I remember is something about a bleed valve and a man called Fred who was nice to her once.      I’d rather stick to my 12-step plan of doing nothing but ordering things with one click. I’ve already got the “Fortnite” avatar look set—just a t-shirt and a duvet slung over the chair like it’s a cape.      You could at least log in to that job site. You’ve got an account from what, 2018?      Oh, that’s right!

Rather skip the new house isn't it?      It's lovely, really. We had to do a bit of work after the previous owners moved out, but it was all minor stuff.      Yes, the condition was very good for a house of its age. Got a bit of charm, I think.      Yeah, I like the kitchen most. That old wooden floor, but I know that's a bit of a faff to keep clean, isn’t it? We had to seal ours when we moved in.      You don’t like sealing floors, George! I still can’t get over how the floor in here is warm to touch now that the heating system's updated. I swear it made a difference this winter.      Aye, and I think the heating system’s one of those ones that’s expected to last for decades, isn’t it? I mean, with a bit of servicing at least. You ever looked at how long you can get out of a boiler these days?      They tell you it’s twenty years, maybe up to thirty if you’re lucky. But let's not think about breakdowns today. We’re here to enjoy the new house, not prepare for the next emergency. Ha – remind me of that when I’m in my 90s!      Haha, you’ll be 90 and still doing your own DIY. Anyway, what's this walk you were telling us about?      Oh right, I was saying—Holsworthy is a great base for some good coastal walks. There’s a loop along the coast path that goes up about five miles to Bideford Bay. I used to walk it when I first moved out here. Nice views, decent terrain. Could be a bit of a challenge depending on how you feel.      Does it go near any villages or cafés? I could do with a slap-up scone halfway through.      You always do. We could make it a bit of a day out. After the walk, head to a little café near the bay—remember the one in Bideford, the one with the homemade jams? They even gave goody bags on Christmas opening if you were there early enough.      Yep, that's the one. Good vibe, and what's better than a free haircut at the Christmas market to cap it off?      Free what now?      Oh, there’s one of those places where they give free haircuts if you pay for a charity voucher.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen anything from the postdoc committee yet on my application for that new role at UCL. I had them all on side at the interview, I thought sure thing.
