Now I'm just stuck waiting and watching other people get advertised for things before I even get a formal rejection or confirmation.      Ugh, that’s so infuriating. I had something similar with a job I applied for in education. Got the in-person interview, felt like I’d nailed it, and then just radio silence. It's the worst. You're never sure when they're going to get back to you, but your confidence just drops each day that passes.      Exactly. You know the system well enough to know it's probably just bureaucracy and not that they've decided against me, but still—it kills your momentum. I’ve been thinking about starting up my own consultancy for health psychology services part-time while I see what happens. It keeps me busy, at least.      That’s actually a good move. You always say the most sensible things when you’re in a stew over something else, don’t you? I’ve been dabbling in that too—sorting out some assessment tools for other schools. Have you spoken to Marcus about it? He'd kill for a services collaboration.      I have, actually. He’s already asked if I'd support his local community centre with some workshops on mental health and stress for families. I said I’d do it if I can find time. It’s nice doing work that doesn’t involve grant applications or data analysis for once.      That is a nice break, honestly. Between you and me, I’m sick of spreadsheets and performance metrics about how many children met their literacy targets. Sometimes I just wish I could get out and see what the kids are actually doing with that data. I mean, it’s important, but it’s just not  me  anymore.      I know what you mean. Work-wise, it feels like something is always missing. At home, though, I’m starting to get a crack on with the kids. My eldest is finally getting the hang of lunches not flying out of the house. Now if the toddler would just learn  not  to shoot them like missiles the second I set the table…      Ha! That’s my world every day.

Rather skip the newfit and go through the request and see what’s the best for the child they’re like... got to go with what’s best for the child. I mean, I've seen so many parents get it wrong. Not all of them, but enough to make you take things slow.      Yeah, I mean we’ve got bigger things to worry about at the moment anyway. Like, I’ve been meaning to talk to you both about this project I’m running in the school. It’s pulling in quite a few private and public schools. But funding is tight.      You’re doing another one of those education system overhauls, aren’t you? I remember you telling me about the last one at our university reunion. It was about integrating left-handed children properly into classroom layouts.      Exactly, and I think it turned out alright. But this one’s a bit different. We’re looking at language learning earlier than most. They’ve taken in French and Mandarin, even some sign language basics.      Oh, that’s actually quite something. I was raised with both English and French, and it was absolute chaos in the house. My mum was left-handed and only started using her right hand in school… it wasn't easy. She says it damaged her confidence somehow. Made her feel… abnormal, I guess?      Oh, I totally hear her on that. I remember taking care of a little left-handed girl once—school had made her use her right hand. She was in tears. I had to calm her down and just let her left hand do what it did naturally. The parents were grateful, but it wasn’t something the school had taken seriously at all.      That’s a real shame. But it just shows how much progress there’s been in understanding kids. Going back to the school project—what we’re doing is not just about the curriculum, but the whole ecosystem: teachers, parents, even the food. They want to introduce balanced meals in school lunches. It all adds up.      You know, speaking of food, we should really discuss what to get out for dinner. Do people want a new recipe or just the same old chicken with… well you know, something green.      Yeah, go for the chicken. But if you’re going to go fancy, make it a Sunday roast. I had a client the other day—nice lady, said her whole family still doesn’t eat much meat because of how her parents cooked it.

Rather skip the newfit meat eh?      Aye, it's all mad these days... got to go with proper beef. Nothing like a good Sunday roast with a bit of gravy, proper Yorkshire pudding.      That's the truth! I wouldn't say no to a good een of that now, I don't think you'd get that if you just ran in to Nando’s.      Fair enough. I'd never say no to a decent stew either, or pulled pork. We had some amazing food the last time me and Sophie went to the Middles East Pub... like, decent enough even for my consultant engineer tastebuds.      You know, like that My turkey, Sophie, back in the day. I remember one of them winters, had the fire on for hours, and I made a whole roast up for us lot, about six of us round the breakfast, no leftovers gone 'til next morning!      Blooming mad. I remember that, Grandad. You told the tale about how the kettle boiled over and nearly took the ceiling, and we all thought it was the washing machine short-circuit.      It wasn’t the washing machine, it was the kettle! You lot never listened when I told you. But at the end of the day, I got me dinner, and the ceiling got a bit soggy — don’t reckon it done it any harm really.      Laugh, I wouldn't want to walk into your house for a bucket o’ trouble just for a bit o’ food. But what made you decide to have a proper roast up again? Still got the oven working?      Aye, still works like a charm. I fancied it the other day, had me son cooking up for me. Proper old-school Sunday roast. I tell you, lad, nothing brings people together better than good food 'n' no guest list.      I have to admit, it is a special feeling. We had this one trip to Bangkok a little while back, stayed in this market side hotel that smelled of street food and fried duck with lunches delivered right to the door. Perched up the aircon, you could hear the tuk tuk’s buzzing all the time goin' on outside.      That sounds brilliant. I just about went mad trying to teach meself box sets and films when I had to self-isolate at the start. Found me a Thai netflix after two weeks of just Coronation Street reruns... to say it made life better is an understatement.

So do you want to take a look at the module plan for next term? I’ve been going through it and I’m a bit stuck on the reading list for the second essay. I was thinking of substituting “The Savage Mind” with some more contemporary postcolonial theory — you know, maybe make it a bit more accessible for the students who aren’t very familiar with theory yet.      Oh yeah, that sounds like a good idea. I was just thinking about that myself actually. It was a bit of a journey last year when the undergrads tried to grapple with Lévi-Strauss — I had to add a couple of supplementary readings just to get them through the first section. Maybe we can add some Sarah Myhill or maybe even something by Homi Bhabha? Not too dense, but still meaningful.      Yeah, Bhabha might be a good bridge. And do you think we should keep the debate format this time? I had some tutors last week ask if we could structure it as a more traditional seminar instead. They’re worried about time management.      Hmm, maybe we can give them both — I mean short debates with a focus on specific topics and then a seminar discussion as follow-up. It gives the students exposure to different modes of engagement. Though I’m worried some of the more nervous students might not speak up in the bigger group. We could introduce some anonymous pre-submitted questions again this term.      That’s not a bad idea. And what about the assessments? I remember last year a few students struggled with the reflective log because it was so different from the more classical essay. I wonder if we should split it into two parts — one reflective and one analytical.      I think you’re on to something there. A reflective part and a more structured analysis could help clarify the learning outcomes. I’m also thinking about sending out a short guidance document, like a reading response example, to guide them into developing their ideas. It’s about scaffolding it without holding their hands too much.      Absolutely. I’ll get on that this week and draft something. Let’s also check if we want to include a new case study next term — maybe something recent in global education policy, something around decolonising the curriculum. I’ve been meaning to get that started anyway.      Perfect. I just started reading this study by Patel and Hassan on academic publishing in sub-Saharan Africa — it’s really eye-opening.

Rather than chuck the entire coffee machine out, I suppose we could glue the bit that's broken back on. It’s still rather fetching really with the dents and all. Not a modernista would say that, but it serves me well.      It does look unique. But it was probably time for a newer model, considering how difficult it was to get working this morning. Almost as if it's a retrofitted Martian rocket. Not that that's a problem, unless you're rushing for a coffee before someone else. We've all got time.      It's the slow drip that reminds me of the Russian space programme! Not that I've much knowledge of the real thing only what I've managed to pick up since university. You know I watched a documentary once on the Mirr station.      Rather pick and choose what you remember? Or rather you've chosen to pick and forget! Wait breakfast, no coffee then? I mean if you're into clocks, and deadlines, you do need to finish shopping, ordering, before eleven so that the packers, or whoever, arrive.      Speaking of deadlines, the removal quote we had came in as £450. For two rooms. Included in that is three hours of packing. We will then be told how much storage is – should we need any storage – will cost per month.      That seems rather quite a deal as long as you don’t want to add anything extra! At most.      And then the storage costs will add up. I do miss the days when one could expect a line in the sand, between professionals and the box tickers.

So do you lot ever just go out clubbing and use pseudonyms? Like, do you even know what you got booked in as?      Oh I just use my actual name. Why would I make one up? I bake for a living, not lie on a guestbook.      I once used "Catherine Cinnamons" at this rave in Birmingham. Reached for a paper towel to wipe my hands and the bouncer just went, “You're not checking in, are you?”      Haha, that’s classically British. We Aussies just show up like, “Hey mate, can I dance?” and forget our name by the second song. On the boat last night, I was called Marco for an hour.      I’m half obsessed with the idea of picketing the Thames or the canal system with an alias, like a floating gig. "Boat: The Boat." It just sounds like a jazz album.      The only law I follow on the water is the non-kosher, non-crumby one.      I mean, if I put shortbread in a cannoli and floated it past the City Livery Club, would that be illegal? Probably. But it’d be delicious.      Real talk, I’m not sure I know the difference between a canal boat and a flatbed barge unless one has pastries on board. Is that what yours looks like, Dom?      No, it’s got a French press and a sock monkey named Dennis. You ever microwaved garlic bread and then tried to explain it through a smiley face emoji?      I did microwave puff pastry once to impress date. Instead it just whispered, “You’re a terrible chef.”      Bread shouldn’t whisper. It should rise up in glory or crumble in despair. No in between.      Speaking of, I’m open to a themed café where the only condiments are espresso, truffle oil, and turmeric. We could market it as  Italian Heritage Necessities陉      That’s better than the “all the meats” condiment station I saw last week. They had the vibe of a go-kart map with sausage improvements.      I swear, some of the Italian menus I see could qualify as secondary literature on Dante. Pass the parmesan.      You know what’s poetic? Getting kicked off a canal boat for singing "O sole mio" in reverse.      Or just trying to explain a homemade mac ‘n’ cheese at a dinner party. “No, the béchamel is kissed by thyme, not made by a thyme.”      All right, no pseudonyms at the dinner table.

I’m just trying to avoid the ones who go all over to M&S for "normal" and still end up sending me 20 selfies after you’ve rejected them for licking their eyebrows at a party.

Rather skip the new series of Doctor Who innit? Seems they’ve gone a bit bonkers with it.      Oh aye, I tried watching it with the wife the other night, and it was full of moon rocks and aliens blinking in and out. Just like “Deary me, I don’t know if I like it.”      I’m all for making it a bit ambitious, love a bit of cerebral science fiction, but honestly, I’d rather just watch some Antiques Roadshow and listen to posh people chat about old things. It relaxes me.      That’s mostly because you can’t handle a bit of real drama, Jo. It’s like that old turkey saying, “Don’t like it? Don’t eat it.” But to be fair, the BBC these days is just trying to patch over a hole with a stick while the wall is crumbling.      Now there’s something worth talking about — the BBC’s state of play! Used to be the bloody beacon of the world, and now it’s just picking up bones and calling it a Christmas cracker.      Aye, it’s the same with the government. Tell me what they’re watching, what they’re reading, then tell me how they run the country. I tell you what, if they were half as organised as the programme scheduler, we’d be doing alright.      And don’t get me started on the benefits system. Last week I had to get a bus to the Jobcentre because they said my claim had a “discrepancy,” and mind you, I haven’t filled in a form in  forty years .      Steve! That’s not true, you still got to fill in forms for your pension, and you grumbled about that like it was the Hindenberg landing in your back garden.      Aye, well if I had a penny for every form I filled in I’d be richer than all those apprentices with their start-up accounts on waiting lists getting spoon-fed while we’re here being told to "give it a bit longer with this machine."      That’s the thing, you remember when the idea of welfare was that the state looked after its own? Now it’s about tick boxes and proving you haven’t made a dent in the earth’s atmosphere.      And what about all this talk about “personal responsibility”? For all the state’s faults, I think those of us who had children, who worked to raise them and have ended up poorer in the process, wouldn’t mind a bit more  state  responsibility to make up for it.

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather. I mean, do we get one proper summer day? One? It’s like the sun decides to pop up for a few seconds, and then it’s over.      You’re not the only one being moaned at. It’s driving me mad too! Well at least you’re trying to get out. I, on the other hand, have been frozen to the sofa since I caught a cold last week. Some people take birthdays too seriously. Honestly, if I could run my own celebration, I’d prefer reading a good book by the window than being dragged to some themed nonsense.      That’s true. Speaking of which, I’ve been looking at your Instagram. You had that beautiful photo of the lake out here with the trees reflected in the water. It’s stunning. I love how it looks like you're in a dream or something.      Yeah, that lake is something. I think it looks better in the summer when the water is green instead of mud brown, but even now it’s nice.

So did you get the results from that stats project yet? I’ve been trying to get my head around p-values all weekend and it's driving me mad.      Eugh, yeah! Got it back Friday. I passed, which is kind of a relief, but the feedback was brutal. I think the professor liked the code but hated the structure. Still, it kept me out of trouble most weekends. Do you ever miss the whole pre-social media world? Like, back when you could write something without expecting it to go viral or derail into go viral or get deep-vialed or something.      All the time. I genuinely miss the quiet bloviation of the ‘90s. It was so much better to just say something and not have every person with a keyboard weigh in. True story: my lecturer once told us over half the posts on TikTok were either job applications or rage posts over gym selfies.

Rather skip the new changes in the NHS funding plans, Jeremy. I read this article this morning that said they're planning to outsource more care to private companies, and I can't say I'm entirely comfortable with that.      No, I heard similar things on the radio earlier. I mean, I'm not against private companies providing care per se, but I reckon it depends on how it's regulated. You’ve got to make sure they’re doing this for social good, not just profit. It's easy for it to go wrong, just like the school meals fiasco in 2018.      Honestly, I’m still trying to get my head around the whole Brexit impact. I mean, that’s what a lot of these funding shortfalls are linked to, right? I had a Professor at Aberystwyth last semester who said the government’s had no real plan about healthcare since the vote. I called it ideological chaos at the time. Maybe a bit harsh, but not far off the mark.      Aye, and it’s not just politics that’s changed over the years, luv. I remember when I was young in Nantyglo, and the NHS was seen as this untouchable, sacred thing. My mam used to say, “If you’re born in Britain, you get medicine fairly, no cheques required!” You don’t hear that spirit much anymore.      That’s a beautiful way to put it, Jeremy. It’s kind of what someone said in one of the books I was editing this week. A character muttered, “The NHS used to be more about people than profit,” and it struck me because I thought  that’s it . We’ve moved about as far from that as the car’s journey from here to Cardiff.      Maybe that’s part of the problem then—how everything’s moved too fast, without much thought. My granddad worked in the construction industry during the building of the M4. He told me the whole project was controversial at the time, but it ended up helping people connect better. Maybe we just need good, long-term planning again. Even if it’s messy at the start.      Some planning, yes, but remember, even the best plans can fall flat with the wrong govt in power. My old professor of social policy once told me, “People in politics today see the NHS like a box to tick on a manifesto.

Right, so today we're going to start working on your very own story, just like the ones in Helen Moss’s books. What do you want it to be about? Girls, what ideas do you have?      A princess and a dragon!      And a magic castle that floats in the sky!      Oh, I like that! A princess, a dragon, and a magical floating castle. Do you want the dragon to be friendly or scary?      Friendly. She’s the princess’s friend and they go on adventures together.      Good choice. Helen Moss often writes about animals and magical creatures who are the heroes, not the villains. So this princess and her dragon will be heroes too. What’s the princess called?      Guardian Darcy! Because she guards the castle.      Guardian Darcy and her dragon friend. What do you think they adventure in? Maybe a place in the sky?      Yeah, the Sky Kingdom! And the castle floats because it’s built on clouds.      We can call it the Castellan of Whimsy.      The Castellan of Whimsy in the Sky Kingdom! That’s brilliant. Now, what happens in their first adventure?      The princess needs to find a magical crown to help a baby cloud grow up.      The baby cloud is lost and the wind isn't blowing its way.      Oh, that sounds like a proper quest! Guardian Darcy and her dragon fl y off to find a wise wind wizard and a forest of singing raindrops to help them. Then, once they find the crown, they sing the cloud a lullaby and it finally grows wings and can fly by itself.      And the wind wizard gives them a superhero cape to fly with.      Yes! And after that, they become the protectors of all the clouds in the land. Do you want to write that down together?      Can you draw the castle?      Of course. I’ll add the floating garden and the rainbow path the dragon walks on too. Once it's all done, we can share it at the Linton Book Festival next month. How does that sound?      Like the best day ever.      And the dragon can wear a funny hat.      Oh, absolutely. Guardian Darcy and her dragon with the funny hat to protect the clouds. What a team! Let’s start writing them into a story. You two are unstoppable.aurus.  The conversation continues with soft voices, laughter, and pencil scratches on paper, as the little girls dictate and the parent helps them shape their tale.

Okay, so I've just got my weekly multivitamin. I still take it even though I’m vegetarian... Well, vegan now, officially. I’m more conscious about it than I've ever been.      Honestly, I don’t even know what a multivitamin is half the time. I just eat loads of kale and runner beans and call it a day.      Please. You probably forgot your own vitamin D levels in this weather. Look at you, pale as a ghost.      Oh, I take vitamins when I run out, but the pills at the chemist like to talk about how they  used  to go to school and now supply only to people with pension numbers—      —And you just left your tablet bottle on the compost heap again, didn’t you?      Honestly, I don’t get how you’ve never had a vitamin breakfast, Rach. You need to up your protein or you'll crash at 2pm and then we’ll have you ordering puff pastry and spam again.      I mean, it’s not like I can afford a whole vegan protein smoothie bar every day. But still, I only started vegan for November. I was thinking of becoming a proper vegetarian before that, but got way too into Curb Your Enthusiasm and thought, “Okay, maybe not tonight.”      It’s not just what you don't eat, it's about what you  do  put in your body. I found an awesome plant-based recipe book from this blog by someone who oddly looks a lot like you, Rach, and they have this delicious looking lentil shepherd’s pie.      Oh, I did make that last week! Except I bailed and just added a bit of mince because I forgot my lentils. Don’t tell Eddi.      You do know, though, that the whole reason I went full vegan was not even for health reasons. It’s the environmental angle. I mean, the carbon footprint of meat is just... mad. My brother sent me this article about how beef farms contribute more to deforestation than entire countries flying.      Yeah, and it's not just that. Then you factor in the manure and methane goenvironmental map stuff. I read this once about how one cow could produce as much methane as a car. And it lives in the air for what, 15 years?      Okay, okay, I get it. It’s not just belly of the beast levels of horror.

Rather skip the new year’s dinner this year to be honest. I’m just knackered with work. Step one: stop feeding your furry children from the side of the sprite bottle. Step two: ignore the 'hey I think it whines when it’s hot' advice from Tom’s cat.      Tom’s cat? He's adopted it for life, bless him. Said he wanted a "ginger-based, primarily self-toilet-training" pet. Time to call the vet about potential renal issues.

Rather skip the oath and just go through the request, madam. I know her solicitor's been asking... What was the question? Oh yes, the butterfly forks. I need to know if you remember where we got them. Not the ones from the bird table—  the   butterfly forks. The ones that matched your grandmother’s cream china. The one you didn’t want to use for fear they'd crumble.      Oi! Why’s she picking on me? I was   nine   when we got them. You were the one who said “they’re conservation grade,” whatever that means. I just brought the box from the attic because you were threatening to throw the bird table into the river if we didn’t dust it again. You remember that?      Yes, well, I was under a lot of stress. The school head teacher called to say she’d found a fork at the back of the classroom—presumably from a picnic with a student in 2006—and it was covered in bird faeces. Also, the two-minute silence for that Russian ballet company’s accident, remember? That was a bad one. I still don’t understand why their tour had to include a stop in Siberia in mid-winter.      Speak for yourself. I remember the silence. I got distracted trying to figure out if the starling in the tree outside was going to fall asleep mid-chirp.      You weren’t even in the room at the time. You were in the shed trying to fix a pipe that wasn’t broken. You just wanted something to do before your birthday tea. You still didn’t come out.      Not my fault. I’m not a fan of “lapware” as you keep calling it. Tea on your lap fails to count as anything you’re fond of.      That is not what   I   call it. I call it tragedy. A tiled floor, open windows, a delicate floral tablecloth, and three very disappointed witches. I distinctly remember passing a spoon to the Daisy from down the road who said she’d never seen such a mess.      Now that you mention it, you  did  run out and shout at the Daisy contingent as if they were Russian spies. I think one of them still calls you “the woman in the orchard.”      Well, what would you expect? The Daisy planting group was outnumbering conservation and we were in full bloom hours after the two-minute silence.

So do you lot ever take a break from sorting all this data or are you just in here like lab rats with highlighters and spreadsheets?      I prefer to think of us as linguistic archaeologists, Lucy. That’s because of blending, isn’t it? I mean, the north and south are colliding in publishing and online, and kids are mixing everything up. Well, let’s be honest — without us, you’d all be out there waving around about "corrupt grammar" while using “they” as a singular pronoun without a second thought.      Not to mention the accent stuff. You remember when we started the dialect project? Everyone thought it was niche. But now? It’s shaping how audio books are written, how AI chatbots talk, and even how spellcheckers are adapting.      It’s fascinating. And yet here we are, at a Cambridge printing house, wondering if we’ll need a new section for "global English" in the next edition of The Concise.      Which also begs the question — what happens to formal English?

So did you go to the doctor yet, Tom? You’ve been off work for three days now.      Yeah, went this morning. Blows! Right, so today we're going to talk about good and evil. I know it's a bit big a topic, but I thought we could start with some stories from British legends and superstitions. How does that sound?      What’s “superstition”?      Oh, it’s when people believe in things that aren’t really explainable by science—like ghosts, lucky or unlucky objects, or creatures that live in forests and mountains. They’re part of our old stories, which are kind of like history and fantasy mixed together.      Like the dragons in King Arthur?      Exactly! King Arthur is a British legend and the dragons are symbols of evil in that story. Now, here in East Anglia, where you were both born, we have some interesting folk tales. For example, the   BuntyBun  , which was a mythical creature said to live in the woods and scare naughty children.      Like a monster?      Sort of, but it's not a monster in the usual sense. More of a guardian spirit, maybe. If you listen to the old tales, the BuntyBun would carry misbehaving children off to hide in the woods—until the parents learned to teach their children properly.      So it was a warning?      Very clever observation. Stories like this weren’t just to scare children—they were tools to teach them about behaving well and respecting the world around them.      But what about the real bad ones? Like ghosts?      Ghosts are a big part of English folklore. There’s a famous ghost in your hometown, Bury St Edmunds—  Abbie Hungrily  . She used to haunt the grounds of St. Edmund’s Abbey and was said to be the spirit of a nun who had a grudge against the abbey.      Why was she evil?      Not evil, necessarily. She was just misunderstood. She was believed to have been wrongly accused or punished, which is why she didn’t rest in peace. Her legend is meant to make people think about kindness and justice—so it’s actually a lesson in how we treat each other.      Oh… goody ghosts?      If you like stories that make you think! Another interesting one is the   Hobbit of the Fen  . It’s a creature similar to the hobbits from Tolkien, but this one was said to live in the fenland, near Ely. He was a shy little fellow, not really evil, but would only come out if you were kind to him and left him a bit of bread and cheese.

So do you ever find it strange working in education when you used to be in recruitment? I mean, first you were matching people with jobs, and now you're matching students with subjects, or trying to help them figure out what they can or can’t read and write?      Honestly, yeah, it’s kind of a mirrored version of the same job. I still love the people stuff, matching individuals with the right environment or task. The main difference now is I’m much more into the  development  side of it. Before, I was like a conveyor belt salesman — "This job suits you!" Now I get to sit down with students who are struggling and see them actually improve. It’s pretty rewarding.      I can see that. I still remember the first week you started here, you had the students do a micro-essay on "What the heck is academic literacy actually for?" And you said it was "the holy grail of student skills everyone thinks they have until they don’t."      Oh, didn’t I say that? That might actually be directly from a student I taught back in Australia. But it’s true — I mean, we all think we can read and write. Until we get to university and read something like, "Heuristic multiplicity in pedagogical paradigms – a deconstructive interrogation," and realize none of us have a clue what the author is saying. All that matters is the ability to unpack what the hell is going on.      Exactly. And when it comes to lecturers trying to evaluate whether their students have it, it can be really hit or miss. Some of them assume the students ‘get it’ if they can paraphrase or make a reference, without actually seeing any evidence the student can do it independently.      Yeah, and that failsafe is that academic literacy is more than just regurgitating a lecture or two. It’s about reading critically, evaluating sources, expressing arguments clearly, and knowing when to use a formal tone versus a passable one. If a student can write an essay that makes a logical case while citing good sources and distinguishing between opinion and fact... that’s the dream.      So how do you actually assess that in a practical way? Because it’s not the same as grading an exam or even an essay if you don’t get into the process.      I’ve found that the best approach is to use what I call a "diagnostic cycle" — short, low-stakes tasks where I can see the process step by step.
